‘Sunflower’ Track Tops
Avco Embassy LP’s
NEW YORK — Avco Embassy Records
announced the release of four new
al-
bums
for May
including
the
label’s
first
original
soundtrack
recording
“Sunflower” with music composed, ar-
ranged and conducted by Henry Man-
cini.
The four new albums were presented
to the distributor by Luigi Creatore of
Hugo & Luigi, V. P. and Chief Opera-
ting Officer for the company and Bud
Katzel,
General
Manager.
Presenta-
tions were made direct to the distribu-
tor and their sales and promotion force
in each market covered.
While
Luigi
Creatore concentrated on covering the
western region, Bud Katzel focused on
the eastern half of the country.
The release included a new rock
al-
bum by a group called Weight entitled
“One Man’s Queen
is Another Man’s
Sweat Hog”. The album was produced
by Vinny Testa of Infinity Productions.
He previously was responsible for Avco
Embassy’s “Liquid Smoke” album and
the group’s chart single “I Who Have
Nothing”. Happy Feeling a pop group
out of Canada was produced by Nor-
man
Petty. A new
single
“Still
Hill”
will be released from the album.
Two key albums
in the release are
Glass
Bottle,
the pop group that has
just
finished
an
extensive
in-person
tour of some ten markets on behalf of
their new
single “Love For
Living”
which is from their new album.
The most extensive promotional cam-
paign
will zero in on the
label’s
first
soundtrack from the parent film com-
pany,
Avco Embassy
Pictures.
The
“Sunflower” soundtrack promotion will
be aimed at every level. Saturation on
radio to garner air-play, publicity and
advertising in both print media and 30
and 60 second radio
spots. The mer-
chandising effort on behalf of the sound-
track will be made in conjunction with
Ampex Stereo Tapes, Avco’s exclusive
tape distributor. It will include posters,
hanging pennants, counter cards, color
stills from the
film and
a
four-color
center window display.
The display material will be used to
initiate a massive national window dis-
play contest in which both Avco Em-
bassy and Ampex will be offering valu-
able prizes. Details on the contest will
be announced shortly.
Ambergris Coast Tour
HOLLYWOOD — Ambergris, the New
York based nine man rock band, has
had a heavy impact on the west coast
in its first tour of the area.
The group, whose first LP on Para-
mount
is “Ambergris,”
left
the
east
for the
first time for engagements up
and down the west coast.
The
opening
performance
was
at
Eagle Auditorium in Seattle on May 15
and
16. On Sunday, May
17 the band
traveled north to Vancouver, B.C.
for
a one
night concert and promotional
work
supporting
the LP
which
has
been released in Canada.
In a major appearance
of
the
tour
Ambergris headlined
at
the Whiskey
AuGoGo,
this
city,
for
four
nights
(21-24)
.
In connection with the release of the
band’s
first
single “Forget
It,
I Got
It” from the LP, the members
of the
group
made
promo
appearances
in
the Los Angeles area. They leave
for
further dates in northern California.
The cross country
tour, which
will
take
the
group back
to
a
series
of
major
eastern
dates,
has them
per-
forming in key cities through the mid-
west as they travel.

Announcing The Release Of Beethoven’s Biggest Hit in
Once every year or so an emphatically unlikely single comes out of
nowhere to render the pop cosmos, well, topsy-turvy.
Such
a record was
Procol
Harum’s “A Whiter Shade
of
Pale”
in
1967, Joe
Cocker’s “With A
Little
Help From My
Friends”
in
the
waning moments of 1968, or the Edwin Hawkins Singers’ “Oh Happy
Day” in 1969.
Such a record
is Miguel Rios’ “A Song Of Joy,” right now.
Unlikely? You bet your booties
.
.
.
Would you, after
all, have ever suspected that a pop adaptation of
Beethoven’s "Ode To Joy” by a Spanish teen heart-throb backed by
an orchestra and chorus under the direction of South American Suite
composer Waldo de Los Rios would so electrify the airwaves from the
Pyrenees to Toronto that even so august an observer as Rolling Stone’s
man in Canada and Beatle confidante Ritchie Yorke would be moved
to exude in
its behalf:
" ...
It
is such an overwhelming
record
that once
you've
heard
it you
will remember
it
for
life ...
It may
well
be-
come the anthem of a generation searching for Utopia ...”
We wouldn’t have either. But unwary though we may have been,
we’re
only
too
delighted
to
bestow
this
marvel
upon
the
United
States, whose pop charts would otherwise have looked
rather barren
during
this, the Beethoven Bi-Centennial, without a
little something
by that unlikely composing chap at their pinnacle.
RECORDS
& TAPES
.
A Song Of Joy
!
by Miguel Rios
Recorded by Hispavox Records S.A. Madrid

Pop Picks
RAINDROPS KEEP FALUN’ ON MY HEAD - Andy
Williams—Columbia CS 9896
Part of Andy Williams’ great success has been
his ability to change with the times. This newest
of
his
long
line
of
LP’s demonstrates
just
this
attribute. Album opens with Mason Williams (the
record was his brainchild)
beautiful "Long Time
Blues.”
Side
one
includes
the
title
cut
and
“Bridge Over Troubled Water.” The second
side
is a medley of six songs, some well known (“Both
Sides Now”), some not ("Little
Boy”).
Full marks
to arranger Al Capps and
of course the golden
vocal chords of Andy, for an excellent album.
EVERYTHING
IS BEAUTIFUL - Ray Stevens -
Barnaby Z12 35005
Seems
like the
hits keep
right on coming for
Ray “Mr. Businessman” Stevens. This time
out,
his
first
for Barnaby,
it’s the
seif-penned
title
tune. As a change of pace, Stevens devotes most
of the remainder
of the LP to other people’s mat-
erial, such as the Youngblood’s “Get Together,”
George
Harrison’s "Something,” and
the
omni-
present “Raindrops Keep
Falling On My
Head.”
Old
fans
and
new
should
find
this
a
reward-
ing listening experience.

in the

follow-up

in a host of tunes which should appeal to
those who like "Little Green Bag.” Watch for this
set on the charts.

Cast-RCA LSO 1169
Here
is the original cast album of the success-
ful off-Broadway musical, "The

Of Isaac”
is a vibrant celebration of

and the record captures the
vitality of the show.
The gospel-like "Yes
I Know That

Alive," the

“I Want To Walk To San Francisco” the

dialogue from the show. Among the
better cast
LPs to come along this season.
ESTHER OFARIM - Esther Ofarim - Philips PHS
600-343
Esther Ofarim here offers a beautifully arranged
and sung album of intriguing songs, fourteen
in
all.
Especially
fine
are
Leonard
Cohen’s
"You

The album

AARON LIGHTMAN — Aaron Lightman—Poppy
PYS 40,010
This is a very well thought out and put together
LP.
It features almost continual music, the ma-
jority of which comes from the talented pen
of
Lightman himself. The songs are mostly soft and
reflective and run into each other without a break.
There are also musical
interludes between
vari-
ous
cuts
which
are
composed
by
producers
Ronald
Frangipane and Dean
Christopher. They
are
usually
lush and
reminiscent
of
film
score
music. The whole adds up to a
clever and very
pleasurable album that
is original and worthy of
attention.
ENTRANCE — Edgar Winter— Epic 26503
Singer and keyboard artist Edgar Winter makes
a strong bid to follow
in the path of
his
brother
Johnny. A blues strain runs through the album,
which consists for the most part of compositions
by Edgar and Johnny. The latter
is heard on har-
monica and for one track on
guitar.
Particularly
effective
is the John
D. Loudermilk song “Tobac-
co Road.” The album
is evidence that Edgar pos-
sesses a formidable talent which should continue
to grow. Watch this one.

Honorary Bruckner
Membership To Frost
NEW YORK — Columbia’s Music
Di-
rector
for
Masterworks Tom
Frost,
has been named an honorary member
of The
Bruckner
Society.
A
special
plaque which was presented to him by
the
Society’s
president,
Charles
L.
Eble, had inscribed upon
it the inscrip-
tion:
“In
recognition
of
signal
services
to
the music
of Anton
Bruckner,
The Bruckner Society of America,
Inc.,
herewith
confers
upon
Thomas Frost the title of Honorary
Member.”
Frost has been responsible for such
momentous
Bruckner
recordings
as
“Bruckner, Symphony No. 5” and “Te
Deum,” a two-record set conducted by
Eugene
Ormandy,
“Bruckner,
Sym-
phony No.
7” with the Columbia Sym-
phony Orchestra under the direction of
Bruno Walter and the soon
to be
re-
leased “Bruckner,
Symphony
No.
4”
conducted by Eugene Ormandy.
As executive Masterworks A&R pro-
ducer for Columbia, Frost has record-
ed such artists as Vladimir Horowitz,
Rudolph Serkin, Isaac Stern and The
Mormon
Tabernacle
Choir,
among
others. He has been a member of the
board of directors
of the Carl Nielsen
Society for the past three years.

Cliff Jackson Dies
NEW YORK —
Clifton Luther
(Cliff)
Jackson,
jazz
pianist,
died
here
last
week
(24)
of a heart
attack. He was
67. Jackson suffered the seizure
after
playing
the
night
before
at
the RX
Room
in New
York.
Jackson,
whose
widow
is the singer Maxine
Sullivan,
had
accompanied
on
disks
several
blues singers, including Viola McCoy,
Lena Wilson, Sarah Martin and Clara
Smith. He performed mostly
at New
York night
spots,
including
Cafe
So-
ciety
(1943-51), Lou Terrasi’s and Jim-
my Ryan’s.
Besides
his widow, Jack-
son
is survived by
a brother and
sis-
ter.

Cash Box — June 6, 1970

---- p42
insigM&soundcontinued
NEW YORK - (Con’t from page 41)
real
I'm doing
it my way. The thing about
large record companies
is that most
couldn't care less about music or people; you’re
a cipher distinguished from
all
the other ciphers
solely by how much money you're
bringing
in.
That's why
I
picked
Bell to distribute Windfall. You're an individual there; they care about what
you're trying to do.”
Along with Windfall, whose business end
is largely handled by Bud Prager, came
Felix’s group, Mountain: born
in
late August,
1969. They opened
in Ungano’s
in
New York after about ten days of being together. Immediately after came a rather
mediocre semi-solo album by Leslie West. By October Mountain had found a new
drummer, Corky Laing, and rehearsals began
in earnest. "We now have a genuine
family unit playing together,"
Felix told me
late
in December, during a recording
session break. “This was the first Christmas
I didn’t spend with my family;
I spent
it with my musical family.”
Out of these sessions spanning four months (Nov-Feb) came “Mountain Climb-
ing!" Painstaking care went into every phase of
its creation, not only
in laying down
the tracks, but in mixing, stereo separation, and the actual placement of the songs
on the record disk. The LP
itself deserves some discussion
in that
it may be the
most important album
in
Felix’s career. Undoubtedly Mountain, as
a group,
will
make better ones, but for Felix, personally, “Climbing!”
is a turning point.
“I believe
so strongly in this project, that
if
it doesn't sell
I’ll pack
it
in,” Felix told me during
the early part of the sessions.
The first track, “Mississippi Queen,”
is Mountain with
its strictly American
roots
showing; a powerful, timeless song of youth
in much the same way as Leon Rus-
sell’s “Delta Lady.” Of Jack Bruce’s “Theme
For An Imaginary Western,” the next
song, Felix says
"I’ll never re-do a song again" (he produced an earlier version for
Jack on
his solo
LP).
Nevertheless Mountain’s version
is superior
in every
way.
Felix’s achingly beautiful voice conjurs up perfectly the wide desolate plains of the
song, and bass, drums, organ, mellotron and guitar all contribute to the loneliness
of the Western wagoneers. “Never
In My
Life” expresses the family’s feelings
at
the sessions.
“For Yasgur’s Farm,” which
starts side two,
is
a major work. A duet between
Felix's smooth
light voice and
Leslie’s deep dark voice,
it has been
in Mountain's
live repertory since the beginning and
first showed where they were going. This
moves
into an acoustic instrumental by
Leslie. “People who said
Leslie sounded
like
Eric
(Clapton
of Cream)
just weren’t
listening very
closely.
This
track
will
prove
it to them," says
Felix. There’s just a
spiral from
this to "The
Laird,” softly
flowing on the bottom, sharp and crackling on top with
Leslie’s guitar to empha-
size
Felix's gently sung but stinging vocals.
After
a
Mountain-hard-rock break of
“Sittin’ On A Rainbow,” the album closes with “Boys
In The Band" also
a major
work and
Felix’s personal
favorite. To say that
it
is classically rooted would be
a
misrepresentation inasmuch as classical music
is so much a part of
Felix.
Every-
thing he does comes from
his mind and
his gut
(writing
is
a
visceral
act; good
writers write as they
feel). So the classics are always there with
him, extending
his range as a musician to infinity.
“Boys
In The Band”
is Chopin, and Bach;
it
is a rondo and a fugue;
it
is saying
goodbye and hello: a dance of death and
life;
it
is an ellipse, a never-ending cycle;
it is Mountain and
it is Felix Pappalardi.
eric van lustbader
Doctors Find Crimso Completely Well
One of the finest albums to come out of Britain last year was King Crimson’s "In
The Court of the Crimson King." And as a
first LP
it
is singular
in the new direc-
tions
in music
it explores. But after
its release and
a short tour of the
U.
S.,
re-
ports stated that the group was splitting up.
Crimso’s leader, Robert Fripp dropped
by
last week
to dispel any such
disas-
trous and unfounded rumors. The group
is indeed
alive and
thriving as witness
their new single “Catfood” and LP, "In the Wake of Poseidon.”
“‘Poseidon’
is the soundtrack for an imaginary film," says Bob. "The idea
is that
from the four elements, earth,
air, fire and water, you can get twelve personalities,
such as the warrior who
is fire and
earth. We personify these characters through
the music."
About Crimso’s personnel changes,
Fripp has this to say: "After the
U.
S. tour
we
split
into three
parts. Greg Lake
(vocalist) joined up with
Keith Emerson
(ex-
Nice); Mike Giles (drums) and Ian McDonald (mellotron) are playing with friends
of theirs and
I am
still here with Pete Sinfield, who does all the lyrics. Basically the
second album
is two people plus friends. What we want to do
is to build up a pool
of musicians to work together on our LP’s.”
“Poseidon”
is a direct progression from “Court." Like Mountain's music, Crimso's
is constantly growing, and therefore, constantly surprising; constantly invigorating.
It
is
total music because
it surrounds and
engulfs the
listener.
It
isn’t,
as Bob
would say, “tap your foot and nod your neck” music.
Upcoming for Crimso:
a
third
LP with
Keith Emerson and John
(Colosseum)
Hiseman,
a second
U.S. tour,
a cartoon made from the "Moonchild” track from
the "Court” LP, and
a film using the “Devil’s Triangle” cut from the new album.
Crimso is in bloom.
Long Short Takes
Talked with some good folks this week. One of them was Karen Wyman, the 17-
year-old
singing
sensation
(beware
of
yellow
journalism!).
Overnight
she
has
launched into a strong career in singing with dates set at the Sands (from June 3)
with Don Adams, and the Shamrock Hilton (from June 17) in Houston as the head-
liner. She’s already tucked a
lot of national TV time under her
belt,
too. Her
first
LP was released
last week by Decca, and provides her with
a
lot of enthusiastic
conversation matter — how the material
is so “now,” how she got what she wanted
in
a
strong,
brassy
instrumental
backing, and how much
she
likes
the
group,
Chicago. We talked a
little about acting, how she sees singing the same as acting,
how she has read for a few parts; and about her Life magazine six-page feature on
her that
is
still up
in the
air. School’s out so
you'll
be hearing a
lot more from
Karen.
Picked up on the staging techniques (among other things) of the Ace Trucking
Company the other day in an interview with the RCA improv comedy quintet. They
explained that they open the show with a suggestion period from the audience for
sketch
ideas. The group says this frees the audience's
inhibitions.
Unlike some
improv groups that work out
in theater surroundings and use improv as an acting
exercise, the Truckers make
it very clear that they work "purely for entertainment
using slapstick and cerebral comedy techniques" and
in saloon atmospheres or
college halls for drinkers and otherwise. Got a
lot of TV and concert action coming
up so be on the lookout for them. They’re a moving experience
(I couldn’t resist).

One of the more interesting disk firm newsletters
is Elektra’s “Touch,”
a
sort of
groupie’s Sixteen combined with a
bit of hype and a sprinkling of trade news. Like
Warner’s fictious Barbie Burbank (though we often got the impression that Barbie
really
lives
in someone’s
mind),
Elektra’s
real-life Josephine takes
her
readers
backstage to share with her the joy of talking to and spending time with
real
life,
major label rock groups. Also,
in the current issue, a very good article on how the
trade paper charts are compiled (which makes the rest of the paper worthwhile.)
This isn’t an official offer, but we don’t think Jac Holzman would be upset
if some
of you concerned readers asked to be put on the mailing
list. Write to Elektra, 15
Columbus Circle (a euphemism for the Gulf-Western Bldg.), New York, N. Y. 10023.

Folkie, Keith Sykes, stopped up this week. Saw his New York debut a couple of
months ago at the Gate with Great Speckled Bird where he was really impressive.

He’ll be hangin' out here
in the summer and then
it’s back
to the concert
trail.
He’s just a shufflin' country boy but he’s learnin’, he’s learnin'.

HOLLYWOOD — Richard Bock, who's
resigned
as
general manager
of
the
World Pacific division
of Liberty/UA,
Inc., intends
to return
to independent

will con-

artists such
as The Buddy Rich
Or-

Richard
“Groove”

pia-
nist George Duke.
Widely regarded as one
of the most
prolific and important contributors
to
recorded jazz, ne created
the Pacific
Jazz
label
in
1952.
Thirteen
years
later, he joined the Liberty organiza-
tion
as
general
manager
of
Pacific
Jazz —
World
Pacific
division,
fol-
lowing
Liberty’s
purchase
of
his
label.
Bock’s

is
to
choose
the
musicians,

the

and

confer
with
sales and promotion people
to assure
that his
original conception
of an
al-
bum
is faithfully represented through-
out the production process.
Bock,
strong
on new

re-
sponsible
for recording
the
first Wes
Montgomery sides
(with
his
brothers
The Mastersounds)
. He introduced on

peter
Bobby
Bryant,
the
original
Gerry
Mulligan-Chet
Baker
Quartet,
Bud Shank-Laurindo Almeida Quartet
(regarded as the first venture of bossa
nova
into
the
United

Chico
Hamilton
Quartet,
Les McCann
Trio,
The Jazz Crusaders,
the Gerald
Wil-
son
Orchestra,
and
pianist
Craig
Hundley.

Successful

for

Robert

as

re-

(Con’t. from page 9)

When an independent company has

Byrds To Studio
For 10th Album
HOLLYWOOD - The Byrds are re-
cording their tenth album for Colum-
bia Records in the label's Hollywood
studios. It will be the group's first
two -record set, comprising live per-
formances as well as studio sessions.
Cover art will be created by West
Coast artist, Eve Babitz. The album
is being produced by Terry Melcher.
It is also the first Byrds album to
be made since bassist Skip Battin
joined the group last October. Now a
quartet, the group also includes gui-
tarist Clarence White and drummer
Gene Parsons, who joined the Byrds in
1968 and Roger McGuinn, the group's
leader since its inception.

NEW YORK (Cont'd from page 37
The British Hit Factory Family has another set of writer -producers in Roger
James Cook .and Roger Greenaway. They are both members of Current Craze for
which they wrote the debut single, "Lady Pearl." Singly, Roger Greenaway is a
member of the Pipkins, White Plains, and Brotherhood of Man, and has just com-
pleted LP's with these groups. Roger Cook is a member (with Madeline Bell) of
Blue Mink and has a solo LP on release in the U.K. and forthcoming here.
Together, Cook and Greenaway started as David and Jonathan a few years back.
Now they are responsible for such hits as the Fortunes "You've Got Your Trou-
bles," Gene Pitney's "Something's Gotten Hold Of My Heart," and Blue Mink's
"Melting Pot" and "Good Morning Freedom." In addition they wrote and produced
the White Plains "My Baby Loves Lovin' " and the follow up "I've Got You On My
Mind." Their own publishing house, Cookaway, handles their compositions as
well as material by other songwriters.
Sue and Sunny, .the pretty songstresses adorning the Brotherhood Of Man,
started out as a group by themselves but got sidetracked by Lesley Duncan (a
songwriter and queen of the British session singers) who persuaded them to go
into session work. Lesley is also responsible for opening the session doors for
Madeline Bell. Madeline came to London with the "Black Nativity" show in 1962,
and met Lesley. Together they backed up Dusty Springfield in all her recordings
for Philips. Later Dusty returned the favor by backing up Madeline for her solo LP.
All in all, the British Hit Factory is a family that looks set to grow into dynastic
proportions. Just the fact that there are so many people of such diverse talents
who have teamed up together, bodes well for the future. While we may not be
hearing from these groups as they are now in years to come, it is quite evident
that all the people involved in this first real musical commune are building a solid
stepping stone towards a bright future.
eric van lustbader
EAST COAST GIRL OF THE WEEK
Would you buy a car from this girl? Would you stop jaywalking at this girl's com-
mand? Mavbe you did. Patty Mizzy, secretary to Ed Kaminski (east coast divisional
promotion manager) at Capitol, has held a number of jobs including one of mak-
ing commercials. One of them was the voice in the Dodge spot-"Come on and
buy a Dodge .
. ." to the tune of "Milord." One other commercial she did the
voice for was the "Don't Cross The Street
In The Middle" jaywalking spot which
she wrote with the help of her father,
ASCAP composer Vic
Mizzy.
For that
spot, they won two awards, one of them
the Public Service Award.
Age 25, Patty attended private schools
and lived on both coasts. She's amassed
a good deal of knowledge about song -
writing from
her dad,
and she
has
worked and continued to work at writing
words through Music Makers Pubs. for
"foreigns"-songs that come from other
countries that are given a new set of
English lyrics (not a translation but en-
tirely new ideas). She devotes an average
of three hours a night to writing, editing
and revising her own lyrics for those
songs.
Before her job at Capitol, which she's
held for five months, Patty worked in the
news departments of KABC and WNEW.
At the latter station she produced a Sun-
day News Close -Up titled "Bogart-The
Man Behind The Cult." Other j61.3s she
has had were ones at Ashley Famous and with Sam Speigel.
Talking a bit more about her work with songwriting, Patty says that the people at
Capitol are expecting her master of the recent foreign she's working on called
"I'm Alive" which she says is kind of like "Those Were The Days." Patty says she
loves her job at the label (this week she brought around the promotion records
because her boss was at the company convention in Hawaii) and tells Ed that
she'll only quit when she has $10,000 in the bank. And, as it looks from here, for
a girl who claims she has had such success simply because she "lucked -out"
every job, that day could be very soon.

for this fine trio

HOLLYWOOD (Cont'd from page 37
PUTTING ONES FOOT IN THEIR MOUTH DEPARTMENT: After the foregoing, it
might be nice to take it safe and not talk about records for a week or two, but,
undaunted, we leap right into the fray to praise two recently released albums.
Rhinoceros has made several personnel changes since their second album, and
their third album finds a smaller and differently motivated group. One of the new
additions is drummer Duke Edwards, who shares vocal chores with John Finley.
Edwards, as well as new producer Guy Draper (remember the Unifics?) is very
soul motivated, and that's the way the group is moving now. We haven't seen the
new outfit in action, but the album is definitely their best yet. From friendly
reports filtering thru this office, several major FM'ers are concurring with our own
quality judgement. For all you Danny Weis fans, don't worry, he's still with the
group.
SPECIAL NOTE TO STEVE HARRIS: As Fred Holman said in the New York column
last week, there's a lot to be said for increasing the quality level of pictures avail-
able to the contemporary press. Let Elektra once more lead the way.
SPECIAL NOTE TO ARTIE KORNFELD - The second album we're going to hype is
the first release on your new Eleuthera label by Bert Sommer. In addition to Bert's
major contribution (he is the artist, after all) we'd like to thank you for turning in
your best production ever.
Bert's first album for Capitol, released last year, almost had what it takes, but
just missed the mark. The quality that makes this a better album is that the art-
ist, who's essentially telling of various situations in his own life, has matured and
now has a better perspective on what is going down around him and inside him.
Of course, anybody can sit down and try to describe what he feels and what he
sees. Not everybody can do it very well, and fewer still can describe their life in
such a way that a lot of strangers can identify with them. Bert is one of the few.
When he describes his pain, you can feel it, when he delights in his pleasures, you
find yourself up with him. To make the listeners feel, that is the great art that
Bert Sommer practices very well.
Jefferson Airplane would be the most sought after recording group in the world
right now, if the Rolling Stones were not up for grabs also. Such is life. As life
goes on, the Airplane go on with it, followed by their press agent sending out head-
lines like "Jefferson Airplane Jets To Europe For Bath," which merely tells how
the Airplane will be playing at the famed Bath Festival in Great Britain on June 28,
right after their appearance at the Rotterdam Festival on June 26. Group's PR
chick was nice enough to note that also appearing at Bath will be John Maya'',
Canned Heat, Johnny Winter, Pink Floyd, Fairport Convention, Colosseum, It's A
Beautiful Day, Keef Hartley and, would you believe, the Maynard Ferguson Big
Band, on the first day; while the second day will see the Airplane joined by Led
Zeppelin, the Moody Blues, Steppenwolf, Frank Zappa, the Byrds, the Flock, San-
tana, Dr. John the Night Tripper and Country Joe & the Fish. Thank you Diane.
Jimmy Webb is said to have finally finished his own self -produced album, at an
outrageous cost, after several months of work. LP is up for grabs, but Reprise
is said to have the inside track.
MOVIE STAR DIVISION - Jason Laskay, who was most recently on view in "The
Graduate" (yeah) and is currently making the neighborhood screens in "The
Grasshopper" (thumbs down on that one) has decided to expand his horizons by
entering the record business. He's just been signed to a contract by Art Wayne and
Howard Boggess' new production firm and will start cutting his first sides this
week.
LEFTOVER DEPT. - Because of tight deadlines, we never did print one of the
nicest pictures of the month, which showed Judy Dyble, former lead singer with
Fairport Convention, and Jackie McAuley, former bass player with Them. Duo was
together for the picture because they now have their own little group, Trader
Home, who've issued a pretty little folky album on Janus.
THANK YOU SPACE -A very nice thank you to Stan Moneiro, an old friend who's
now promo head at Metromedia. Stan dropped us a nice line in response to a
recent column on the 50's, of which he was an integral part. Hope to be seeing
you soon.

Colgate-Palmolive Co. Launches
Giant -Sized LP Premium Offer
HOLLYWOOD - One of the largest
premium record album program in
history will be launched by the Col-
gate-Palmolive in supermarket
and
drug chains throughout the country
this month.
The offer of three exclusively pro-
duced LP record album will be made
through coupons printed on 40 million
packages of the company's products.
The program is expected to prove
out to be the biggest single record
promotion in the history of the pre-
mium and recording industries,
ex-
clusive of the various annual Xmas
programs. It will be in effect for ap-
proximately six months.
Harry Mynatt, president of Official
Creative Productions in Los Angeles,
which conceived the promotion
for
Colgate-Palmolive, estimates that
2
million to 5 million albums will be
distributed. Four record companies,

Amaret Sets Two
June Album Releases
HOLLYWOOD - Amaret Records,
running hot with both single ("Cottage
Cheese")
and
album
("Crow
By
Crow") by Crow, has set two addition-
al albums for June release.
"Fresh Air," featuring the group
of the same name, is being released
this week. LP was preceeded by a
single, "For What It's Worth," cur-
rently picking up airplay around the
country. Set for June 29 release is the
debut LP by Dave Antrell, with an
initial Antrell single, "Straight From
A Rainbow," out this week.
Crow is currently in the midst of
their heaviest concert tour ever, and
will be showcased at the Whisky in
L.A. for five days starting July
8.
While in Los Angeles, they'll also go
into the studio.
Decca, Kapp, Motown, and Uni, are
involved
in the
project,
with MCA
Special Markets coordinating the man-
ufacturing. The albums feature two
artists on each record: Diana Ross
and the Supremes and Neil Diamond;
Roger Williams and Bert Kaemfert;
and Peggy Lee and Jack Jones. The
recordings feature groups of numbers
never before offered on one record.
The public may obtain, without ad-
ditional charge, one of the three re-
cord albums by purchasing any four
of ten Colgate-Palmolive products, in-
ccluding Fab,
Axion,
Cold
Power,
Punch, Palmolive soaps and dishwash-
ing liquid, Ajax liquid cleaner, Handi
Wipes, and Baggies.
Another unique aspect of the pro-
motion is Colgate's request for only
four proofs of purchase to obtain either
of the three records offered. And it is
the first time that Colgate or in all
probability any company of compa-
rable size, has offered the same pro-
motion with 10 of its best-known and
normally high -selling products.
Official Creative Productions creates
sales -stimulation
promotional
pro-
grams tor industry, concentrating on
premiums, dealer loaders, continuity
programs, games, and original pro-
motional concepts.
In developing the Colgate Palmolive
promotion, formery directory of cre-
ative
products
at
Capitol,
Mynatt,
stated that the plan was implemented
through the cooperation of 10 different
brand managers. The 10 brands in-
volved represent 80% of Colgate-Pal-
molive's business.
At the National Premium Sales Ex-
ecutives seminar in New York last
month, Mynatt, who co-chaired the
meetings, revealed that a goal of 4
billion dollars in sales had been set
by the association for 1970. Mynatt
added, "And we have not scratched
the surface in the use of records as
premiums. 85% of the homes in Amer-
ica have record players, accounting
for more than
a
billion dollars
in
record sales last year." The Colgate-
Palmolive free record plan includes
a bounce -back offer whereby the con-
sumer may purchase a 3 -pack, 5 -pack,
or 10 -pack set of records in a deluxe
wood -grain vinyl case. The case
is
free. Records are offered on a 10 day
free trial at a special price. If the
records are returned, the consumer
may keep the deluxe case.
Official Creative Productions is a
subsidiary of Official Industries, Inc.,
a New York based, publicly owned
company with offices
at 445 Park
Avenue headed by eastern sales man-
ager Bernie Woods, who worked with
Mynatt in coordinating the promotion.

ALONE TOGETHER - Dave Mason - Blue
Thumb BTS 19
This fabulous poster package contains
an
equally fine record, the first LP by Mason since
his departure from the original Traffic group.
The artist is an accomplished lead guitarist, a
gifted songwriter and an extremely capable vo-
calist and all these talents are readily apparent
in this album. All eight tunes on the deck were
penned by Mason; several of the easier ones
("Can't Stop Worrying, Can't Stop Loving," "Sad
And Deep As You") are among his best works.
First rate set.
MINNIE'S BOYS - Original Cast - Project 3 TS
6002 SD
Show music buffs have Project 3 to thank for
saving two unsuccessful musicals so they can
live on in their cast LP versions. The first was
"Cry for Us All," and now several months later
we have the recently -shuttered "Minnie's Boys,"
based on the careers of the Marx Brothers, who
still have quite a following. The Larry Grossman -
Hal Hackaday (two writers to watch) score is
winningly
merry and
sentimental,
with
four
fine ballads ("Empty," "Mama, a Rainbow," "Be
Happy," and "They Give Me Love").
Shelley
Winters stars.
THE CHAMBERS BROTHERS GREATEST HITS -
Vault 135/2
Hard core Chambers Brothers fans will be in-
terested in this two volume package of old tracks.
There are 21 cuts in all, among them such ef-
forts as "You've Got Me Running," "Hooka Tooka,"
"Baby, Please Don't Go," "Pretty Girls
Every-
where," "Girls, We Love You," "Johnny B. Goode"
and "House Of The Rising Sun." Set should do
nicely in the marketplace.
PRIMORDIAL LOVERS - Essra Mohawk - Re-
prise 6377
The first thing to say about Essra Mohawk is
that she sounds like nobody else. The second
thing to say is that she is not only a beautiful
singer but an excellent and original writer.
All
the songs are hers, from the acoustic, "I Am The
Breeze," featuring a haunting oboe backing, to
the heavier and electric "Spiral," with its deep
booming bass line. This is an LP to listen to
carefully. It's an eclectic set that has obviously
had a lot of time and love go into it. The result
shows it.

84338
The pianist who gained recognition with the
John Coltrane Quartet and then went on to head
his own groups is heard here with his newest
assemblage - and a fine gathering it is. With
Wayne Shorter blowing tenor sax and Ron Car-
ter working the cello (to name just two of the
fellows), Tyner leads the charge through a twelve
minute up -tempo number, "Vision," serves up
an Oriental -flavored "Song Of Happiness" and
C tops it off with the delicate "Perisina." An out-
standing jazz outing.

of

of each foreign market.” He
feels
the
“initiative must

and the

licensees uncovered
in

Dowden & Co. Custom
-Anniversary’ Albums
PHILADELPHIA — Two custom
“Col-
lector’s Edition” record albums, creat-
ed exclusively for U.
S. corporations
and groups celebrating 25th or 50th an-
niversaries in 1970 and 1971, are being
produced by Dowden & Company, Phil-
adelphia anniversary consulting firm.
The 50th anniversary album, entitled
“Golden Hits for a Golden Anniversa-
ry”, includes 19 classic old and new all-
time best
sellers, spanning the years
from 1920 to 1970. Included:
“Charles-
ton,”
(1920), “Night and Day”
(1932).
“Oklahoma!”
(1943), “76 Trombones”
(1957),
“Hello,
Dolly”
(1964),
“Hey,
Jude”
(1968),
and
“Raindrops Keep
Failin’ on My Head”
(1970). Artists in-
clude Benny Goodman, Harry James,
Aretha
Franklin,
Kostelanetz, Robert
Goulet, Ray Cmckf, Peter Nero, etc.
The 25th anniversary album features
the Academy Award Winners song for
each of the past 25 years, by top
re-
cording stars.
Both records are designed for use by
the golden and
silver corporate
cele-
brants
as executive
gifts,
premiums,
traffic
builders,
self-liquidators
and
incentives.
The entire
right inner panel
of the
gate-fold record jacket is reserved for
any custom use a celebrant
dictates:
a letter from the president, a concise
corporate history, etc. The other inner
jacket panel traces the evolution of the
music
- and the nation’s history over
the 25 and 50 year time periods respec-
tively.

Mansueto De Ponti, former A. & R.
Manager of E.M.I. Italiana, has joined

will become effective on June 15th.
At Riccione, a town on seaside
(an

saggeri Musicali held their

a)

ries, c) Schaub-Lorentz, d) retail shops.

to
a)
and b) divisions. Messaggerie Musicali
distributes the lines CBS Italiana and
CGD,
which
includes
Reprise,
WB,
Festival, Scepter, etc., as well as Union
Carbide products. Record distribution
is organized through 45 salesmen, 3 in-
spectors and a division manager and
operates through 10 stores.
According
to

manager
S.
de Gennaro there was an increase of
3.05%
in the distribution organization.

183,531

Two-Way Information
On

initial

Alexenburg
will supply information

rection

and areas or outlets that have begun

This gives MOR

forty, R&B

a

country

TOP HITS OF THE YEAR
A COMPILATION OF THE YEAR'S BIGGEST HITS TO DATE
Because Cash Box is continually asked to supply a
list of the year’s leading hits to A&R men, record producers
and radio stations, etc.. Cash Box offers a continuing feature that lists the year's Top 50 titles as of the date the
feature appears. The feature is published in the last issue of each month and
is compiled from the Cash Box Top
100 Sales Chart Point system operates as follows: For each week a song
is #1 on the Top 100
it receives 135
points. Each #2-record is awarded 124 points. No. 3 gets 123. No. 4 gets 122. No. 5 gets 121. From No. 6 thru
No. 10 songs get 115 to 111 points respectively. No. 11 song gets 90 points and so on down the line
till the No. 50
song which gets 51 points. Only the top fifty titles of any given week are included
in the survey. Survey begins
with the first issue in January.

NEW YORK (Cont'd. from page 38
)
In the
fall, the company plans to start an intermediate priced concert program
which works on the same idea as the coffeehouse but
in
a concert format. The
deal would be for one or two nights packaging one or two performers
for each
concert. Act might get from $200 to $1,500 for a concert.
Again,
it’s something
that the schools could afford, concerts that big agencies wouldn’t bother to handle
because of the money involved and
it also gives the performer someplace to go
after the coffeehouse circuit.
The Bitter End network
is the only circuit of this nature
in the country. Thirteen
circuit coordinators handle the colleges
in the various areas throughout the coun-
try.
All the colleges are kept informed
of what’s happening by
a monthly news-
letter.
One of the other things
in the works
is a film circuit
in which specialized films
like an Incredible String Band concert film, or a film on woman’s liberation could
be passed around the circuit. A part of the plans call for a Movie Or^ which em-
ploys a concept of piecing together
bits of film and sound
for a
six hour show
that has no plot but a central theme, so that anyone could enter or leave during
its runningtimeand not miss anything.
The main thing about Campus
Directions
is that out of one office comes the
management, booking and
publishing facilities necessary for an
act. The whole
idea of the company
is sound and
is one of the most promising things to actually
be working within the American folk and rock scene. Such artists as John Denver,
Jerry
Jeff Walker, McKendrie
Spring,
Keith
Sykes, Townes Van Zandt and
Don
Crawford have been a part of the coffeehouse circuit and have gotten the proper
exposure each of them needed from
it. As a certain
publicity director said about
Mike Brovsky and his whole idea: “His head
is
in the right place.” Maybe instead
of going
after the
big,
big money and
the
big,
big
bands, some
other heads
throughout the country could start turning in the right direction.
fred holman
EAST COAST GIRL OF THE WEEK
Would you
call a Swedish
girl who married an
Italian a Swedish Meatball? Not
if she was Karin Grasso of Tonsil
Records, where she
is a production
assistant,
sales person, bookkeeper, song publishing aide,
etc. Married
to BMI
songwriter
Richard Grasso of Beechwood Music, Karin
is 25 years old. She says, though, that
she’s been in the record/entertainment business for a hundred years!
As a teenager she worked
in
her home
town Miami with three dj’s as Radio
Girl,
giving
nightly
reports
on
the
Top
10
songs and the local scene. Upon gradua-
tion (two days after to be exact) she was
on a plane to New York where she turned
up
a
job
as
a
dancer—something
she
had done
in Miami. She was a
"twister”
at the Peppermint Lounge, The
Round-
table,
Trudy
Heller’s
and
other
clubs
around
town.
She
also worked
at
free
lance fashion modeling during what she
calls her “ultra-skinny days” and appears
on a few Blue Note album covers. For 3
years she worked as
Roulette
president
Morris Levy’s secy, and for 2Vz years she
held
a
job
at
Liberty.
The
opportunity
came up
late
last
year
to work
with
a
new
record company from
scratch
and
took it—Tonsil, started
in January, 1970,
and now has one LP and two singles. She
loves her work and, between her hobbies
of
cooking
and
athletics,
finds
a
few
hours a day for
it.
SHORTTAKES
When a group sits down to create a name that
it can go under, the members
must always have things to say about words and phrases that
will be associated
with
it — complimentary or derogatory.
Gulliver, a new group on
Elektra, must
have had fun thinking about record
reviews
that would say ”...
a group that
stands
tall” or “Watch for this one to travel way up the charts.” The possibilities
are endless depending on your familiarity with English
literature (Jonathan
Swift
in particular) or your talent for making puns. While you mull over a few ideas on
this matter,
let me
fill you
in on the group.
I mentioned their album several weeks
ago and
it is
still one of my favorites to come from an American (Philadelphian
in
particular) group
in a long time. They came up and rapped about how they
re-
corded
it to get such clarity on the recording. The quartet, composed of ex-music
students, an ex-art student and an ex-transient apple picker/drive-in theatre
at-
tendant, have
all worked among one of the three dies of Philadelphia studio men
over the past two years. Together they have cut with The Electric
Indian, Assem-
bled Multitude and others. So, studio techniques are very familiar to them and the
group uses them to their
fullest to enhance their songs. And they say that the
strongest thing working
for them
is each
of
their songs which
are simple and
flowing without a single unnecessary
frill added. Harmonies and choise of instru-
mentation are tactfully chosen and worked out. The group says they go
into the
studio knowing what to do and go
after
a
tight,
full and coherent sound. The
quietly amplified set-up
of the studio makes
it their creative workshop and
the
album they have produced
is a masterpiece.
It’ll be out soon and the group
will
be promoting
it on-stage.
(I’ll
not end
this item with
a
blasted pun about these
potential giants.)
Two of the most promising happenings slated
for the New York area this sum-
mer — Mountaindaie and the New York Pop Concerts — are beginning to turn less
turn
less promising each day.
It seems that Brave New World, the producers of
the NYPC,
is forcing several top acts slated for both tests on the July 11 and 17
weekends to be withdrawn from the Mountaindaie
bill because of a lOO-mile/21-
day exclusivity clause
in the contracts they signed with various agencies. Moun-
taindaie is trying to replace the acts with others, and seems to be doing a good job
of
it considering the odds. This is one to keep an eye on. Meanwhile the only peo-
ple who are really suffering from the rip-off are ticket holders who are anxious of
HOLLYWOOD (Cont’d. from page 38
)
official
photographers
of Concert
Associates,
California’s
leading
promoters.
In
addition to album covers, concerts and P.R. pictures, Emerson-Loew are also work-
ing with writer Kathy Orloff on some stories.
The pictures on the lower two-thirds of this page were
all shot at the Who con-
cert at Anaheim Stadium, and represent rock photography at its best.

LOUIE, LOUIE “As
long as those
pearly teeth
hold
out,
Louie’ll
still
be
playing
something new, and
all the others
will be running after him, trying to catch up.”
(Jazz pianist Richard M. Jones)
If anyone should ask we’d say that Louie Armstrong, Duke Ellington and Benny
Goodman are the Bach, Beethoven and Brahms of jazz. And
if we had to name
one guy alone, we’d
give
Louis the
title as the greatest jazz
personality ever
to
raise a horn to his lips and blast a rooftop.
Armstrong
is 70 years old — today. He has been blowing
into a trumpet (and
cornet) for nearly 60 out of those 70 barrelhouse years. The history books
tell us
that he started
in New Orleans, fooling around with a beatup trumpet and trying
it on for size. He was twelve when he was sentenced to the Waif’s home for “firing
firearms within the city limits.” And it was there that he learned to read music.
By 1917 he was playing
in the excursion boats that moved up the Mississippi’s
muddy waters. By 1922 he was
a member of King Oliver’s band
at the Lincoln
Garden
in Chicago. And two years
later he was the
star attraction with
Fletcher
Henderson’s band at the Roseland in N.Y. By 1927 he had moved
into the Sunset
Cafe with his own band. But Louis was always — and
will always be — the main
attraction. So eloquent, so unique that kids who had jazz within them came nightly
to listen
in awe-struck devotion. Kids who were screwballs at the time — Muggsy
Spanier, Bing Crosby, Frank Teschmacher, Bix Beiderbecke, Jess Stacy and Benny
Goodman.
What Armstrong did those nights at the Sunset he
is
still doing. And
if he occa-
sionally hams
it up a
bit, we understand.
It was
in the mid-thirties when
Holly-
wood finally discovered him — handed him a scene or two in a Crosby flick (“Pen-
nies From Heaven”) and Louis became a kind of clown. And
in “Going Places” he
crooned Johnny Mercer’s “Jeepers Creepers” (where’d you get those peepers?”) to
a horse. Louis probably came off best in “Nnew Orleans,” a film based loosely on
his
life. To our recollection
it was (and probably
still
is) the most authentic jazz
incorporated into a film score.
Now he can be caught on TV occasionally, guesting on shows helmed
by far
lesser talents than him. And
in Europe, where he
is revered,
he’ll tour to standing
room only crowds with pick up
all star combos. Soon
he’ll be
in town, we hear, to
celebrate his 70th with us, concertizing and compelling.
This then (since we don’t have his home address)
is our open-adoration birthday
greeting to the King. Stick with the Swiss Kriss, man. Happy 70th.
A post-script on Ellington (also celebrating his 70th this year) who
is currently
represented with a two pocket Solid State (Transamerica)
LP, cut
in Manchester,
England
last November. We heard the LP just this morning. And we’re planning
to take
it to bed tonight. To our ears they’re the best Ellington sides since he
left
Victor ...and that’s a long longtime.
AND HOWE — Last week’s announcement that Macey Lipman and Bones Howe
had joined forces to form a new production firm (Mr. Bones Productions), we hear,
has been
in the works for months. As a matter of fact songsmith Norman Gimbel
mentioned
it to us when we were
in N.Y.
in April.
“It’s not definite,” said Norman.
“I called Macey the other day but he refused comment.” Another case of Macey
nottellingGimbel — no?
harveygeller

SICAMERICANA — Operating

Kasenetz & Katz Map
New British Invasion
NEW YORK — Kasenetz & Katz have
added Billy J. Kramer and The Mind-
benders
to
a growing
list
of
British
acts
for Super K
records. The
pair,
who
in recent weeks returned to
rec-
ord
production,
are
beginning
what
they feel could be the start of the big-
gest
British
artists’ movement
in the
U.S.
They have already signed Graham
Gouldman,
a
pioneer
of
the
English
underground
movement
with
his
songs,
“For Your
Love”,
“Heartful
of
Soul”
recorded
by
Eric
Clapton
and
his Yardbirds
in
1965. The
first
release by a British artist on Super K
will be Graham Gouldman, who
will
be getting the most extensive promo-
tion in the history of K&K.
Other artists include the Ivy League
of
“Tossing
and
Turning”
fame,
Freddie and the Dreamers “I’m
Tell-
ing You Now” and “Do The Freddie,”
Eric
Wolfson,
writer
of
“Sunshine
Games,” “Carnaby
Street Runners,”
“Shark”
and now
Billy
J.
Kramer,
who had two
hit records with
“Little
Children,”
“Trains
and
Boats
and
Planes,”
and
the
Mindbenders,
who
had smash hits with “Game of Love”
and “Groovy Kind of Love.”

in N.Y. prior to the singer’s headline
stint at the Apollo Theater. Flanking Hayes are Jim Stewart
(r.)
president of
Stax and A1 Bell
(1.) executive v.p.
of the label. This
is Hayes’ second consecu-
tive Gold Record LP, the first being “Hot Buttered Soul,” which
is, at present,
heading for the Platinum mark.

producer George

and Fantasy Train.

stressed

would

its

of
acquiring
only
artists who have the ability to sustain
themselves
in
personal
appearances
as well as on records. Commenting on

“Through

with

Record

I
have

to

an
intimate
and
closely

try’s most formidable marketing and

organization
at
our
disposal.”
Kinetic’s
second
single,

Just
Begun” by The Jimmy Castor Bunch,
is the subject of a full-scale promotion
effort.
The
first
Kinetic
album
by

Chris
Moon
is

'Rock’s’ Roxon Tells
Biz Execs To Turn On
To Rock Generation
NEW YORK — Lillian Roxon,
author
of the “Rock Encyclopedia,” has warn-
ed business executives that the “busi-
ness community must tune in to youth
before youth tunes the business com-
munity out.”
Miss
Roxon
made
these
remarks
last week
(24) while serving as moder-
ator of a discussion on the “Impact of
Rock Music on Business,” held at Trin-
ity Church on Wall Street. She empha-
sized that the “youth of today not only
possess a major portion of the buying
power in our economy but are also the
trend setters. Wide
ties, tie-dyed fash-
ions,
1970
cars
and
most
up-to-date
fashions can be directly traced to our
youth and to their idols
.
.
. rock musi-
cians.”
Miss Roxon further suggested, “It is
time
that middle
class,
middle
aged
business executives, who for the most
part control business, give youth a big-
ger break.” She called for the creation
of a “Little Brother Program.” Young
people would “adopt”
a Businessman
and thus serve as a direct
line to the
pulse of the younger generation.
Appearing
on
the
panel
with
Miss
Roxon were:
Bruce Morrow, TV and
radio
personality;
Herb
Goldberg,
president of Contact Slacks Division of
Miller Bros. Hat Coim.;
George Kias,
Coca Cola
Bottling Company
of New
York; Miss R. Vivian Sargent, Person-
nel Officer at Chemical Bank; Alan M.
Augustine. Plymouth Motors; and Fa-
ther John Moody, Trinity Church.
Presenting a copy of the “Rock En-
cyclopedia” to Father Moody of Trini-
ty Church, Miss Roxon expressed the
hope that her book would serve as a
useful guide to business executives who
wish a bridge to the world of the young.
Farrell Completes
'Partridge Family’
Dates For 6 Shows
NEW YORK — Wes Farrell, president
of the Wes
Farrell
Organization,
has
completed the recordings for the
first
six segments of the up-coming ABC-TV
situation comedy
series,
“The
Part-
ridge Family.” According
to a rough
estimate by Farrell, the writers of the
first
six music segments
of the show
have been responsible for record sales
of over $75 million.
In selecting material
for the
series
(which
will
introduce
a minimum
of
one
new
contemporary
song
each
week)
Farrell established a complete
open-door policy,
inviting the top wri-
ters on the record scene today to con-
tribute original songs. Some of the wri-
ters whose material has already been
recorded are Tony Romeo, Barry Mann
and Cynthia Weifi, Jack Keller, Cash-
man and West, Diane Hildenbrant, and
Mike Appel, as well as Farrell himself.
The first Bell single to be released by
the group
is Tony Romeo’s “I Think
I
Love You,” which
is
slated
for mid-
August
release.
With
the
series
pre-
miering on Sept. 25, the album is being
readied for an early Oct. release.
Farrell returns
to the coast
in mid-
July to complete further recordings for
the “Partridge Family,”
series which
stars Shirley Jones and David Cassidy.

AF Embarks On
The Local Touch
NEW YORK — Audio Fidelity Records
armed
with
nine new
full-line
distri-
butors,
is embarking on a program of
promo on
behalf
of
all
of
its
distribs
built
around
aid
at
the
local
level.
Herman
D.
Gimbel,
president,
says
“the
time
has come
for
the
record
manufacturer to realize that his promo-
tional efforts must be pin-pointed and
developed for each specific area in the
country rather than being generalized
on a buck-shot basis,” noted Gimbel.
He
further
pointed
out
that
a
lot
of promo money and time are wasted
when the record manufacturer tries to
blanket
all areas
with
the same
ap-
proach. He
feels
that
the
distributor
in New York or Chicago has
entirely
different
problems
than
the
one
in
Dallas or San
Francisco,
and
that
it
is
the
responsibility
of
the
record
manufacturer
to
better
understand
each
distributor's
situation
and
to
apply
specific know-how and
aids on
a personalized basis.
This can be
ac-
complished he believes, by the manu-
facturer’s sales and promo execs and
staff spending more time
in the
field
at
the
local
level
with
the
distribs,
and this is the manner in which Mitch
Manning,
national
sales manager
of
Audio Fidelity and
his
staff,
are now
working with the company’s
distribu-
tors
“In this manner, the experience and
knowledge gained by the parent com-
pany can be disseminated to all distri-
butors to the mutual advantage of the
entire
organization,”
explains
Mann-
ing.

Jonz Sets R&B Tone At Scepter
NEW YORK —
Chris Jonz
has been
named
as
general
manager
of
all
R&B product and promo for Scepter
Records and
its
affiliated
labels,
re-
ports Sam Goff, exec vp.
In addition to complete promo activi-
ty, Jonz
will be
seeking master
pur-
chases and
surveying
live
talent.
In-
creased
relations
with
distrib promo
men,
the
co-ordination
of advertising
media
and
campaigns,
will
also
be-
come Jonz’ responsibility.
A graduate
of Ohio
University,
his
prior experience
includes
time
spent
in the advertising department at Decca,
music director of WOUB
in
the
Mid-
west,
and
manager
of
publicity
for
E. B. Marks Music.
He started with Scepter in the spring
of
1968 as east coast regional R&B
manager, assuming national responsi-
bilities less than a year
later. He
be-
lieves
the whole R&B market
has
been
relatively
overlooked
but
has
been given more deserved recognition
of late. “The fact that the entire R&B
market
has become more
and more
significant recently is unquestionable,”
he says.
Building increased relationships with
new artists has
to be a primary aim,
according to Jonz. However, these
re-
lationships must be
established
on
a
career basis, not merely with the hope
of producing a single
hit. In this area,
Jonz believes that the creative aspects
of product
responsibility can
only be
achieved by treating each case as an
individual, staying away from the rigid
lines governing product and promotion.
Launching
his
first major
push
in
his new
position, Jonz has
a
full
line
of product to be released. Already out
is “The Border Song” by Tony Middle-
ton,
produced
by
Peter
Schekeryk.
Dionne Warwick’s new
label, Sonday
Records,
will premiere The Constella-
tions
with
“In
Love
Forever”.
The
debut release was co-produced by Guy
Draper and Miss Warwick. John Mada-
ra
Enterprises
will
unveil
“Rain-
maker”
by The Moods.
The
Profiles
on Bamboo
are
releasing
“A
Little
Misunderstanding”
in
addition
to
the
Tiffany LP
release,
“Toussaint”
by
songwriter/musician, Alan Toussaint.
In conjunction
with
the
Tiffany
re-
lease,
Jonz
feels
that
the
fusion
of
Gold For Family
TWO POINTS
for
N.Y.
Knicks
star
Cassie Russell as he
lifts RCA record-
ing artist Carolyn Franklin at a party
thrown by the
label
at Soul East
for
the
songstress
during
her
recent
engagement
at the Apollo Theater
in
N.Y.C.
R&B which
accents
on
the
under-
ground
sound
will
be
an
important
direction
in the future of R &
B. The
co-ordination
of
these new
directions
in music along
with
increased
distri-
butor
relations
hold
the
initial
keys
to Jonz’ philosophy.
Prophesy Blues Series
HOLLYWOOD — The first five LPs
in
Prophesy Records series of specialized
blues album product have been com-
pleted and are currently being packag-
ed and readied for release.
The
five
are
by
Lightin’
Hopkins
(“Lightin’
Strikes
Again”),
Clifton
Chenier
(“Clifton’s
Cajun
Blues”),
Billy
Biser
(“The
Late,
Great
Billy
Biser”), Calvin “Loudmouth” Johnson
(“After
Hours
Blues”)
and
T-Bone
Walker (“Farther On Up the Road”)
All were recently recorded
in Hous-
ton and A&R’d by Roy Ames, original
producer
of Columbia’s Johnny
Win-
ters. The Biser LP
is the
last one
re-
corded by the Blues singer prior to his
death late last year.
Each
of
the
tracks
contains
short,
candid
introductions
by
the
artists
themselves. The “intro” facet was
in-
cluded because
of Prophesy’s regard
for the product as being
“historically
important to the recording industry/’
The LPs
will be packaged separately
but released together and
distributed
by Bell.
“These
are performances by
great
blues
artists who
have
been
greatly
overlooked by the recording industry,”
said Mickey Shapiro, Prophesy
presi-
dent. “Each of the artists has made a
significant contribution to music today
and the influence they’ve had on other
performers
becomes
apparent
once
you
listen
to
the LPs.” According
to
Don Altfeld, Prophesy A&R
chief,
the
LPs
will
all
carry deluxe packaging.
Tim
lane, merchandising head
of the
label,
said
that
the
label surveyed
a
number of distributors as to packaging
and release pattern.
Shapiro took dubs
of
the
series
to
Europe
last week
in order
to
set up
European
distribution
for
both
the
Blues series and Prophesy’s
first LP,
“Black Pearl
‘Live’,
’ which has
just
been released.
Merc/Harrison
Production Deal
NEW YORK — R&B recording
artist
and producer Wilbert (“Kansas City”)
Harrison and Mercury Records
have
negotiated
a
multi-record
agreement
between
Mercury
and
Harrison
and
Chuck
Rubin’s
production
company,
Action City.
The
first record from
the deal
will
be a single, songstress Joann Gentry’s
rendering
of
the Ruth Brown
classic,
“Mama,
He
Treats
Your
Daughter
Mean,”
backed
with
“Hummin’
and
Cryin’ for Peace,” a Harrison tune.
Harrison, just back from a European
tour
with
the
Creedence
Clearwater
Revival,
will
produce
Miss
Gentry’s
solo effort before beginning a summer
tour with the Revival!
Kinney Dividends
NEW YORK —
Directors
of Kinney
National
Service,
Inc.
have
declared
regular
quarterly
cash
dividends
on
its Common Stock, Series A Preferred
Stock, $4.25 Series B Preferred Stock,
and
$1.25
Series D
Preferred
Stock.
Firm
is the parent company
of War-
ner Bros. Pictures and
its music
divi-
sions.
The
dividends
are
as
follows:
6*/4
cents a share on the Common Stock;
22
2
cents
a
share
on
the
Series A
Convertible Preferred Stock;
$1.0625 a
share on the $4.25 Series B Convertible
Preferred Stock; and 3D/4 cents a share
on the $1.25 Series D Convertible Pre-
ferred Stock. All dividends are payable
on
Aug.
15,
1970,
to
shareholders
of
record July 15, 1970.
The Common
Stock,
Series A
Pre-
ferred Stock, Series B Preferred Stock
and Series D Preferred Stock are listed
on the New York Stock Exchange. The
dividend
on
the
Series C
Preferred
Stock, which is listed on the American
Stock Exchange,
is payable on an an-
nual basis.

for this summer have been having their share of difficulties. One apparent excep-

is being

is
only
$12.00. A
good
deal
of
planning
has gone
into

festival:
more
than
enough sanitary facilities will be constructed and there will be an ample supply of

firmed as signed: Joe Cocker, Led Zeppelin, Jethro
Tull, John Sebastian, Grand
Funk Railroad, Doug Kershaw, Canned Heat, Johnny Winter and Ten Years After.
There will also be a substantial representation of Canadian talent. The promoters
are anticipating a crowd of 200,000.

CoghBoK Great Britain
The June 18th election
of a Conser-
vative Government has infused much
of
the
music
business
here
with
the
same
rosy
glow
of
optimism
that
upped share prices on
the Stock Ex-
change when the Conservative victory
became
obvious.
Hopes
are
high
for
the
abolition
of
the
widely
detested
Selective Employment
Tax,
and
the
possibility of a Value Added Tax being
introduced
is already looked on favor-
ably in some music industry quarters.
VAT would benefit retailers to the ex-
tent
that
disks,
cassettes,
musical
instruments
and
the
like
could
be
stocked and the tax due on them paid
over the counter by the customer and
retailer at the time of sale instead of
dealers
having
to pay
it
as now,
in
advance of actual sale. The Conserva-
tives are also firmly committed to the
introduction
of commercial
radio
as
an
alternative
to
the
present
BBC
monopoly. Pundits expect commercial
stations to be operating by
1972 on
a
regional basis licensed and
controlled
by an additional department within the
existing
Independent
Television
Au-
thority. The BBC’s
local
stations
al-
ready
in
operation
are
expected
to
continue, but the new ones planned for
later this year may well be diverted to
commercial broadcasting outfits in the
areas concerned, and the final total of
forty or so BBC local stations covering
the
entire
country
will
obviously
not
be
attained
now.
But
a
serious
ob-
stacle to the implementation of a com-
mercial radio pattern
for the country
is the continuing intransigence
of the
Musicians
Union
on
the
question
of
needle
time,
the
allocation
of
hours
permitted for the broadcasting of rec-
ords.
This
restriction
has hamstrung
the BBC for years in its program plan-
ning and policy, and there is no reason
to suppose that the change
in govern-
ment has mellowed the MU’s attitude
in any way. Indeed Hardie
Ratcliffe,
MU
general
secretary
due
to
retire
next spring,
has
just candidly
stated
that
the union would
like
to
see
the
BBC’s present needle time
ration
re-
duced
still
further,
and
there
is
no
indication that his successor amongst
the
three candidates
for
the job
will
endeavor
to modify
this
outlook
and
attitude. Nobody
has
yet given
voice
to a solution that will circumvent this
stand-off
imposed
by
a
union
with
32,000
paid-up members,
but
in
view
of the
fact that
it seems
likely that a
few
million
recently
enfranchised
young voters
put
their
cross
against
Conservative
candidates’
names
on
account
of
that
party’s
advocacy
of
commercial radio
if for no other
rea-
son, then a solution
will assuredly Ue
found.

Spain
Everybody sings
(not swings) nowa-
days in Spain. Well, maybe not exact-
ly everybody, but many people already
well-known
in
their own
professional
field
(theater,
football,
bullfighting,
radio,
TV,
etc.)
have
decided
to
in-
crease
their
popularity
through
pop-
music. This increased popularity is not
always,
alas!
,
positive. The
latest
re-
cruits
are Manuel
Galiana,
a
young
actor
produced
by
Alain
Milhaud
(Spanish Barclay) and Marisa Medina
(Belter),
a famous TV
presentatrice.
Galiana
has
recorded under Milhaud
a
comic
version
of
“Je
t’aime,
moi
non plus”
with Elsa Baeza. The
title
is “I hate you
.
.
.
, me too.” Marisa
Medina has
released her
first
record
coinciding with her wedding. The title:
“Jolly
nights.” There
is
also now
in
Madrid
a
“Hair”
which
has
nothing
or
little
to
do
with
the
original
one.
“Piccadilly,”
a
booming
discotheque
three
years
ago,
is
sponsoring
the
Spanish “Hair.” They are doing rath-
er well,
it seems. A new female singer
is
born.
She
is
called
Tara,
comes
from
Galicia,
records
for Fonogram
and
people who were
invited
to
the
“premiere”
at
J.J.
say
is
a
sort
of
Janis
Joplin,
though
a
little
bit
raw.
She
is produced by Maryni Callejo—
a
very
famous
lady
indeed
in
the
Spanish show-business—and managed
by Emilio Santamaria, who
is becom-
ing
very
quickly
a
managers’
man-
ager. Andee Silver (Columbia) has
re-
corded
“Teno
saudade,”
by
Andres
do Barro, a song with Galician
lyrics.
Very
original.
Manolo
and
Ramon,
formerly
El Duo
Dinamico,
forerun-
ners
of
all
Spanish
pop
music,
have
released a new single after two years
of silence
(record-wise)
. They
record
now
for Movieplay and hope
to make
a
shattering
come-back. The
title
of
the A
side
is
“Lagrimas,
sonrisas”
(Tears, smiles).
Valerio Lazarov,
the
boss
of
“Especial
Pop,”
a
Spanish
TV musical program,
is in Osaka with
Massiel,
Karina,
Julio
Iglesias
and
Miguel Rios filming a
still more
spe-
cial production, which
will eventually
be released
in Latin America. By the
way,
Miguel
Rios
is
climbing
both
quickly and steadily up the American
charts
with
a
“Song
of
Joy.” He
is
on
the A & M
label
over
there,
and
Hispavox in Spain.

Tuning In On .. . 
WDGY-Minneapolis 
Getting Younger By The Hour 
"We get younger as the day gets 
older," says general manager Dale 
Weber in describing the policy of 
WDGY, a 50,000 kw. station serving 
the twin cities of Minneapolis and St. 
Paul, Minnesota. Working off what is 
basically a Top 40 format, WDGY 
shifts by small degrees throughout the 
day, moving from an adult -directed 
approach during the morning and 
early afternoon hours to strictly teen 
programming by evening time. 
The changes are reflected not only 
in the type of music which is broad- 
cast, but in the personalities of the 
deejays doing the platter spinning. So 
the morning jock is cummuter-ori- 
ented while the mid -day man is one 
with a knack for communicating with 
the housewives. Nighttime disk jockey 
Jimmy Reed, himself a young man, 
closely identifies with the teen audi- 
ence. 
WDGY-Minneapolis, Minnesota. 50,000 
kw. Robert 
H. Storz, pres.; 
Dale 
Weber, general mgr.; Scott Burton, 
program dir.; Johnny Canton, music 
dir. 
Format: Top 40: Playlist: 
30 hit 
records, selected oldies, occasional al- 
bum tracks. 
On -Air -Personalities: Scott Burton, 
6-9 a.m.; Johnny Canton, 9 to noon; 
George Young, noon to 3 p.m.; Gene 
Leader, 3-7 p.m.; Jimmy Reed, 7 to 
midnight; King Michael, midnight to 
6 a.m. 
On the public affairs front, the sta- 
tion has spearheaded a campaign to 
lower the Minnesota voting age to 18. 
This weekend the station is airing a 
telethon on this topic, with listeners 
urged to call in their opinions and 
direct questions to prominent mem- 
bers of the community who will be 
sitting on a WDGY panel. 
The station has also been active in 
winning support for Minnesota's Aqua- 
tennial celebration. It has sponsored 
the sale of Skipper pens, donating 
profits to the community committee.

GIRLS' NIGHT OUT - An evening at 
the Copa with Columbia artist Gary 
Puckett was the prize for three young 
New York girls, winners of a WMCA- 
Columbia 
sponsored 
contest 
pro- 
moting the singer's engagement at 
the supper club. Backstage before the 
show (standing, left to right) : Colum- 
bia's Matty Matthews; 
WMCA jock 
Jack Spector; 
Puckett; 
Karen Di -

Though the station's basic strength 
is among 18-35 year old listeners, it 
has also done well with the 35-49 age 
market. "We take an approach to 
contemporary music which does not 
alienate the older adult audience," ex- 
plains Weber. "Rather than confining 
ourselves, we have tried for a broader 
appeal." 
The station has refrained from 
many of the traditional Top Forty 
devices, such as the use of giveaway 
contests and emphasis on breaking 
records. Promotions stress audience 
involvement rather than cash hand- 
outs. Currently WDGY is running a 
Summer Pleasure promo, requesting 
listeners to describe their plans for 
the summer and awarding prizes to 
those which are broadcast. 
Listeners are also encouraged to 
request oldies. When the deck is aired, 
the person who requested received a 
copy as a prize. 
`Space Age Radio' l.D.'s 
Completed And Available 
LOS ANGELES - The "Space Age 
Radio" station I.D.'s which were pro- 
duced by singer Mark Lindsay, ar- 
ranger Artie Butler and electronic mu- 
sic specialist Alex Hassilev, are now 
ready for presentation to AM and FM 
stereo -multiplex stations throughout 
the U.S. 
Over 125 station I.D. tracks are part 
of the package, with vocal stylings by 
Lindsay, announcer slates by KHJ-Los 
Angeles jock Don Steele and voice 
impersonations by Paul Frees. 
The package will only be given to 
one station in an individual market 
and that station will have exclusivity 
for one year. All sales are being coor- 
dinated through the Charles H. Stern 
Agency in Los Angeles. 
Sullivan Show To Host 
Annual AGVA Awards 
NEW YORK - The Ed Sullivan Show 
will devote its entire September 20 
premiere show this fall on CBS -TV to 
AGVA's "Entertainer of the Year" 
Awards. Bob Precht, producer of the 
Ed Sullivan Show has reached an 
agreement with the American Guild 
of Variety Artists (AGVA) acquiring 
television rights to their first annual 
awards presentation show. It is plan- 
ned to tape the show in the Las Vegas 
Convention Center on Labor Day 
weekend. Stars of the entertainment 
world, who belong to AGVA, will be on 
hand to perform on the telecast.

SUPREME AID - Motown's Supremes were special guests of newly -elected 
Mayor Kenneth Gibson of Newark, N.J. at his inaugural ball last week. The girls 
announced that they would perform a benefit concert in Newark in the near 
future with all monies going to help defray expenses incurred by Gibson in his' 
campaign for the mayoralty. 
Stevie Wonder To Wed 
LONDON - Singer Stevie Wonder has 
formally announced his engagement 
to wed songstress Syreeta Wright. No 
date for the wedding has been set as 
yet. 
Miss Wright, 23, recently began re- 
cording as a singer and lyricist. She 
collaborated with Wonder on the lyrics 
for "Signed, Sealed and Delivered," 
and is part of the trio which sings 
this song with, him nightly onstage at 
The Talk of the Town in London. She 
was formerly a member of Motown's 
musical arrangement department in 
Detroit, where she and Stevie origi- 
nally met three years ago. 
Stevie Wonder remains in London 
until July 11 when he returns to the 
States to record a television special. 
Spring Records 
In Sales Streak 
NEW YORK - Spring Records is cur- 
rently enjoying an unprecedented 
sales streak. Chart climbers on Spring 
include "The Boys In The Band" by 
the Boys In The Band and "I Gotta 
Get Away" by Ray Godfrey. The lat- 
ter, which has been active on the soul 
front, was co -produced by Grammy - 
winning vocalist Joe Simon. "We' Got 
A Problem" by Robert Bands, which 
has just been released, is also showing 
strong action around the country. 
"Our flexibility and ability to act 
fast when a record begins to break," 
said label president Julie Rifkind, "is 
responsible for the firm's success."

Hartman To Address COPME

stage 
Modern Jazz Quartet 
RAINBOW GRILL, NYC - The Mod- 
ern Jazz Quartet found itself in what 
even for this group was a slightly un- 
familiar setting when they opened an 
engagement last week at the Rainbow. 
But although the MJQ is not a tradi- 
tional supper club attraction, and de- 
spite the occasional misplacing of a 
fork or spoon during the set, the Quar- 
tet kept the audience intrigued via 
their musical expertise and the sheer 
dynamics of their instrumental inter- 
action. 
The MJQ opened with a few stan- 
dards, "Willow Weep For Me," "It 
Ain't Necessarily So," before doing a 
couple of more contemporary items, 
Tim Hardin's "Misty Roses" and Len- 
non-McCartney's "Yesterday." On the 
last named song, pianist John Lewis 
set down the melody, while vibist Milt 
Jackson overlaid a particularly imag- 
inative improvisational track. 
Turning to some original material, 
the group offered an excerpt from 
Lewis' score for the film, "Kemek," 
which was premiered in its entirety 
during last year's Christmas concert at 
Lincoln Center. Also from the Lewis 
catalog were "The Jasmine Tree," 
"Visitor From Mars," and the even 
more astral "Visitor From Venus." 
These offered Connie Kay the oppor- 
tunity to work with a variety of per- 
cussive instruments and the remark- 
able sounds he produced are probably 
still reverberating lightly somewhere 
in the room. 
The MJQ has been playing together 
for close to two decades now. But 
whereas many groups would have set- 
tled into a comfortable rut, this in- 
credible foursome has shunned the 
easy and obvious, opting instead for 
the adventurous. Both individually and 
collectively they have continued to 
strike out along new jazz routes and 
apparently they plan to continue walk- 
ing point. As well they should. 
e.k. 
The Kinks/Toe Fat 
WHISKY A GO-GO, L.A. - Head Kink 
Ray Davies generously told an enthu- 
siastic audience at a recent Whiskey A 
Go Go outing, "We're not a good group 
and we know it, but we enjoy ourselves 
His statement was half right. The 
Kinks do enjoy themselves and get 
further into it when the people out 
there get turned on to their music and 
performance, as they did at the Whis- 
key. The Kinks are a good group, ac- 
tually two different groups, in effect, 
with different approaches on records 
and in concert, putting out an incred- 
ible amount of energy in both capaci- 
ties. 
I've been a Kinks fan right from the 
beginning, when they unleashed "You 
Really Got Me" and "All Day and All 
of the Night" about five years ago, 
during the first wave of the British in- 
vasion. They epitomized raw rock and 
roll with those tunes and witi the fire 
and appeal of lead singer Davies and 
his cohorts in personal appearances. 
Strangely 
enough, 
they 
never 
achieved complete recognition, even as 
their music got more subtle and com- 
plex, from "Well Respected Gentle- 
man" and "Sunny Afternoon" to the 
recent "Arthur," scored for a televi- 
sion drama and a monumental contri- 
bution to recorded rock. 
The current Kinks include, besides 
Davies, John Dalton on bass, Dave 
Davies playing lead guitar and adding 
vocals, Mick Avory on drums and elec- 
tric piano -organist John Kirksey. On 
wax, most notably with "Arthur," the 
band exhibits an always -changing in- 
ventiveness over a solid, energetic rock 
base, whether using full brass or a sin- 
gle delicate harpischord line. 
On stage the Kinks harken back to 
their early days, still lively, explosive, 
appealing, even lovable, when, for in- 
stance, Ray Davies winks and points 
naughtily at the audience or when 
brother Dave shakes his shaggy locks 
and belts his raucous off-key vocals. 
(A note: Ray Davies has to be one 
of the most exciting singers in pop mu- 
sic. His wobbly, almost drunken deliv- 
ery and his beautifully timed move- 
ments put him up there beside the oft - 
lauded theatrics of Jagger, Morrison 
and Joplin.) 
At their Whiskey gig, the Kinks con- 
centrated on pure energy flow, using 
mostly old material and molding two 
guitars, bass, piano, drums and vocal 
harmonies into 
a 
pulsing electric 
machine. They did a haunting, strong 
"Waterloo Sunset; " "Brainwashed," 
from "Arthur," which equals Kinks in 
its unrelenting drive; the mystical 
"Big Sky," from the "Village Green 
Preservation 
Society" 
album 
and 
ended the set with a "Really Go Me - 
All Day" medley which almost blew 
them off the stage. 
They also fell into a fifties rock jam 
and kicked it all out with Chuck Berry - 
Little Richard licks. Dave Davies' 
playing, while not jaw -dropping, was 
consistently together. 
It might also be noted that drummer 
Avory holds his left hand stick in the 
time-honored manner, cradled in the 
crotch of his thumb and forefinger, 
rather than using it overhand like a 
club, an all too annoying mannerism of 
many rock drummers. And what could 
be heard of Kirksey's keyboard was 
pretty and powerful. 
As a publicity representative said 
later, most of the audience was made 
up of old Kinks fans. "You're either a 
Kinks freak or you're not," she said. 
She's probably right. 
I only caught part of Toe Fat's set. 
That new English group played before 
the Kinks minus their lead singer, who 
blew his voice in earlier sets. What 
was left was an electric blues instru- 
mental trio, adequate but all too famil- 
iar. 
s.s. 
Leon Thomas 
VILLAGE VANGUARD, NYC - When 
Leon Thomas arrives on the stage, you 
get the feeling something good is about 
to take place. Maybe it's the clothes he 
wears, which are beautiful and multi- 
hued. But you think, no, it's the man's 
exuberance, which is evident in his 
shuffling gait and his expression. Then 
he gets to shaking a cowbell, blowing 
a panpipe and throat articulating and 
you forget about the whys as you ex- 
perience the performance of an impor- 
tant new talent. 
During his five day stint at the Van- 
guard, Leon was working with 
a 
smaller group than the one heard on 
his recently released Flying Dutchman 
album. The compactness of the unit 
was well suited to the Vanguard. Off 
the LP came "One" and "Echoes," 
two songs written by the artist, fol- 
lowed by "The Creator Has A Master 
Plan (Peace)," co-authored by Phar- 
aoh Sanders. On this one Leon soon 
had the audience joining in; it spiraled 
upward to a joyful ending. The artist 
also offered an eloquent reading of 
Horace Silver's "Song For My Father." 
Leon deals in a sound which reaches 
into the consciousness of his listeners. 
Using his voice as an instrument and 
weaving his percussive patterns, the 
artist calls up spirits of his ancestors 
and creates an atmosphere which is 
as mental and spiritual as it is musical. 
Not exactly your run of the mill jazz- 
man, Leon Thomas.

Bass Promoted To 
Chess Exec Producer 
CHICAGO - Ralph Bass has been pro- 
moted from producer at Chess Rec- 
ords to executive producer with the 
label. Bass will now supervise the en- 
tire Chess staff of producers for the 
Chicago -based record complex's Chess, 
Checker, Cadet and Cadet/Concept la- 
bels. 
A producer with Chess for 26 years, 
Bass brought Etta James, Moms Mab- 
ley, Pigmeat Markham and Mitty Col- 
lier to the label. 
Before joining Chess, Bass produced 
for Black and White, Savoy and King 
Records. He produced James Brown's 
"Please, Please, Please" for King as 
well as Earl Bostic's instrumentals for 
that label. Records by the Dominoes 
and the Royals on King were also pro- 
duced by Bass. ("Open The Door Rich- 
ard" by Jack McVey was his first hit 
production.) 
Other major R&B acts that Bass 
has produced are T -Bone Walker, 
Hank Ballard and the Midnighters, 
Johnny Otis and Winonie Harris. With 
Chess, Bass has worked in jazz as well 
as R&B, producing records by such 
artists as Ramsey Lewis.

Composer Tobias Dies 
NEW YORK - Charles Tobias, com- 
poser, author and music publisher- 
died in New York at the age of 72. He 
was the writer of such songs as "Miss 
You", "When Your Hair Has Turned 
To Silver", "Don't Sit Under The 
Apple Tree" and "Those Lazy Hazy 
Crazy Days of Summer".

S Million Orders For Atco Albums 
NEW YORK - Atco Records had 
written over $1,000,000 in orders on 
eleven new albums issued last week. 
Orders were taken at sales meetings 
held at Atco distributorships through- 
out the country by teams of Atlantic 
executives. 
The eleven new albums included re- 
leases by Eric Clapton, Lulu, Johnny 
Jenkins, Donny Hathaway, Otis Red- 
ding, Livingston Taylor, The Unspoken 
Word, Jerry Jeff Walker, Dee Dee 
Warwick, King Curtis and Cactus. 
Strongest orders were for Eric Clap - 
ton's new album, which features .the 
musician on vocals as well as guitar, 
and also includes Delaney and Bonnie, 
Steve Stills, Bobby Whitlock, John 
Simon and Leon Russell; Cactus, the 
new group comprised of Carmen Ap- 
pice and Tim Bogert from the late Va- 
nilla Fudge, and Rusty Day and Jim 
McCarty from the Detroit Wheels; and 
Livingston Taylor, on his debut album 
for the label. 
Atlantic Records is backing up these 
new Atco Releáses with a substantial 
promotion, publicity and advertising 
program. Firm has also created a 
number of dealer aids for these new 
releases including window displays, 
counter displays and point -of -sale mer- 
chandise. Advertising program will 
include print, radio and TV media. 
World Youth Assembly 
Convened At `Hair' 
NEW YORK - More than 500 youthful 
delegates to the United Nations World 
Youth Assembly, all under age 25, 
from over 100 nations attended a spe- 
cial invitational performance of "Hair" 
Sunday, July 12. 
Michael Butler, producer of the show 
pledged over one hundred thousand 
dollars to help defray the costs of the 
World Youth Assembly when its future 
was in jeopardy for lack of funds.
