NEW YORK - SHORT TAKES BY THE NUMBER, SHORT ACHES BY THE SCORE 
Last week's column was all short takes. Because of the large number of them 
left over, though, we'll print another lot of them heavily interdíspersed with some 
first-hand bits (including a Cannonball Adderley interview). Read on, read on. 
Blood, Sweat & Tears was more than just the name of a band the other day in 
Bucharest, Rumania. It was also a pretty fair description of the proceedings as the 
Columbia group gave a performance which wound up in a virtual riot. Apparently, 
the Bucharest police aren't used to what has become the standard audience par- 
ticipation closer for rock concerts in the Western world. When enthusiastic fans 
attempted to storm the stage, the cops reacted by wading into them with flying 
clubs. When the smoke cleared, a number of young people had been injured and 
ít was announced that the remainder of the band's State Department sponsored 
tour had been cancelled. BS&T had planned to do an additional concert in Ploesti. 
Other news of the week ís of the Newport Jazz Festival on July 10 to 12. Set to 
go on Saturday is Ike And Tina Turner and, ín celebration of his birthday, Bill 
Cosby will present his group, Badfoot Brown and The Bunions Bradford Marching 
and Funeral Band. Also on tap for their predominantly blues performances are 
Roberta Flack, Albert King and Shuggie Otis. All are "first -timers" at the festival 
who will take their place among a full slate of top jazzmen. 
About the Cosby band: Uni ís going to release the group's first album this week 
on which the actor/comedían performs on a number of instruments and com- 
poses all the music. Produced by Gil Rodin, the set features Cos in a serious vein. 
Still on a jazz note, Warner's Herbie Hancock is heading up a group of show 
business people to build a Harlem Jazz Center in that community. The pianist/ 
composer wants to start the center to provide professionals and students of the 
Arts with the opportunities to research, create and present their work to the public. 
Julian "Cannonball" Adderley just visited us to talk about his black music semi- 
nar program and his upcoming Capitol release. The LP will include the group 
playing with a symphony orchestra. Three major pieces will be presented: one by 
his producer, David Axelrod; another by Lalo Schifrin; and the Viennese composer 
Jawinul penned a work that takes 22 minutes of album time. The album gets into 
a lot of free -form stuff into which is worked all types of music - rock, R&B, bal- 
lads, old swing, and styles of Archie Shepp, Ornette Coleman, Don Ellis, etc. 
Cannonball comments on his change of direction on this LP in the following way: 
"Music has so many characteristics and the band can play anything very well. 
(Con't. on Page 40) 
HOLLYWOOD - THEY SHOO-IN HORSES, DON'T THEY? 
Songsmiths maintain that their most gratifying experience ís to come across 
kids in the street who are humming, whistling or singing their compositions. We 
agree. Back ín the fifties, when we were adding words to music, we would con- 
stantly encounter saplings singing our songs and ít never ceased to amaze and 
enchant us - even though they were our kids. 
It was a dozen years ago when we wrote our one and only horse -race song. 
It began "Well, 
I bet my bottom dollar on a nag called Sarah Rose/In the fifth at 
Caliente/Fifty dollars on the nose/On our parimutual ticket she was 95 to 1/And 
I 
wondered why the odds were high/then 
I saw her run ... 'They're off,' the grand- 
stand shouted/As they started in to race/Sarah Rose took off like 'Lightning'/ 
'Lightning' was ín 14th place/As they headed for the backstretch/In a final burst 
of speed/01' Sarah Rose, by just a nose/Was a mile behind the lead ... " It was 
titled "Monkey on a Donkey" and íf you consider the first two of thirty-four verses 
as undeserving, we'll hum a few bars. 
We showed them to a number of music biz people and, almost without excep- 
tion, they took exception to one word in the song. "You're on the wrong track," 
they said, "there are no parimutuals at Caliente." We had no idea how knowledge- 
able our trade was - about horse racing. 
Since, we have discovered that a great many industry execs and artists escape 
from the weekday record rat race to a weekend Hollypark horse race. And the 
list of horse racing owners ín this biz is impressive and prodigious. It includes 
(and we're sure this ís only a partial list) exec -producers Snuff Garrett, Ken Rever - 
comb, Joe Saracino; D.J. Bob Hudson; music pubs and producers Sy Heller, 
Ray Harris, Bill Lowery; execs Jerry Moss, Russ Regan, Herb Alpert; pressing 
plant proprietor Nate DuRoff; record promoman Mike Borchetta; songsmíth-con- 
ductor-producer Burt Bacharach; former label prexy (in the process, we hear, of 
forming his own new label) Alvin Bennett and vocalist Tommy Roe. 
A couple of years back, at the NARM convention, Bacharach abashedly excused 
himself from a panel discussion, explaining that he had to leave a little early be- 
cause he had his first horse racing at Del Mar. Since Burt has seldom done wrong 
with a song, half of NARM figured his nag was a sure thing. And many wandered 
out of the auditorium to contact their local bookies, laying a sawbuck or two on 
Bacharach's entry. From the flick and disk trades Bacharach gets Oscars and 
Grammys. But from his horses - mostly promises, promises. 
He owns six at the moment, including one that recently ran in the San Juan 
Capistrano Handicap. "I'm planning to spend this summer at Del Mar," Burt re- 
cently told L.A. Times nightclub editor Bob Hilburn, "we've rented a house right 
on the beach ... racing is the only thing that lets me forget music completely." 
Snuff Garrett ís one of very few ín our trade who is actually ahead of the game 
with his stable. In the past few months Snuff has had more horses than records 
ín the top three. His trainer, George Hartstone (former president of Hart Distrib- 
utors) insists that Garrett is simply enjoying beginner's luck. "Hardly anybody 
ever makes money racing horses," says Hartstone. "That's why it's the sport of 
Kings." George also trains the Jerry Moss, Nate DuRoff, Al Bennett and Herb 
Alpert stables. 
Mike Borchetta, involved ín split ownership with Bill Lowery and Bob Hudson, 
contends that he ís turning a neat profit on his weekend venture. "But that's only 
because 
I also board horses." Still Borchetta's colors have reached the winner's 
circles on numerous occasions - three times this year. 
Tommy Roe, we're told, recently coughed up ten grand for a horse - a yearling

NEW YORK (Con't. from Page 39) 
Everybody loves every kind of music - a comprehensive style of musical tastes." 
Then we spoke on his seminar work at colleges. He makes it clear that the text- 
book is one thing and his field work is another as far as jazz and all black music 
goes. Time was, even when he was in a black, Southern college himself, when jazz 
and other forms of black music were frowned upon by the faculty and he even 
cited that it was a matter for discipline if you were caught playing jazz in the re- 
hearsal halls. That's a lot of lost heritage which he says exists in some colleges 
even today. His whole band, all college graduates, take part in the two day semi- 
nar which includes several lectures on the roots and history of jazz and black 
music, concerts and workshops. It is usually set up in conjunction with a concert 
by the group at the college that week, sometimes being set up by the Black Stud- 
ies Program, a music or sociology or other department. In most cases the group 
does it free - Cannonball stated "There's no charge for the experience in black 
music." The concert generally pays it back. We talked about his thoughts on stu- 
dent unrest and things he observed during the heat of last semester. He claims 
he's non-violent and does not condone classroom burnings and the like because 
"It denies others of the right to study in that space." He talked about one incident 
at Berkeley where the rioters and administrators called a temporary truce in order 
to hold the annual two day jazz festival. For his seminar during the festival at- 
tended by 12,000 people, he drew 6000 of them in one day. This year his black 
music seminar program will be condensed into one four hour period. He's also 
trying to coordinate week-long workshops for credit, and a Southern black music 
festival which he would like to play with Clara Ward, Jerry Butler, Staple Singers, 
etc. Look for his new album and watch for him on campus and in concert hall - 
he knows what he's doing. 
EAST COAST GIRL OF THE WEEK 
For two years, Bonnie Belville has 
worked with Dave Glew and Sal Uterano 
of the Atlantic Album Sales Dept. Maybe 
you've heard her recently doing a Mott 
The Hoople, radio spot, or maybe you 
heard her a couple of years back at 
Palisades Park and other show spots 2nd 
soprano-ing with her singing group. 
She's also used that talent to land some 
session work. There's a whole story to 
the start and finish of that venture that 
is too long to get into now, but it does 
show off her go-getter spirit that served 
to land her jobs with CBS News and with 
several fashion shows as a model. On 
weekends she still uses the services of 
the Barbizon School of Modeling which 
she attended to get local fashion show 
work. Only recently did she begin taking 
guitar lessons but Bonnie claims, "Give 
me six months and 
I can truly boast of 
a little guitar."

Mountaindale was presented this week with an injunction by Sullivan County to 
foil plans for their summer activities, claiming a general lack of facilities to handle 
the crowds that are expected. So, the opening night Van Cliburn concert was can- 
celled until a later date, and the Mountaindale people are trying to iron things out 
in time for this weekend's rock fest. Set to appear is The Grateful Dead who will 
also be doing a set of concerts at The Fillmore this weekend, billed as "Dead At 
Midnight" - four nights of midnight concerts which will also feature a sub -group 
of Dead members performing under the title of The New Riders Of The Purple 
Sage. 
Mentioned the new McKendree Spring album last week. Well, this week 
I was 
able to hear one of the three acetates in existence of that group's Decca LP slated 
for August. All but two of the songs were penned by the group but one of the out- 
standing cuts is their interpretation of James Taylor's "Fire And Rain." Generally a 
fine album, it features a more fulfilling sample of their style than was found on 
their debut album. The group gave a tape of the new deck to the underground 
radio station at Cornell University. Requests for airplay was so strong after initial 
broadcasts, that one song went on the Top 30 charts there overnight, despite an- 
nouncements that the record was unavailable. The group appears at the Capitol 
Theatre very soon. 
Was also able to sneak a listen to the new Jerry Jeff Walker album on Atco. 
Recorded down South, there are some very strong production numbers that break 
up the "single" image of the singer -composer. Some say he will have a hard time 
trying to follow "Mr. Bojangles," but 
I think there is a lot in this album that could 
secure his career as a singer/songwriter. 
The Village Gate is onto a new rock format which will feature new groups 
throughout the week and weekends. Sunday nights will be set aside for experi- 
mentation in contemporary music forms, particularly jazz-rock fusion. That pro- 
gram kicks off on July 12 and 19 with groups Farmer Brown and The 7th Cen- 
tury. Call for reservations at GR 5-5120. 
A new horn section is working in the Muscle Shoals Studios in Alabama. Dale 
Quillen, Mike Stough, Stacy Goss and Sonny Royal play trombone, trumpet, fluegel- 
horn and tenor sax respectively, and double on F horn, bass trombone, tuba, 
Bari sax, alto sax and clarinet. The Shoals Horns have also been doing work at 
Tupelo, Mississippi's Triangle Sound Studios and at Quinvy Studios. 
This week's shows at the Schaefer Music Festival in the park are Ike & Tina 
Turner/Voices Of East Harlem on July 13, The Four Tops/Eddie Holman on the 
15th, Stan Kenton/Four Freshmen/Chris Connor on the 17th, and Little Richard/ 
Wayne Cochran & The C.C. Riders on Saturday (18). 
Les McCann and His Trio will play in the Garden of the Museum of Modern 
Art on the 16th. Muddy Waters is coming with his Blues Band on August 6th. 
There is a series of free concerts set for Tompkins Square Park on four con- 
secutive Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m. starting July 22 with two others on August 16 
in the afternoon and evening. Various concerts will feature gospel, folk, rock and 
jazz with a lot of local talent. Bring blankets and chairs. 
Poet/novelist/songwriter/singer Leonard Cohen will make his New York debut 
at the Forest Hills Music Festival on July 25. He'll be playing with his newly -formed 
band, The Army. He's now in Nashville recording his third Columbia album.

at that. Not an exorbitant figure when you consider that Fred Astaire, who has 
been known to cut records (he also backed a label in the 60's - remember 
Ava Records?) owned a horse that earned more than a quarter of a million dollars. 
"Triplicate" was his name and he won the Gold Cup and the Golden Gate Handi- 
cap among others. "Racing is a lot of fun," says Astaire. "But an owner runs into 
a good many hazards and irritations at times, Some people can't understand why 
the horses they bet on should be beaten. They blame the jockey, the track, the 
horse - in fact everybody but themselves - and often take it out on the owner. 
One day 
I was leaving Hollywood Park after Triplicate had been beaten and, as 
I 
drove by in my car, a man walking along the toad said in a loud voice to be sure 
I'd hear, 'There goes the son -of -a -bitch who owns Triplicate'." 
Russ Regan owns a trotter and a pacer, currently racing the California Fair cir- 
cuit. But they'll be at Hollywood Park in September. Regan says the horses are at 
least "earning their oats." Which is more than most equestrian shareholders 
should expect. Still we can't help but wonder - with all the execs involved ín 
racing why our "Monkey on a Donkey" song wasn't ever cut. For anyone out there 
interested, we still have a few faded leadsheets. But no demo - we blew all the 
demo money on that Bacharach horse back at NARM convention.

"WUSA." Flick stars Paul Newman, Joanne Woodward, Tony Perkins and Laurence 
Harvey. This is the first time that Diamond has sung his own comp in a motion 
picture ... Jimmie Haskell, the omnipresent arranger -conductor, may now be 
labeled the west coast catalyst for the Muscle Shoals sound. Having recently com- 
pleted the charts for Bobby Gentry's Capitol LP "Fancy," and her chart single 
"Apartment 21," in Muscle Shoals, he's just finished work on the string arrange- 
ments and conducting chores for the Rick Hall -produced Clarence Carter single

tower on Fame which Hall also produced. Haskell has recently cut Laura Nyro in 
N.Y. and B. B. King in L.A. as well as the Shoals dates ... Glen Campbell returns 
to the International in Vegas this week with Eddy Arnold set to follow on July 27th.

Can you identify our Mystery Man? Within the next two weeks a certain record 
industry individual will embark on a cross country bicycle trip. Though some have 
called his venture foolhardy, he has turned a deaf ear to their comments. He is 
undaunted. Having assembled the necessary items (tent, air mattress, maps, 
etc.) he stands tall, prepared to face the long and winding road to Los Angeles. 
Does the Easy Rider fate await him too? Or will he emerge as a modern day 
Lewis And Clark? And can you guess his identity? First correct answer received 
here at Cash Box will receive a special prize, donated by the Mystery Man him- 
self, a rare recording by Dolly Holiday. More clues next week.

Blue Thumb Readies 
2nd `Color Collage' LP 
LOS ANGELES - Having introduced 
its "Stereo Color Collage' multi -hued 
record with Dave Mason's album, 
"Alone Together," Blue Thumb Rec- 
ords next "Color Collage" LP will be 
"Buddy And The Juniors." This al- 
bum will be released in August. 
"Buddy And The Juniors" is the 
first time teaming of Buddy Guy, 
Junior Wells and Junior Mance. The 
project was conceived by Philadel- 
phia disk jockey Michael Cuscuna of 
WMMR-FM and financed by Blue 
Thumb. 
The colors used in this package 
differ significantly from those used 
on the Mason LP which is now Blue 
Thumb's top selling and fastest mov- 
ing album. Various grades of black 
and white are blended into the blues 
album, which features all accoustic 
instruments and no drums. 
The repertoire performed by ran- 
ges from "Talkin' Bout Women Ob- 
viously" to "Riffin," "Buddy's Blues," 
"Hoochie Coochie Man," "Five Long 
Years," "Rock Me Mama" and "Ain't 
No Need." 
Creedence Gold Album 
Heads Fantasy Release 
OAKLAND - "Cosmo's Factory," the 
new 
LP by Creedence Clearwater 
Revival-fifth in the series of LPs by 
Creedence-is a Gold Album as of 
the moment of release. Advance or- 
ders on the LP, which was released 
July 8, totaled over $1 million. 
The new Creedence LP contains 
seven original compositions by John 
Fogerty, lead singer and guitarist. 
Four of the songs in the LP have pre- 
viously been out on singles: "Up 
Around the Bend," "Run Through the 
Jungle," 
"Travelin' 
Band" 
and 
"Who'll Stop the Rain." Three of the 
songs are new. Fogerty produced the 
album. 
Included in the material on the LP 
is a Fogerty arrangement of "My 
Baby Left Me," a composition of vet- 
eran blues singer Arthur "Big Boys' 
Crudup, "Before You Accuse Me," 
one of Bo Diddley's hits, and "I 
Heard It Through The Grape Vine," 
standard. 
Also on the Fantasy July release 
schedule are two other new LPs, one 
by Billie Joe Becoat, "Let's Talk for 
Awhile" and "Parish Hall." 
Becoat's LP is his second for Fan- 
tasy (his first was released in 1969) . 
It was produced by Jesse Osborne. 
Parish Hall is a new group making its 
first recording debut with the Fantasy 
LP.

NEW YORK - Jazz artist Joe Farrell 
has been signed to an exclusive con- 
tract by CTI Records. He is now re- 
cording his first album for the label, 
set for an August release. Farrell 
won the 1970 Down Beat readers poll 
as top soprano sax player.

Pop Picks 
HELLO DARLIN' - Conway Twitty - Decca 
DL 75209 
Another country artist crosses the border into 
pop territory. Actually, Conway Twitty's done it 
before, but not in a while, and it was a surprise 
to find his single, "Hello, Darlin'," on the Top 
100. Now the album of the same name has hit 
the Top 100 Albums chart. Twitty is obviously 
an artist to be watched closely. His career may 
take some sudden turns. 
BLACK TALK! - Charles Earland - Prestige 
7758 
Jazz organist Charles Earland has come out 
of nowhere onto the charts. Assisted by Virgil 
Jones, trumpet; Houston Person, tenor sax; Mel- 
vin Sparks, guitar; Idris Muhammed, drums; 
and Buddy Caldwell, conga, Earland has made 
an album that has a wider appeal than any jazz 
organ set we can remember. LP has five selec- 
tions, including "Aquarius," "More Today Than 
Yesterday" (just released as a single) and the 
title tune. Watch this one closely for further ac- 
tion.

GREAT EXPECTATIONS - Kiki Dee - Tamla 
TS303 
Take one established British session singer, 
add an excellent record company that knows 
what it's about, sprinkle in arrangers and mu- 
sicians of style and taste building on rock solid 
songs and you have some idea of what this 
premier LP from Kiki Dee is like. But not quite. 
Here's a girl with one of the finest new voices 
around who has been struggling for some time 
in England with the wrong material. Suddenly, 
as happened when Dusty Springfield moved 
to Atlantic, Kiki's voice is finally liberated. Best 
cuts include "I Can't Give Back The Love and 
the moving "Jimmy."

Jazz Picks 
THE SIXTH SENSE - Lee Morgan --Blue Note 
BST 84335 
Lee Morgan, who as a teenager was already 
playing to acclaim in Dizzy Gillespie's band, 
has continued to seek out fresh musical direc- 
tions. The trumpet player adds another chapter 
to his story with an album which never lags 
in intensity of feeling and musical spirit. Though 
Morgan's presence is everywhere, the talents 
of his comrades in sound, four of whom are 
alumni of Art Blakey groups, contribute consid- 
erably to the LP's overall sound. Solid jazz entry. 
A DAY IN COPENHAGEN - Dexter Gordon - 
Prestige 7763 
Tenor sax man Dexter Gordon assembled a 
uniquely talented group of expatriate jazz musi- 
cians and they have come up with an album 
which is as refreshing as its title. Three Slide 
Hampton originals highlight a set which also in- 
cludes the contemporary standard, "The Shadow 
Of .Your Smile." Slide is heard on trombone and 
Kenny Drew offers some neat piano work. Gordon 
himself is in characteristically fine form on this 
worthwhile LP.

Leslie Grade, a veteran figure in the 
British entertainment industry, has 
formed his own independent company 
Leslie Grade Ltd. just a month after 
resigning his active responsibilities 
within the EMI leisure group. The rea- 
son given for his withdrawal was 
health, and Grade has recently said 
that his new enterprise will enable him 
to function in a favorite area without 
the pressure of his EMI duties. He has 
named Albert J. Knight and Ron 
Ricardo as directors of the new com- 
pany, and Knight will again produce 
this year's Christmas pantomime at 
the London Palladium which Grade is 
presenting in association with Pye 
Records and Moss Empire chief Louis 
Benjamin. Grade is also setting up a 
major British concert tour for singing 
comedian Des O'Connor before pre- 
senting O'Connor in "The London Pal- 
ladium Revue" in Toronto next Febru- 
ary. Grade, whose brothers are Sir 
Lew Grade of Associated TeleVision 
and Bernard Delfont of the EMI orga- 
nization, has been named exclusive 
European entertainment representa- 
tive for the International and Flamingo 
Hotels in Las Vegas. His company 
will also be active in film work, with 
projects already lined up which will 
star Mireille Mathieu and Cliff Rich- 
ard. Richard will also be the main at- 
traction of the new show which Grade 
will tour around the provinces. 
Competition for available American 
disk catalogues is warming up as Bri- 
tish majors seek replacement reper- 
toire for American labels that have 
started independent operations here. 
EMI has captured the Holland-Dozier- 
Holland-Invictus and Hot Wax labels 
under a long-term deal, with Ian Mc- 
Lintock being named Invictus label 
manager in addition to his Capitol du- 
ties and Richard Smith taking charge 
of Hot Wax. As already reported Phi- 
lips has signed a pact negotiated by 
managing director Fred Marks with 
Sun vice president Noble Bell to re- 
lease Sun repertoire over the next 
three years. 
Joan Baez, The Who, Chicago, Leo- 
nard Cohen, The Doors, Mungo Jerry, 
Jimi Hendrix, Arrival, John Sehastian, 
James Taylor, Richie Havens and Pen- 
tangle are among the star names con- 
firmed to appear at the third Isle of 
Wight Music Festival on August 26th 
through 30th. Aminimum quarter mil- 
lion people are expected at the open- 
air event, whose bill last year was top- 
ped by Bob Dylan, and rumors of legal 
moves by residents in the area to ban 
the fest have not yet been confirmed. 
The shows are organized by Fiery Cre- 
ations, headed by Ron and Ray Roulk, 
who have named Tony Barrow to han- 
dle press representation for the event 
in conjunction with Fiery Creations 
publicity director Peter Harrigan. It 
will be Joan Baez's first British visit 
for three years and her only appear- 
ance here. 
Monument Records president Fred 
L. Foster and vp Bobby Weiss were in 
London for parlays with Monument 
disk licensee Decca and KPM Music, 
the affiliate of the company's Combine 
Music, where they spoke with KPM 
overseas division manager Peter Phil- 
lips and Combine's UK professional 
manager Johnny Gordon. Foster and 
Weiss were also seeking product for 
release on Monument in the States and 
other overseas markets. 
MCA Records will release in Sept- 
ember a double album entitled "Jesus 
Christ Super Star" with music written 
by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim 
Rice. Those taking part are Ian Gillan 
of Deep Purple as Christ, Yvonne Elli- 
man as Mary Magdalene, Murray 
Head as Judas Iscariot, Mike d'Abo as 
Herod, and Barry Dennen as Pontius 
Pilate. Groups involved in the project 
are Juicy Lucy, Quartermass, Nucleus, 
and the Grease Band plus a symphony 
orchestra, The City of London Ensem- 
ble, pianist John Lill and a Moog Syn- 
thesizer programmed by Mike Vickers, 
Madeline Bell, P.P. Arnold and Lesley 
Duncan are in the chorus for the work, 
which presents the last six days of 
Christ's life as observed by Judas 
Iscariot. 
Management Agency and Music has 
consolidated its recent entry into the 
music publishing field by concluding a 
deal to handle the compositions of 
Leonard Cohen in the U.K. and the 
British Commonwealth with the exclu- 
sion of Canada. The three-year pact 
was completed after three months of 
dickering between Cohen's personal 
representative 
Marty 
Mac hat 
and 
Cyril Simons, manager of Leeds Music 
which is administering the MAM pub- 
lishing operation. 
Warner -Reprise celebrated its first 
birthday by purchasing 
a 
London 
Transport bus for countrywide promo- 
tional purposes. The double-decker ve- 
hicle bears the words "The Warner Re- 
prise Road Show" and the Warner 
logo, and will be used to take product 
to retailers throughout the country and 
to promote acts and records at festi- 
vals. The lower deck is being equipped 
as a discotheque and the top deck will 
be employed to sell disks at certain 
events. Warner -Reprise chief Ian Ral- 
fini revealed that the British operation 
had paid off the loan from its Amer- 
ican parent after just three months of 
business, and notched £11/4 million in 
sales during its first year. 
EMI's first cassette to be entirely 
produced in the UK has been released 
and it's "Let It Be" by The Beatles. 
The company has been tooling up for 
the last four years to manufacture its 
own tapes, and has been producing 
eight -track and four -track at its Hayes 
plant, but until now its cassettes have 
been made by the Philips factory at 
Walthamstow. EMI plans a total of 500 
cassettes on the market by the end of 
the year, predominantly pop and mid- 
dle of the road repertoire and some 
classics, with a monthly release pat- 
tern averaging twenty. Deputy mar- 
keting manager Barry Green disclosed 
details of the country's first sampler 
cassette, containing fourteen tracks by 
well known artists and selling at 29 
shillings and eleven pence. 10,000 cop- 
ies are being pressed initially for dis- 
tribution to stores with special promo- 
tion racks. 
Argo has released a two -LP boxed 
album entitled "The Wonder of the 
Age" - Mr. Edison's New Talking Pho- 
nograph" presenting the early history 
of the gramophone and including the 
voices of William Gladstone, Florence 
Nightingale, Enrico Caruso, 
Nellie 
Melba, George Bernard Shaw and P.T. 
Barnum. The album was compiled and 
produced by Kevin Daly. 
Evolution Records are launching a 
promotion campaign on two singles 
"Lovely To See You" by The Informa- 
tion and "You're Only Out To Hurt Me" 
by Abbe Jones. For the RCA van sales- 
man achieving highest sales a prize of 
£50 will be given; £25 second prize and 
£10 third prize. For the dealer with 
highest sales first prize is 2 weeks in 
Majorca; second prize one week and 
third prize a weekend in Paris. Cam- 
paign will run from July 1st thru Au- 
gust 31st. The Pathe Sound Library, 
one of the most comprehensive in 
Europe, is to be incorporated into KPM 
Music, an associate company within 
the EMI group of which Pathe is a 
member. The move will involve the 
transfer to Denmark Street of thou- 
sands of quarter inch master tapes 
containing an enormous variety of 
sounds from the splash of a drop of 
summer rain to the roar of a full scale 
battle.

ing Jazz Non -Stop series in fall

NEW YORK —

sharing community
plan”
in-

BNW’s

Randalls
Island rock fest. New York Pop, held

The
Coalition

Lords

Workshop,

oth-
ers. The

centered around
the

represented by the

to
become
involved
in

running
of
the Fest.
According

Don
Friedman,

of the three co-producers
of the con-

were being hired as ushers, baggage

In

has

I.
Coalition an
undisclosed sum
as
“rent”
for using
Downing Stadium, inasmuch as Ran-
dalls
Is.
is
technically
part
of East
Harlem and community groups were
denied
use
of
the
stadium
for
the
weekend
in
question.
Further
two
hours each night
(5-7)
are being
set
aside by BNW for use by community
groups
in
the way
of
speakers
and
local acts.
“This is the only way a festival can
go
on
in
this
country
without
vio-
lence and crowd problems,”
said Bob
Gardiner,
also a BNW producer. “By
involving
everyone
we’re
setting
a
precedent here.”
According
to
spokesmen
from
the
Young Lords and the Ryp
Collective,
all
money
they
receive
from BNW
will
be
used
to
further
community
projects.
In
the
case
of
the Young
Lords
this means mainly health pro-
grams to help detect and fight again-
st TB and
lead
poisoning which

major
problems
among

Latin
population
that
constitutes
East
Harlem. Some money will be
utilized

L. Wolfe Gilbert
Dies; Wrote First
Film Main-Title
NEW YORK —
L.
Wolfe
Gilbert,
veteran writer-publisher, regarded as
“The Dean of Tin Pan Alley,” died on
Sunday,
July
12,
in
Beverly
Hills,
Calif,
at
the
age
of
83.
His
song,
“Ramona,”
written
with
Mabel
Wayne,
is
considered
the
first
film
theme song
(see this week’s editorial,
“It
All
Started with Ramona”). The
writer
of
such
other
well
known
songs as “Waiting for the Robert E.
Lee,” “Down Yonder,” “Marta,” “The
Peanut
Vendor,” “Hitchy
Koo,’_’
Gil-
bert was born
in
Odessa,
Russia, on
August 31, 1886. He came to America
as an infant and lived in Philadelphia
with his family, then
later moved to
New York City.
Interested
in
theatricals
from
childhood,
Gilbert
worked
his
way
from copyboy for the New York Post
to
cafe
entertainer
in Coney
Island,
then
later as an actor
in Vaudeville,
where
he
toured
with
the
John
L.
Sullivan
Show,
also writing columns
for the New York
Clipper.
After 11
years
of seeing the Broadway lights,
he
wrote
his
first
song
in
1912,
“Waiting
for
the
Robert
E.
Lee.’
This
publication
_ established
his
career as a song-writer. Gilbert wrote
the script for the Eddie Cantor Chase
and
Sanborn
Show
and was
recog-
nized throughout the years as a spe-
cial material writer for many leading
stars,
collaborating
with
such
per-
sonalities
as
A1
Jolson,
Paul
Whiteman, George _M.
Cohan, Irving
Berlin, and Frank Sinatra.
Other
successes
include,
Lucky
Lindy,”
which
he
composed
about
Charles
A.
Lindbergh’s
solo
flight
across the
Atlantic, “Oh Katharina,
“My
Sweet
Adair,”
“Shades
of
Night,”
“Jeannie,
I Dream
of
Lilac
Time,” “By Heck,” and “My Mother’s
Eyes,” which became George
Jessel’s
theme song.
Mr.
Gilbert was
a member of the
American
Society of Composers, Au-
thors and
Publishers (ASCAP)
since
1924 and served on
the_ Board
ot Di-
rectors since 1953, previously serving
from
1941-44. He was
also chairman
of the ASCAP West Coast Commit-
Surviving are his widow Rose,
five
children and three brothers.
Funeral
services were held Wednesday
(15th)
in Temple
Israel
of Beverly
Hills at
12:00
noon, with burial
following
at
Hillside Memorial Park in Los Ange-
les.
Doors' Sixth Gold LP
NEW YORK —
“Absolutely
Live,”
the
Doors’
sixth
Elektra album
has
achieved advance sales of over a mil-
lion and
is already certified as a gold
record.
With
the
release
of
“Morrison
Hotel”
last
January,
the
Doors
be-
came
the

to

gold albums,
and
with
the
gold
certification
of

Live,”

become
the
first American rock group
to achieve
six
straight
ones.
“Absolutely
Live”
is
a
two-record
set
compiled
from
live Doors performances over the past
year.

Granger Trek Signals Tangerine Expansion
HOLLYWOOD —
Ron
Granger,
head of Tangerine Records, recording
artery
of Ray
Charles’ RPM
Inter-
national, leaves next week
(27)
on a
two week cross-country trek to select
four
regional
independent
promo
men
to
represent
Tangerine
product
throuhgout
the
U.S.
In
addition
to
hiring
reps
on
the
east
coast, midwest,
south, and west
coast.
Granger
will
also
be
promot-
ing label’s most recent single and LP
releases, “Universal Rhythm” by The
Rhythm
Rebellion
and
Tangerine
prexy Ray
Charles’
“Love,
Country
style.”
Prior
to
his two week
trip. Gran-
ger reviewed his
first year with Tan-
gerine
Records
at
his
office
at
2107
West Washington Boulevard.
“This
past
year
has been
a
good
one
for
Tangerine,”
he
remarked.
“We’ve
really
worked
at
getting
things together, and as we’ve grown,
we’ve
taken
on
more
responsibility
than
before.
In
contrast to the
past,
Tangerine
is now a truly autonomous
label. We
place
all
advertising from
west
coast
headcjuarters.
My
trip
next
week
will
finalize
Tangerine’s
decision
to push
its own product
in-
ternally on
a
full-scale
basis.
In
ad-
dition,
we’ve
inaugurated
a monthly
newsletter from Tangerine, which
is
sent
from
our
office
to
distributors
and deejays across
the nation.
“Currently we are negotiating with
foreign
contacts
for
licenses
in
Eu-
rope,
South
America,
and
the
Far
East,
and
I
anticipate
being
able
to make a concrete announcement re-
garding
these
deals
within
the next
month. This
is a big step forward for
Tangerine, as we will be distributing
other
labels here
as
well
as expand-
ing our own market.
“The Raeletts have new product in
the can to follow up their chart item
T Want
To,’ which we
will
be
re-
leasing
in
August
to
coincide
with
their
appearance
with
Ray
at
the
Grove
here
in
Los Angeles.
‘Ray
himself
is
riding
high.
‘My
Kind
of
Jazz,’
his
first instrumental
LP in years, is showing up across the
board,
on
Top
LP,
Soul,
and
Jazz
charts.
“And
his new
country-themed
al-
bum,
‘Love,
Country
Style,’
should
go
straight
to
the
top.
“In
one week we’ve
sold over
50,-
000
albums,
and
reorders
are
now
being shipped to San Francisco, Dal-
las, New York, and here in Los An-
geles.”
Acuff-Rose,
wffiich
has two
tracks
on “Love, Country
Style,”
is putting
its promo men on
it; Wally Schuster
of the Big Three has hired extra men
to work on “Show Me the Sunshine;”
United
Artists
has
“Don’t
Change
On
Me,”
and
Clyde
Otis,
publisher
and writer of “I Can’t Take
It Any-
more,”
is
giving that a push.
NEW POLYDOR STARR
is
Brenda
Starr whose
first single for the label,
“Soldier
Boy,” .was
just
released.
With

are

(1.) and Rudy

(r.).

CHICAGO CHATTER
Wagner Van Vlack, president of Interstate United, unveiled lU’s new restaurant,
Fritzel’s Steak House,
at a
press luncheon
in the posh
eatery
last Tuesday
(14).
Guests enjoyed cocktails, luncheon and
a tour of the premises. The steak house
is located
at 2121 South Arlington
Heights Road
in suburban Arlington
Heights,
Illinois. The
initial
Fritzel’s
in Chicago’s Loop area, has long been, and continues
to
be, one of the coin industry's most popular eating places
in town. Van’s com-
pany
owns
this one
also. The
Arlington
Heights
location
will
no
doubt
enjoy
similar success.
As
of this morning
(20)
the
Bally Manufacturing Corp.
plant
is back from
its

CALIFORNtA CLIPPIJAGS
The
transformation
of Hank
Tronick’s
office
at
C.
A.
Robinson
is now com-
plete
with
a new
desk,
chairs,
sofa,
drapes,
lights and
wall
to
wall
carpeting.
Geographically,
the
office
is
still
situated
in
a
strategic
spot— next to the
play-
room
and
bar.
C.A.R.
gourmets
are
a
bit dismayed
because
Friday
playroom
luncheon
buffets have been discontinued for the summer. But cold refreshments
are
still
plentiful for hot and
thirsty customers.
Al
Bettelman
reports
that June was
the
biggest
sales volume month
in
the
history
of
C.A.R. &
Co. He
credits the
successful month
to
sales
of Midway’s
“S.A.M.I.”,
Bally’s “Space
Flight” and “Bowl-0,” and
Valley
billiard
tables. The
combination
of
heavy
orders
for
these
hot
recent
items and
a
spurt
of
used
equipment
sales, mainly for new summer
locations, have kept the C.A.R.
staffers
jumping.
Perhaps
in
response
to
the
business
increase,
C.A.R.
service manager
Mike
Hall
is
heading
for the
hills—with
his family on
a
weeks’ camping
trip
in the
high
Sierras.
After
the
pressures
of
recent
months,
Mike wants
to
get away
where there are no coin machines
or telephones—for a week anyway!
From
the San
Francisco area
record
racks we
are
getting
strong
reports
on
“Groovin’ With
Mr.
Bloe”
by
Mr.
Bloe on the DJM
label. Also doing
well
in
the
Bay
area
is “Candida”
by Dawn
on
Bell,
Reports
out
of
Seattle
are
showing
strong one-stop action on “Some Things
a Man’s Gotta Do”
by Shango on Dun-
hill,
“Patches”
by
Clarance
Carter
on
Atlantic and
“We’re
All
Playing
in
the
Same Band”
by
Bert Summer on
Eleuthera.
Portland
is getting some calls on Neil Diamond’s “Solitary Man” on Bang. We
recall
this was the
first
hit for Diamond about four years ago.
It’ll be
interesting
to see what happens the second time around. The number one breakout album
everywhere
is “Cosmos Factory” by Creedence Clearwater Revival with
stiff com-
petition from “Blood, Sweat and Tears #3” on Columbia and
“Eric Clapton” on
Atco.
HOFSTOA HAPPENINGS
A.
F.
(Al) Lemke,
82, dean
of Houston
music operators,
died
July 3
after
a
long
illness.
Our
sincerest
sympathy
to
his
widow,
Pauline,
three
sisters and
one
brother. Son
of German
immigrants,
Al was
a
machinist
before he opened
Al’s
Cafe,
a
large downtown Houston
restaurant which
he successfully operated
along with coin operated counter games as a sideline. When electric coin operated
phonographs appeared
he
sold the cafe to devote
full time
to operation
of that
type
equipment.
Reportedly
he was
the
first
person
here
to
put
electric
coin
operated
phonographs
on
locations. One
of
his
prized
possessions was
a
per-
sonal
letter from the Seeburgs thanking him
for
his volume
of business, always
on
a cash
basis.
Lemke’s honesty and
professional
ethics as an
operator were
never
questioned.
He
was
a
lifelong member
and
regular
attendant
of
First
Evangelical
Church.
The
recent
three-day Rowe vending machine
service school
at Central
Sales,
Inc., 91
Dennis
St.,
Houston, was super
in attendance;
also
in
real and
fringe
benefits.
Average
attendance was 30
operators
per
meeting
and
23
attended
every session. A
gift was awarded each 100% attendee. Drawing was held, open
to
all ops who attended every meeting, for a stero record console. Each meeting
was
followed
by
a
buffet
dinner.
Instructors
for
the
school were
Ralph
Phipps
and John
Pentecost.
Don Carter and
Bill Cooke
justly proud
of
their new Scepter Records
offices
on
Southwest
Freeway.
Both
are
active
in
Houston
music
promotion
Danny’s Gifts and Records, 3219 Airline
Dr.,
bearing down on
mail order promo-
tion.
Owner
Danny
Hall
always
seeking
artist
to
record
Visited
long
established
Bluebonnet
Music and
Cigarette
Service
but owner
K.
T.
Park was
out
(as most good ops
usually are) tending to business.
Did enjoy
cordial chat
with attractive
little office secretary Vicki
Lewis.

Butler,
president Gulf Coast
Dist.
Co., together with wife and daughters,

Abe Susman,
Dallas,
state distributor for Gottlieb
line, on
a combined business
and
pleasure
visit
here
with

of ABC

While
visiting with Marge

wholesale record store, had occasion to meet Willie D. Pate, P & M Record Shop.
From load

Houston, while

Local

as many middle

trips and
spent
their money
locally.

Outburst
Dist. Goes To Mercury
LOS ANGELES—Mercury Records
has
entered
into
an
exclusive,
long-
term agreement to distribute the new
Los Angeles based independent
label,
Outburst Records Ltd.
The
deal, announced by
Mercury’s
president Irwin Steinberg, was nego-
tiated by Mercury’s recently appointed
Los Angeles A&R Director, Bob Todd.
The Outburst
artist roster
initially
contains
three
acts,
all
of which
are
represented
by
the Agency For
the
Performing
Arts
(APA)
under
the
supervision
of Howard McElroy. The
initial Outburst
release,
a
single
en-
titled “Stoney Mountain” by a group
called
Therpay,
is
already
available,
Todd
said. Other acts signed
initially
to
Outburst
starring Len
Jewell
in-
clude The Show and Jupiter.
Therepy started a concert tour last
week and
is featured in
all venues on
the
same
bill
as
Metromedia
star
Bobby Sherman.
Heading Outburst
is long-time LA
producer
and
songwriter
Hal
Winn.
Winn has been responsible for
chart
hits on both the pop and R&B levels.
Among
his
successes
have
been:
“Gimme
Little
Sign,”
by
Brenton
Wood; “Psychotic Reaction,” by Count
Five,
and
“The
Ooogum
Boogum
Song,” also by Brenton Wood.
Warner GM Of
Record On Film
Winn
said
Outburst
initially
will
maintain
offices
in
Los
Angeles and
Dallas.
Winn and Todd
said
the
Outburst
roster would contain a minimum num-
ber
of
acts
to
allow maximum
con-
centration
on
each.
Winn
has
been
involved
in the record industry
since
1962.
In
addition
to
its
own
in-house
labels—Mercury, Philips, Smash, Fon-
tana,
Limelight
and
Intrepid—Mer-
cury also
distributes the independent
labels, Virtue, Wayside, Peachtree and
Odax
labels.
Steinberg said the addition of Out-
burst
was
another
strong
step
for
Mercury
aimed
at
strengthening
its
position in the
total marketplace and
especially on the West Coast.
Weiner Heads Sales
For Metromedia Label
NEW YORK — Mort Weiner has been
promoted to director of national sales
at Metromedia Records. According to
label veep, Tom Noonan, Weiner
will
now be responsible for all sales activi-
ties and will work with the promotion
and
advertising
departments
to
de-
velop marketing concepts for all label
product.
Previously
Weiner
was
Eastern
promo manager at Metromedia. Before
joining
the company he was national
singles
sales
manager
for
Verve/
Forecast.

Capitol Names Schwartz
Creative Services VP
HOLLYWOOD—Capitol Records
Dis-
tributing
Corp.
has
announced
that
Marvin Schwartz has been elected vice
president,
creative
services,
CROC.
For the past ten years Schwartz has
served
as
Capitol’s
director
of
crea-
tive services.
In
his new
position
Schwartz
will
supervise the packaging of all Capitol
product
and
coordinate
all
support
functions
relating
to
the
graphic
presentation of that product. This will
include
over-all
supervision
of
the
label’s art, photo and editorial depart-
ments,
which
also
combine
under
Schwartz
to
furnish
collateral
ma-
terials
to
Capitol’s merchandising de-
partment, as well as
special products
and
custom
services.
Schwartz
will
continue to serve as Director of EMI’s
International Design
Center.
Schwartz
first came
to
Capitol
in
1949.
Under
his
direction
the
com-
pany’s
graphic
arts
department
has
grown from
a one-man
shop.
It has
also been the
source,
to
the
label,
of
many awards for album cover design.
Schwartz,
himself,
has
received
four
Grammy Awards.

Simon & Garfunkel
FOREST HILLS TENNIS STADIUM,
N.Y. — “I am just a poor boy, though
my
story’s
seldom
told ...
I
have
squandered
my
resistance,
for
a
pocket
full
of mumbles.
.
.
.”
Paul
Simon’s
“The
Boxer”
the
opening
number
of
the
night, was
the most
appropriate song they could do. With
a
little imagination you can
see
the
similarity
of
the
song
and
their
childhood
beginnings
in
that
very
same
Forest
Hills.
So
that was
just
the start of one of the finest concerts
nine dollars could buy.
It was about
nine
o’clock
(a
half
hour
late)
when
they
appeared
on
stage and started to sing before any-
one
even
noticed
them.
Paul
Simon
wearing
blue
jeans,
a
striped
shirt
and
a New York Yankees
cap.
Art
Garfunkel
wearing
the
same
blue
jeans, and a worn button down
shirt,
looking
very
Forest
Hills,
followed
The Boxer with “59th
Street Bridge
Song” and “Fakin’
It.” By
this time
the well dressed and extremely quiet
crowd knew they were in for an extra
special treat. Maybe because they were
playing
in
their own back yards and
their mother was there to watch them,
but perfection was
the
only way for
them. Paul
Simon, a
bit of an
actor
& comedian
also,
felt
it necessary
to
stop
one
song and
start
over
so
he
could
do
it a
different way,
best
de-
scribes the altitude they were aiming
for.
The moon
was
burning
a
fiery
orange in the sky and the warm night
The Byrds
Van Morrison
grew hot as everyone strained to listen
to Paul Simon’s guitar and Art Gar-
funkel’s
beautiful
vocals.
They
did
all
their famous
songs,
covering
all
five
of
their great Columbia albums,
which
brought
back
memories
to
many. As extras were some rock and
roll greats like “By By Love.” Before
intermission they
did
one from
their
new
album,
a
folk
song
from
Peru
called “El Condor Pasa,” and finished
the
first half with the great “Home-
ward Bound.”
For
the
second
half
of
the
show
the
boys
concentrated
on
solo num-
bers, and both showed the profession-
alism
they
have.
The
highlight
of
the night, was the million selling (and
Art’s
finest
solo)
“Bridge
Over
Troubled Waters.” This brought him
a thunderous and well deserved stand-
ing
ovation.
After a
set
of
encores,
the show ended
just as
strangely
as
it
had
started,
with
the
boys
just
walking
off. They came back
to take
bows,
with
sheepish
grins
on
their
faces
as
if
uncertain
as
to
whether
the crowd enjoyed them. They are un-
equaled by any other act around and
.they know
it! By
this time the moon
was a
golden glow
standing
high
in
the sky and a strange setting for the
quiet crowd to
file out onto the sleepy
streets surrounding
the
stadium, and
back
to
the
desolation
of
their
cars
and homes
to discuss one
of the few
real music
treats
they had
ever wit-
nessed.
m.h.
Blood, Sweat
<& Tears/John Hartford
HOLLYWOOD BOWL, L.A. — “Peo-
ple
say
that we
sound
‘too
precise.’
Well, anybody who’d
spent
six years
at
Juilliard
is trained
to sound
‘pre-
cise.’
Actually,
the members
of
this
band
probably
have much
individual
free blowing space as any other rock
group.”
David
Clayton-Thomas’
statement,
made at a press conference the after-
noon
before,
was
at
least
partially
proven
during
the
course
of
Blood,
Sweat and Tears’ Hollywood Bowl con-
cert. Each member
(except drummer
Bobby Colomby)
did
indeed
have
at
least
one
lengthy
solo.
Contrary
to
their
recorded performances,
though,
the band sounded far from precise. In
fact, they were quite—and consistent-
ly—ragged. This, they explained, was
because
it was their first U.S. appear-
ance following their Iron Curtain tour,
and
they
really
hadn’t much
oppor-
tunity to perform material from their
new Columbia album.
Whatever the excuse, their audience
didn’t seem
to mind a program char-
acterized by performers tripping, fall-
ing mikestands, occasional out-of-key
playing
and
an
extremely
obvious
showbiz approach
to the whole thing.
BS&T did, however, have the decency
to
make
a
sound
check
during
the
afternoon
(something
that
the Band
hadn’t
done
the
week
before,
with
really unfortunate results). Four care-
fully-planned encores were taken, with
the real chestnuts (“You’ve Made Me
Arlo Guthrie/Manhattan Transfer
So
Very
Happy”
and
Wheel”)
saved for
last.
‘Spinning
The “showbiz approach” mentioned
above
was
typified
by
the
group’s
presentation
of “Symphony
for
the
Devil”
done
up
with
lots
of
mood
lighting and
sinister instrumental
ef-
fects; the only thing the piece lacked
was the sight of Clayton-Thomas pop-
ping up
in long red underwear and a
horned headpiece.
Possibly because he was brought in
as a next-to-the-last minute substitute
for broken-wristed Gordon
Lightfoot,
R.C.A.’s John Hartford presented
his
45 minute sock-it-to-’em set of proven
audience-pleasers.
Comprising
about
nine
numbers,
it
was
virtually
the
same program
presented
at
his
last
couple
of
local
club
appearances.
Hartford’s
group,
Iron
Mountain
Depot,
performed
with
competence;
their
lack
of
inspiration
understand-
ably may have
been symptomatic
of
the boredom brought with
repetition.
Probably
the
most
unexpected—and
for
that
reason
memorable—feature
of the whole
set was their playing “I
Want You (She’s So Heavy)” as Hart-
ford
left
the
stage following
his
en-
core
of
(surprise!)
“Gentle
On My
Mind.”

CENTRAL PARK, NYC — The Byrds
just keep on, adding a few new things
here, doing an extended improvisation
there, and
generally generating good
feelings among themselves and
their
listeners.
At
the
Schaefer
Festival
they were right up to
snuff.
Roger McGuinn and the crew opened
the set with a Bob Dylan song, “You
Ain’t Goin’ Nowhere.” The Byrds are
always
at home
doing
Dylan’s
ma-
terial
and
this
number,
from
their
“Sweetheart
Of
The
Rodeo”
album,
usually
gets
things going
for
every-
one.
Roger
then
introduced
a
new
song “Welcome Back Home,” a coun-
try
flavored item which was given a
nice gently rocking treatment.
Somehow
the
Byrds’
version
of
“This
Wheels
On
Fire”
seems
to
get
more
prophetic
with
each
per-
formance. Shifting winds of a building
rainstorm gave
it even more intensity.
But no rain
fell on
the Byrds.
The
medley
portion
of
their
set
featured a good deal more solo work
and improv playing than
usual.
Fol-
lowing “Turn, Turn, Turn” and “Mr.
Tambourine Man,” and
serving
as
a
prelude to “Eight Miles High,” there
was
a
ten minutes
plus jam by the
bass
guitarist and the drummer. Ap-
parently the Byrds would like to move
further along in
this direction,
so
al-
though
this
break was
a
trifle
too
long,
it augurs well for the future.
To
cries
for an
encore, Roger and
friends
ambled
back
onto
the
stage
to sing “So You Want To Be A Rock
And
Roll
Star.”
More
than
just
a
spoof
and
a
goof,
this
has
always
been
an
excellent
plain
old
happy
tune, and
the
Byrds’
rendition
of
it
on this not quite stormy night was a
treat. The
group
exited,
once
again,
to prolonged applause. Obviously the
audience
would
have
stayed
for
a
dozen more encores.
Also
on
the
program
was
Van
Morrison who, while raindrops fell
all
around,
offered
a
well
balanced
set
comprised
of
numerous
selections
from
his
“Moondance”
album. We
particularly
liked
his
singing
of
“Brown Eyed Girl.” Morrison records
for Warner
Brothers.
e.k.

PARK,
NYC —
Arlo
Guthrie brought many smiles to many
faces
as
he
performed
in
his
own
inimitable
fashion
at
the
Schaefer
Music
Festival
this
week.
Playing
both guitar and piano and singing
in
the manner
to which
he has become
accustomed, Arlo was .... well, Arlo
was just Arlo.
What
is
it about a New York City
audience that there are people so rude
as to demand songs and insult artists
who
don’t cater
to
their whims.
Sev-
eral
noisy
and
obnoxious
people
did
their damnedest to disrupt Arlo’s
set
with
continued
cries
for
“Alice’s
Restaurant” (“See the movie,” advised
Arlo)
and
the
“Motorcycle
Song,”
neither
of which
got
done.
This
Re-
prise
artist
is
moving
forward
into
different material now and
it
is good
material.
Still
there
are
some
who
prefer the security of the past. At any
rate, Arlo was scarcely ruffled by the
outbursts and calmly went about
his
business.
One
of
the
real
highlights
of
the
set came very early with the singing
of
“Okie
From
Muskogee,”
the
GARDEN
STATE
ARTS CENTER
N.
J.—Despite
serioas
social
turmoil
in
nearby
Asbury
Park
last
week,
British
songstress Petula Clark drew
admiring swarms
of summer concert
goers
throughout
her week-long
en-
gagement
at
the
handsome
Garden
State Arts
Center. Her
act was
pol-
ished, combining wit and nonchalance
with a
distinctive and
sensitive
sing-
ing style and
it no doubt pleased her
fans as well
as winning her new
de-
votees who had thought
of her
only
as the
girl who
sings “Downtown.”
Basically,
Miss
Clark’s
set
is
con-
structed around her personal
hits
“I
Know A Place,” “Don’t Sleep
In The
Subway,”
“This
Is My
Song,” “My
Love,”
“I
Couldn’t
Live
Without
Your
Love,”
but
she
also
delivered
standards
and
near
standards
like
Paul
McCartney’s
“Yesterday”
as
well as newer material
including
Si-
mon
and
Garfunkel’s
epic
“Bridge
Over Troubled Water.” Highlights
of
the evening were a moving
interpre-
tation
of
the
(vastly
underrated)
Leslie
Bricusse
ballad “You And
I”
and
a
“Beat
Goes
On”
medley,
an
preachy and overly self-righteous song
which has become a hit in the country
market.
After hearing
Arlo’s tongue
in
cheek, deadpan
version
of
this,
it
seems hard
to
believe
that
the
song
was originally written in earnest.
Some
equally memorable moments
came with “Percy’s Song,” which film
freaks
will
remember
as
the
tune
which Bob Dylan was
in the midst of
writing and Joan Baez was singing in
the movie “Don’t Look Back.” Arlo’s
treatment
was
even-keeled,
benefit-
ting greatly from
his rhythmic piano
technique.
Returning
to
the
guitar,
Arlo
offered
another
Dylan
piece,
“Don’t
Think
Twice,
It’s
Alright.”
Arlo’s own “Ring Around The Rosey”
and “Coming Into Los Angeles” were
thoroughly enjoyable as well.
Preceding
Arlo
Guthrie was
Man-
hattan
Transfer,
the
new
Capitol
quartet. They have a sound not unlike
the early Mamas & Papas, not quite a
fair comparison, but one which
is cer-
tain
to
strike most
people upon
first
hearing them. They performed several
songs
accompanied
by
Gene
Pistilli,
lately of Cashman, Pistilli & West.
e.k
historical
review
of
rhythm
which
had the singer performing everything
from
Strauss-like
waltzes
to
Elvis-
flavored
rock.
Backing the vocalist was a
fine
or-
chestra made up
of brass and
reeds
from
the
Buddy
Rich
band,
plus
strings,
plus
Clark
regulars
Hugh
McCracken
on
lead
guitar and
Kirk
Hamilton
on
bass.
Frank
Owens,
Petula Clark’s Musical
Director, con-
ducted
from
the
piano
neatly
co-
ordinating
the
overall
blend.
First half of the evening was am-
ply
filled with
the
tightly
disciplined
yet
musically
explosive
orchestra
of
Buddy
Rich.
The
big
band
format
was standard but the sound was 1970
as
the
group
ambled
through
spun
out versions
of “Keep The Customer
Satisfied” and
selections from “West
Side
Story,”
both
of which
included
brilliant
solos
from
band
members
and
powerful
percussive
inventions
from
Mr.
Rich. The
orchestra
plays
in
the
States
this
summer
before
heading for a
tour
of
Britain
in
the
fall.

WESTSIDE
ROOM,
CENTURY
PLAZA, CENTURY CITY—If it’s the
teens who
dictate
the
tastes
of
the
recording
industry,
it’s
still
their
affluent
establishment
elders
who
support the supper
clubs. John Gary
knows the buttered side of his bread.
He’s more of a MOR entertainer than
most. His repertoire is aimed squarely
at Mr. Businessman and his Mrs.
In-
terweaving
pop and
(mostly)
stand-
ard
ballads
with
nimble
notes
for
change
of
pace,
he
has
managed
(with
nary
a
single
chart
record,
though his RCA album
sales are sub-
stantial)
to
command
and
please
large
audiences.
Gary
is
a noteworthy
note-holder.
And
it’s refreshing
to watch him,
so
secure
in
his
own
element
that
he
doesn’t feel compelled to also
(like
so
many
others)
be
a
comic.
It makes
the
spontaneous humor between him
and the audience a pleasant extension
of
his
personality.
He’s
perfectly
at
ease
in handling the ringside reparte.
His
voice
is
melefluous
without
being monotonous. His low notes are
full
of timbre
and
are
demonstrated
best
in such songs as “Don’t Let Me
Go”
and
“For
Once
In My
Life,”
while his head tones remain pure and
easy with the
likes
of “Malegena Sa
Le
Rosa.”
He
handles
the
lighter
tunes
nearly
as
well.
“She
Loves
Me,” for example,
is done with both
warmth
and
humor. A
Bacharach-
David medley
is
particularly impres-
sive as he uses Hal’s words
to Burt’s
tunes—not
necessarily
together,
as
they were
written. What
issues
is
a
melodic
montage
of
such
items
as
“Raindrops
Keep
Falling
On
My
Head”
played
in
counterpoint
to
a
vocal rendition
of
“I’ll Never Fall
in
Love
Again.” The
medley
is
one
of
the high
points
in an engaging
flow
of good
songs performed
with
com-
pelling
proficiency.
Gary
is
backed
by
A1
Pelgrini’s
band
with
tasteful
arrangements,
well
controlled by
pianist-musical
di-
rector John Hammond.
Eddie
Duran
is featured
on
guitar and
he’s
obvi-
ously
one
of
the
best
sidemen
around.

Spaniels Are Back; Master To Calla
NEW YORK—A
master
released
less than two weeks ago on the North
American
label
by
the
Spaniels
has
been acquired by Calla Records, sub-
sidiary label of Roulette.
“Fairy
Tales”
produced
by
Lloyd
Price and Ricky Burton garnered air-
play,
listener
calls and
sales
in
ex-
cess
of eight thousand
in the Wash-
ington,
D.C.
area
and
interest
has
spread
to
the
Philadelphia
market.
Seeking widespread
distribution
and
concentrated promotional
effort,
pro-
ducer
Lloyd
Price
entered
negotia-
tions with
Roulette president Morris
Levy who purchased
the master
for
immediate
release
on
the
company’s
Calla label.
Both “Fairy Tales” and its flip side,
“Jealous
Heart”
were
penned
by
Richard
Barrett,
writer
of
the
cur-
rent Roulette
hit with the Three De-
grees, “Maybe.”
National R&B
promotion
director,
Rocky G.
is immediately undertaking
a
promotional
campaign
with
visits
planned to the Philadelphia, Washing-
ton, Baltimore area followed by trips
to Detroit, Chicago and St. Louis with
other markets possibly following.

A week
or
so back
I happened
to
receive
a
card which came
to me
at
my home address
in a pink envelope.
The letter read: “My very dear Peter,
no doubt
it
is a surprise to hear from
me;
time has passed
so
quickly and
so
many
things
have
happened
to

of

sweet, do you
recall
those mad marvellous days we spent

Everything
was
such
an
adventure!
I
hope
you
remember
those things with the same warmth
I
do,
because
of
all
the
men
I’ve
known,
you make me
feel
like some
one. My
Love,
Eloise
Laws.”
I
had
never
heard
of
the
girl,
but
under-
standably my wife thought otherwise
and was decidedly “cool” towards me.
Imagine my
surprise
a month
later
when reading through
a publicity
re-
lease
from

.
.
.
yes

Eloise

lieved and delighted that the mystery
had

Perhaps

I was very pleased

that the promoting
of records
is not
a
thing
of

Record
promo-
tion has never been a strong feature
of the business here.
In the
last few
years
“hand-outs”
to
disc
jockeys
and reviewers, and to people who are
generally
accepted
as
being
able
to

in promoting records, have be-

a
rarity. Some companies
only
get one or two albums to hand out in
this way. Certain people will be quick
to
label
the
practice
“payola”,
but
give-aways
are
only
one
side
of
the
story.
Promotion
is
the
life-line
of
the recording industry overseas, par-
ticularly
in
America;
and
those
in-
volved
in
the
trade
in
this
country
could do well
to keep
it
in mind.

Jacques Helard, general sales man-
ager at Pathe Marconi’s
is more than
happy these days about the growing
importance of the import department
headed by Richard Peisac. Peisac who
imports an average
of 40,000 LP’s
a
month has witnessed a regular rise in
sales.
French
people seem now more
and more
interested
in imported
rec-
ords for various reasons:
1) The
rec-
ords
are
available
before
they
are
pressed
and
released
in
France.
2)
The
quality
of
the product
is
rather
better
than
the French
one.
Richard
Peisac has now several deals
all over
the
world
with
various
labels
inter-
ested.
Being
released
in
France
as
fast
as
possible. Best
sellers can
top
the 35,000 copies sold in a very short
time.
An
amazing
figure
for
the
French
market
latest
imported
LPs
released
include: Pink Floyd, Beatles,
Temptations, Rare Earth (a top seller
here),

Crow
and

Funk. After the summer
holi-
days

is

on the Tamla Motown label to make
it
even more popular
in
France. Other
plans
include new
deals
with many
American
labels to meet the increas-
ing public demand for imported
rec-
ords. As seen from the public
side
it

that the

in France of

is a very good way to
make popular label since people tend

teresting and of a better quality. We
are sure that this technique of import-
ing

more an more popular in France.

'Professionalism Is Our Format' 
The most recent Pulse survey in 
the Toledo area shows WTOD a 5,000 
kw country station at the top of the 
ladder among listeners in the 18-49 
age bracket. But the picture was not 
always as rosey for WTOD; in fact, 
for years they had remained on the 
bottom rungs. Then, in September, 
1968, they decided to convert from a 
top forty to a modern country format, 
a good decision in the light of their 
phenomenal upsurge since then. 
WTOD's accomplishment is note- 
worthy since it has faced consider- 
able competition in the Toledo mar- 
ket, including three Top Forty sta- 
tions. In accounting for a country 
format station winning out in the 
ratings race, WTOD's program direc- 
tor Jim Wight commented, "At the 
same time country grew. more sophis- 
WTOD 
Toledo, Ohio. 5,000 kw. 
John Booth, pres.; Robert Martz, 
general 
mgr.; 
Charles Fleishman, 
commercial mgr.; Jim Wight, pro- 
gram dir. and promotion mgr.; Bill 
Manders, 
production 
mgr.; 
Chuck 
Wheeler, music dir.; Dick Lambert, 
news dir. 
Format: Modern Country. Playlist: 
85-90 singles, selected albums and 
Oldies. 
On -Air -Personalities: 
Jim 
Wood, 
6-9 a.m.; Jim Wight, 
9 to noon; 
Chuck Wheeler, noon to 3 p.m.; Bill 
Manders, 3-6 p.m.; Les Bortell, 6-9:15 
p.m. 
ticated, rock began to become less 
palatable to all but the teenage lis- 
teners." The inevitable result was 
that older members of the audience 
became more attracted to modern 
country sounds. 
Wight cited another important fac- 
tor, "We pay our jocks more than 
some stations in major markets. They 
work hard in promoting the station 
while they're on the air and while 
they're off. Professionalism is our 
format." 
Using the NAB recommended com- 
mercial load of 18 minutes, WTOD 
walks a line between rock or extreme 
sounding country music and what 
Wight termed "hard" or very tradi- 
tional country. Basic policy is to play 
two album tracks and two oldies per 
hour, using the remaining time to 
play selections from a playlist of 
85-90 singles. 
DROP RIGHT IN-That's what Cer- 
tron Records' Pozo Seco did at the 
studios of the Larry Kane Show in 
Houston. KTRK-TV personality Kane 
was on hand to welcome the pair, who 
brought along a copy of their new 
LP. 
Promotions are heard often on the 
station. A recent one, with the im- 
probable title "Send A Friend To 
Hell," rewarded winners with an all - 
expense paid weekend at the Satan's 
Holiday Fair in Hell, Michigan. A 
Country Clunker contest featured a 
run down 1957 station wagon as the 
first prize, while "Hi -Low" gave lis- 
teners the chance to zero in on an 
exact money figure in a fashion sim- 
ilar to the one used in the card game. 
Currently WTOD is involved in a 
whirlwind preparation for the Miss 
Lucas County Fair contest which is 
sponsored by them. In addition to 
selecting applicants, the deejays have 
the 
somewhat 
enviable 
task 
of 
screening them 
and choosing the 
finalists. Winner of the competition 
receives a bevy of WTOD-donated 
prizes. 
During the month of December, the 
station goes all out on a "Penny 
Pitch" campaign to raise money for a 
local crippled children's home. Jocks 
shovel walks, wash cars, allow pies 
to be thrown in their face, all for 
donations. "It's simply an emotional 
appeal for money," explained Wight. 
Last year the station was directly 
responsible for raising over $4,000 
for this charity. 
ABC newscasts are heard on the 
hour in addition to two minutes of 
local news. Editorials are aired four 
times per day and changed every oth- 
er day. 
Claim Unauthorized 
Lennon Video Tape 
NEW YORK - Screenings of an 
hour-long video tape on John and 
Yoko Lennon to sponsors and net- 
works in the U. S., England, and 
Japan by Anthony Cox, are being 
conducted without authorization or 
consent from either of the Lennons 
or ABKCO Industries which rep- 
resents the Lennons, according to 
ABKCO. 
It was also added that John Len- 
non is not preparing a score for the 
tape, as reported. 
Sperber & Scene '70 
Set For 26 More Weeks 
NEW YORK - Betty Sperber's op- 
tion as producer of the rock TVer, 
Scene '70, has been renewed for an- 
other 26 week cycle. Other options 
which were renewed at the same time 
include Mike Gargiulo, director, Ani- 
ta 
Tricarico, 
talent 
coordinator, 
Susan Gottlieb, production supervi- 
sor, and Danny Aharoni, production 
coordinator. Stephanie Gray has been 
named associate producer and Dave 
Rogers and John M. Kinsellagh re- 
main as executive producers. 
Scene '70, which is now seen in 84 
markets recently began a policy of 
having guest hosts for each of the 
shows. Kicking off the new format 
was James Brown. Subsequently Me- 
lanie, Johnny Maestro, Jerry Butler, 
Kenny Rogers and the First Edition 
and Oliver have served in the capacity 
with the 'Chamber Brothers, Sam 
Moore (formerly of Sam & Dave), 
Andy Kim, the Grass Roots, Richie 
Havens, Genva Ravan & Ten Wheel 
Drive and Ray Charles slated for fu- 
ture hosting duties.

individually inscribed, 
and printed 
matter carried the legend that the

Major Push On 
New 'Canned' LP 
HOLLYWOOD - "Future Blues," a 
new Canned Heat album slated for 
immediate release, is the object of a 
major ad, publicity, promo and mer- 
chandising push by Liberty/UA, Inc. 
The 
album 
cover 
for "Future 
Blues" features 
an Iwo-Jimo-type 
flagraising with the flag flown upside 
down, a universally -accepted distress 
signal. Accordingly, the label is in 
the process of mailing the attention - 
getting slicks to radio stations, retail 
outlets, and to all field employees. 
Bumper stickers for cars and for 
motor bicycles, mailings, radio spots, 
heavy consumer advertising on the 
underground level, displays, posters, 
and local store advertising round out 
the Liberty/UA push. In addition, the 
company's key exec are so impressed 
by the performers and packaging 
of "Future Blues" that a special 
mailing of the album is being under- 
taken to a great quantity of opinion 
makers in the music industry. 
"Canned Heat," one of the first 
underground groups to emerge as in- 
ternational best-sellers, are currently 
on a national personal appearance 
tour, after which they will headline a 
major rock festival in Japan in late 
summer.

Dome To Distribute 
Stonegood In N.Y. 
NEW YORK - Dome Distributors, 
Long Island, New York record dis- 
tributors, have been signed as the 
eastern representatives for Stone - 
good Records and all subsidiary la- 
bels, it was announced by Monk Hig- 
gins, president of the new label. Hig- 
gins is due in New York this week 
for meetings with Bernie Block and 
Barry Reznick of Dome to setup 
eastern sales policies for the compa- 
ny's initial product. 
Higgins has just completed swings 
through 
San 
Francisco, 
Seattle, 
Houston, Dallas, Denver and Miami 
coordinating distribution assignments 
in those areas, while Stonegood ex- 
ecutive Fred Stone has toured Mexico 
and Hawaii setting up similar inter- 
national arrangements. 
Stonegood had originally planned 
to market initial product through 
their own national sales force, ac- 
cording to Higgins, but have now 
decided independent distributors in 
each market will be better suited for 
the company's needs at present.

LOS ANGELES - Kent Records has

sively with Little Richard, Gladys

Mitchell, singer; Bobby Harrell, gui- 
tar; 
Theodore 
Toney, vocals; and 
Otis Taylor, lead singer.

Women's Lib Theme 
Of Decca's Single 
NEW YORK -A new Decca single 
praises 
the 
Women's 
Liberation 
Movement. The record, "I Am A 
Woman" and "Liberation Now," was 
co -produced by Tom Morgan, Decca 
A&R head, and Joe Rene, indepen- 
dent producer. "I Am A Woman" is 
narrated by Sandy Duncan, recent 
star 
of 
Broadway's 
"The 
Boy 
Friend." "Liberation Now," was co- 
authored by Betty Freidan, authoress 
of the best-selling non fiction book 
"The Feminine Mystique"; Jackie Re- 
inbach, authoress of "¡Carefree Cook- 
ing," and Joe Rene. 
According to Rene, who published 
the song in his Claro Music Corp., 
300 copies of the sheet music are 
being mailed to the various women's 
liberation groups around the coun- 
try. 
The song will be introduced next 
Saturday (8) at the home of noted 
art collector Ethel Scull in East 
Hampton, at a special press confer- 
ence. 
Among the sponsor's of this event 
is Mrs. Wyatt Cooper, (Gloria Vand- 
erbilt) .

LOVELY RITA-Well-known session singer Rita Coolidge has been signed to 
A&M Records as a solo artist. The songstress has just completed a nationwide 
tour. With Rita at the signing are (clockwise) Gil Friesen, veep of ad- 
ministration and creative services, Herb Alpert, president of the label, Chuck 
Kaye, v.p. of A&R and publishing, and David Anderle, Rita's producer. 
Steve Jerome Heads 
Groove Sound Studio 
NEW YORK - Groove Sound Studio 
has named Steve Jerome as new op- 
erating head of the studio, effective 
immediately. In addition, Jerome will 
also engineer all sessions. 
Groove Sound Studio has under- 
gone an extensive maintenance over- 
haul recently and new equipment has 
been installed. The addition of 
a 
16 -track console is being condisered 
for installation this fall, with a com- 
plete revamping of rental fees now 
being formulated said to offer sub- 
stantial savings 
to 
producers 
of 
demos, recordings and commercial 
jingles. 
Jerome, along with his brother 
Bill, will continue to produce for Mu- 
sicor Records, in addition to his new 
duties for Groove Sound Studio. The 
Jeromes have been responsible for 
such hits as "Brenda" by the( Cupids; 
"Whenever 
A Teenager Cries" and 
"Tommy" by Reparata and the Del- 
rons; "Walk Away Renee" and "Pret- 
ty Ballerina" by the Left Bank; 
"Ding Dong the Witch Is Dead" and 
"Heigh Ho" by the Fifth Estate; and 
"Happy" by the Blades of Grass, 
among others.

Jazzists Dig Tunes 
Out Of Gopam Ent. 
NEW YORK - Gopam Enterprises, 
Inc., the music publishing arm of 
John Levy Enterprises, is getting 
through to jazzists with its tunes. 
These tunes, "Pharaoh's Dance" and 
"Country Preacher", are both written 
by Joe Zawinul. "Pharaoh's Dance" 
encompasses one entire side of Miles 
Davis' "Bitches Brew", two record set 
on Columbia, among the biggest sel- 
ling album's in ;Davis' career. The 
second number is the title song of the 
"Cannonball" Adderley Quintet's pop- 
ular "Country Preacher" album on 
Capitol. 
Zawinul, the vet pianist with the 
Adderley Quintet, is also the author 
of such previous hits as "Mercy, Mer- 
cy, Mercy", "Walk Tall" and "Money 
In The Pocket". His tunes are pub- 
lished by Zawinul Music, a division 
of Gopam Enterprises, Inc. 
In addition, Nat Adderley has writ- 
ten "Hummin' ", featured in Quincy 
Jones new album on A&M, "Gula 
Matari." Adderley is also the writer 
of the hit "Work Song". His songs 
are published by Upam Music, anoth- 
er division of Gopam Enterprises, Inc. 
Among the other divisions of Go- 
pam Enterprises, Inc. are Taggie Mu- 
sic Company, which 
contains the 
songs written by the late Wes Mont- 
gomery. 
The Managing Agent for Gopam 
Enterprises, Inc. is Joan Shulman, 
headquartered in the New York office 
of John Levy Enterprises. Worldwide 
representatives of 
Gopam 
include 
companies throughout Europe, South 
America, Japan, and Australia. 
Capitol Signs If 
NEW YORK - Capitol Records has 
announced the signing of If, a seven 
member English group. The deal was 
negotiated with the group's pro- 
ducer -manager Lew Futterman and 
his Concert House organization. 
The group's first LP, "If" was re- 
leased on the Island label in Eng- 
land. Capitol will release it here on 
July 20. 
If, which includes Dick Morrisey 
(tenor) and Terry Smith on guitar, is 
presently appearing in concerts and 
festivals in England and the Conti- 
nent, and has an 18 date tour set 
with Traffic. 
This agreement is a further part of 
Capitol's new New York product ac- 
quisition set-up. Through this ar- 
rangement, Capitol New York handles 
total work on new acts, from singing 
through release follow-up. In con- 
junction with release of the "If" al- 
bum, Capitol is planning a massive 
multi -media campaign. 
Blue Horizon/Sire 
To New World HQ 
NEW YORK - Ground breaking has 
begun on the new home of Blue Hor- 
izon/Sire group of record and music 
publishing companies. The premises, 
an entire building, located at 165 
West 74th Street, New York, will be 
called Blue Horizon House. 
Housed there will be 
executive 
offices and rehearsal rooms, as well 
as a modern fully equipped eight 
track recording studio. In addition, 
there will be a record shop at the 
location that will specialize in blues, 
progressive rock and imported rec- 
ordings. The main purpose of the 
shop will be to feed back to Blue 
Horizon and Sire a pulse of what is 
happening at the retail level. 
Among the companies headquar- 
tered at the new address in addition 
to Sire and Blue Horizon, will be 
their 
affiliated publishing 
houses, 
Uncle Doris, Doraflow, Bleu Disque, 
Sanah, Goodie Two Shoes, Pandora, 
Geordie, as well as various interna- 
tional 
publishing 
companies 
rep- 
resented 
by the 
group including 
Heathside and Saravat (both United 
Kingdom) and Angle and July (both 
Australian). 
Distrib. Deal 
Sire Records will be distributing 
product by Focus, a new Dutch group, 
as the result of an agreement reached 
between Sire's 
managing director, 
Seymour Stein, and Hubert Terheggn, 
of Radio Tele Music the publishing 
arm of Radio Luxembourg, who holds 
a worldwide production contract on 
the group. Sire and their licensees 
throughout the world, with the ex- 
ception of Benelux, will handle Focus 
product. 
In another move toward strength- 
ening their internptional roster, Sire 
will 
produce 
and 
distribute 
rec- 
ordings 
by 
Dutch 
vocalist 
Ben 
Cramer throughout the world. The 
deal was set with Robert Aardse of 
Dureco in Holland and Sire will dis- 
tribute Cramer's product worldwide 
with the exception of Benelux and 
France. Cramers' initial session is set 
for mid -August in New York. 
Craig Braun, Inc. 
To Open On Coast 
NEW YORK - West Coast oper- 
ations are scheduled to begin in late 
fall for Craig Braun, Inc., a New 
York based sales promotion/advertis- 
ing agency working exclusively with 
the record industry. 'In association 
with their subsidiaries, Sound Pack- 
aging Corporation, and 888 Advertis- 
ing, they develop all phases of record 
merchandising, including album jack- 
et design/printing, posters, point of 
purchase displays, trade advertising, 
and unique album stickers. Some of 
their clients include A & M, Atlantic, 
Bell, Chess, Columbia, Elektra, Lon- 
don, 
Metromedia, 
Motown, 
RCA, 
and Scepter. 
Recently hired to assist in east 
coast operations was Cheryl McIn- 
tosh, formerly with Columbia Records 
and their advertising agency since 
1966. Miss McIntosh will head the 
advertising production department 
Managing the L. A. office will be 
Ken Sasano, formerly a merchandis- 
ing project manager at Capitol Rec- 
ords in Hollywood. Prior to joining 
Capitol, Sasano was associated with 
their 
subsidiary, 
Merco/iCollegiate 
Record Co. in New York.

THE JULY FIFTH ALBUM -5th Dimension- 
Soul City 33901 
Although Soul City seems to be rapidly 
running out of the group's tracks this latest 
5th Dimension 
LP release should be 
set 
for 
a 
sizable chart run. 
Set consists of 
tracks from 
previous albums like 
"Sun- 
shine Of Your Love," "California My Way," 
"Go Where You Wanna Go," and "Lovin' 
Stew," and some 'B' side songs, such as 
"Don'tcha 
Hear Me Catlin' 
To Ya," and 
"Those Were The Days." 5D's sound is un- 
mistakable and fully as potent as ever as 
evidenced by the fact that the set is already 
on the charts. 
THIS IS HENRY MANCINI-RCA VPS -6029 
Henry Mancini's 
huge following will be 
ecstatic over this specially priced two record 
'Best Of" set. Happily, much of Mancini's 
pioneering early works are included for the 
listener's delectation such as "Peter Gunn," 
"Dreamsville," "Mr. Lucky," and "My Friend 
Andamo," as well 
as the maestro's later 
triumphs like "Moon River," Dear Heart," 
"Love Theme From 'Romeo and Juliet,' " 
and "Days Of Wine and Roses." This is a 
retrospective set of herculean accomplish- 
ments by one of our most popular writer/ 
conductors. It can't fail to do well.

ELTON JOHN-Uni 73090 
The 
question 
before 
us, 
dear friends, 
is all we've heard about Elton John true, or 
are we again the unwilling victims of the 
Hype Machine? And the proof, as they say, 
is in the pudding. Elton and his lyricist (in- 
deed 
everyone 
connected 
with 
it) 
have 
poured their lifesblood into this LP. It is 
a genuine labor of love. It is also one of 
the two or three most beautiful albums re- 
leased this year. Everything starting with 
the songs themselves (many of which are 
being covered) through Elton's infinitely sen- 
sitive voice and piano, through Paul Buck - 
master's constantly exciting and inventive 
arrangements to Gus Dudgeon's inciteful pro- 
duction blends to form that rare unity that 
only great projects achieve. Album is already 
receiving strong airplay. 
GONE IS LOVE-Paul Mauriat-Philips PHS 
600-345 
Paul Mauriat has few peers in the field 
of orchestrating contemporary ballads and 
this album may well be his finest effort to 
date. 
Along with 
"Bridge 
Over Troubled 
Water," "Let It Be" and "Raindrops Keep 
Fallin' On My Head," the maestro serves up 
a bouncy "Classical Gas" and a hum -able 
tune of his own composition entitled "My 
House And The River." Those who prefer 
their music MOR will give this decker 
a 
warm reception. 
URIAH HEEP-Mercury 61294 
Those lil Dickens, Uriah Heep, lay down 
some of the 'heaviest' music this side of 
Led Zeppelin and Mountain. "Walking In Your 
Shadow" 
is 
all 
pounding 
rhythm, 
fierce 
double -tracked guitar from Mick Box and 
echoing harmonic vocals by David Byron. 
"Come Away Melinda," the poignant Fred 
Hellerman tune, is given a delicate but un- 
usual treatment and shows off to excellent 
effect the full range of Byron's strong voice. 
And "Dream -mare" starts off with quiet or- 
gan work from Ken Hensley which leads into 
much flaming guitar fireworks. This one is 
definitely not for the folk -freaks. But for the 
hoards of PLAY IT LOUD fans this will be- 
come a staple.

BRIDGES-The 
Nice-Mercury 
SR - 
61295 
The farthest out of the rock classical col- 
laborations and decidedly one of the most 
successful is this blending of the Nice and 
the Sinfonia of London under the direction 
of Joseph Eger. "Five Bridges Suite," an 
original work by Nice organist Keith Emer- 
son, is presented in live performance as is 
"Country Pie/Brandenburg Concerto No. 6." 
Latter combines Dylan and Bach in a most 
unusual fashion. Emerson has since left the 
group so this represents the last Nice album. 
Set has done extremely well in Britain and 
should do likewise on this side of the water.

highlight the track that features excellent 
ensemble horn playing. On another level, 
"Raise The level of Your Conscious Mind" 
with a good vocal workout by J. W. Hodg- 
kinson would make a fine single. Set should 
be picking up FM airplay almost immediately 
with substantial sales to follow. No ifs about 
it.
