CashBox Country Music Report 
Opry Celebrates 
45th Birthday 
NASHVILLE-WSM's 45th 
Grand 
Ole Opry Birthday Celebration and 
Disk Jockey Convention, a fast -paced, 
well planned event which attracts 
more than 6,000 official delegates and 
hundreds of curious spectators will 
start on October 15th. 
WSM's Grand Ole Opry has been 
phenomenal since its beginning in 
1925. This show is the most unbelieva- 
ble and enduring radio program any- 
where. From all over the world rep- 
resentatives employed in the produc- 
tion, promotion, or distribution of 
country music, as well as the indus- 
tries greatest stars and other celeb- 
raties will attend the birthday festivi- 
ties. 
As in the past, this celebration will 
be designed for the enjoyment of the 
DJ's, artists and guests. 
The actual convention begins on 
Thursday, October 15, and is climaxed 
by the cake -cutting celebration on 
stage at the Saturday Grand Ole 
Opry. 
In order to attend all official Opry 
anniversary events, one must send a 
registration form along with a check 
for $10.00 payable to the Opry Trust 
Fund. This fee permits registrants 
access to dinners, luncheons, buffets, 
etc. at the Municipal Auditorium, of- 
ficial headquarters, plus, the oppor- 
tunity to rub elbows with singers, 
DJs and other industry people who 
market the country music product. 
The $10.00 registration fee is a 
contribution and all revenue received 
is channeled to the Opry Fund, which 
was established in 1965 to give finan- 
cial assistance in time of need, emer- 
gency or catastrophe to country mu- 
sicians or their families. 
For further information on advance 
registration write: 
The Opry Trust Fund 
WSM Radio 
P. 0. Box 100 
Nashville, Tennessee 37202 
Slim Whitman 
To Ireland 
NEW YORK-Slim Whitman, one of 
America's most established country 
and western artists, has just em- 
barked on an intensive tour of Ire- 
land. The tour began in Dublin, on 
September 1st, and hits twenty key lo- 
cations. It will close in Galway, on 
October 11th. 
Since beginning his career in 1952, 
Whitman has recorded 39 albums and 
over one hundred singles, including 
"Indian Love Call" and "Rose Marie", 
both of which earned him million sell- 
ing gold disks, as did a pair of his 
albums. 
ON THE DOTTED LINE-Buddy 
Lee looks on as Liz Anderson signs 
an exclusive management, booking 
contract. Anderson, who records for 
RCA Records, has had many hit sin- 
gles, including "Game Of Triangles," 
with Bobby Bare and Norma Jean, 
"If The Greek Don't Rise," "Husband 
Hunting," and her current single, 
"All Day Sucker." 
Country Series 
BBC Programs 
NASHVILLE-George Hamilton IV 
has officially signed with BBC in Lon- 
don to do a Country Music television 
series this Fall on BBC -TV in Eng- 
land. 
In accordance with the show's for- 
mat, the RCA artist is to be featured 
as host and emcee. in addition to per- 
forming on each program. Hamilton 
stresses that emphasis will be placed 
on British country talent and he will 
primarily act as host. 
Hamilton, who was a regular on the 
CBS -TV Jimmy Dean Show, and later 
host of his own ABC-TV series in 
1959, is expected to be an extremely 
important 
factor 
in 
helping 
the 
country music industry eliminate Eng- 
land's "exposure gap" caused by very 
limited radio and almost no TV cov- 
erage to date. 
In spite of a lack of previous ex- 
posure in England, country music has 
been gaining tremendous popularity 
in recent months as was witnessed by 
the addition of London's own "Nash- 
ville 
Room", which was 
officially 
opened last year by Chet Atkins. 
It was during Hamilton's perform- 
ance of this year's festival that the 
idea for his forthcoming TV series 
originated, as a result of coverage 
given to the event by BBC -TV.

The record dispute which has the ma- 
jor record manufacturers and com- 
mercial broadcasters at logger -heads 
is still very much a part of the scene 
in this country. The dispute arose out 
of a new copyright act which enabled 
the record companies to seek a royal- 
ty from broadcasters for the right to 
play their records. Right from the 
start, broadcasters from 114 stations 
refused to pay a royalty and there- 
fore have not been able to broadcast 
any material originating from Aus- 
tralia or from any other country 
where such a copyright act exists. 
Since mid May when negotiations be- 
tween the parties broke down, the 
only disks played have been Ameri- 
can, apart from an ever increasing 
number of local sides produced here 
by newly -formed independent com- 
panies. (These independents are tak- 
ing advantage of the current dispute 
by not asking for any royalty for the 
performance of their records.) So, 
the dispute wears on with no signs of 
any agreement, although regular dis- 
cussions are still taking place with 
neither side eager to make a state- 
ment for fear of making the situation 
worse. Much worse it could not be, 
because every day that the dispute 
continues, puts the new independents 
in a stronger position, while the ma- 
jor companies continue to lose valu- 
able ground on the local recording 
scene.

"All I Have To Offer You Is Me." It 
was a big hit in America last year 
for Charlie Pride. "Comic Conversa-

composer John Bromley has been 
recorded by EMI's Columbia label as 
a new singles vehicle for Johnny 
Farnham. Visiting Decca, recording 
star Englebert Humperdinck (alias 
Gerry Dorsey) was presented with 
six gold awards for sales of his rec- 
ords in Australia. Deputy general 
manager of EMI (Australia) Mr. Ar- 
thur Major made the presentation 
which consisted of three 12" plaques 
for sales exceeding 10,000 copies for 
the albums "Release Me," "The Last 
Waltz" and "Man Without Love." 
Humperdinck was also 
given 
7" 
awards for his singles "Release Me" 
and "The Last Waltz," as well as a 
plaque for sales of 35,000 on his 
"Last Waltz" extended-play disk.

Mr. Kiyoshi Nishi, the chairman of 
the board of directors of Columbia, 
and Mr. S. Watanabe, the foreign la- 
bel director, left for U.S.A. on Sept. 
16. Mr. Masami Nakayama, the pres- 
ident, and Mr. T. Shigesawa, oper- 
ating director, leave for Europe on 
October 2. They planned the trip for 
the purposes of market research and 
goodwill with affiliated companies. 
CBS/SONY has planned a "Gift -back 
Sale" as an expanding sale of year- 
end and New Year and has already 
closed its advanced orders to dis- 
tributors. The label examined the ex- 
panding sales in view of covering 
their first half year's weak sales. 
They picked up some strong cata- 
logs which are already on sale and 
packaged 20 sets (30% of classics, 
70% of pops) of double -albums in 
gorgeous double -jacket. They will be 
on the market in the middle of No- 
vember. The cost is Y3,000 ($8.33). 
Nippon Victor has been getting ready 
to release foreign labels and has 
completed the recording of the first 
catalogs. They are scheduled to rep- 
resent foreign labels and special clas- 
sic catalogs as of December. The first 
release includes 7 LP's, including dou- 
ble -set -albums and triple -set -albums. 
Price is Y2,000 ($5.56) for one piece. 
This foreign label is based on the 
upward trend that current Japanese 
artists have been making around the 
world, while Japanese modern music 
has been highly estimated overseas. 
Moreover, export of Japanese records 
has been increasing.

LONDON GALA-London Records national sales convention at N.Y.'s Summit 
Hotel held recently, produced plenty of color and action. AT TOP (1. to r.) 
D. H. Toller -Bond, president of London Records opens the convention by greet- 
ing the assembled district men and distributors; discussing the new label prod- 
uct are Bud Daily and Bill Ham of H. W. Daily Dist. of Houston, Walt Maguire 
national pop a&r chief; Herb Goldfarb national sales and dist. manager for 
London, delivers the basic product presentation to the guests. CENTER (1. to 
r.) Surprise guests who added more than a touch of charm and glamor to the 
proceedings were famed opera divas Renata Tebaldi (2nd from 1.) and Joan 
Sutherland (2nd from r.) shown here with Terry McEwen label's classical a&r 
chief, Toller -Bond, and Herb Goldfarb; Marcel Stellman (seated) exec from 
parent firm British Decca, greets famed conductor Stanley Black. BOTTOM 
(1. to r.) Jack Welfeld of London's sales force at the home office talks with 
export manager Helmut, and N.Y. production exec Bernie Fass; Distribs 
listen as London execs Goldfarb, McEwen and Maguire introduce the com- 
pany's new albums. 
Liberty/UA 
(con't from P. 7) 
hopes to attract recording personnel 
that will realize that Liberty/UA is in 
a position to do for them what can't 
possibly be done through an indie 
company relying on an indie distribu- 
tion pattern. 
"Our job," says Elliot, "is to be 
able to fulfill with reasonable imme- 
diacy the required sales needs of any 
place in the U. S. We are therefore 
establishing fulfillment centers. We 
were originally in New Orleans with 
a stocking location, fulfilling Hous- 
ton from that source. Now we have 
collapsed New Orleans as a stocking 
center, retaining it as a sales office, 
moved to Dallas, collapsed the inde- 
pendents in Dallas, collapsed the in- 
dependents in Kansas City. Now out 
of 
Dallas 
(which 
is 
our 
south- 
western fulfillment center) we take 
care of Houston, San Antonio, New 
Orleans, Oklahoma City and Dallas. 
We have sales offices or resident sales 
representatives for those accounts in 
those areas." Elliot adds that if an 
account should 
move, Liberty/UA 
will transfer its product representa- 
tives to that new area. Firm has 
made similar switches in Atlanta 
(now serving Atlanta, Charlotte and 
Miami) and Union, N. J. (now serv- 
ing 
Phil., 
Baltimore -Washington, 
Richmond and Newark). 
"Our concept is minimum stocking 
locations that will economically sup- 
ply the needs and demands out in the 
field." 
Elliot sees a marketing move to- 
wards expanded mama 
and papa 
stores. "Most of the major racks are 
looking for supportive basis and are 
creating their own full line retail 
stores. A rack to be totally efficient 
realizes that it has to have minimum 
inventory in those places. They de- 
velop a sameness with little chance of 
exposure. The next expansion :in the 
record business will be towards ex- 
panded mama and papa stores. But 
they're going to be controlled by ma- 
jor suppliers." 
Maher RCA's Rock 
Manager In East 
NEW YORK - Jack Maher has been 
appointed manager of rock music on 
the east coast by RCA Records. 
Gary Usher, rock music vp, said: 
"Maher's extensive experience in the 
planning, advertising, 
and promo- 
tional areas highly qualify him for 
this vital post. His ability to deal 
both with rock artists and their prod- 
uct is important asset to our East 
Coast rock operation." 
Maher, who has been in the music 
and recorded entertainment business 
for 14 years, joined RCA in January, 
as manager of advertising. In this 
position he handled advertising for 
all of the label's records and recorded 
tape products as well as those labels 
manufactured 
and 
distributed 
by 
RCA. 
Maher has held the post of creative 
director of The Music Agency, and 
has headed up creative services and 
advertising for MGM Records. At the 
Music Agency, Maher was responsi- 
ble for the creation, production and 
placement of radio spots for all rec- 
ord accounts of the agency. At MGM, 
he was responsible for all advertising 
and graphics and was instrumental in 
the firm's early participation in un- 
derground and college press and ra- 
dio media. Previous to his association 
with MGM, he had been an account 
executive with West, Weir and Bartel 
and was an editor for Billboard. 
`Box' Merchandising 
HOLLYWOOD - Target Marketing 
Inc. has completed negotiations with 
Kendrew Lascelles to merchandise 
items related to his original poem, 
"The Box." 
Lascelles delivered his original poem 
about war and how it hurts the 
children of the world when he was 
a guest on "The Smothers Brothers 
Summer Show" on ABC-TV. 
The 
poem, as recited by its author, is 
now a single record on the Mediarts 
label. 
3 Boston Symphony Sets Mark 1st 
Deutsche Grammophon U.S. Sessions 
NEW YORK - Deutsche Grammo- 
phon has marketed its first three rec- 
ordings with the Boston Symphony, 
marking the 
German label's first 
American sessions. 
The sessions, debuting the orches- 
tra under its exclusive contract with 
the classical arm of Polydor, Inc., 
were made in Boston Symphony Hall 
last spring under the direction of 
four 
engineers, 
headed by 
Karl 
Faust, who were flown in from Eu- 
rope. Though taped in the U. S., mas- 
tering, processing and pressing were 
done in Germany, after which the 
artists approved the final versions. 
The sets include Italian conductor 
Claudio Abbado's versions of Ravel's 
Daphnis & Chloe, Suite No. 
2 and 
Pavane for a Dead Princess, along 
with Debussy's Three Nocturnes (Fe- 
tes, Nuages and Sirenes) ; Michael 
Tilson Thomas, associate conductor 
of the Boston Symphony offers Ives 
and Ruggles "Three Places in New 
England" and Sun -Treader, respec- 
tively (a second Thomas set is planned 
for early next year); and the Boston 
Symphony Chamber Players 
offer 
three Debussy sonatas and Syrinx. 
Big Push For Sets 
To launch the release of these first 
Boston Symphony albums, Deutsche 
Grammophon has set a heavy adver- 
tising and promotion campaign. A 
limited number of advance test press- 
ings were made available for pre -

Tape Progress 
On the tape front, Laginestra is 
pleased with the global response to 
the firm's Stereo -8 cartridge catalog. 
In Europe, for instance, he cites the 
fact that sales of Stereo 8 there ac- 
count for 10% of tape sales despite 
the fact that 100 cassette players are 
sold to every 10 Stereo 8 units. Total 
tape sales account for 40% of RCA's 
pre-recorded business, with a 75% to 
25% ratio of Stereo 8 sales over cas- 
settes. U. S. cassette sales, Lagines- 
tra believes, have been over forecast 
by the business. As for 
Quad -8, 
RCA's

Von Karajan Returns 
To EMI: Renews Pact 
With Deutsche Gram. 
LOS ANGELES-Herbert von Kara- 
jan has signed a new exclusive con- 
tract with EMI and Deutsche Gram- 
mophon Gesellschaft giving both com- 
panies rights to record Maestro Von 
Karajan and the Berlin Philharmonic 
Orchestra, of which he is the chief 
conductor. The EMI recording pro- 
gram will include not only orchestral 
works and concertos, but also com- 
plete operas. 
Sir Joseph Lockwood, chairman of 
EMI, said, "I am delighted at this 
renewal of our long association with 
one of the great musicians of the 
age." 
Karajans first EMI recording was 
in 1946, and he remained an exclusive 
EMI artist until 1961 making a total 
of seventy LP's, 35 orchestral, the 
remainder including twelve complete 
operas. 
In anticipation of the new agree- 
ment, EMI has already made three 
new Karajan recordings under indi- 
vidual negotiation: 
the Beethoven 
"Triple Concerto," with David Oi- 
strakh, Mstislav Rostropovich, Svia- 
toslav Richter, and the Berlin Phil- 
harmonic, due for U.S. release by 
Angel in November; Tchaikovsky's 
B -flat minor piano concerto, with 
Alexis Weissenberg and the Orchestre 
de Paris, a January, 1971, release; 
and the Frank D -minor symphony, 
also with the Orchestre de Paris, re- 
leased here last month. 
Anderson To SM 
NASHVILLE-Dick Patterson, presi-

nounced the appointment of Scott 
Anderson as director of client rela- 
tions for the Nashville based radio 
commercial production firm. In that 
capacity Anderson will head the com- 
pany's sales force.

Chandler Gets 
New A&R Post 
At Wand Label 
NEW YORK-Chris Jonz, general 
manager in charge of R & B product 
for Scepter Records, announced the 
appointment of Gene Chandler to 
head the A 
& R activities of the 
Wand label. 
In Gene's new capacity, he will be 
producing acts as well as reviewing 
new masters for purchase on the 
Wand label. Final approval of all 
masters will 
be made at product 
meetings under the supervision of 
Chris Jonz. A strong effort will be 
made with Jonz, to whom Chandler 
will be reporting, to insure maxi- 
mum productivity through co-ordi- 
nated promotional activity. Chand- 
ler's operation will continue from his 
Chicago based office at 1321 S. Michi- 
gan Avenue. 
A year 
ago, 
Gene brought to 
Scepter the "Backfield In Motion" 
single which sold over a million 
copies. Gene, 
who dates back 
to 
"Duke of Earl" fame, will continue 
producing Mel & Tim, The Profiles 
and The Voicemasters for Bamboo 
Records, a Scepter subsidiary. Wand 
has no immediate new releases, al- 
though several major deals are pend- 
ing at this time. Chandler was named 
Producer Of The Year at the 1970 
NATRA Convention. 
Pictured (from left to right) are: 
Chris Jonz, Sam Goff, Denny Zeitler, 
and Gene Chandler.

MINIM el/N 
Jan van Schalwijk, managing di- 
rector of Ariola-Benelux and two of 
his staff members visited last week 
the A&M Records Affiliates Meeting 
in London. Lou Adler, president of 
Ode '70 Records and Chuck Kaye, 
A&M's vice president in charge of 
recorded product, visited the Ariola- 
Benelux office in Haarlem. 
Penny Farthing's Larry Page and 
Brian Hall visited Holland, meeting 
various execs from N. P. Phonogram 
and Philips' Phonographic 
Indus- 
tries. Island groups Mot the Hoople 
and Bronco were in Holland for ap- 
pearances in various parts of the 
country. The groups played a.o. in 
the Amsterdam Paradiso Club. 
Ten Dutch newspapermen and Pho- 
nogram's Anton Witkamp flew to 
Hamburg to attend a Rolling Stones 
press reception thrown by Teldec, 
Hamburg. The group is currently 
touring on the European continent 
and will do a concert in Amsterdam 
on Oct. 9. N. V. Phonogram reports 
fantastic sales for the new Rolling 
Stones Decca album "Get Yer Ya- 
Ya's Out". The company shipped 16,- 
000 albums on release date to Dutch 
dealers. 
The Keef Hartley Band did con- 
certs in Arnhem and Rotterdam. On 
Sept. 16 German Television shot a 
film of the band on locations in Am- 
sterdam and Zandvoort. 
Bospel Music NV undoubtedly now 
has the biggest hit of 1970 in The 
Netherlands `Huilen is voor jou to 
laat' by Corrie & De Rekels. Though 
the record has been in the charts for 
already 23 weeks, it suddenly climbed 
up to the 4th position with a red 
arrow. In view of the number of 
weeks this year counts, this original 
Bospel Music copyright will probably 
become no. 1 title on the top 100 of 
1970 in Holland. The Bospel Music 
ballad De Dag Dat Jij Verdween with 
which song Ben Cramer obtained the 
3rd slot in Spain during the 'Interna- 
tional 
Songfestival, 
Barcelona 
in 
1969 has now been recorded in Ger- 
many on the Metronome -label and it 
has appeared in a Danish version in 
Scandinavia. Armada Records con- 
tracted a very young instrumental 
talent: the 
13 -years old trumpet - 
player Tineke Van Tongeren who at 
the moment gives concerts with the 
Haarlem' youth -orchestra in Berlin. 
Tineke's first record will appear in 
October and it will be presented in a 
TV filmproduction of Gert Timmer- 
man which will be shot in Germany. 
Joe Miyasaki of the Japanese rec- 
ord label Nippen, was in Holland last 
week, with regard to the Japanese 
plans of the female singer Wilma (13 
years old). Klaus Lorenzen was also 
present. 
Metroname-producer 
Ben 
Cramer has returned from a visit 
to New York, where he recorded 4 
songs for Sire records. According to 
managing director Stein of this com- 
pany: "Four hits". 
MATCHING COLORS-What goes with Shocking Blue so well as regal gold ? 
Thus, it isn't surprising to find the group outfitting itself with a new flock of 
platina awards for reaching 5,000,000 international sales on "Venus" and a 
gold LP for their "At Home" album which topped the 25,000 mark in the 
Netherlands. Their reception at the Amsterdam Hilton also marked official 
release of the new "Scorpio's Dance" album.

EAST SIDE STORY-Overwhelming audience response greeted famed com- 
poser -conductor Leonard Bernstein at Osaka Japan Festival Hall when the 
maestro, in the midst of a Far East tour, led the orchestra in Mahler's Ninth 
Symphony. More than half the crowd rushed the stage to shake hands with 
Bernstein. Similar fantastic reactions occurred in Fukuoka, Kyoto, Nagoya 
and Tokyo. Bernstein attended a dinner given by Mr. Morita, chairman of 
CBS/Sony Records and two dealer parties in Osaka and Tokyo. He is shown 
here at one of these.

---- p28
eashbuac/ singles reviews 
(Picks of the Week 
STEVIE WONDER (Tamla 54200) 
Heaven Help Us All (3:07) (Stein & Van Stock, ASCAP-Miller) 
Super Wonder surges back with another step into the total performer 
portrait that he has been cultivating. No longer limited to R&B or teen, the 
artist turns up with another all -format effort that will win across the board 
acceptance. Excellent contemporary lyric and Wonder's delivery wrap up 
blockbuster results. Flip: "I Gotta Have a Song" (2:32) (Jobete, BMI- 
Hunter, Wonder, Hardaway, Riser) 
BARBRA STREISAND (Columbia 45236) 
Stoney End (2:57) (Tuna Fish, ASCAP-Nyro) 
One of the most unlikely combinations yet, Barbra Streisand tackles Laura 
Nyro's "Stoney End"; and what a fusion. Transformed by the material, Miss 
S. becomes a whole new artist filled with a power of top forty and blues 
never before even hinted at in her performances. Flip: no info. 
SMOKEY ROBINSON & THE MIRACLES (Tamla 54199) 
The Tears of a Clown (2:56) (Jobete, BMI-Cosby, Robinson, Wonder) 
A brilliant return to the heyday sound of the Miracles has already brought 
the Detroit team #1 honors in Great Britain and now soars into the American 
marketplace. Side is a giddy taste of the bright blues rock that hasn't been 
heard here for a long while, too long. Flip: "Promise Me" (2:59) (Jobete, 
BMI-Tarplin, Robinson, Cleveland) 
FIFTH DIMENSION (Bell 940) 
One Less Bell to Answer (3:29) (Blue Seas/Jac, ASCAP-Bacharach, David) 
Sparkling fare from the Bacharach/David sampler gives the Fifth Dimen- 
sion a taste of the wine that had once been Dionne Warwick's alone. Melan- 
choly reminders in the crafted lyric and a dramatic production top off the 
group's follow up to "On the Beach." No flip info. 
JERRY BUTLER (Mercury 73131) 
Special Memory (3:08) (Butler/Chappell, ASCAP-J & B Butler, Wade) 
Saying that the new Jerry Butler record is a dazzler has by now become a 
taken -for -granted description; but the latest lights an extra spark which is 
bound to make it one of the artist's best received in quite some while. 
Especially powerful ballad production. Flip: no info. 
RONNIE DYSON (Columbia 45240) 
I Don't Wanna Cry (3:00) (Ludix/Betalbin, BMI-Dixon, Jackson) 
Already on playlists from his "Why Can't I Touch You" LP, Ronnie Dyson's 
new side features a tempting rock oldie done up with an eye toward cornering 
top forty, blues and even MOR markets once more. Flip: no info. 
JOE TEX (Dial 4098) 
The Only Way 
I Know to Love You (3:13) (Muscle Shoals/Cotillion, BMI- 
Soule, Woodford) 
One of Joe Tex' most dramatic offerings yet, this ballad features a mag- 
nificent performance and intense production to create a blues and top forty 
masterwork. None of his tongue-in-cheek humor or power rhythm, this time 
it's all silk Tex-ture, and a marvel. Flip: "I'll Never Fall in Love Again" (3:45) 
(Blue Seas/Jac/E. H. Morris, ASCAP-Bacharach, David) 
THE LETTERMEN (Capitol 2938) 
Hey, Girl (2:53) (Screen Gems/Columbia, BMI-Goffin King) 
One of the choice tracks in the Lettermen's "Reflections" LP, this from - 
the -past parade is glossed by their inimitable styling. Delightful material and 
a superb performance should assure potent MOR receptions, strong enough 
to cause top forty tremors. Flip: "Worlds" (2:40) (20th Century, ASCAP- 
Rose, A & M Bergman) 
COUNTRY COALITION (ABC 11279) 
Take to the Mountains (2:45) (Dick James, BMI-Hazzard) 
Country Coalition's subtle magnetism is brought back to life in the group's 
shot at a second single success. New side is a brilliant ballad offering spot- 
lighting the team's harmony strength. Should fare very well with top forty 
and FM audiences, possibly MOR as well. Flip: "Age of Angels" (2:30) 
(Pamco, BMI-Loggins) 
MAMA CASS ELLIOT (Dunhill 4253) 
The Good Times Are Coming (2:53) (April/Barwin/Jac, ASCAP-Barry, David) 
Attractive ballad fare from the unlikely team of John Barry and Hal David 
gives Mama Cass a gem to work with. Featured in the upcoming Lee Marvin/ 
Jeanne Moreau western, the material should have a headstart in attracting 
sales notice with top forty and MOR listeners. Flip: "Welcome to the World" 
(2:18) (Helios, BMI-Segal, English) 
STEAM (Mercury 73117) 
Don't Stop Lovin' Me (3:19) (Little Heather/MRC, BMI-Frashuer, DeCarlo, 
Leka) 
Pulsing teen dance side with the polished delivery ,of Steam make this 
new offering a powerhouse top forty entry. Team's work gives the song a 
sparkle that should open the doors at top forty stations for a bright sales 
initiation. Flip: "Do Unto Others" (3:05) (Same credits) 
JOE SIMON (Sound Stage 7 2667) 
That's the Way I Want Our Love (2:31) (Cape Ann/Jabee, BMI-Beavers) 
A little of the soft Joe Simon and a bit of the rousing man are both brewed 
in this easy moving new track from the artist. Mellow mixture for R&B and 
top forty action. Flip: "When" (2:17) (Cape Ann, BMI-Wilson, Gayden) 
LOU RAWLS (Capitol 2942) 
Win Your Love (3:20) (Kags, BMI-Cooke) 
One of Lou Rawls' sparklers, this renovation of the Sam Cooke goldie puts 
the song in a whole new rhythm perspective. Bright, vivid performance and 
the material's strength should put Rawls back in the top forty as well as 
R&B sales spotlights. Flip: "Coppin' a Plea/Cool Train" (4:02) (Lou Rawls/ 
Kags, BMI--Rawls/Cooke) 
DEAN MARTIN (Reprise 0955) 
Detroit City (3:45) (Cedarwood, BMI-Dill, Tillis) 
A giant song in the country and pop fields, "Detroit City" is revisited, this 
time by Dean Martin. His familiar enchantment and the power of the ma- 
terial should earn powerful exposure on adult and MOR levels. Flip: "Turn 
the World Around" (2:24) (Fingerlake, BMI-Peters) 
(Newcomer Picks 
ONE G PLUS THREE (Paramount 0054) 
Poquito Soul (3:05) (Hot Shot, BMI-Miller) 
From the Gordo people who turned up "Viva Tirado" comes this similarly 
moulded instrumental side. Stylish organ funk and an insistent rhythmic 
magnetism should open ears at blues and MOR stations as a portal to top 
forty breakthrough. Flip: "Summertime" (3:15) (Gershwin/New Dawn, ASCAP 
-Heyward, Gershwin) 
GARRY BONNER (Faithful Virtue 7001) 
There's a Place & It's as Green as Any Country Mountain (2:37) (Koppelman- 
Rubin, BMI-Bonner, Lana, Margolis) 
Garry Bonner comes up with a marvelous way to end the summer. His 
first artist appearance in over a year shows the composer working with a part 
reminiscent/part melancholic pastoral that should touch teen audiences. 
Livelier, but mindful of his hit compositions for others. Flip: "Remember 
How the Sun Felt" (3:16) (Same pubs, BMI-Bonner, Lana, Finiz, Margolis) 
THE OUTSIDERS (Kapp 2104) 
Tinker Tailor (2:07) (Noma, BMI-Reid) 
Bright teen fare with an especially hypnotic rhythm track and instrumental 
polish behind sparkling vocals. Top forty exposure should spring this side 
into the best seller running and the team could also nab FM notice. Flip: 
"You're Not So Pretty" (2:05) (MCA/Spice Box, ASCAP-Simonell, Cavan- 
augh, King)

'On The Street' Album 
Is No Laff-ing Matter 
LOS ANGELES - In a radical de- 
parture from its standard comedy 
fare, Laff Records will release an al- 
bum of serious black poetry, written 
and recited by four Black Panthers. 
It will be titled 'On the Street in 
Watts' by the Black Voices. 
Album producer 
(and Laff vice 
president) Dave Drozen described it 
as "the heaviest, deepest soul poetry 
ever produced. We call it Watts poet- 
ry 
. 
. 
. the language of the street. 
They pull no punches." 
Drozen will call a press conference 
for Oct. 15th, inviting both consumer 
and trade press to meet the four Pan- 
thers and hear the why's behind the 
album. 
The set should create no 
small amount of controversy, consid- 
ering a sampling of the titles in- 
cludes 
"Response to 
a 
Bourgeois 
Nigger", "Kill" and "Funny How 
Niggas Can Change Things". 
The spoken word is accompanied 
by Afro -styled music, which Drozen 
said complements the bed -rock mes- 
sages of the poetry. "You could trip 
on the music alone," he stated. 
'On the Streets in Watts' will be 
released on Laff's newly -created Ala 
Label. 
Mirettes Join Zea 
HOLLYWOOD - The Mirettes' first 
single under their new label affilia- 
tion, Zea Records, has been mar- 
keted. The femme trio, NATRA's 
choice as "most promising female 
group," previously recorded for UNI 
where they enjoyed two hit albums 
"Whirlpool" and "Midnight Hour" as 
well as several singles. 
Hosea Wilson, Zea president, said 
their first release, "Ain't My Stuff 
Good Enough?," was produced by 
Fred Smith. Smith, producer of Bill 
Cosby's albums, is also the producer 
of Jackie Lee, The Olympics and The 
Watts 103rd Street Band.

DETROIT - Marvin Figgins and

Womack Has `Everybody 
Talkin' ' In Liberty/UA 
Promotional Campaign 
LOS ANGELES - Bobby Womack 
has just been slated as recipient of 
an Liberty/UA all-out drive. Push 
centers 
on his new "Everybody's 
Talkin' " R&B single version of the 
hit from "Midnight Cowboy" and the 
just -released album, "The Womack 
Live", on Liberty. 
During 1970, Womack established 
himself both as a singer with his 
waxings of such tunes as "Fly Me To 
The Moon" 
"California Dreamer", 
and "More Than I Can Stand"; as a 
guitarist with Aretha Franklin, Wil- 
son Pickett and Ray Charles; and as 
a songwriter, with material that has 
hit for Pickett and 
The Rolling 
Stones. 
Liberty/UA is dividing the Womack 
campaign 
into three catgories to 
stress his power in rhythm and blues, 
top forty, and underground. 
At present, Womack is preparing a 
new night club act; and Liberty and 
his talent representative, Internation- 
al Famous Agency, are in the process 
of setting up an extensive cross- 
country personal appearance 
tour, 
plus network television guest shots. 
Further proof of the Womack ver- 
satility is the fact that he produces 
his own recordings with his personal 
manager, Ed Wright.

licity and artist relations.

HOLLYWOOD - Mercury Records

Glory 
single 
would 
be 
available 
shortly.

with a five piece instrumental back- 
up group.

THE BEST OF GORDON LIGHTFOOT - U.A.- 
6754 
Gordon Lightfoot is one of the most brilliant 
singer, songwriters alive today. His style and 
delivery are both incredibly unique. Included 
in this Best of LP are "Go Go Round," "The 
Way 
I Feel," "Early Mornin' Rain, 
"Black Day 
In July," "Canadian Railroad Trilogy," "Did 
She 
Mention 
My 
Name," 
and 
five 
other 
sparkling performances. This album is a must 
for all Gordon Lightfoot fans, and is even 
more important for those who are still unfa- 
miliar with the artist and his material. 
GIMME 
SHELTER - Merry 
Clayton -Ode 
70-77001 
Underground fans the world aver rejoiced 
when 
the first 
Merry Clayton solo single 
"Gimme Shelter" was released some time ago 
and have waited in anticipation for her first 
LP. They may not be happy with it but a host 
of MOR people will love it. Merry's voice is 
indefatigable as she sings her way through 
"Bridge Over Troubled Water," Doors' "Tell All 
The People," Hair's "I've Got Life," and so on. 
Rather a surprising easy listening set that is 
fine in its own right but whether goest pro- 
ducer Lou Adler? 
IDLEWILD SOUTH - Allman Brothers Band 
- Atco 33-342 
In this, their second, album, the Allman 
Brothers have taken their music a step fur- 
ther. Side one opens with a country gospel 
number called "Revival," 
and 
ümrrediately 
goes into a funky rock tune "Don't Keep Me 
Wonderin'." The remaining five selectons are 
composed of two ballads, two jazz flavored 
songs, and the traditional "Hoochie Cooche 
Man." Idlewild South should earn the Allman 
Brothers Band all the respect they rightfully 
deserve. 
THE GLOBETROTTERS - Harlem Globetrotters 
- Kirshner KES 108 
The World famous Harlem Globetrotters, 
masters of trickery on the basketball court, 
and the basis of an animated Hanna-Barbera 
CBS -TV series, have now entered the music 
field with the release of their first LP. Included 
in this deluxe fold out package is the Trotters 
single, "Gravy," and a dozen other delightful 
tunes. Set is produced by Jeff Barry and is 
packaged in a special fold -out sleeve. 
THE GENE CHANDLER SITUATION - Mercury 
SR 61304 
Gene Chandler, producer, label prexy and 
entertainer can be proud of this album, his 
most recent achievement. It's a study in con- 
trasts, the gentle, very soulful likes of "Am 
Blue" and "Unforgettable" with the swinging 
"Hallelujah, 
I Love Her So" and, of course, 
Gene's recent single hit "Groovy Situation." 
This is an artist who certainly has a way with 
a song. Expect this decker to see multo ac- 
tion.

KILN HOUSE - Fleetwood Mac - Reprise 
6408 
What makes Fleetwood Mac so interesting is 
their ability to always produce new and inven- 
tive material. This album is no exception. Dan- 
ny Kirwan, Jeremy Spencer, Mick Fleetwood, 
and John McVie lay down 10 new tracks rang- 
ing from hard rock to soft blues. Pay close 
attention to "This Is The Rock," "Blood On 
The Floor," "Jewel 
Eyed Judy," "Buddy's 
Song," and "One Together." 
CLYDIE KING - Lizard A20104 
The renaissance of the back up singer con- 
tinues with this release by Clydie King who 
along with Rita Coolidge, Merry Clayton, and 
Claudia Lennear has previously provided the 
finishing touches to many a hit. Clydie's voice 
is deep and husky and is used to good effect 
on the driving Otis Redding -Steve Cropper 
number 
"Direct 
Me," 
through 
the softly 
flowing Gabriel Mekler (he also coproduced the 
set) tune "First Time, Last Time," on to the 
sonata -like "B Minor," to the r&b flavored 
"You Need Love Like 
I Do" to her version of 
Paul McCartney's "Long And Winding Road." 
A good debut. 
THE SECOND DAMNATION - Damnation - 
United Artists 6773 
Rock Fans should waste no time in picking 
up on this new LP that contains 10 hard and 
heavy tracks. Damnation gets right into it with 
the driving rhythms of "No Way," and "Death 
Of A Virgin," and keeps the pace for the 
remaining nine cuts. Also included are "Driv- 
er," "Back To The River," "New York City 
Woman," "Money Tree," "Everyone," "Ba- 
Dup," "Smile," and "In The Morning." 
ANY WOMAN'S BLUES - Bessie Smith - 
Columbia G30126 
These may be "any woman's blues" but 
they are unmistakably Bessie Smith's inter- 
pretations, expertly produced and remarkably 
clear, though they were recorded more than 
forty years ago. This is the second of five two - 
record sets Columbia is issuing, tracing the 
career of the great blues singer. It includes 
more than two dozen vintage recordings, about 
half of which employed a large conical horn 
rather than a microphone. Still Bessie sounds 
like the very personification of the blues. An 
important and valuable release which all real 
blues fans should want to own. 
THE ASSEMBLED MULTITUDE - Atlantic - 
SD 8262 
Coming off the singles chart with their ver- 
sion 
of Pete Townshend's "Overture From 
Tommy," The Assembled Multitude try their 
luck with an interesting first album release 
featuring the hit single. Also included in the 
LP are 10 rather popular tracks. McCartney's 
"Singalong Junk," Harrison's "While My Guitar 
Gently 
Weeps," 
"I 
Want 
You 
(She's 
So 
Heavy)" by the 
Beatles and Neil Young's 
"Ohio" are the tunes that should make this 
debut a best seller. 
BEETHOVEN EDITION 1970 -Deutsche Gram- 
mophon 
As almost everyone knows this is the Ulti- 
mate Beethoven: seventy-five albums in twelve 
volumes of the entire works of the master 
composer under the inspired direction of Her- 
bert von Karajan. His interpretation of Beetho- 
ven is well nigh the definitive one and the 
Berlin Philharmonic is spectacular. The vast 
set is broken down into the Nine Symphonies, 
the Concertos, etc. and can be bought by the 
consumer in separate boxed sets. Also in- 
cluded is a gorgeous hard bound book replete 
with b&w and color photos and drawings cov- 
ering the life and works of Beethoven. What 
else can we say; our cup runneth over.

ARIADNE AUF NAXOS - Richard Strauss - 
Deutsche Grammophon 2709 003 
Packed in a plush mauve fabric with gold - 
tooled box this version of the Strauss Opera 
is masterfully directed by Karl Bohm. Stand- 
out voices include Dietrich 
Fischer-Dieskau, 
Tatiana Troyanos, and Franz Stoss. According 
to the excellently written notes in the large 
libretto, "Ariadne Auf Naxos" represents the 
composer's 
successful attempt at breaking 
away from 
the Wagnerian influences that 
marked his earlier works. In this work, as in 
Strauss' 
famous 
Rosenkavalier the 
vocals 
predominate over the 
scored 
instrumental 
passages.

Pop Best Bets 
GULF COAST BOUND-Blues Magoos-ABC- 
ABCS 710 
The Blues Magoos return with an interesting 
package of fine Latin flavored material. There 
are six tracks on the LP, but each is relaxing 
and should make for hours of pleasant listen- 
ing. "Gulf Coast Bound," "Slow Down Sun- 
down," "Tonight The Sky's About To Cry," 
"Can't Get Enough Of You," "Magoo's Blues," 
and "Sea Breeze Express" are included. 
WORTH WAITING FOR-Joe Williams-Blue 
Note-BST 84355 
Joe Williams is a brilliant vocalist with a 
range that defies description. 
His style, it 
seems. was created to fit any song he chooses 
to sing, and his powerfully emotional voice 
keeps you pinned to your seat. All the selec- 
tions on the LP are treated brilliantly. "Some- 
thing," "Can't Take My Eyes Off You," "Oh 
Darling," "I'd 
Be A 
Fool Right Now," and 
"Lush Life," are remarkable. 
Jazz Picks 
SOULED OUT- Dizzy Gillespie-GWP 
ST 
2023 
Here's the new album from Dizzy Gillespie 
and what more need be said. This gentleman 
has been doing it all for so many years, you 
come to expect the exceptional from him. This 
LP fits the bill. The ten tunes are new ones, 
but Dizzy brings to them the wealth of experi- 
ence and soul which has established him over 
the years as a jazz giant. Gillespie's recent re- 
surgence 
should 
become 
even 
more 
pro- 
nounced with this release. A first rate item. 
SUMMUN 
BUKMUN UMYUN-Pharoah San- 
ders-Impulse 9199 
Pharoah has been doing some excellent work 
of late, especially on the last Alice Coltrane 
LP. Here he comes up with an album of his 
own of two long tracks. Side one is the title 
tune built around some fine Latin percussion. 
With the saxophonist 
are Woody Shaw on 
trumpet, Gary Bartz on alto sax, Lonny Liston 
Smith, piano, Cecil McBee, bass, and Clifford 
Jarvis, Nathaniel Bettis and Anthony Wiles 
on drums and African percussion. Side two is 
Smith's adaptation of "Let Us Go Into The 
House Of The Lord," which has a more re- 
laxed atmosphere to it. 
THAT HEALIN' FEELIN'-Horace Silver Quin- 
tet (With Vocals)-Blue Note 84352 
Subtitled 
"The United 
Phases 
Of 
Mind 
Phase 1," this LP marks a turning point in 
the career of the man who composed the 
:lassic "Song For My Father." Vocals are ably 
handled by Jackie Verdell and on one number 
by 
Gail 
Nelson. 
Horace, of 
course, 
plays 
superior piano and has written all the tracks. 
They're all very different with side one being 
slower while side two picks up the pace con- 
siderably. Fine LP. 
MARRAKESH EXPRESS-Stan Getz-MGM SE 
4696 
Stan Getz turns to a catalog of recent hit 
songs and applies his smooth styling to them 
with pleasant results. Title tune is neatly ar- 
ranged and rendered, ditto "I'll Never Fall In 
Love Again," "Both Sides Now," "The April 
Fools," and "Love Theme From 'Romeo And 
Juliet'." Getz has stepped out more clearly 
into the MOR spotlight and with this George 
Martin produced LP, he should do quite nicely.

always -pleasant, but still true "Tin Pan Alley"-ish qualities of "Strangers in 
the Night," "Sunny," "Those Were The Days." 
Rock music, as Okun explains, did reach its maturity in the 60's, and did 
represent a revolution of sorts-more in what is said, perhaps, than its melodic 
vehicle. But, Okun's dismissal-and that's the right word-of the great pop 
music of the 20's, 30's and 40's is an assessment that's more the after-effect 
of reviewing the "Hit Parade" of the past rather than a real study of the 
pop songs of the period-the songs that may not have emerged as hits, 
but do reflect an awareness of the world around them, if that's what Okun 
must have in his pop music. 
PAUL MAURIAT: DOORS OPEN - WORLD WIDE 
Doors are bound to open for the man who conducted what is believed to be 
the biggest instrumental seller of the decade of the 60's. The man is Paul 
Mauriat whose Philips recording of "Love is Blue" sold about 5 million copies 
following its release in 1968. The orchestral sound of this Frenchman, thanks 
to the hit, is a global "live" attraction, now playing the U.S. and set through 
next May for dates in Japan, Latin America and South Africa. One aspect of 
concerts, Mauriat explains, is the need for arrangements that differ from his 
recording scoring. For best concert -hall effect, this means a greater emphasis 
on brass. Programming involves contemporary tunes and a bit of the classics 
mostly, Pagannini and Chabrier. Also there's comic relief from saxist Gaston; 
he and pianist Andre Borly are the only other Frenchmen who tour with Mauriat. 
Another door opener for the thin, mod -dressed performer is the opportunity to 
do U.S. film scores, a field he's already been into in France. He likes the "mu- 
sical freedom" of working in this medium. A door has also opened for Mauriat to 
lend his name to good -works. This includes his participation as one of five mem- 
bers of a committee to advise Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan, high commissioner 
for refugees of the United Nations Organization, on the next LP, "World Star 
Festival," that's sold to benefit UNO. "Many more recordings" are promised 
during 1971. 
PETER HAS A HOUSE IN SWEDEN BUT . 
. 
. 
It constantly amazes me how closed off to new sounds many people are. 
I mean you can play them the greatest cut in the world and if they don't want 
to hear it they just turn off. Consequently it's usually a tremendous uphill climb 
for most new artists. It shouldn't be that way for Clive Sarstedt because he, 
like Elton John and John Buck Wilkin, is a writer and singer of rare power, 
grace and style. 
His RCA album, recently released contains some beautiful songs, like the 
"It'll Always Be Winter -Looking For Jesus" tracks that really pack a wallop. All 
the material is not, admittedly, that good but it hardly matters because, as 
Clive says, "I'm way beyond the songs on that album." 
Clive stopped by last week on his way to the Coast, 
I remarked that the LP 
had a good feel to it. "That's because everyone that 
I knew that happened to 
be in London when the sessions were in progress dropped by to sing or play. 
So the atmosphere was relaxed and happy," said Clive. "The next LP will use 
much fewer people. Just a rhythm section, I think." 
Clive will be here about a month. And if Work Permit problems came be 
overcome will do some touring with an American group consisting of bass and 
drums. We're looking forward to that.

of Yao" with a possible hit song, "Zinge Zinge" which'll be sung by Mbulu

He credits Hank Mancini for "busting down the doors," bringing in the new 
a 
wave of screen composers. Since Jones was born in Chicago in '33, he was a 
little late for the Chicago jazz scene (and, for that matter, the heyday of 52nd 
Street jazz) but like Louis Armstrong before him, he started blowing into a 
trumpet as a teenager and by the time he was 21 was playing in Lionel Hamp- 
ton's band. When he left Hampton in '53, he freelanced in N.Y., did arrange- 
ments for Ray Anthony and others. In '55 he took up the trumpet again, tour- 
ing with Dizzy Gillespie. Again he quit the band trail and spent a year and a 
half in Paris, composing, arranging and conducting, for Barclay Records. He 
visited the Scandinavian countries in '56. And in the fall of '59 was hired as 
musical director for the Harold Arlen blues opera "Free and Easy." He arrived 
on the coast in '65. His style is not exploratory. Unlike many composers who 
have experimented with atonality and extended forms, he has remained within 
the classic jazz framework. He continues to champion "the jazz thing" explain- 
ing that "there's too much fertility in that ground, music must return there in 
order to grow."

ances in London. This week they're scheduled to play the new Winterland in

Underground City 
Goes Underground 
NASHVILLE -A new "hard rock 
and psychedelic" night club will open 
in about two weeks at Underground 
City, U.S.A., at Burns, Tennessee, 
near Nashville, with the Tulip Grove 
booked for the opening. 
Ron Holt is resident manager for 
the proposed $18 million, 230 acre 
entertainment complex which will in- 
clude the new club, with Larry R. 
(Rick) 
Key, 
son 
of Underground 
City, U.S.A., Inc. President E. Jimmy 
Key, as operator of "The Inferno." 
A limited supply of food will be 
available with no alcoholic beverages 
to be sold at the club, which will 
open at 7:30 P.M. Fridays and Satur- 
days. "The Inferno" will host jam 
sessions at 1:00 P.M. Sundays. 
The club will be in one of the many 
large underground rooms created by 
limestone mining, and will be ori- 
ented 
toward 
those nearing, 
and 
over, twenty-one years of age. 
The first phase of development at 
Underground City, U.S.A. includes 
the club and an existing seafood res- 
taurant and eight acres under the 
ground, in addition to rides, exhibits, 
and camping -picnic areas in the fami- 
ly -oriented complex. 
Later plans include a motel, con- 
vention 
hall, 
golf 
course, 
pools, 
stables, and other tourist attractions.

Editorial: 
CMA'S LOSS 
The Country Music Association has done so much for Country Music since its 
inception. 
Imagine what it could have done were it not bogged down by constant politics, 
in -fighting, harmful by-laws and the like. 
The original concept of CMA, when it was formed, was to benefit Country 
Music as a whole. All in the Association and on the Board were asked to dis- 
associate themselves from company affiliations and personal benefit, and think 
in terms of the how all of Country Music would be improved by any decision, 
appointment, expenditure and the like. 
Unfortunately, it seems as though too many people in the association have 
lost sight of its original principles and goals and are involved in personal power 
struggles and politicking either for their own selfish desires or to prevent more 
deserving business competitors from getting into a position whereby their work 
for the improvement of country music might be detrimental to their day-to-day 
business activities. 
We saw vivid evidence of the politics and games CMA people play at the 
annual CMA election of directors in Nashville last week 
. 
. 
. especially in our 
own "Publications" category. 
After three deserving candidates desireous of working hard for Country Music 
were nominated from the publications field at a board meeting a few months 
ago, and were put onto the ballot for all to scrutinize and think about, a last 
minute move was made by a large block -voting member of the publication field 
to elect a dark horse, nominated just before the secretary closed nominations, 
giving no one time to investigate who the individual was, whether he was quali- 
fied, or whether his election was in the best interest of Country Music. As a 
matter of fact a number of the members in our vicinity were overheard asking 
"who is her" 
Did you ever hear of him?. 
. 
and fearful of exhibiting 
ignorance mumbled, "I never heard of that publication" or "I never knew it 
was involved in Country music." 
Why wasn't this nomination to such an important job made months ago like 
the others. So it too could be examined by members. Why was it saved for the 
very last second, for Country Music Week, when Nashville goes thru the turmoil 
and confusion caused by over population and a schedule of events that makes 
one desireous of "getting done quickly" with such things as nominations and 
elections so he can get to his next bit of business on an overloaded schedule of 
events. 
Needless to say, the big block vote of the one publication, which, each year, 
seems to have more votes than all the other publications combined (a situation 
very unlike our constitutional approach to things that gives Delaware as many 
Senators as New York has in Congress) pushed through its favorite son, de- 
priving CMA of anyone of the three previously nominated candidates who would 
have given so much to the Association. 
This editorial may smack of sour grapes. But it's not that. It's just the result 
of years of frustration that sees worthy people, who want to serve, (a rare breed 
in this day and age) prevented from doing so by politics. It's unfortunate that 
a block vote of the membership of one company, that could include the firm's 
window washers, receptionists or mail -room clerks, can control an election. And 
keep, possibly more deserving people who might pose a business threat, out of 
the limelight. 
For its own benefit, we advise the CMA Board to re-examine its by laws and 
consider a more constitutional election process before we find an editor from 
"Facist Party Daily" or some sexy girly magazine nominated and elected to the 
Board before anyone realizes it has happened.

Harold Hitt Reports 
CMA Progress 1970 
NASHVILLE - Harold Hitt, pres- 
ident of the Country Music Associa- 
tion opened the 12th Annual CMA 
Membership Meeting last week by 
reflecting upon the recent achieve- 
ments made by country music during 
the past year. Following, are ex- 
cerpts from Mr. Hitt's speech: 
"The year of 1970 has been a year 
when Country Music has attained its 
well deserved place in American soci- 
ety, the world and even the cosmos. 
Your board of directors, at their 
own expense, has carried the banner 
of country music into many different 
sections of our continent this year. 
Our first meeting, in January, was 
held in Hawaii, the second in Atlan- 
ta, where significant gains in mem- 
bership fron this active area in coun- 
try 
Music was accomplished, our 
third meeting was in Toronto, Cana- 
da, with 29 top executives from this 
country 
sharing 
ideas 
with 
our 
neighbors to the North. To show the 
strength of your board, I would like 
to point out that we have 41 execu- 
tives 
from 
the 
west 
coast, 
the 
southeast, the mid -west, and the New 
York City area. With this caliber of 
persons and broad regional support, 
your country music association will 
continue to be a sounding force in 
the industry. 
Membership records have been set 
during this 1970 year with 157 life- 
time members, (including Pete Con- 
rad, our moon -walking astronaut), 
186 organizational members, and 2,- 
516 individual members. This gives us 
a total membership of 2,859, a gain 
of 423 during the past year. Member- 
ship chairman Ralph Emery and his 
weekly meeting committee, and Mar- 
raret Beeskau, CMA Membership Di- 
rector, deserve a 
special vote of 
thanks for their devotion to the 
cause, and those of you who have 
brought new members into our fold 
are to be congratulated and com- 
mended for your efforts in this area. 
TV has become, and is becoming 
each day, a more important medium 
for displaying our product to the na- 
tion. After the highest audience ra- 
ting yet, (a 40 percent share) for our 
annual Kraft 
Awards 
Show, 
the 
Madison Avenue executive has truly 
become aware of Country Music in 
the industry. More talent has been 
presented on network TV this year 
than ever before in the history of the 
industry. The high ratings of the 
Johnny Cash Show, The Hee-Haw 
Show, and the Glen Campbell Show 
have brought interest from such 
prominent personalities as Ed Sul- 
livan, Lawrence Welk, Andy Wil- 
liams, 
Dean Martin, Mery Griffin, 
Joey Bishop, Mike Douglas, David 
Frost, Flip Wilson, Dick Cavett, Len- 
non -Durante, Donald O'Connor and 
Bob Hope as well as the Kraft Music 
Hall. Both The Cash Show and Hee- 
Haw are rated in their networks 
among the top five programs. In the 
ten major cities of the east coast, 
both shows are rated two and three 
in the top five of their networks. 
Recently, a variety magazine survey 
shows that these country shows rate 
with the public as family entertain- 
ment, variety shows, comedies, and 
musicals, all rolled into one.

rector of King Records, one of the

got back from a 35 day tour in Eu- 
rope and U.S.A. on October 3. 
At Tokyo Airport, he said as fol- 
lows; "I visited 20 record companies 
and talked with about 200 people in 
Europe and America. The purpose of 
his tour was to attend the A&M 
meeting in London and observe the 
movement of video disk and talk with 
companies 
which 
we 
have 
con- 
tracted."

meeting." 
"We exchanged opinions about vi- 
deo disk with the companies includ-

Communicating Face -To -Face Is 
Elektra Sets Judy Collins Drive 
Uttal Answer To Electronic Age 
NEW YORK - In this era instan- 
taneous electronic global communica- 
tion, Larry Uttal of Bell records still 
believes that creativity functions best 
on a face to face basis. 
New York -based Uttal believes in 
being where the records are pro- 
duced, meeting people on a regular 
basis and taking an active part in the 
creation of hits. He finds it necessary 
to schedule a full week in London 
and a week in Los Angeles each 
month in order to meet with all the 
executives, artists, producers and new 
talent he has to see in those cities. 
His global visits have helped Bell to 
more than double their chart activity 
in the past year. 
Two of the label's most recent gold 
singles, "Love Grows (Where 
My 
Rosemary Goes)" by Edison Light- 
house and "Hitchin' A 
Ride" by 
Vanity Fare, are from England. The 
Fifth Dimension, the Partridge Fami- 
ly, Seals & Crofts and other Califor- 
nia -based artists have contributed 
enormously to Bell's steady growth. 
As his roster of artists in London 
and Los Angeles increased, Uttal 
found himself traveling cross country 
and across the Atlantic more fre- 
quently. 
`Can't Wait For Hits'

Nat'l Tape Profits 
Slide, Sales Rise 
Over Nine Months 
BROOKFIELD, WISC. - Sales at 
National Tape Distributors increased 
over the nine months ended July 31, 
but profits slipped appreciably below 
those of the same period a year ear- 
lier. 
Jim Tiedjens, president, reported 
that sales for the period reached $30,- 
718,939, compared with $20,878.546 a 
year before. Profits came to $104,000 
compared with last year's $366,000. 
Earnings per share were 4¢ on 2,- 
305,906 average shares outstanding, 
compared to last year's 18¢ on 1,- 
989,373. 
Tiedjens 
said 
the disappointing 
earnings of the third quarter were, in 
part, due to a reduced gross profit 
resulting from price increases 
by 
several major suppliers with a "cor- 
responding hike to our customers." 
In addition, he said, subsid consolida- 
tion economies have not yet been 
achieved. "Looking ahead, we are an- 
ticipating a breakeven fourth quarter 
and substantial improvement thereaf- 
ter," he predicted. 
To enhance its management team, 
Tiedjens announced that Harold P. 
Thomson, a member of the law firm 
of 
Whyte, 
Hirschboeck, 
Minehan, 
Harding & Harland of Milwaukee, 
has been elected chairman of the exec 
committee. He's been a secretary and 
member of the board of directors of 
the company since 1966. 
"We are also exploring several 
other business programs that show 
promise," Tiedjens said.

NEW YORK-Michael Kagan has 
been appointed director of national 
promo Epic and Columbia Custom 
Labels, according to Ron Alexenburg, 
vice president of Epic and Columbia 
Custom Labels, sales and distribution. 
Kagan will be responsible to Alex- 
enburg for the directing of all activi-

direct the local and regional promo-

on breaking and establishing new 
catalog artists, as well as sustaining 
already established artists.

bia Custom Labels as branch promo 
manager in the Chicago -Milwaukee 
area, then was promoted to midwest- 
ern regional manager for Epic and 
Columbia Custom Labels. His most re- 
cent position with the company was 
national promo manager.

NEW MORNING-Bob Dylan-Columbia 
KC 
30290 
I've finally come to realize that first im- 
pressions of a new Dylan album are rather 
meaningless. He changes so much from LP 
to LP and there's so much to pick up on that 
it just can't be done the first time 'round. 
Think of Bob in a transitory stage between 
'Highway 61' and 'Blonde On Blonde' add the 
country flavoring of 'Nashville Skyline,' and 
you'll have a rough idea of where this set is 
at. More instrumentation, especially organ and 
piano, herald the new morning. Dylan's songs 
and vocals are now more Band and less Nash- 
ville. Got it? Now you're on your own.

Stock market circles have been dis- 
cussing the implications of the huge 
EMI money -raising issue announced 
by chairman Sir Joseph Lockwood 
and managing director John Read. It 
is a £21.2 million right isue of 81/4% 
convertible unsecured loan stock 1981, 
with 
ordinary 
shareholders being 
asked to pay for £3 nominal of the 
convertible for every ten ordinary 
shares held. The appeal of the exer- 
cise is in its generous conversion 
terms, which permit loan stock hold- 
ers to switch into one ordinary share 
for every £2 of stock in any year 
from 1973 to 1980. But the decision to 
raise money in this manner, coupled 
with the news that Capitol is experi- 
encing difficult trading conditions and 
is most unlikely to repeat its impres- 
sive first half results which boosted 
EMI earnings appreciably last year 
has cast a gloomy shadow. Some other 
areas of EMI activity did not fulfill 
earlier rosy hopes with the result 
that the year's pre-tax profits rose 
from £17.6 million to £20.96 million, 
considerably less than previous esti- 
mates had forecast. 
The Oxford Circus studio complex 
owned by AIR London, the production 
consortium headed by George Martin 
was officially opened at two cham- 
pagne receptions recently. There are 
three studios and a film dubbing the- 
ater. The latter has a Neve desk and 
Philips 35 mm projectors, and is de- 
signed for the mixing of movie tracks 
and post synchronisation. The studios 
have Neva 16 -track desks and Studer 
and 3M tape recorder. The largest 
can accomodate up to seventy musi- 
cians and will shortly have film facili- 
ties. A second has room for up to 
thirty musicians, and is primarily in- 
tended for group use. The third 
studio can be linked with the tape 
reduction room or to the second and 
its desk, and can also be used in 
conjunction with any other part of 
the complex by means of closed cir- 
cuit TV. The studio staff is sixteen 
strong and will be increased to twen- 
ty-five over the next few months. 
Martin and the AIR London consorti- 
um of Peter Sullivan, John Burgess 
and Ron Richards will be using the 
studios extensively, and now that the 
five-year deal with EMI has been 
completed, they are seeking an exclu- 
sive production pact with a major 
American company with the option 
of an AIR London logo when results 
warrant it. Martin will visit the 
States before Christmas with this end 
in mind, and meanwhile will be spen- 
ding three weeks in the studios with 
the San Francisco progressive group 
called Sea Train. He is also produc- 
ing an album for RCA with the Ed- 
wards Hand duo and planning an or- 
chestral LP of his own. There is a 
possibility that he may produce an 
album at the AIR studios with Sergio 
Mendes and Brasil '66 before the end 
of the year.

Dubreg Studio, which 
manufac- 
tures the pocket -sized miniature elec- 
tric organ known as the Stylophone, 
lost a High Court battle with the 
Customs authorities in which Dubreq 
sought a ruling that the Stylophone is 
a keyboard instrument and not liable 
for purchase tax. Justice Thompson 
in his ruling declared that a keyboard 
instrument had 
to comprise 
keys 
which move and act as a lever to 
achieve the vibration of a string or 
the opening of a valve or completion 
of an electric contact. The Stylophone 
(which is played with a pencil -type 
implement with no movement of the 
keys) did not come within this defini- 
tion. Dubreq managing director Bert 
Coleman said after the judgment that 
his company would appeal and drew 
attention to numerous foreign instru- 
ments with button and other actions 
that are being imported into Britain 
and evading tax because they are 
classified as keyboard instruments. If 
the Dubreq appeal fails, the company 
will have to pay over £78.000 in back 
tax.

An attempt is being made to per- 
suade the musicians union to reverse 
a six -year -old ruling preventing the 
recording of mood music for sound 
libraries in Britain. Behind the move 
is Keith Prowse-Peter Maurice Music 
library chief Robin Phillips. The MU 
ban was imposed originally because 
the union declared that music for ra- 
dio, TV and films should be recorded 
by British musicians and not selected 
from the resources of the sound li- 
braries. Ever since the latter have 
recorded their material overseas, and 
Philips hopes the MU will relax the 
ban on the grounds that recording 
overseas is depriving British musi- 
cians of work and that foreign li- 
braries might well invade the British 
scene. He added that radio, TV and 
film producers seldom had budgets 
permitting the commissioning and 
recording of special music and if 
they could not use the mood music 
libraries, it was likely that they 
would dispense with music altogether.

At the launching of Rare Earth 
records one year ago in Detroit, Mo- 
town exec vice-president Barney Ales 
predicted the new label would be- 
come "a significant factor in the in- 
dustry." Today, that prediction is a 
fact, and the skyrocket success of 
Rare Earth has heralded an exciting 
new era in record histroy. 
In its first year of operation, 55% 
of Rare Earth's single releases have 
scored on best-seller charts across 
the natibn. The label's album success 
is even more impressive, with "Get 
Ready" and "Ecology" by the Rare 
Earth, "Bedlam" by the Rustix and 
"S. F. Sorrow" by the Pretty Things 
all enjoying prolonged chart activity 
coast -to -coast. 
Int'l Signings 
Movi g from a solid base of do- 
mestic talent that includes the Spin- 
ners and Chuck Jackson on V. I. P. 
and, of course, the Rare Earth group 
from Detroit, Rare Earth has bran- 
ched out into an operation of inter- 
national scope. From England, the 
label has added Sounds Nice, Toe Fat 
and songstress, Kiki Dee; from Hol- 
land, the Cats; and from Toronto, 
Canada, R. Dean Taylor, currently 
thrusting to the top spot with his 
smash single, "Indiana Wants Me." 
Hearts of Stone, an exciting group 
out of Boston, and Poor Boys, from 
New York, are two 
more 
high- 
powered talents recently added to the 
Rare Earth stable. But, Rare Earth 
doesn't overlook its own backyard. 
Tapping the seemingly limitless 
pool of Motown City talent, Sunday 
Funnies and the Power of Zeus have 
become exciting additions to the 
growing list of Rare Earth artists, 
seeking to repeat the phenomenal 
success of the Rare Earth group, five 
natives of the Detroit rock scene. 
With two No. 2 hits in a row and two 
hit albums in their first year, Rare 
Earth has become one of the hottest 
rock groups in record history, setting 
a scorching pace for the other Rare 
Earth artists. 
The international 
significance 
of 
the operation and the evolution of 
the label have induced three of Eng- 
land's top record producers to be- 
come creatively involved with artists 
in the Rare Earth stable. Tony Clark

Major Label, Talent Acquisition Drive 
Is Accelerated By Capitol's lannucci 
NEW YORK - There's a new ag- 
gressive attitude at the Capitol Rec- 
ords organization. It first showed its 
colors when the company tied -in with 
Holland -Dozier -Holland for the In- 
victus label just about a year ago, 
and was re-emphasized last week 
with the announcement that Capitol 
would handle the hot Island Label of 
England in America. Island has such 
acts as Jethro Tull, Traffic, Spooky 
Tooth, and a host of others. 
Up to a year ago, Capitol seemed 
to prefer to have artists signed only 
to its own label, the major exception 
being the distribution agreement with 
the Beatles' Apple Records. 
An 'In -Fighter' 
However, after the Invictus deal 
the company actively went after and 
completed agreements with Rick Hall 
for Fame Records, with Chips Mo - 
man for the Chips and Trump labels, 
with Bob Krasnow, Don Graham and 
Tommy LiPuma for the Blue Thumb 
label, with Denny Cordell for the 
Shelter label and most recently with 
Chris Blackwell for the Island label. 
Thus, Capitol has become one of 
the "in -fighters" at all of the negoti- 
Fast Pace Set 
In US, Abroad 
ations for leading artists and labels 
making themselves available for new 
distribution deals. 
Why this new success in bringing 
in the winners? "We're willing to 
deal," says Sal Iannucci, president of 
Capitol Records. "We are sensitive to 
creative people and their needs and 
we're very aware of the atmosphere 
they prefer to work in. And we're 
making that atmosphere available to 
them." 
"There are no rules, other than 
good business judgement in any of 
the deals we are making," Iannucci 
continued. "And we go in to negotia- 
tions with no predetermined concepts 
as to how the deal must shape up. 
There are no set rules for any agree- 
ment," in our restructuring of Capi- 
tol Records as we shape it to become 
a more vital force in the record and 
music industry of tomorrow."

sive aspect of Capitol is the "new 
freedom" Capitol in America has to 
NARM 'Emergency Meet' Sets Industry 
Drive To Pass Anti -Bogus Legislation 
NEW YORK - The cash register 
tape at the Tape Hut in Wilmington, 
Dela. showed a sale of $76.28 for 18 
8 -track cartridges. The purchaser was 
Jules Malamud, 
exec director of 
NARM, who quickly identified the 
merchandise as bootleg tapes of such 
stars as Jimi Hendrix, Temptations, 
Joe Cocker, 3 Dog Night, Santana, 
the Carpenters, the Rolling Stones 
and soundtracks of "Woodstock" and 
"M.A.S.H." Some of the cartridges 
were selling at $3.98, others at $4.39. 
The same store offered authorized 
cartridges of the same product at 
$5.69. 
In 
an 
ultimate 
act 
of 
"chutzpah," 
one cartridge warned 
against unauthorized duplication. 
'Epidemic' Proportions 
Enraged at this open-handed dis- 
play and sale of bogus tapes, Mala - 
mud decided to call an extraordinary 
meeting of NARM reps and leading 
manufacturer execs in New York last 
Monday 
(2) 
consider 
emergency 
measures to combat an "industry evil 
that has reached epidemic propor- 
tions." (See this week's editorial). 
The meeting, to which Malamud 
brought his purchase, has resulted in 
an all -industry attempt to pass legis- 
lation during the special session of 
Congress that convenes later this 
month that would make the manufac- 
ture and sale of bogus disks and tapes 
a criminal and/or civil offense. A 
legal sub -committee formed within a 
newly -organized Record & Tape Leg- 
islative Committee has been assigned 
the task of drafting such legislation 
for approval this week by the full 
committee. 
Earl 
Kintner, 
NARM 
counsel, who appeared at a post -meet 
press conference along with Mala - 
mud, Jim 
Schwartz, president of 
NARM, and Jack Grossman, 1st vp,

NEW YORK - The Grammy awards 
presentations by NARAS, the record

Cossette and Burt Sugarman will 
produce the TV show, marking the 
13th annual Grammy awards. Many 
tradesters have called for a "live" 
telecast of the Grammys as a device 
to give the awards greater impact, 
both within the business and out to 
the consumer. 
A TV network 
& 
sponsor are expected to be named 
soon. 
Cossette and Sugarman will pro- 
duce for NARAS under their CoBurt 
Corporation banner, a major world- 
wide entertainment, communications 
and leisure time organization. Bell 
Telephone's Special, "The Switched 
On Symphony," produced by CoBurt 
in 1969, won an Emmy and two addi- 
tional nominations, including one for 
Cossette and Sugarman. According to 
Townsend, "The highly imaginative 
production was a motivating factor 
in the selection of Cossette and Sugar-. 
man to produce the Academy's live 
telecast. The show featured some 300 
performers; 
a well -assembled cast 
that virtually scanned all musical 
tastes from 'symphonic' to 'acid -rock' 
musicians. This is a feat in itself." 
Since the inception of CoBurt in 
July, 1969, Cossette and Sugarman 
have produced several hour-long tele-

TV webs,

sion, president Robert Brockway last 
week declared that "our inquiries 
have convinced us that hundreds of 
millions of dollars in new revenues 
will be derived from the best of the 
backlogs" of Hollywood studios on 
video cartridge. The division head's 
statement was made last week in re- 
futation of Tom McDermott's com- 
ment that the RCA SelectVision sub- 
sidiary is not interested in the issue 
of backlog films or satisfied that the 
area would provide revenue from the 
public. 
Brockway added that the monies 
CBS sees in releasing feature-length 
films on video cassette will come both 
from audiences that have never seen 
"these films and from those who will 
want to see them again -under condi- 
tions and convenience factors never 
available before." 
He pointed to the market for mo- 
tion pictures in television, saying 
"there were those who predicted that 
the product would never make it. 
What television has shown, EVR will 
prove again, that the audience for 
Hollywood films has been scarcely 
tapped." Aside from the students of 
drama, fans and film buffs who will 
enjoy an added perspective in the 
medium; any audience through video

album.

though the cassettes are being manu- 
factured 
to 
allow longer playing

quality." The process now enables

one side of a cassette, and eventual- 
ly, will permit the label to release

requires fewer side changes and in 
the case of symphonic works elimi- 
nates the turn -over break between 
movements.

ogue.

'Year Of Retailer' Program Turns 
Into Ampex Year For The Consumer 
ELK GROVE VILLAGE - What had 
earlier been termed Ampex' "Year of 
the 
Retailer" has developed, 
ac- 
cording to E. Peter Larmer, into the 
year of the Consumer. Originally, the 
program had been designed to be un- 
like 
the 
push -through 
promotion 
with offers and pressures aimed at a 
one -time -only level. Rather, it was 
presented in terms of "consistent 
growing effort with a key on accep- 
tance," the consumer equipment divi- 
sion's vp and general manager noted. 
As a result of keying on customer 
confidence and establishing person to 
personnel acquaintences for tape and 
equipment, the plan has showed itself 
to be bearing rapid as well as long- 
range fruit. 
Larmer gave extra credit to the 
"Year" program for turning this into 
one of Ampex' best year in the con- 
sumer tape recorder business in spite 
of "tight money, extreme competi- 
tion, and a generally confused and 
bewildered consumer." 
He said that the dealer support 
program is meeting with sizeable ac- 
ceptance with "the desired effect of 
sales and consumer satisfaction." 
New Consumer Step 
From the original concept of mak- 
ing the retailer more familiar with 
the equipment and accessories he was 
handling, with the goal of having 
him deal more effectively with his 
buyer's 
needs; 
Ampex 
is 
now 
stretching its "Year" into a new 
phase with direct surveying of the 
customer. From questionnaires and 
interviews, Ampex is now seeking to 
find out about the users, their im- 
pressions and ideas about equipment, 
service and product for future de- 
velopment. The new survey -step was 
instated, Larmer said, "so we aren't 
engaged in pushing products through 
dealers that they can't sell."

One of the main points of the issue is 
the LRA's assertion that a local com- 
mercial station could be viable oper- 
ating in a sales conurbation of 75,000 
people and charging an advertising 
rate of two shillings per thousand 
people per thirty second advertising 
spot. CBC says that the minimum 
formula for economics viability is a 
sales conurbation of at least 125,000 
people and 
a thirty second spot 
charge of four shillings per thousand 
population. 
At a press conference held to give 
CBC's views 
on the LRA paper, 
Green drew attention to the LRA's 
proposal to amend the Copyright Act 
of 1956 as a means of obtaining un- 
limited needle time for broadcasting 
disks and circumventing objections 
by the Musicians Union and other 
interested 
bodies. 
Green 
expressed 
the CBC's disagreement with this, 
and its preference to reach agreement 
with the MU and others rather than 
"do away with them". CBC had ap- 
proached the Mechanical Copyright 
Protection 
Society, 
Phonographic 
Performance Ltd. and the Performing 
Right Society to discover what rate 
of royalty they would demand from 
commerical radio operations. MCPS 
had specified 61/4 %, PPL would require 
121/2%, and the PRS figure was 8%, 
providing the PPL lowered its own 
demand accordingly. 
If not, PRS 
would also seek 121/2%. Green em- 
phasised that the CBC figure of four 
shillings per thousand, twice the LRA 
estimate, was essential to meet the 
costs of operating commercial radio 
and show a reasonable profit. He 
pointed out that the BBC local sta- 
tions in operation cost £75,000 per 
year for six hours of daily broadcas- 
ting, and they had no sales staff to 
maintain. CBC envisages a ration of 
70% national and 30% local advertis- 
ing, with seven main program pro- 
duction areas feeding shows to a net- 
work of about sixty stations serving 
the major sales conurabation areas. 
Green declared the advertising should 
be on a patronage basis, that is, ad- 
vertisers buying time in shows over 
which they have no control or influ- 
ence with regard to style and con- 
tent. 
Virtually all activity on the com- 
mercial radio front is now at a 
standstill while a Government White 
Paper on the subject is awaited. Pub- 
lication is expected at Christmas or 
early in the New Year. 
Meanwhile, back at the BBC, talks 
are continuing between the Corpora- 
tion and the Musicians Union on the 
question of needle time for the new 
BBC local stations. Eight of them 
have a weekly allocation of seven 
hours, but newer ones now opening 
or due to over the next few months 
have none. The seven hour ration has 
proved inadequate for programming 
requirements, but it is unlikely that 
the MU will concede a larger share 
of time. 
The new stations without the seven 
hours are confined to review pro- 
grams, soundtracks and coded music 
for their record shows. Coded music 
refers to recordings obtained on a 
reciprocal basis by the BBC from 
other European and North American 
broadcasting 
organisations, 
and 
much of it is unknown material rec- 
orded generally by equally unknown 
artists and orchestras. A growing 
number of leisure industry people be- 
lieve that a showdown with the MU 
is becoming inevitable on the thorny 
question of needle time. In the event 
of an MU strike, the BBC could the- 
oretically broadcast as many disks as 
it wished because there is no legal 
commitment to limit such program- 
ming, but such a development might 
lead to the Electricians Union and 
other unions taking sympathy strike 
action and putting the BBC off the 
air. 
David Carter, music producer of 
BBC's Radio 
London station, has 
stated that MU members had ap- 
proached him with program ideas for 
the station, but he had told them 
Radio London could not afford to 
book them at present MU rates. 
When they said they were prepared 
to negotiate their fees, he told them 
to check it out with the MU, and 
when they did, they were threatened 
with expulsion.

company secures registration of the

in

with

identity because it is not an r and b 
specialist.

Met Bruno Coquatrix, manager of 
the famous Olympia music hall. Co- 
quatrix has been enjoying a very 
good 
season this year with such 
names as Gilbert Becaud, currently 
appearing at his music hall. Becaud 
has a tremendous reception for his 
latest appearance, said to be his best 
in 10 years. However, Coquatrix still 
regrets that nothing has changed in 
the past years to bring something new 
to the scene: "we are still watching 
the same numbers we have seen for 
the past 35 years, he says. In America 
it is the same thing, with Broadway 
still presenting the same shows or at 
least similar ones. I would like to 
know which countries will bring a 
new life to music halls all over the 
world. We need new ideas; when 
nothing moves, it means a general 
weakening of the general scene." For 
the coming season Coquatrix plans to 
have such top names as Sammy Da- 
vis Jr., Paul Anka (back in Paris 
after a huge success for a one-night 
stand last month), Dionne Warwick, 
Liza Minelli, Jerry Lewis, Leonard 
Cohen, Dean Martin, Elvis Presley, 
Frank Sinatra, Peter Paul And Mary 
and Bob Dylan.

During a high sea -party on the 
Baltic Sea, the International Dis- 
cotheken Organization 
(I.D.O.) was 
founded. The I.D.O. will represent the 
discotheques, one of the three musi- 
cal mass mediums. This organization 
will get from the German record in- 
dustry a sample of each new released 
record, which will be tested by com- 
petent experts. Results of this test 
will 
be published 
in a brochure 
which will appear monthly. Further- 
more, they plan the foundation of a 
record -quick -service. 
Members 
of 
I.D.O. can buy as first delivery rec- 
ords at a special price. The most 
important thing of the whole pro- 
gram is the foundation of a disk- 
jockey -school, because the kind of 
presentation of records through the 
disk-jockey is decisive for the success 
of the record and its interpretation.

(PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS (L -R) Manager ARC New South Wales, Des Steen 
and Managing Director ARC Australia, William Smith.) 
The Australian Record Company Limited recently held their annual Na- 
tional Sales Meeting this year at the Broadbeach International Hotel on
Queensland's Gold Coast. 
Fifty delegates from all states of Australia and Rabaul, New Guinea, at- 
tended the Convention which ran over five days. Highlight of the meeting was 
the sound and visual presentation of the company's product which included 
sixty specially selected album tracks as well as accessories, pre-recorded 
cassettes and eight track tapes. 
Another big moment was the announcement of the winner of this year's sales 
competition-Mr. Barry Bull, manager of ARC's Queensland branch. ARC 
chief William Smith unveiled six Gold Records which the company has awarded 
to Simon and Garfunkel's "Bridge Over Troubled Water" LP. Each gold record 
represents sales of 10,000 albums, a truly great achievement. 
ARC have held similar functions annually since their inception.
