`Pre -Beatles No Trend, Economy' 
Spurs `Packaged' Show Revival 
NEW YORK - A pre -Beatles no 
trend and tight -money combination is 
affording a new look at the "pack- 
aged" concert tour. 
To Ira Blacker, vp of American 
Talent Int'1, a six month old booking 
agency 
here, 
the 
situation 
is 
"rough." Besides the tight -money sit- 
uation, Blacker sees a present "rough 
time" for concert tours because "mu- 
sic needs a boost" on the order of 
exciting new acts which leads 
to 
emulation, which, in turn, creates ac- 
tivity. 
The concept of reviving the "pack- 
RIAA Gold Awards 
Hit High In 1970 
NEW YORK - RIAA gold awards 
reached a new high in 1970. A total 
of 169 awards were made, compared 
to 158 in 1969. In 1970, 113 albums 
and 56 singles earned gold, while the 
year before, 94 albums and 64 singles 
earned awards. The leading record 
label in the gold derby was Columbia 
Records, with 21 awards, 16 for al- 
bums, five for singles. Gold awards 
are determined either by $1 million in 
sales for LP -tapes, 
and 
1 million 
units in the case of singles. 
FRONT COVER 
A phenomenon like Chicago doesn't 
happen frequently but when it does, 
America, and the world sit up and 
take notice. Columbia Records is re- 
leasing the third double -album simply 
entitled Chicago by the seven -man 
group with the Midas -touch. 
Each of Chicago's earlier Columbia 
double -record sets, C.T.A. and Chi- 
cago, have recently sold over two - 
million copies each, and both have 
been awarded Gold Records for sales 
exceeding one million dollars as cer- 
tified 
by 
the 
R.I.A.A. 
(Record 
Industry Association of America). In 
addition, both albums are still riding 
high 
on 
the 
national 
best-seller 
charts nearly two years after their 
initial release, thus attesting to the 
group's 
ever-increasing popularity. 
All of Chicago's albums are produced 
by James William Guerico for Posei- 
don Productions.

Saffian, Blacker notes. "It's a ques-

pointing to an upcoming "package" 
tour by Savoy Brown, Small Faces 
with Rod Stewart and the Grease

To Blacker, the current pop music 
vacuum is exemplified by the emer- 
gence to the surface of traditional 
`undercurrent" sounds, like R&B mu- 
sic and standard pop sounds. He 
claims a "conservative white back- 
lash" that prevents the booking of 
strong R&B acts. The lack of show- 
cases, Blacker adds, is giving the 
booking agency business a hard time, 
too, especially 
on the west coast. 
Says Blacker: "Promoters used to bid 
for acts, now they bid for big halls." 
Blacker also sees a trend toward acts 
becoming more involved in "small, 
tightly run agencies." 
Among other contemporary acts 
booked by ATI, whose president is 
Jeff Franklin, are Badfinger, Curtis 
Mayfield, Dawn, Four Seasons, Im- 
pressions, Jay & the Americans, Ras- 
cals, Mungo Jerry, Potliquor, Spooky 
Tooth, Tokens, among others.

HOLLYWOOD - U. 
A. Records 
made a rusty rumor official. It has 
abandoned the Liberty logo for the 
U. S. and Canada and henceforth will 
be known as U. A. Records. At a 
press conference held at the Beverly 
Hills Hotel last week, David Picker 
made this announcement, adding that 
only the Blue Note and the firms 
international Latino labels would be 
continued along with U. A. "We are 
starting with a fresh look, using the 
name of one of the most successful 
film firms in the world," said Picker. 
With this change, Picker added, there 
is a new direction and philosophy.

Elektra Into Multiple Tape Dist 
Posner Cites 
More Outlets 
NEW YORK - Elektra Records, 
which previously held exclusive dis- 
tribution of its tape, has established 
a system of multiple distribution on 
its tape product only. 
Mel 
Posner, 
vice 
president 
in 
charge of national sales, explained 
that Elektra tape distribution would 
now operate through Elektra's 
21 
distributors across the country and 
through certain key tape rack ac- 
counts. Elektra's regional salesmen, 
Stan Marshall on the east coast, Stan 
Schoen in the midwest, and Scott 
Ross on the west coast, as well as 
Posner himself and assistant George 
Steele, will be calling on these ac- 
counts. 
Posner declared that the reason be- 
hind Elektra's decision was twofold. 
"First of all," Posner stated, "we 
have found over the years that the 
present distribution system excludes 
certain very important tape accounts 
that are simply not serviced by rec- 
ord distributors." 
But Posner alluded to a further 
problem 
with 
tape 
merchandising 
that 
influenced Elektra's 
decision. 
Both Elektra president Jack Holzman 
and Posner feel that one of the great 
problems with tape merchandising 
revolves around the fact that there is 
a serious lack of means of exposure 
for tape product, a shortage of facili -

licity at all. As Posner pointed out, 
"A hit tape is always preceded by a 
hit record." 
Posner further indicated that the 
time is over when tape sales can be

Artistic Cut 
U. A. has cut its artists roster 
drastically in recent months from 265 
to 71, said Picker, in order to offer a 
heavier concentration to new and es- 
tablished acts. Those recently signed 
to the label include George Gerdes 
from the folk-rock field, El Quintet 
(the group that backed Sir Douglas) 
and Eric Burdons hard rock combo, 
WAR. WAR will be the initial album 
to be released with U. A.'s new logo 
and is said to ship Feb. 15. Picker 
said there had been some confusion 
about U. A. signing Eric Burdon. The 
group known as Eric Burdon and 
War is signed to MGM Records for 
the U. S. and Canada, but U. A. has 
foreign release rights.

be a home but will be an outlet for 
inventive performers,"

McCartney Seeks 
To Dissolve 2 
Beatles' Firms 
LONDON - The New Year opened 
with final irrefutable confirmation 
that the Beatles are no more as one 
entity. 
Paul 
McCartney 
initiated 
High Court action to dissolve the 
Beatles and 
Co., formed in April 
1967, and Apple Corps. He wants 
a full rendering of accounts and 
assets 
and 
a 
four-way 
split 
of 
these between himself and the other 
three erstwhile group colleagues. It 
has been common knowledge that the 
Beatles have been glaring eye to eye 
more often than seeing eye to eye 
since soon after the death of their 
manager Brian Epstein. It's under- 
stood that McCartney wanted Lee 
Eastman, now his father-in-law, to 
succeed Epstein in guiding their for- 
tunes, but John Lennon, George Har- 
rison and Ringo Starr overruled his 
choice in favor of Allen Klein. That 
decision was it as far as McCartney 
was concerned, and Lennon went into 
detail about his change in attitude 
towards the rest of the group in a 
recent interview published in an un- 
derground magazine. 
Lennon's friendship and marriage 
to Yoko Ono also is said to have 
taken a disruptive effect on the four- 
some, and the rather sorry end to the 
twenthieth/century's most spectacular 
and legendary pop partnership will 
be a probably prolonged and acrimo- 
nious spell of litigation. The exact 
monetary value of the Beatles and 
Apple Corps has not yet emerged, 
but some quarters estimate it at 
being in ex-ess of £40 million. Ex- 
perts in such matters have already 
pointed out that, in the event of a 
division of the assets between the 
foursome, the capital gains tax is 
likely to make fearsome inroads into 
each share unless some satisfactory 
formula can be found to circumvent 
this hazard.

Firm Expanding 
Student Owned 
Record Shops 
LAWRENCEVILLE, 
ILL. - By 
working with student governments, a 
new company has helped to establish 
seven student -owned and 
operated 
record shops on seven different Mid- 
western campuses and expects to see 
the number boom to 30 or more loca- 
tions in '71. 
Student 
Economic 
Development 
Corp. in Lawrenceville, Ill. not only 
functions as a rack jobber for stu- 
dent record shops but also offers stu- 
dent aid in the selection of locations, 
accounting procedures, inventory and 
traffic control, merchandising, adver- 
tising, and promotion. 
"This is an entirely new concept in 
record distribution," said H. Stephen 
Landau, Jr., president of the corpora- 
tion. "We're interested 
in helping 
student governments and organiza- 
tions enter the business field, so we 
not only supply the records but also 
the expertise to initiate and conduct 
a successful business." 
Student 
Economic 
Development 
Corp. is working primarily with or- 
ganizations in the Midwest, including 
Michigan State University at Lan- 
sing, Southern Illinois University at 
Carbondale, University of Missouri 
at Columbia, and Case Western Uni- 
versity at Cleveland, but expects to 
expand westward in 1971. 
SEDCO was formed in 1970 as a 
consortium of students and recent 
students who were interested in hel- 
ping student organizations develop 
co-operative 
business ventures on 
college campuses. It offers a variety 
of college -oriented services and pro- 
ducts in addition to records. SEDCO 
was capitalized to the extent of $250,- 
000 by Executive Systems, Inc., also 
of Lawrenceville, 
socially 
oriented 
management consultant firm which 
provides the more mature business 
expertise for the student ventures.

and has signed its first writer, Ken- 
dall Hayes. Hayes has enjoyed con-

rus" and "Your Mother Should Know" 
by Lennon and McCartney.

Albarano Is GM 
Of Janus As Part 
Of Expansion Move 
NEW YORK - Nick Albarano has 
been 
named 
general manager 
of 
Janus Records as part of a reorgani- 
zation and expansion program at the 
abel. 
Albarano, Mary Schlachter, pres- 
ident, said, will direct all promo, 
sales, marketing and production ac- 
tivities. "Janus has grown," 
Sch- 
lachter said, "to the point where a 
general manager is necessary. Nick 
Albarano has helped get the label off 
the ground and, as general manager, 
he will continue to consolidate all the 
factors that have contributed to our 
success." Schlachter said other ap- 
pointments will be announced. 
Albarano had 
been 
director 
of 
marketing for Janus since the label's 
inception in Aug., 
1969. He was 
formerly national sales manager fo' 
Epic Records as part of a seven year 
association. He was also with Capitol 
Records for six years. 
Dick Jacobs To 
Roulette; Tops 
A&R, Creative Svc 
NEW YORK-Dick Jacobs has joined 
Roulette Records in the dual capacity 
of director of A&R and creative serv- 
ices. 
Roulette president Morris Levy de- 
tailed Jacobs' assignment as one of 
varied responsibilities including the 
screening of new talent, supervision 
of recording dates and maintaining 
liaison throughout all phases of pro- 
duction with the many independent 
producers working with the company. 
In addition, Jacobs will be deeply in- 
volved with graphics on all album 
covers and merchandising displays 
and coordinate LP production and 
packaging. 
Jacobs joins Roulette following an 
association of 17 years with MCA 
during which he headed the A&R 
staff of Coral Records and was, in 
1968-69, exec producer for the MCA 
special markets division. 
Beginning his career in the music 
business as an arranger, Jacobs work- 
ed with many top artists including 
Louis Armstrong and the Tommy 
Dorsey Band. His arrangements were 
evident contributors to many hits by 
numerous Coral, Brunswick and Decca 
artists with whom he worked includ- 
ing The 
McGuire Sisters, Teresa 
Brewer, Buddy Holly, Jackie Wilson, 
Rod McKuen. Debbie Reynolds, Steve 
Lawrence & Evdie Gorme and many 
more. At one time a recording artist 
himself, Jacobs scored with several 
instrumental hits among which were 
"Petticoats of Portugal". "Man With 
the Golden Arm" and "Fascination."

NO GAP HERE-Richard Rodgers (1.) America's top composer for the mu- 
sical theater and Andrew Lloyd Webber, the young English rock composer

POST CAMPAIGN-"Quit Dreaming Of A White Christmas-Stop Pollution" 
is the word from Post Records, the Philadelphia -based manufacturer and dis- 
tributor of the "Solid Gold Sound" album series. In wrapping up its usual 
Christmas promotion, Buzz Curtis, president of Post Records, says that he re- 
alizes the billboard campaign is a small contribution but in conjunction with 
their new "stop pollution" message inscribed on each label hopes that it will 
alert the public of the concern in the music industry for this crucial problem.

Cash Box - January 23, 1971 
www.americanradiohistory.com

---- p22
cash bar/singles reviews 
(Picks of the Week 
THE JACKSON 5 (Motown 1177) 
Mama's Pearl (3:09) (Jobete, BMI-The Corporation) 
Tapping their special keg of pop energy, the Jackson 5 roars into the lists 
once more with a blazing bubbly -soul surger that has already bounded into 
the top forty in its first week on the market. Super side as a new year follow 
up to their Christmas hit. Flip: "Darling Dear" (2:37) (Jobete, BMI-H&R 
Gordy, Story) 
CREEDENCE CLEARWAIER REVIVAL (Fantasy 655) 
Have You Seen the Rain (2:39) (Jondora, BMI-Fogerty) 
Hey Tonight (2:43) (Same credits) 
Showing their first major change since establishing themselves on the 
rock front, Creedence Clearwater slows and softens their sound in this single 
from the "Pendulum" monster. While "Have You Seen the Rain" comes as 
close to a ballad as anything from CCR, the flip features their unique power 
to turn this into a two-sided giant. 
THE GUESS WHO (RCA 0414) 
Hang on to Your Life (3:20) (Dunbar/Cirrus/Sunspot/Expressions, BMI- 
Cummings, Winter) 
One of the most aggressive vocal and musical singles from the Guess Who 
brings the group's top forty visage closer to that presented in their LP's. 
Side is already a strong from -LP choice with FM stations and should explode 
into AM sales lists. Flip: "Do You Miss Me Darlin' " (3:54) (Same credits) 
DEREK & THE DOMINOS (Atco 6803) 
Bell Bottom Blues (3:10) (Casserole, BMI-Clapton) 
Shrugging off the 50's styling of their earlier side, Derek (Clapton) and the 
Dominos come up with a progressive ballad that should see powerful top 
forty reception. Instrumentally enticing and surprisingly melodic, the piece is 
certain AM/FM dynamite. Flip: no information. 
CHRISTIE (Epic 10695) 
San Bernadino (2:54) (Leeds, ASCAP-Christie) 
Having faced a long haul up the sales lists with "Yellow River," Christie 
should find it easy sailing with this second -time outing. Side is a British 
best seller loaded with rhythmic magnetism for teens and a good performance 
to add extra FM impetus to the single. Flip: no info. 
CANNED HEAT (Liberty 56217) 
Wooly Bully (2:30) (Beckie, BMI-Domingo, Samudio) 
Taking the Sam the Sham hit of last decade, Canned Heat pours out a 
fine follow-up to their "Together." This side still features the top forty dance 
and humor of the original, but Heat's instrumental additions should add 
enough FM impact to give the side widespread playlist magnetism. Flip: 
no info. 
JERRY BUTLER (Mercury 73169) 
If It's Real What 
I Feel (2:38) (Ice Man, BMI-Jackson) 
Jerry Butler takes on two aids in this side, giving him his most moving and 
commercial sides in about a year. First, he had gone back to a slightly faster 
pace, and second, he's accompanied by a girl who gives the side that extra 
hit icing Flip: no info. 
GARY PUCKETT (Columbia 45303) 
Keep the Customer Satisfied (2:40) (Charing Cross, BMI-Simon) 
A heavily programmed "flip" from Simon & Garfunkel, "Keep the Customer 
Satisfied" has become identified with Gary Puckett as the opener for his 
appearances. The grand vocal ability of Puckett, the song and a production 
plus should put this new side high in the top forty picture. Flip: no info. 
DAVE MASON (Blue Thumb 7122) 
Waitin' on You (3:05) (Coachhouse, BMI-Mason) 
Superb mixture of blues and exuberance gives Dave Mason an outstand- 
ing new side to captivate the teen audiences at AM and FM dials. Brightly 
paced and nicely performed, the side should catch enough attention to climb 
onto sales lists. Flip: "Just a Song" (2:59) (Same credits) 
JANIS JOPLIN (Columbia 45314) 
Me & Bobby McGee (4:09) (Combine, BMI-Kristofferson, Foster) 
The ready -known "Me & Bobby McGee" becomes an intensely personal 
thing in this Janis Joplin reading from her newly issued "Pearl" LP. This, on 
top of the entire Joplin cult anticipation assures overwhelming receptions to 
the performance. Flip: "Half Moon" (3:50) (Open End, BMI-Hall) 
JIMMY RUFFIN (Soul 35077) 
Maria (You Were the Only One) (2:56) (Jobete, BMI-Gordy, Brown, Story, 
Glover) 
Brilliant production, a sparkling piece of material and Jimmy Ruffin's glow- 
ing vocal should excite immediate R&B and top forty notice for this ballad 
offering. One of the most powerful sides from this artist in a long while. 
Flip: "Living in a World 
I Created for Myself" (3:10) (Jobete, BMI-Story, 
Brown, Gordy) 
TAMIKO JONES (Metromedia 205) 
Cross My Heart (2:25) (Muscle Shoals/Cotillion, BMI-Soule, Woodford) 
Having gained MOR play with her first single in two years, Tamiko Jones 
aims at adding the pop and blues areas without dropping that easy, MOR 
appeal. Bright new side that could find a variety of spotlights on its way up. 
Flip: "Since I Don't Have You" (3:05) (Bonneyview, ASCAP-Rock, Skyliners) 
(Newcomer Picks 
J 
DREAMS (Columbia 45300) 
Devil Lady (2:50) (Crunchy Grenola, BMI-Kent, Lubahn) 
Muted horns with a '30's tingle and arrangements built on the Sly Stewart 
rhythm power give Dreams a wild premiere backdrop in this side from the 
group's LP. Powerful top forty effort that should break loose with teen 
audiences. Flip: "The Maryanne" (2:25) (Crunchy Grenola, BMI-Lubahn) 
C.C.S. (Rak 4501) 
Whole Lotta Love (3:40) (Cotillion, BMI-Page, Plant, Jones, Bonham) 
C.C.S. arrives with its British best seller only to become locked in a cover 
fight with King Curtis' instrumental version of the same hit. Top forty reaction 
is already building sales for this electric -flute and power -percussion treatment. 
Flip: "Boom Boom" (3:30) (Conrad, BMI-Hooker) 
BRASS MONKEY (Rare Earth 5022) 
Sweet Water (2:51) (Hill & Range, BMI-Flett, Fletcher) 
Imagine Creedence Clearwater performing after a year of tutoring by 
English musicians. That's the musical blend that comes out clearly in Brass 
Monkey's own brand of rock. Excellent teen side with strong top forty poten- 
tial. Flip: "You Keep Me Hangin' On" (3:47) (Jobete, BMI-Holland, Dozier, 
Holland) 
DAVID ALLEN COE (SSS Intl 825) 
Tobacco Road (2:30) (Cedarwood, BMI-Loudermilk) 
The Nashville Teens' early rock giant has been revived by a handful of 
progressive artists in LP's, but the arrangements on this latest performance 
could prove right in breaking the version with top forty and FM stations for 
the first time since the original. Flip: no info. 
FRANK LEWIS (Beverly Hills 9358) 
Year of War (2:56) (Markari, BMI-Lewis, Castle) 
An interesting lyric with contemporary enticement is fitted to the "Bar- 
carolle" from Tales of Hoffman in this unusual side for top forty considera- 
tion. The Australian artist here could follow Miguel Rios' pattern of breakaway 
sales. Flip: 'Indianapolis" (2:51) (Same credits)

check list of best selling pop albums other than those appearing on the CASH BOX Top 100 Album chart. Feature is designed to call wholesalers' & retailers' 
attention to key catalog, top steady selling LP's, as well as recent chart hits still going strong in sales. Information is supplied by manufacturers. This is a weekly 
evolving list presented in alphabetical order. It is advised that this card be kept until the list returns to this alphabetical section.

Canadian Theme In Columbia 
Toronto Showcase Of Product 
TORONTO - Columbia's A&R head 
Johnny Williams and the company's 
national director of advertising and 
promo, Bill Eaton, put together an 
impressive product presentation (4) 
at Toronto's new posh Don Valley 
Holiday Inn. 
Attending the presentation were 
the label's sales and promotion peo- 
ple as well as some of the new artists 
signed with Columbia. 
Unlike previous years, this product 
presentation spent more than 80 min- 
utes of its 4 hour show on new Cana- 
dian product. 
Williams, who is responsible for 
Columbia's successful entry into the 
domestic market with perhaps Mash- 
makhan as the leading force, also 
introduced a new Hamilton group 
known as Smyle with a sampling of 
their waxed 
sound. Almost every 
province was represented at the 
event. The label's involvement with 
Canadian product covered all fields, 
MOR, MOT and country. The most 
impresive new act is that of Gordie 
Tapp, now an important supporting 
actor with "Hee Haw," popular U. S. 
TVer now returned for another year. 
Single and album product is expected 
shortly. 
Canada's newest city Thunder Bay 
was represented at the meet by Don 
Grashey and Chuck Williams of DMG 
Sound. They have recently signed a 
production deal with Columbia and 
their first act, Carrol Baker, a lovely 
Liberty To 
MCA Canada 
TORONTO - MCA Records (Cana- 
da) has taken over national distribu- 
tion of the Liberty line and all allied 
labels which include: Blue Note, Im- 
perial, Sunset, Minit, World Pacific, 
and World Pacific Jazz. 
Arrangements have been made with 
London records (former distributors) 
to take over the existing inventory, 
making all current Liberty product 
fully exchangeable under MCA's cur- 
rent exchange policy. 
Shipment of product from MCA's 
national warehouse in Cornwall has 
already begun with complete invento- 
ry servicing to the trade by the early 
part of February. 
A complete inventory order form is 
now in the printing stages which will 
be mailed to retailers across the 
country. 
Final negotiations for the distribu- 
tion deal were kinalized by MCA's 
vice-president Product Development 
Lee Armstrong and Liberty/UA's 
exec vice-president Mike Stewart.

Guess Who's Hunter Lays It 
On Line To Radio In Canada 
TORONTO - The record producer 
versus radio station record producer 
controversy continues to be the chief 
topic of conversation with music peo- 
ple in Canada. 
Don Hunter, manager of the inter- 
nationally famous Canadian group, 
The Guess Who, recently made wvail- 
able his views on the subject. This is 
the beginning of a trend of influen- 
tial 
figures 
making 
known 
their 
views on the Canadian music scene 
which appears to be facing a survival 
crisis. Canadian disk and production 
luminaries heretofore have remained 
silent with regard to criticising those 
in 
the important 
radio industry. 
There always looms the threat of 
blacklisting by radio stations. This 
may be prevalent in Canada, but like 
any country, hard to prove. Hunter 
was quite outspoken, noting: "At this 
stage in the development of a Cana - 
Farrell, Grever Launch Joint 
Latin Production, Pub Venture 
NEW YORK - Wes Farrell, pres- 
ident of The Wes Farrell Organiza- 
tion and Bob Grever, president of 
Grever International of Mexico City, 
have set a joint venture for the pro- 
duction and publishing of Latin ar- 
tists for distribution in Central and 
South Amerida. 
Farrell indicated that the duo will 
"discover 
and 
develop 
Spanish- 
speaking performers who are right 
for the Latin 'pop' market." "Few 
people," he adds, "are aware yet of 
what the growth of a middle class, a 
phenonmenon of the 1960's, has done 
to the record -buying potential in 
these countries. Today a hit single in 
these combined markets can easily 
reach the million dollar mark. This is 
an audience that is worth a great 
deal more effort than is currently 
being directed towards it and one 
that we will grow with. We want to 
develop a minimum of three acts dur- 
ing the first year and more after 
that. 
Bob Grever and Wes Farrell have 
an association stretching back many 
years. In addition to representing 
Farrell's Pocket Full Of Tunes pub- 
lishing firm in the Mexican market, 
Grever also represents such major 
publishing houses as E. B. Marks, 
Chappell Music and the Big Three 
(Robbins, Feist and Miller). 
New Label Planned 
Farrell indicated that it is very 
likely that he and Grever will estab- 
lish a new record label to market 
their product. According to Grever, 
several established Latin artists have 
already been approached to record 
for them and for other producers in 
the Wes Farrell Organization. 
It was pointed out by Farrell that 
"we will, in many cases, be making 
cover -records of contemporary Eng- 
lish -language pop hits as well as

Sell Satchmo Fest 
Salute To German 
Video Company 
HOLLYWOOD - The Newport Jazz 
Festival's 70th birthday salute to 
Louis Armstrong has been sold to 
Sudwest Television in Germany by 
festifilms, the George Wein -Sid Sti- 
ber production company. 
Wein is presently on a five week 
tour of the Far East showing the 
four 45 -minute programs to govern- 
ment television systems. He is also 
promoting concerts with the Count 
Basie Band in that area. 
Wein is producer of the TV spe- 
cial, shot in conjunction with Euro - 
Films, a Los Angeles -based producer 
of jazz films for overseas TV ex- 
posure. 
Nordvision in Scandinavia; ORTF 
in France and the national networks 
in Holland and Belgium have all 
screened 
the 
four programs, 
ac- 
cording to Wein, who anticipates sel- 
ling the programs to these VER - 
SEAS OUTLETS. 
Wein has met with officials of the 
National Educational Television net- 
work (NET) about showing the color 
spectacular in the United States. A 
one hour special is planned for com- 
mercial TV before the program is 
aired over NET. 
Armstrong narrates all four shows 
and apnears in all the segments. Ar- 
tists appearing with Satchmo include 
Mahalia Jackson, the New Orleans 
preservation Hall Jazz Band, 
the 
New Orleans Eureka Brass Band, plus 
trumpeters Dizzy 
Gillespie, 
Bobby 
Hackett, 
Wild Bill Davison, 
Ray 
Nance, Joe 
Newman and Jimmy 
Owens. 
dian record industry, there must be 
distinct separation-record compan- 
ies must be record companies and 
radio stations must be radio sta- 
tions." He added, 
"The 
Canadian 
scene is too young, too much in a 
state of flux. Anyone who expands at 
this time, too rapidly into too many 
fields has to be hurt." 
Hunter pointed up the fact that 
record sales of Canadian groups have 
improved over the past year. The 
Guess Who's "These Eyes" although 
receiving certification for U. S. Gold 
failed to make the 100,000 mark in 
Canada but both "Hand Me Down 
World" and "Share The Land" have 
topped this previously hard to cap- 
ture figure. 
Hunter outlined a personal experi- 
ence which indicated to him that in 
the U. S. it was nearly impossible for 
a group (associated with a record 
company having a tie-in with a radio 
network) to get exposure on that 
media because of a very good and 
strong anti-trust law. He indicated 
there were no such laws in Canada, 
noting: "We don't have the same 
laws in Canada. In the U. S., every- 
one is faced with the possibility of an 
anti-trust suit, and they're terrified 
of even appearing like they're help- 
ing an act from an associated com- 
pany." 
Zeroing in on broadcasters Hunter 
expressed: "I don't think radio sta- 
tions should be allowed into record 
production, and especially not into 
publishing, not at this time. It can do 
nothing, but hurt the situation now. 
Later on it might be fine, but right 
now it should not be allowed. No 
matter what anybody says, there has 
to be a potential conflict of interest. 
It can't be anything else." 
In summing up Hunter was of the 
opinion that "The fate of the Canadi- 
an record industry depends on the 
CRTC. One of two things is going to 
happen in the next 12 months-we 
will have a record industry or we'll 
be right back where we started- 
nowhere at all." 
Lang To Europe 
NEW YORK - Michael Lang, pres- 
ident of the newly -formed Just Sun- 
shine label, embarked last week (14) 
on a three-week European trek. 
During his stay Lang, who recently 
completed a deal with Paramount 
Records for distribution, will meet 
with foreign distributors, publishers 
and concert promoters and generally 
familiarize himself with the Europe- 
an markets. He will additionally set 
up European tours for the artists 
signed to Just Sunshine. Former Mi- 
ami concert producer and producer of 
the 1968 Miami Pop Festival, Lang 
was responsible for the conception 
and development of the Woodstock 
festival, which he also produced. Lang 
will visit Paris, London, various cit- 
ies in Germany and will also attend 
the MIDEM conference.

5 New Albums From Roulette 
NEW YORK - Five new albums 
will spearhead a late Jan. release 
from Roulette Records. 
These include new packages from 
Don Cooper and Don Crawford, both 
of whom have had prior albums with 
Roulette and, says the label, are en- 
joying consistent sales, particularly 
from college bookstore and campus 
outlets where they have frequently 
appeared in concert. Cooper toured 
last season with Blood, Sweat & Tears, 
appearing at 
numerous 
collegiate 
functions and accompanied BS&T to 
Europe.

Happysad Opens 
Western Office 
NEW YORK - Recently formed in 
New York, Happysad Records last 
week 
disclosed 
expansion 
of 
its 
working staff and the opening of a 
second office in Los Angeles. 
The western 
quarters 
at 
3264 
Overland Ave. are headed by Scott 
Howard whose first project will be 
initiation of the company's first re- 
lease, "Raincheck" and "Merri-Goes- 
Round" by the Trousers. 
Stepping up coverage on the sin- 
gle, Happysad has also made a series 
of appointments 
in the sales and 
promotion 
areas 
including: 
Bob 
Garelick for the Eastern seaboard; 
Tony DeSanto in east/central; Joe 
Mauriello covering progressive out- 
lets; Rick Bock and Alan Feinstein 
in sales. 
According to the company's heads, 
Paul Levinson and Ed Fox, the re- 
lease is being serviced with emphasis 
on the "Merri" side for top forty and 
"Raincheck" to FM stations. 
A reserve is currently in prog- 
ress with pressings showing the new- 
ly adopted 
logo 
designed by Ira 
Rubin. 
Also in the works at Happysad is 
an album from the Trousers, "Ideal 
Compromise," now being primed for 
February release. The group has al- 
ready made a few media appearances 
in New York and has finished the 
taping of a "Komotion" tv'er to be 
aired in Pa. on the 30th. 
album and the release also includes

Three Degrees LP 
Roulette Records has also initiated 
a company -wide campaign in behalf 
of 
The 
Three 
Degrees 
album, 
"Maybe" based on activity surround- 
ing 
their 
current 
chart 
single, 
"You're The One" which is among 
the album's selections. 
The LP was originally titled for 
the group's hit single "Maybe" and, 
with the breakout of a second single, 
has reaped large reorders from nu- 
merous areas throughout the coun- 
try. 
Sales and marketing vice president 
Sonny Kirshen stated that pressure 
sensitive stickers denoting inclusion 
of "You're The One" in the album 
have been shipped to all distributors 
for attachment to stock and efforts 
are being made to affix the stickers 
to existing stock at racks and retail 
outlets. Image posters of The Three 
Degrees have been designed and are 
in production for immediate ship- 
ment as well. 
Further 
enhancing 
the 
album, 
noted Kirshen, is the great amount 
of attention focusing on still another 
selection from the album which, co- 
incidentally 
is 
the 
flip 
side 
of 
"You're The One." Their current hit 
is coupled with what is believed to be 
the 
first new 
vocal rendition 
of 
"Stardust" in well over five years 
and is capturing one stop activity in 
response to juke box demand.

Pickwick's 'Super Sales' Drive 
NEW YORK - Rich Lionetti, direc- 
tor of marketing for Pickwick Inter- 
national, Inc., has launched the com- 
pany's "Super Sales" new release 
campaign for 1971. 
Heading up the release is the first 
economy version of "Jesus Christ/ - 
Superstar," priced at $1.89, which 
features full orchestra, chorus and 
soloists in musical excerpts of the 
highly acclaimed rock opera. 
Another outstanding feature 
of 
this release will be the album, "I 
Walk the Line," by Johnny Cash, 
which features, in addition to the 
title tune, such big hits as "Born to 
Lose," "Cry, Cry, Cry," "Straight A's 
in Love," "Remember Me," and oth- 
ers.

to California, Harold Berkman's arrival became cause for a stream -in of both 
label executives and old friends who had worked with Berkman in New York. 
Set up in his 7165 Sunset Blvd. quarters, Berkman is shown at left with Dave 
Greenman (left), and (from right) Sol Greenberg, Sammy Vargas and Ben 
Scotti. Photo at right has him joined by Ed Beulike (right) and (from left) 
Al Lewis and Mel Price.

Humblebums Albums 
NEW YORK - United Artists Rec- 
ords 
is 
repackaging the 
"Lenny 
Bruce Midnight Concert" album re- 
corded at Carnegie Hall, in New 
York, in 1961, and is scheduling it 
for a Feb. 15 release. The album will 
combine Bruce's humor with a con- 
temporary art cover, and UA expects 
the new pakckage to do well in prog- 
ressive and underground markets.

bum by the Humblebums, a folk/rock 
group consisting of Gerry Rafferty 
and Billy Connolly. The LP, "Open 
Up The Door," will be tried in with 
the groups cross country tour and 
extensive promotional campaign.

Project 3 LP's 
NEW YORK - Project 3 Records 
has announced its forthcoming album 
release which will consist of LP's by 
Tony Motolla, Urbie Green, and Ka- 
thy Gregory. 
Tony Motolla's LP entitled "Close 
To You" will feature the title tune as 
well as "We've Only Just Begun," 
"Didn't We," and "Yesterday When I 
Was Young." Urbie Green's "Green 
Power" 
will 
be 
highlighted 
by 
Green's 
performance 
on 
the 
new 
King/Vox Ampliphonic Unit; and Ka- 
thy Gregory's debut LP will contain 
her 10 original compositons. 
Enoch Light, president of the la- 
bel, has announced that Project 3's 
semi 
monthly 
auditions 
have 
provided the label with many new 
and interesting acts including Rock 
Island, and The Spectras. Kathy Gre- 
gory was also discovered at these au- 
ditions. 
Capitol Prod. 
Deal w/Double 0 
NEW YORK - Dick Asher, vice 
president, Eastern Operations, Capi- 
tol Records, Inc., announces that the 
label has entered into an independent 
production agreement with Double 0 
Productions of New York. 
The indie pact calls for Double O, 
operated by Barry Oslander and Don 
Oriolo, to produce Sunshine Express, 
formerly known as The Mel Win 
Trend. Win is lead singer and writer. 
Sunshine 
Express, 
which 
hails 
from Scranton, Pa., has played dur- 
ing the past year in clubs, colleges, 
and concerts throughout the North- 
east. Capitol is preparing a single for 
release in the near future.

Nat Barnett Dies 
BALTIMORE - Nat Barnett, foun- 
der and operator of the HiFi Record 
Shop here, died recently at Sinia 
Hospital. His large operation, also 
known as the Record & Tape Collec- 
tor, is especially noted for its im- 
ported recordings. A native of New 
York, he moved to Baltimore in 1931. 
He started out as a distributor and 
formed the retail operation 15 years 
ago. 
Survivors 
include 
his 
wife, 
Mary, two sons Saul and Mort (who 
is associated with RCA Records in 
Hollywood); and a daughter, Ruth 
Lee 
of 
Rockville, 
Md., 
and four 
grandchildren.

AL DE LORY: HE WEARS MANY HATS 
What can you say about a guy who records a single of "Theme From 'Love 
Story' " only to find himself in competition with seven or eight other versions? 
That he already has a group of gold records to his credit, many of them gained 
as Glen Campbell's producer. That he produced one of the Lettermen's finest 
recordings, "Hurt So Bad." That his version of "Song From M*A*S*H" was 
one of the more refreshing singles of last year. That he recently composed the 
music for the film, "Norwood" (starring Glen and Joe Namath) and that he 
looks to more film scoring assignments in the future. 
We discussed motion picture soundtrack trends with Al De Lory when he was 
in town on a promotional trip for his "Theme From Love Story." He feels that 
movie music is going through a transitory stage and cites "The Graduate" and 
"Easy Rider" as examples. Both of these films, as well as many others, have 
tied together hit songs which were not written specifically for the screenplay. 
In the case of the former, they were all the work of Simon & Garfunkel, while 
in "Easy Rider" they were from a number of composers. "This is a little thing 
that happens in the middle," says Al, "while movie scoring is moving from one 
trend to another." 
Whichever way it moves, Al feels that he will become more involved in film 
scoring. He found his experience with "Norwood" more than a little uplifting. 
"I approach each melody with the idea of writing what the specific scene calls 
for," explains Al. "When I'm writing for a film I'm also writing something that 
may become popular." Al is a talented young man who has moved from playing 
piano for others, into production and now into composing and performing on 
his own. His future looks bright.

JAMES TAYLOR AND THE ORIGINAL FLYING 
MACHINE 1967-Euphoria EST -2 
So popular has James Taylor become. This 
album, loosely strung together from studio 
sessions of four years ago, looks like it will 
gather lots of sales potential. Certainly it is of 
interest as a collector's item, but it includes a 
distracting amount of false starts and mean- 
ingless chatter. For the record, Taylor is heard 
on lead vocal doing now familiar material such 
as "Rainy Day Man" and "Brighten Your Night 
With My Day," as well as some less powerful 
songs. Taylor fans may want to have it in their 
collections. 
ROGER WILLIAMS GOLDEN HITS VOL. II- 
Kapp-KS 3638 
A collection of Roger Williams' golden hits 
reads like the academy awards nominations 
for best songs of the year. "Gentle On My 
Mind," "Alfie," "Galveston," "The Impossible 
Dream," "A Taste Of Honey," "Up Up And 
Away," "Softly, As 
I Leave You," "This Guy's 
In Love With You," and the "Love Theme From 
Romeo And Juliet," are all included. Album is 
perfect for the easy listening audiences and 
MOR stations. 
NEW GENERATION-Chambers Brothers-Co- 
lumbia-C 30032 
The Chambers Brothers get it all together 
for this new and impressive package of funk - 
rock. Highlighting the set is their latest release 
"Funky," which is destined to become their 
biggest single to date. Also included are "When 
The Evening Comes," "Are You Ready," "Prac- 
tice What You Preach," "Reflections," "Young 
Girl," "Pollution," "Going To The Mill," and 
the title tune, 
"New Generation." Album 
should do well considering their large com- 
mercial and underground following.

THE PRICE YOU GOT TO PAY TO BE FREE- 
Cannonball Adderley Quintet-Capitol SWBB- 
636 
Here are four new sides by Cannonball and 
his cohorts, and a very nice double album set 
it is. All the selections, and there are twenty, 
were recorded "live" at an open studio ses- 
sion, and audience reaction is enthusiastic. 
Cannonball intro's Nat Adderley, Jr., his 15 
year old nephew who does justice to the title 
song, which he also wrote. Nat, Sr. vocalizes on 
several tunes and there you have it, a spirit 
of family which endows the album with a to- 
gether sound not easily forgotten. As for the 
Quintet, their sound is as tight as ever. A 
choice jazz package. 
RAHSAAN RAHSAAN-Rahsaan Roland Kirk- 
Atlantic SD 1575 
Roland Kirk has been in the vanguard of 
contemporary jazz musicians for some time 
now and this album, his latest, gives evidence 
that he intends to stay there. Which is good 
news, as he is one of the most inventive free 
spirits recording today. Here he turns his magic 
on the classic "Satin Doll," endowing it with 
new vibrancy, and 
a medley which includes 
"Sentimental Journey," "Lover" and a Dvorak 
piece must be heard to be perceived. Kirk is 
very much into the potential of instruments 
and his piano styled saxophone is only the 
latest of his devices. A special album from a 
genuine artist.

Six Albums In Mercury's Feb. Package; 
British Label Vertigo To Be Distributed 
CHICAGO -Albums by Patto and 
Jimmy Campbell, the first to be re- 
leased by Mercury Records on the 
Vertigo label, highlight a six -LP re- 
lease for February. Other albums are 
by Randy Burns and the Skydog 
Band, Gene Chandler and Jerry But- 
ler, Chuck Mangione and Jackson 
Heights. 
Vertigo one of England's labels for 
progressive music, is being distribut- 
ed by Mercury in the U.S. 
Patto, whose LP is called "Patto," 
is a jazz-rock act produced by Steve 
Winwood's brother, Muff while Jim- 
my Campbell's "Half -Baked," is a 
folk -oriented album by a folksinger/ 
songwriter from Liverpool. 
Blue Note Sets 
Five Jazz Releases 
HOLLYWOOD -LP's from five jazz 
artists 
have 
been 
scheduled 
for 
February release by Blue Note, the 
jazz label of United Artists Records, 
according to an announcement made 
by Mike Lipton, UA's vice president 
for marketing. 
The artists involved 
are Elvin 
Jones, Jeremy Steig, Candido, Or - 
nette Coleman, and Chick Corea. Al- 
bums, 
tapes, 
and 
cassettes 
are 
shipping now and will be in retail 
outlets throughout the nation im- 
mediately. 
Drummer Elvin Jones, is repre- 
sented by a collection entitiled "Coal- 
ition", avant-gardist Omette 
Cole- 
man, a leader in contemporary music, 
is presented in "Love Call", while 
Candido, is showcased with "Beauti- 
ful". Jeremy Steig's third set for 
Blue 
Note 
will 
be 
"Wayfaring 
Stranger", and "The Song Of Sing- 
ing" by Chick Corea, will round out 
the Feb. release. 
Blue 
Note will be backing the 
quintet of LP's, tapes, and cassettes. 
According to Lou Simon, senior 
V.P./director of marketing and Jules 
Abramson, national sales manager, 
both LPs will receive heavy support 
on the merchandising, promotion, ad- 
vertising and publicity level. 
Another LP set for heavy support 
is Randy Burns and the Skydog Band. 
The LP, produced by Mercury staffer 
Barry Seidel, features Burns and his 
group. 
The Gene and Jerry LP, the first 
done by the pair as a team, features 
their single, "You Just Can't Win." 
The album was produced in Chicago 
by both of the artists. 
Also 
included 
in the release is 
"Friends and Love," by Chuck Man- 
gione. The two -LP package, was re- 
corded during a nationally -televised 
concert with the 
Rochester 
Phil- 
harmonic. The album is a blend of 
numerous forms of music, including 
jazz, rock and classical. 
Rounding out the February release 
is Jackson Heights, a new British 
rock group, led by Lee Jackson, for- 
mer bass player for the Nice. 
Stockhausen Concert 
NEW YORK -Deutsche Grammophon 
artist Karlheinz Stockhausen will be 
performing 
his 
"Hymnen" 
at 
a 
special non -subscription performance 
with the New York Philharmonic at 
Philharmonic Hall in Lincoln Center 
on February 25. On the following 
Sunday afternoon, February 28, he 
will be presenting a program of pre- 
mieres and new works of his own 
composition at Alice Tully Hall in 
Lincoln Center. 
In conjunction with his personal 
appearances, Polydor 
Incorporated, 
importers of Deutsche Grammophon, 
has arranged for special promotion 
for their two record album of "Hym- 
nen" along with several other Stock- 
hausen works.

cash baac!talenton stage 
Free 
Sir Lord Baltimore 
CARNEGIE HALL, NYC-Before I 
attempt to describe one of the most 
unusual rock concerts ever produced, 
a few words about the audience are 
in order. The audience that attended 
the Free concert on Jan. 25, was one 
of the most disrespectful audiences 
ever gathered in a hall-anywhere. 
They came, supposedly, to hear music, 
but succeeded only in completely fill- 
ing the aisles of Carnegie Hall with 
shreds of papers and airplanes made 
of 
the 
program 
booklets. 
They 
shouted and whistled and smoked and 
screamed and threw more papers. 
They did everything but listen, and 
if no more rock shows are to be 
booked at Carnegie Hall, I will com- 
pletely sympathize with the manage- 
ment. 
As for the show itself, it was really 
good and really bad. The opening act, 
Mercury Recording artists Sir Lord 
Baltimore, were as far from a musical 
group as one could imagine. They 
were loud, unmelodic, sloppy and bor- 
ing-from beginning to end. Balti- 
more performed "Kingdom Come," 
"Master Heartache," "Hell Hound," 
and "I Got A Woman," from their 
equally sloppy first album. The fact 
that the show was the first for the 
group is no excuse at all. Louis Dam - 
bra, Gary Justin, and John Garner 
just don't have what it takes. But I 
do like the name-Sir Lord Baltimore 
-it's catchy! 
Following a rather lengthy inter- 
mission, England's Free made their 
New York debut. Their music is a 
cross between the past and the future 
-it's blues oriented, with plenty of 
rock thrown in tastefully. Free is 
one of the most refreshing acts to 
come along in some time. They are 
professional in every sense of the 
word. Their performance is second to 
none. "All Right Now," "The Stealer," 
"Highway," a new tune-"My Brother 
Jake," and virtually every cut on their 
"Fire And Water" LP was performed. 
Free's music is very widespread in 
its appeal. They blend blues, rock, and 
funky dance music into a nuiquely in- 
teresting package. It's all there for 
the taking. It's Free. 
k.k. 
Tim Hardin /Victoria 
VILLAGE 
GASLIGHT, 
NYC-We 
hadn't seen Tim Hardin in some time 
when we arrived at the Gaslight for 
his opening night. He has changed 
and all for the better. He is into a 
funky blues style of playing, he ap- 
proaches each song with an uncom- 
monly thoughtful attitude, he delivers 
it with intensity and feeling, and per- 
haps most important, he seems to like 
being on stage and performing for 
the people. 
Along with self -penned items such 
as "Black Sheep Boy" and "Reason 
To 
Believe," the 
Columbia artist 
treated us to an extended "Stormy 
Monday," which had members of the 
audience clamoring for more. Then 
abandoning his guitar for the moment, 
Tim sat down and proceeded to play 
some incredible bar room piano, doing 
up "I Got News For You," a song 
which benefitted greatly from his ir- 
repressible humor. An exceptional set 
from this gifted artist. 
The capacity house got an added 
bonus in the appearance of Victoria, 
a young singer/composer from the 
West Coast. She impressed with a 
four song cycle on piano and per- 
formed several selections from her 
debut album on the San Francisco 
label. We particularly liked the in- 
strumental interplay between her on 
guitar and David Hayes on bass. Vic- 
toria is an important new talent. 
e.k. 
James Taylor 
FILLMORE EAST, NYC-As far as 
his audience was concerned, James 
Taylor could do little wrong on Mon- 
day when he appeared at the Fillmore 
for a benefit concert. Since Taylor ac- 
tually did very little that was wrong, 
the whole thing amounted to a pleas- 
ant, if not overly exciting evening. 
Taylor is an engaging personality, 
completely relaxed and often quite 
amusing. Off -hand comments and brief 
snatches of songs (including a com- 
mercial for snuff and one for Coca 
Cola) were injected into the proceed- 
ings with wit and style. 
He opened his set playing solo on 
familiar material, "Something In The 
Way She Moves," "Carolina In My 
Mind," "Blossom" and "Sunny Skies." 
All were effective but none more so 
than "Sunny Skies," which is a very 
thoughtfully conceived and well exe- 
cuted reminiscence. 
During the second part of the pro- 
gram, the Warner Bros. artist was ac- 
companied by a few friends, including 
Russ Kunkel who contributed some 
super and controlled drumwork, as 
well as Danny Kootch, an old friend 
of James' and a former partner of 
his in the Flying Machine, who played 
some fine guitar. One of the highlights 
of this portion was "Steamroller," 
which we're not sure is the funky 
blues tune it was designed to be, but 
is a pretty funny song. 
Opening the show was Victoria, the 
young singer on the San Francisco 
label. A review of her Gaslight per- 
formance appears somewhere else on 
this page. 
e.k. 
Spencer Davis -Peter Jameson 
Poco/Jo Mama 
SANTA 
MONICA 
CIVIC 
AUDI- 
TORIUM - Last Friday evening's 
concert in Santa Monica proved to be 
in some ways a disappointment, but 
was the debut of what may well be 
one of 1971's brightest new attrac- 
tions. 
For the highlight of the show, in- 
disputably, was the duo of Spencer 
Davis and Peter Jameson. Accom- 
panied by pianist Richard Landis and 
bassist Steve Sloane, the two guitar- 
ists and vocalists provided a generally 
low-keyed and acoustic mixture of 
original material and songs from 
what might be regarded as the bluesy 
Hot Tuna bag. It's a change -of -pace 
for anyone who might have been ex- 
pecting the early British 
electric 
blues -rock of earlier Spencer Davis 
groups, but a change that went down 
very well with the audience. Davis 
and Jameson will probably find their 
greatest acceptance in clubs, small 
auditoriums and colleges. Their first 
album, on Mediarts, should sell well 
upon exposure of the group through 
personal appearances and FM air- 
play. 
Atlantic's Jo Mama continue to 
impress as a highly professional unit. 
Fine musicians all, they keep things 
moving onstage with a minimum of 
interruptions and distraction. Most of 
their songs are originals from their 
first 
album, written 
by guitarist 
Danny Kootch alone and in combina- 
tion with other members of the 
group. The music is rock and roll, 
reminiscent in a way of the old Hold- 
ing 
Company, but not quite 
so 
"heavy." And lead vocalist Abigale 
Haness bears a physical resemblance 
to Janis Joplin that can't be all un- 
intentional. 
Jo Mama's upcoming tour with 
James Taylor and Carole King should 
be of great assistance in spreading 
their reputation. If they can upgrade 
the general level of their already 
pretty good material a bit, and dig 
into the music a bit more, they could 
be around for some time to come. 
Poco, headlining, turned in their 
most disappointing Los Angeles per- 
formance to date. Vocal ensembles 
were sloppy, and the instrumental 
Buck Owens Concert 
"NOW" GROVE, LOS ANGELES- 
Buck Owens, Don Rich & the Bucka- 
roos, Kenni Husky, Susan Raye, Bud- 
dy Alan and the Bakersfield Brass 
kept opening night customers more 
than merely satisfied with a fusion of 
country, pop, country -rock and blue 
grass; actin' and doin' what comes na- 
turally in this adventurous booking, 
the first all country -styled concert at 
the elegant Grove. 
It was a lengthy but rewarding eve, 
from Rich and the Buckaroos' opening 
free wheelin' instrumentals to the 
grand finale with all on stage, singing 
along to "Johnny 
B. Goode" and 
"Bridge Over Troubled Water." 
There were more than a dozen high- 
lights: "Kenni" (Catherine) Husky's 
powerful belting of "Mule Skinner 
Blues," Buddy Alan's treatment of 
"Big Mama's Medicine Show," The 
Bakersfield Brass' "Act Naturally," 
Susan Raye's "Rose Garden" (and her 
latest Capitol side, "L.A. International 
Airport") and practically everything 
Owens offered during his seemingly 
brief appearance. If one has to fault 
the show at all, it could be tightened: 
shorter stays, perhaps, for Alan, Rich, 
Raye and the Brass and a few more 
minutes with Owens. Husky is a defi- 
nite find and you should be hearing 
chart titles from her in the near fu- 
ture. Raye is surely the most attactive 
country oriented vocalist to come to 
these parts since Lynn Anderson ar- 
rived in Anaheim. And her voice is 
caressingly warm. 
Owens is not the first Grove act to 
walk on stage wearing blue denims 
and leather jacket. Bobby Darin es- 
sayed just about the same uniform a 
few years back. On Owens it fits even 
better. 
He is a totally relaxed performer. 
Much of his success must be attributed 
to a casual, unslick and subdued de- 
meanor. But musicianship is also in- 
volved. And if his verbal asides are 
occasionally as corny as Kansas in 
August, the total effect is bromidic 
and bright as the moon. Some of the 
titles he effortlessly branded during 
his stay on stage: "Tiger By The 
Tail," "Act Naturally," "Together 
Again," "Cryin' Time" and "Truck 
Drivin' Man." 
Along the way he traded quips and 
memories with Roger Miller, one of 
several country -directed celebs who 
were in the audience. KLAC (most 
recent station to switch to a country 
format in these parts) broadcast the 
event "live" with Jay Lawrence Mc'- 
ing, adding to the evening's excite- 
ment. 
Four years back, when he reviewed 
Eddy Arnold's very successful Grove 
debut, we wrote, "if Arnold is here, 
can Owens, Cash, Haggard and James 
be far behind ?" It's been a long wait 
-but worth it. 
Owens is booked for just six nights. 
Our educated guess (based on word 
of heavy advance reservations) is that 
Grove (to be shuttered starting in 
April) will be making him an annual, 
more extended, affair. Incidentally it 
was Buck's manager, Jack McFadden, 
who first approached Sammy Davis 
and the Grove, offering the "concert" 
approach starring Owens. Certainly 
one of the most totally satisfying 
evenings at the Grove in years. 
h.g. 
Bobby 
DESERT INN, LAS VEGAS-This 
was the first chance I had to see 
Bobby Darin since he became Bobby 
Darin again, and I must say he's 
almost like Bobby Darin was when 
he was first Bobby Darin. He also 
bears a slight resemblance to Bob 
Darin, not to mention Robert Waldo 
whatever. 
There was only one real weakness 
in Bobby's show, and I really don't 
think that there were too many people 
in the audience who noticed it. What 
it was was chick singers, three of 
them, and while they weren't bad, 
they weren't really background sing- 
ers, not like the kind of real pros 
(which Darlene Love calls the three 
black singers complex) who you'd find 
behind Elvis, Tom Jones, Bill Medley 
and Wayne Newton. That wasn't all 
Bobby's fault, though, because he 
started his stint in Vegas with real 
background singers, but they walked 
out. Anyway, Bobby 
opened with 
Laura Nyro's "Save The Country," 
and it was a gas, even though the 
chick singers didn't have too much 
soul. 
Just as the audience, mostly middle- 
aged middle America, was trying to 
decide what Bobby was up to now, 
what with this song about freedom 
and 
all 
("ain't thet hippie 
talk 
Maude?"), he hit "Mack The Knife" 
and became the Bobby of old. Cool and 
casual as always, but with a touch 
more humility. James Taylor's "Fire 
and Rain" is an excellent song, but 
somehow it didn't quite seem to work 
in Bobby's hands (and it was the 
only song on the set that didn't). 
"Hi -De -Ho," on the other hand, came 
off as an excellent change -of -pace, 
picked up by Bobby's harmonica work. 
A Lennon -McCartney medley, built 
around "Hey Jude," was the highlight 
of the set, but his rendition of "High - 
Darin 
er and Higher" clearly showed that 
he hasn't lost that old R&B touch 
that marked some of his earlier disk 
successes. Bobby switched gears for 
Bob Dylan's "I'll Be Your Baby To- 
night," turning in a highly sensitive 
performance accompanied by his own 
acoustic guitar work. The folk hat 
stayed on for Tim Hardin's "If I 
Were A Carpenter" and his own "Sim- 
ple Song Of Freedom" (a hit for 
Hardin but ready for another go - 
round on the charts). 
I didn't want to clutter up the nar- 
rative, but it should be mentioned 
that in addition to all the music that 
was going on, there were also a few 
other things, like bits and pieces of 
Bobby's impersonations, some very 
hip and funny rapping that surpassed 
the outdated material of Dick Lord, 
the comedian who preceeded him and 
and some of the other cute Darin bits. 
To resume, Bobby ended with some 
all out rock: an Aretha medley ("Re- 
spect" and "Chain Of Fools,") and, to 
the pleasant surprise of many, "Splish 
Splash," which he boogie-woogied on 
the piano, throwing in a little of "I 
Hear You Knocking" for good meas- 
ure. 
Bobby Darin has always been a 
supreme entertainer, and he's gone 
through some head changes that have 
made him an entertainer for all ages, 
both super -hip and Spiro -hip. He's 
had his ups and downs, though his 
ups haven't been as high as they 
should be and his downs (at least as 
a performer) haven't been too much 
so, but he's on the upswing again, 
heading for the top once more, and 
wouldn't it be nice to see him on tv 
with his own show for awhile. Even 
a summer show. Maybe he could team 
up with Linda Ronstadt. 
a.r. 
work was careless, even though they 
can be one of the most exciting and 
musical bands around. The McCune 
sound system, by the way, was of a 
decidedly inferior quality, which may 
have contributed to the group's be- 
low -par set. Audience reception to the 
Epic artists was, however, enthusi- 
astic. 
A special commendation should be 
made to Concert Associates, pro- 
moters of the event, who have started 
supplying programs with artist bi- 
ographies, news of upcoming events, 
and the like to the audience at no ex- 
tra cost. It's a policy that is appre- 
ciated by the attendees, and a good 
piece of self -promotion.

Gallis Midwest Conclave 
Draws 225 Execs To Chi 
CHICAGO - Independent 
promo 
representative Paul 
Gallis 
reports 
success of the Midwest Music Con- 
clave, held recently in Chicago a cou- 
ple of weeks back. Conceived by Gal - 
lis about a year ago, the event, first 
of its kind in this area, attracted 
more than 225 executive and person- 
nel representatives from the various 
radio stations, record labels, produc- 
tion firms, racks, etc. in the three 
state market of Illinois, Indiana and 
Wisconsin. 
"I'm 
completely 
overwhelmed", 
said Gallis, "I expected a turnout but 
not of this magnitude. When you 
consider the fact that a national 
meeting usually draws in the neigh- 
borhood of 700-800 people, the 225 
attendance figure for our conclave is 
very impressive." 
Gallis has been in promotion since 
1953 and, although he's quite well 
known across the country, most of 
his work activity has centered in the 
midwest market. "Let's face it," Gal - 
lis says, "this is where it's at, only 
there are some areas in the country 
that refuse to recognize the fact. 
Ours is a very important and power- 
ful market, exposurewise, saleswise, 
you name it. References are constant- 
ly made to the east coast and the 
west coast but seldom does our area 
receive the recognition it deserves." 
Our purpose in setting up the con- 
clave was to provide 
a sounding 
board for the radio and record people 
in this area and, of course, to discuss 
Col Is Rushing 
'Nanette' Caster 
NEW YORK - Columbia Records is 
rush -releasing the original cast LP 
of the smash revival of "No, No 
Nanette." Disk was cut at Columbia 
Records 30th St. studios in New York 
under the supervision of Tom She- 
pard, Columbia A&R producer. David 
Frost has scheduled a TV special on 
the show to be taped Feb. 22.

were erroneously 
omitted from last week's Grammy 
nominations list in the category, Best 
Contemporary 
Group 
Performance, 
for their A&M disking of "Close To 
You."

radio station managers, program di- 
rectors, deejays, from the participat- 
ing markets gave unhesitatingly of 
their time and effort to make this 
thing a success." 
Among the meaty topics discussed 
at the meeting were "With So Many 
MOR And Stations Going Pop, Has 
The Top 40 Stations Lost Its Identity 
And Effect On Sales and Listeners", 
"What Is The Black Man's Position 
Both In Radio And In The Recording 
Industry", and "Is Radio Going Back 
To The '50's And Hiring Personality 
Deejays, Or Where Is It Going". 
Guest speaker was Bob Hamilton, 
publisher of Radio News. 
"In view of the reaction to our 
first session", said Gallis, "we are 
planning a second conclave to pos- 
sibly encompass an even wider range 
of the area. Within the next month 
we hope to meet and appoint a board 
of 
directors to start laying the 
groundwork for future activities."

By Kristofferson 
NEW YORK - Kris Kristofferson 
will be making his most extensive 
series of personal appearances during 
Feb. and March, announced his per- 
sonal manager Bert Block. The com- 
poser of such hits as "Me And Bobby 
McGee," "Sunday Mornin' 
Comin' 
Down," "For The Good Times" and 
"Help Me 
Make It Through The 
Night," Kristofferson recently com- 
pleted his first starring movie role in 
"Dealer," co-starring Karen Black 
and Gene Hackman, which will be 
distributed by Columbia Pictures. 
Concert dates for Kristofferson in- 
clude Harvard, Cambridge (Feb. 12); 
the Gaslight, New York (13-22); the 
Riverboat, Toronto 
(March 
9-14); 
Lenny's Boston (15-21) ; Shady Grove 
Music Theatre, 
Gaithersburg, 
Md. 
(26) and Westbury Music Theatre, 
Westbury, New York (27). 
Kristoffersons 
second 
Monument 
album will be released during the 
next few months. Cover versions of 
Kristofferson songs now number in 
the hundreds. 
'SWEETHEART' OF AN IDEA:-With a rush, pre -Valentine's Day (Feb. 14) 
release of Engelbert Humperdinck's latest Parrot LP, "Sweetheart," London 
Records has prepared a special promo to tie-in with the holiday. Twenty- 
five thousand kits containing a shopping bag, mobiles, stickers, LP cover 
displays are on their way to distributors, one -stops and deejays. There are 
also an additional 100,000 shopping bags available. In New York last week 
(4), young ladies were hired to hand out 250 kits to passers-by at the Am- 
ericana Hotel, the Royal Box of which is the songster's New York showcase. 
Displaying the items in the kit are (left to right): Milton Friedman, local 
London promo rep; Lenny Meisel, national LP promo; and Mel Richmond, 
local promo rep.

Blue Note Sets 
Jazz Sales Promo 
HOLLYWOOD - The announcement 
of a special sales program for all 
catalog and new releases on Blue 
Note Records, was made by Mike 
Lipton, UA's vice president for mar- 
keting. The campaign will last the 
entire month of February and is the 
first such program even instituted in 
Blue Note's over three decades of 
leadership in jazz recordings. 
In- 
cluded in the deal are not only all 
Blue Note LP's, but all jazz tapes 
and cassettes via the entire United 
Artists family of labels. 
The Blue Note catalog contains 
performances by artists who have 
dominated the jazz polls for many 
years. These include Ornette Cole- 
man, Jack Wilson, Horace Silver, 
Freddie 
Hubbard, 
Don 
Cherry, 
Wayne Henderson, Jackie Mc Lean, 
Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Mc 
Coy 
Tyner, 
John 
Patton, 
Bobby 
Hutcherson, Art Blakey, J. J. John- 
son, Kenny Burrell, Donald Byrd, and 
many others. 
The just -issued sets which are en- 
compassed in the new Blue Note pro- 
gram are "Coalition" by Elvin Jones, 
"Love Call" by Ornette Coleman, 
"Wayfaring Stranger" 
by Jeremy 
Steig, "Beautiful" by Candido, and 
"The Song Of Singing" by Chick 
Corea, late of the Miles Davis group.

INTERNA TIONA L MUSIC SECTION 
Canada's CIRPA Shows Impact RiFi Withdraws From San Remo 
TORONTO - The newly formed 
Canadian Independent 
Record Pro- 
ducers' Association got together for 
its third meeting (20) and under 
elected chairman 
(president) 
Jack 
Richardson released its aims and ob- 
jectives. In short, "C. I. R. P. A. is a 
national, democratic and non-profit 
Association whose purpose is to aid 
and support the Canadian Indepen- 
dent record producer and the re- 
cording industry in Canada through 
cooperative measures." 
Their aims are as follows: 
1. 
To act as a forum for the 
gathering, discussion and dissemina- 
tion of information relating to the 
business of independent record pro- 
duction. 
2. To corporately strive for a high- 
er standard of production quality in 
Canada resulting in greater rewards 
for the entire Canadian music indus- 
try. 
Rose 
WB -Pioneer Is 
Off To Big Start 
HOLLYWOOD - Reaction to the 
new Warner Bros. -Pioneer Corp. rec- 
ord company in Japan is both "over- 
whelming and far beyond our most 
optimistic projections," reports Phil 
Rose, managing director of the Kin- 
ney Record group's newly formed in- 
ternational operation. 
Now back at his desk at company 
headquarters in Burbank, Rose was 
in Tokyo for a fortnight on activities 
surrounding the Jan. 25 "official" un- 
veiling of the new company in the 
Japanese market. 
In addition to the artists roster 
from the Atlantic and Warner/Re- 
prise labels in the Kinney Record 
Group, the new diskery also has a 
roster of 60 Japanese artists specifi- 
cally signed to the new label to draw 
from. 
"Fact is," Rose said, "we had two 
chart singles in Japan both over 100,- 
000, after our first week in oper- 
ation-one English and the other 
Japanese. Led Zeppelin on Atlantic 
and Mari Hemni on Pioneer". 
The new company is headquartered 
in Tokyo and completed its total dis- 
tribution facilities throughout Japan 
prior to officially opening. 
AWARDING EXPERIENCE-Andre 
Kostelanetz, CBS recording star, re- 
cently visited Australia enroute to 
New Zealand for a series of orches- 
tral concerts. 
During his brief stay in Sydney he 
did press, radio and television inter- 
views; was guest artist on a national 
TV show and hosted to a cocktail 
party by Australian Record Company 
(CBS people down -under). 
Photographed at the party Ray 
Bull (left) ARC's general sales man- 
ager presented the maestro with a 
gold record award representing sales 
in excess of 10,000 records for his 
album of "Strauss Waltzes." 
3. 
To 
collectively 
support 
the 
growth of the talent community in 
Canada. 
4. To make available to Canadian 
independent record producers an or- 
ganization within which 
they can 
combine their talents, reputations, 
present and potential financial and 
political 
forces 
and 
direct 
them 
towards the 
solution 
of problems 
faced by independent record pro- 
ducers as a group. 
5. To represent its membership to 
the recording industry, press and in- 
formation media 
and the 
general 
public of Canada and the world in a 
forceful, 
truthful 
and 
impressive 
manner. 
6. To protect the interests and 
rights of the Canadian independent 
record producer. 
This third meeting saw the forma- 
tion of a membership committee and 
one for looking after press releases. 
It was pointed up that this is not a 
secret organization and that it is no 
way launching a vendetta against 
any other faction of the entertain- 
ment industry. Their reason for form- 
ing is to improve the status of the 
independent producer and collectively 
form a strong voice enjoyed by other 
groups in the industry. 
National reaction to the organiza- 
tion has been running high. Mail and 
telephone enquiries have been exten- 
sive and members of the Toronto 
branch have moved out into the field 
to form regional cells across Canada. 
Island Artists 
Funk Euro Rep 
NEW 
YORK - Capitol's 
Grand 
Funk Railroad have granted exclu- 
sive agency representation rights for 
Europe to Chris Blackwell's Island 
Artists Limited. The group's manag- 
er -producer, Terry Knight noted that 
Island Artists first represented Grand 
Funk by negotiating their debut Eu- 
ropean appearance in London, which 
was standing -room -only. 
Island Artists is negotiating an ex- 
tensive European tour for Grand 
Funk in the summer. However, rather 
than follow the standard practice of 
playing every known club and uni- 
versity in Europe for the exposure, 
Grand Funk will concentrate mainly 
on the large football stadiums and 
auditoriums which are as centrally 
located as possible and where the 
greatest number of people can assem- 
ble together at one time to see the 
group. "We hope to secure a permit 
to give a free concert in Hyde Park 
to close the tour on our way home," 
Knight said. 
Island Artists offices are located at 
38 Basing Street, London W., 11. 
Electrola Promotes 
Artists In Germany 
COLOGNE - Capitol's McGuiness 
Flint visit to Germany on Feb. 11, 
12, 13. Group will be doing TV, radio 
and press promo for both its current 
single and album, handled by Elec- 
trola. Electrola recently had visits 
from Andy Kim, Ashton Gardner & 
Dyke, 
Country Joe McDonald-all 
here doing TV promotion. Touring 
the country are the Edgar Broughton 
Band. 
Also, German TV produced in co- 
operation with the BBC London a 
series of 13 Rolf Harris Shows. The 
special service department of Elec- 
trola is promoting the Harris LP's, 
"Life At The Talk Of The Town" and 
"The Best Of Rolf Harris"; He sings 
songs from this Album in his shows. 
MILAN - RiFi Records, among Ita- 
ly's top labels, has withdrawn from 
the San Remo Song Festival, (Feb. 
25-27) and, as a consequence will not 
present any of its artists or songs to 
the festival committee. As for RiFi 
artist participation, it's understood 
that they would have to pay their 
own way to the festival if they de- 
sired to make an appearance. As it 
now stands, the San Remo Festival, 
heading for its 21st year, will not 
witness any big names, and will rely 
mostly on a roster of newcomers. 
RiFi's 
announcement 
contained 
four points in explanation of its re- 
fusal to support the event: 
1) Ri -Fi does not want to accept 
the principle, according to which the 
festival organizers, taking advantage 
of the TV presence in San Remo, ask 
the industry for "huge" amounts of 
money. 
2) Ri -Fi does not want to accept, 
for the 
reasons 
already 
publicly 
stated and notified to the Italian Fed- 
eration 
of Phonographic Industry, 
the festival rules. 
3) Ri -Fi does not believe that the 
"21st Festival of San Remo", orga- 
nized according to the old system, 
may answer public expectations as 
well as the reality of the market- 
place.

YUKO NAGISA 
Yuko Nagisa reached the top of the Japanese best sellers and sold over one 
million records with her first release, "Kyoto No Koi." She is seen here with 
her award the "1970 Record Prize of Japan." Yuko is contracted to Toshiba 
Records, which has now issued her follow up single, "Kyoto Bojou."

Ann Murray Special 
NEW YORK - Anne Murray, who 
has made seven guest appearances 
this season on the Glen Campbell 
Goodtime Hour, has been set to star 
in her own one hour color TV special 
rolling this week for the Canadian 
Broadcasting 
Corp. 
Sponsored 
by 
Nestles and produced and directed 
by David Acomba, the program will 
be taped entirely on location with 
Miss Murray performing in natural 
settings and in concerts throughout 
Canada, with as many as six to 
eight cameras covering the action 
at one time. The program, to air in 
March, will feature selections from 
her second Capitol Records album.

porary appointment of a receiver as 
caretaker of the partnership business 
and for an order that McCartney be 
supplied with information about the 
par nership finances. Mr. Hirst de- 
clared in court that "the latest ac- 
counts suggest there probably is not 
enough in the kitty to meet even the 
individual Beatlees' income tax and 
surtax liabilities." He said that on a 
conservative estimate the foursome's 
surtax liability must be £500,000. The 
action by McCartney seeking dissolu- 
tion of "The Beatles and Co." was 
adjourned on undertakings by Apple 
Corps to procure payment of money 
due to the Beatles into a solicitors' 
joint account pending a full hearing 
in about two weeks' time when the 
evidence has been completed. 
Mr. 
Hirst 
told 
Justice 
Stamp 
that 
McCartney had never trusted the 
group's manager Allen Klein, or ac- 
cepted him as manager. Klein's coun- 
sel, Mr. A. J. Balcombe QC said a 
bank letter revealed that on January 
15th 1971 Apple Corps had something 
over £2 million on deposit account. 
Rumors suggesting an impending 
takeover bid for Management Agency 
and Music empire have been dis- 
counted by MAM managing director 
Bill Smith. He stated that there have 
been no enquiries with regard to 
takeover of the company. Hints of an 
offer valuing MAM shares at 50 to 55 
shillings each sparked off a flurry of 
buying recently, and EMI was alleged 
to be interested. Smith explained the 
buying spree by attributing it to 
news that MAM was actively seeking 
to add other companies to its roster. 
Thirty employees, mostly female 
office staff, have been declared redun- 
dant, and left at the end of January 
from the EMI -owned World Record 
Club operation in Richmond. WRC 
chief Derek Sinclair explained the 
situation arose from the company's 
decision to phase out pre -selection 
single LPs and tapes by July this 
year in favor of concentrating on 
box sets of LPs, which have won 
substantial marketing success. The 
first of the latter was a Frank Sina- 
tra collection just over a year ago, 
released on an experimental basis, 
and has been followed by similar box- 
es featuring Nat King Cole, the Holly- 
wood 
Bowl 
Symphony Orchestra, 
Dean Martin and a particularly suc- 
cessful Herb Alpert collection. Sin- 
clair said that operation of box set 
marketing lent itself to computeriza- 
tion and reduced the need for the 
present volume of staff. As many as 
possible of the redundant employees 
were being relocated elsewhere with- 
in the EMI organization. Forthcom- 
ing box sets from WRC include some 
featuring top Polydor middle-roaders 
Bert Kaempfert and James Last and 
French 
maestro 
Franck 
Pourcel. 
Eric Burdon, stormy long-playing 
petrel of the Midem galas, has caused 
more controversy with the "P.C.3" 
track in his "Black Man's Burdon" 
album just released. The track in 
question refers to Queen Elizabeth in 
what some quarters regard as an 
offensive manner, and EMI, which 
distributes Liberty/UA product here, 
has refused to handle it. Consequent- 
ly, the LP has been re -pressed with 
"P.C.3" omitted for the EMI distribu- 
tion system, and initial pressings in- 
cluding the controversial track are 
being handled by Liberty/UA's own 
sales force and independent distribu- 
tors. 
Paul Rich, chief of the Carlin Mu- 
sic Corporation's British office, has 
been completing deals initiated at 
MIDEM. 
European 
sub -publishing 
pacts he has tied up are worth in 
excess 
of $20,000, 
and Rich has 
placed material by David Lewis and 
Andwella, who are Reflection Records 
artists, in many areas of the Conti- 
nent. The same applies to another 
Reflection group, Dogfeet, and Rich 
reports $70,000 worth of business 
done on copyrights in Tony Strat- 
ton -Smith's 
Stratsongs 
catalogue, 
which 
Carlin 
administers. 
Groups 
whose writing is involved include 
Brian Davies and Every Which Way 
and Genesis. 
The British record industry seems 
to be coping well at the time of 
writing with the effects and hang-ups 
caused by the strike of Post Office 
employees in pursuit of a wage 
claim. Distribution and collection of 
disks and orders has continued with- 
out major interruption, and record 
company executives envisage no seri- 
ous problems while the automatic 
telephone 
service 
functions 
ade- 
quately. 
The Robert Stigwood Organization 
has completed a deal with Universal 
Pictures for a movie version of the 
"Jesus Christ-Superstar" rock op- 
era. Universal is grubstaking the 
movie and partnering the RSO enter- 
prise in staging the work on Broad- 
way in September at an estimated 
cost of up to $750,000. As part of the 
deal, Universal will collect half the 
worldwide theater and film profits of 
the operation. 
Ian Matthews (ex Matthews South- 
ern Comfort) has been signed to 
Philips. Fred Marks negotiated the 
deal with Matthews' managers Ken 
Howard and Alan Blaikley, and the 
deal makes the first world-wide solo 
signing by Philips for the progres- 
sive Vertigo label. The contract is for 
three years and first product will be 
an L.P. and a single release early in 
the spring. 
Quickies: American producer James 
Bowen in town for five days during 
which time he cut tracks with Kenny 
Rogers and the First Edition which 
will result in a single release espe- 
cially for the British market entitled 
"All God's Lovely Children."

The first New Year's meeting of 
chiefs from nationwide agencies was 
held at the conference room of the 
King Record Company. 
There they reported the conditions 
of the record market of the year-end 
and gave the interim report on 1970's 
sales gains. They will expect to gain 
sales projects of $30,555,556 made up 
of record sales of 80% and music tape 
sales of 20%. 
LP sales (Japanese LP record sales 
of 40% and foreign ones including 
popular ones, 60%) have been more 
successful 
in 
each record market 
area, and especially LP records of 
$2.80 have shown double sales as the 
company has expected. 
In addition to these favorable suc- 
cesses, 2 or 3 records sets have been 
good sellers. Even single records of 
foreign, popular singers, which have 
been said unsuccessful these years, 
have been successful, too. For exam- 
ple, LP and single records of Carpen- 
ters, Tom Jones, G. Nazzaro, D. Vi- 
dal, E. Humperdinck and Nick & Ni - 
chola have been good sellers. 
As for Japanese LP and single rec- 
ords, Yoko Kishi and Ritsuko Abe 
have been outstanding sellers. And 
what's more 'Hann No Meruhen' by 
Dark Ducks, `Tokyo No Onna' and 
`Osaka No Onna' by the Peanuts and 
'Ai Wa Fushicho' 
and `Fuyu No 
Teishajoo' by Akira Fuse. 
Also, records of children's songs 
and folk songs sales have been high- 
er than usual.

ONLY JUST BEGUN-Shown is Arthur Rubinstein celebrating his 84th 
birthday at a party given by RCA Records at N.Y.'s La Cote Basque res- 
taurant by cutting the piano -topped cake. Rubinstein talked only of the future 
at the event which he called one of the happiest moments of his life. 
'Fillmore At NARM' 
Set For February 
PENNSYLVANIA - "Fillmore at 
NARM", a special late -night party 
at the 13th Annual NARM Conven- 
tion, will star Aretha Franklin, At- 
lantic Records recording artist. She 
will be the featured performer in a 
show which includes Cold Blood and 
Tower of Power, two groups on the 
San Francisco label, and James An- 
derson, who records for Cotillion. 
"Fillmore at NARM" will be held 
on Saturday evening, February 27 and 
is sponsored by Fillmore Corporation. 
Bill Graham, President of Fillmore 
and originator of the Fillmore East 
and West, will be there in person 
to present the performers. Fillmore's 
executive vice president, David Ru- 
binson, coordinates the evening. 
Two special light shows will be 
part of the evening's entertainment. 
Fillmore posters will be distributed 
to all who attend. This is the first 
time such an evening has been planned 
at a NARM Convention. Casual dress 
is requested.

Zager & Evans 
To Vanguard 
NEW YORK - Bob Reno, pop A&R 
director at Vanguard, reports the 
signing of Zager and Evans to an 
exclusive contract. Irwin Levine and 
Larry Brown have just produced their 
first LP for the label which will be 
released during 
March. 
A 
single 
culled from the album has been 
shipped world-wide. 
Zager and Evans' first single, on 
RCA, was "In The Year 2525," which 
sold 2 million in the II.S. and an ad- 
ditional two million in foreign coun- 
tries. They come to Vanguard with 
a large portfolio of new material 
they've put together during the past 
year. In addition to their own ma- 
terial, the first LP is comprised of 
several cuts written by Levine, Brown 
and Al Cooper. 
The deal was negotiated through 
Jeff Franklin's American Talent In- 
ternational office with Reno. Zager 
and Evans are represented by Man- 
agement III.
