SANTA ANA, Calif.-The Wurlitzer 
service school program is in high gear 
on the west coast where field service 
engineer Leonard Hicks is keeping 
busy spreading the news about the 
Company's new Model 3600 Super 
P.R. Wisc. Style 
A good example of grass -roots pub- 
lic relations for our industry comes 
from Green Bay, Wisconsin where 
Empire Distributing 's manager, Bob 
Rondeau and Bob Greatens, ,partner 
in Hallada Coin, spent an entire Sat- 
urday with Boy Scout Troop No. 42 
picking up paper to help the scouts 
get enough money to continue their 
Christmas projects (see photo above). 
Both Greatens and Rondeau, who 
are active MOA members, believe 
that the best public relations program 
for our industry is sincere civic in- 
volvement and both are following 
MOA's public relations programs.

M -O -R Shines At Columbia Festival Of Stars 
THE STARS ... Johnny Mathis, Vikki ('arrPeter Nero and Percy Faith in an unusual M -O -R night at Madison Square Garden. (See review below.) 
Clive Davis, master of ceremonies for the Columbia Festival of Stars at the Garden. A party for the celebrities held at New York's leading M -O -R room, the 
Rainbow Room, followed the Garden event. Davis is seen greeting David Clayton -Thomas of Blood, Sweat & Tears; Steve Popovich is behind David. Davis with 
Ornette Coleman with Larry Douglas and Bob Altschuler on right. Al Aronowitz of the New York Post with Davis. And on far right, Johnny Mathis with C.D. 
eashbodcltarlenton stage 
Columbia's Festival Of Stars 
MADISON 
SQUARE 
GARDEN, 
NEW 
YORK-Middle-Of-The-Road 
Music Lives! And it's greatly loved by 
what might be called a Musical Silent 
Majority. They're out there, folks. 
They may not make themselves no- 
ticed as much as the rock music en- 
thusiasts, but more than 18,000 came 
to Madison Square Garden last Fri- 
day to hear "Good Music Mathis, 
melodies, Vikki Carr, Peter Nero and 
Percy Faith all presented by Colum- 
bia Records. 
Clive Davis, president of Columbia 
Records, and m.c. of the evening, 
clarified the intent of the special Fes- 
tival of Stars event. Although he rec- 
ognized the dynamic changes that 
have taken place on the musical scene 
during the past decade, he pointed to 
the fact that the soft, romantic sound 
has been a "mainstay of American 
Music and we felt we owed an eve- 
ning to this kind of music." 
"This is not an evening of nostal- 
gia," Davis went on, "this is an eve- 
ning of Today." And he went on to 
point out how every one of the per- 
formers on the bill was very much a 
"today" performer. 
From that point on, the artists 
proved the point to the Garden audi- 
ence. First onto the circular, raised 
stage located smack -dab -in -the middle 
of the Garden Floor was Percy Faith 
and some sixty musicians. The lights 
dimmed, and Faith put the orch thru 
a hoedown. And on the downbeat, the 
huge stage began to revolve, making 
one full revolution every seven min- 
utes. The fact that everyone could get 
a closer glimpse of the stars was 
greeted with tremendous applause. 
Percy was beautiful with a soft, lush 
version of "The Rest Of Your Life" 
and his (plug) latest single "Dia- 
monds Are Forever." It was unusual 
sitting in the Garden and watching 
people in gowns and suits pass by. 
And we got a kick out of the ice 
cream pitchman whispering his "Ice 
Cream, Ice Cream" chant. He too 
sensed the dignity of the evening. 
The Hanley Sound System was 
magnificent. So clear was the sound 
that one could even pick up an occa- 
sional imbalance in the orchestra dur- 
ing a number or two. 
Peter 
Nero followed 
the short 
Faith opener (Percy came back to 
open the second half) with his usual 
professionalism. No, he even sounded 
better than usual. Or, as some wise 
old music business veteran once put 
it, they sound better when they have 
something on the charts. And with 
"Summer of '42" a smash for Nero, 
he sounded more like a star. We also 
noted that the kids have nothing on 
the MOR folks as far as recognizing 
a song is concerned. The applause 
from the Garden group burst into a 
polite roar when Nero touched the 
first four notes of the hit "'42" sin- 
gle. He was cool through a jazz ori- 
ented 
"What 
The 
World 
Needs 
Now;" warm thru "Never My Love;" 
hot thru "Lucretia McEvil;" dramatic 
thru a "J. C. Superstar" medley and 
humorously classical thru "I 
Got 
Rhythm" performed as the great clas- 
sical composers might have presented 
the number. Nero is a showman. 
Clive Davis beautifully filled the 
pauses (while the stage was being 
reshuffled) with interesting facts and 
figures about record sales by some of 
Columbia's leading performers. And 
then Vikki Carr burst onto the stage 
with "I Want To Be Happy." The 
feminine change -of -pace was a de- 
light, 
and Vikki's 
low-cut 
brown 
gown drew a number of whistles. But 
it was her voice that drew the ap- 
plause. Vikki belts with the best of 
the belters and can tear your heart 
out with those Women's Lib favor- 
ites, "It Must Be Him," "With Pen In 
Hand" and her current release "I'd Do 
It All Again." Vikki has found her - 
Clive greets Allen Ginsburg and Percy Faith. 
self a niche with this type of "tor- 
mented woman" material. She pro- 
jects them well and they drew the 
biggest applause. The fans seem to be 
moved when Vikki cries her heart and 
eyes out. She does both, and it comes 
across 
with 
sincerity. 
"Cuando 
Caliente El Sol" is always an audi- 
ence favorite, as is her "Judy Garland 
Medley" including "You Made Me 
Love You," "Trolley Song," "Swanee 
River" and the "Over The Rainbow" 
finale. 
After some other lush and beautiful 
arrangements by Percy following the 
intermission ("Quiet Night," "Sun- 
rise, Sunset" "Fiddler on the Roof") 
out came the obvious star of the show, 
Johnny Mathis. Greeted with a roar, 
Johnny assumed his familiar bent 
knee, 
crooked 
elbow 
stance 
and 
sounded 
magnificent 
on 
"Misty" 
which was also welcomed with ap- 
plause after only the first three notes 
by the orchestra. He did John Len - 
non's "Love," swung thru "If You 
Really Love Me," and did a beautiful 
job on "Summer Me, Winter Me," and 
the sophisticated Mabel Mercer classic 
"Over The Weekend." But Johnny is 
at his best when you can be close to 
him and we got the feeling that this 
intimate material and the tremendous 
distance between the performer and 
most of his audience wasn't working 
to maximum advantage. It was obvi- 
ous that what his fans wanted to hear 
were his oldies, and when he did 
"12th of Never," "Wild Is The Wind," 
"When Sunny Gets Blue," "It's Not 
For Me To Say," "Tonight" in medley 
form, they felt satisfied. When he 
concluded this medley (that really 
offers only a smattering of each of 
the above songs) with "Wonderful, 
Wonderful," the presentation 
was 
greeted with a roaring cheer and 
standing applauders. Some thought 
should be given to re-recording this 
classic. It's about fifteen years now 
since it was first released and it might 
be the strongest new thing Mathis 
could record. "Sleigh Ride" and the 
Jacques Brel "If We Only Had Love" 
concluded the evening. 
Although Mathis sounded great, he 
probably would have had this audi- 
ence roaring if he had only sung his 
past hits. Because it seemed that the 
Garden was loaded with Mathis lovers 
who have been listening to his rec- 
ords through the years but were nev- 
er able to pay the tab for seeing him 
line in such clubs as the Copa or the 
Waldorf Empire Room. It's amazing 
how this master of "kissy-face mu- 
sic" (as one teenager once called it) 
can bridge the musical generation 
gap. 
The audience was extremely well 
behaved and Clive Davis told the 
folks how marvelous they were as he 
bid them farewell. 
Cash Box -January 1, 1972

NEW YORK: WHAT HATH ROY LICHTENSTEIN WROUGHT? 
Ninety three million people per year. Yeah? More than the populations of 
France and Luxembourg put together? No fooling? And that figure is only the 
number of buyers and we should times it by three for the total readership? What? 
Two hundred and seventy odd million? Can this be real? 
Actually it is very real although the product itself is in the realm of fantasy and 
imagination. Marvel comics have just that sort of audience, according to Steve 
Lemberg, youthful president of National Copacetic, the company which recently 
acquired rights to the characters in the series. 
Already in the works is a sixty-five installment, five minute radio show format 
which will be distributed nationally and aimed at the 16 to 25 year olds who 
constitute 75% of Marvel readership. This is the opening salvo in a broad 
spectrum of multi -media projects based on the Marvel heroes. All will employ 
top -grade ultra -contemporary scores. 
"We are doing a Carnegie Hall multi -media show January 5," says Lemberg, 
"and are working on a tv special featuring Alain Resnais, a film, and a $2,500,000 
giant arena spectacular. Albums are obviously a major part of the picture, and 
we're also planning a mixed media book package. There is almost no limit to the 
way the Marvel characters can be presented." 
If that is true (and who are we to gainsay it) then such heroes of the cosmos 
as Thor, son of the regal Odin, from the far dominion of Asgard, the Spider Man, 
The Hulk and The Fantastic Four will reach an even wider audience during the 
coming year. Certainly the upcoming Carnegie Hall show is already shaping up 
as one of 1972's first must -see events. 
Slated to appear at that Gotham showplace are film director Resnais, a long 
time Marvel addict; Peter Boyle of "Joe" fame; the Beach Boys' Dennis Wilson 
(who will introduce new musical material inspired by the Silver Surfer); drummer 
Chico Hamilton, who will improvise background music; Australian illusionist Geof 
Crozier; actor -comedian -talk show host Earle Doud; WPLJ's disk jockey Zacherle 
who will read a Dr. Doom narrative. And, of course, Stan Lee, the creator of 
Marvel Comics. 
According to Lemberg, "The center of the Carnegie stage will be a giant Mylar 
throne, around which will weave the weird and wonderful works of Peter Nevard, 
who will create a cacophony of Asgardian effects with film, slides and lighting. 
Magician Crozier has devised some never -before -seen illusions for the show, 
which will be the most elaborate production ever staged at Carnegie Hall. Two 
Marvel artists, John Bessman and Herb Trimbe, who originated the Fantastic Four 
and The Hulk, will animate a fight sequence on the spot. Eddie Carmel, the nine 
foot, eight inch man will improvise poetry dedicated to his Marvel heroes and in 
the lobby the audience will be surrounded by 128 huge panels, an exhibit created 
by Stan Lee to show the evolution of the comic book." 
If that sounds like fun, imagine what might follow. Or let Lemberg imagine it 
since he will be the one to do it. He has already proved himself a capable pro- 
duction manager, having served in that capacity at Fillmore East as well as at 
numerous rock festivals. He got the idea for the whole Marvel project while 
browsing in a San Francisco book shop. "I saw these comics while I was just 
hanging out there and I bought a few and then it came to me." 
As it will come to us and the countless millions too. Welcome to the apocalypse! 
ed kelleher 
DAWN-MUSIC YOU CAN GET YOUR TEETH INTO 
"I think that our biggest difficulty now is with our image. People in the trade 
tend to think of us as 'bubble -gum', when really we're doing something quite 
different." The speaker was Tony Orlando, leader of Dawn, in town for a couple of 
days' quick promotion work and an American Bandstand taping. 
Tony's back as an artist after a period of activity with Columbia's publishing 
arm, April -Blackwood. Dawn, he explains, was an accident. "Hank Medress, who 
produces the group, has been a friend of mine for some time. He occasionally 
bounces ideas off of me. He had made a record called 'Candida'. It was com- 
pletely finished, with a full instrumental track and a lead vocalist. He asked me 
if I thought it would appeal to any record company in particular. I told him that 
it sounded like a Bell record to me. He took it to Larry Utall, who flipped for it, 
except for the lead vocal. Hank came back and asked me to put one on. I did, and 
the single became a hit. We thought it was just a one-shot thing. Then we made 
'Knock Three Times'. That sold more than four million internationally, and we 
felt that we might be on to something." 
We asked Tony what he felt his music was, if not bubble -gum. "We're into a 
1960's Drifters kind of thing. When 
I was recording for Epic, twelve years ago, 
the first four sides 
I cut were new Carole King -Gerry Goffin tunes-'Some Kind 
of Wonderful,' 'When My Little Girl is Smiling,' 'Take Good Care of My Baby' and 
the hit, 'Halfway to Paradise.' Carole was 18, and she arranged the session, play- 
ed piano on it and sang background vocal. I think that what we're doing now 
has the same kind of feel. It explains why a large part of our audience is in their 
30's ... they grew up on that stuff. You go to our shows, and you'll find that it's 
not mostly kids who show up." 
Besides Tony, Dawn includes two girl singers, Telma Hopkins and Joyce 
Vincent. Both were established session singers before joining the group; it's Telma 
singing 'Shut yo' mouth' on Isaac Hayes' "Shaft." They've been with Dawn, 
though, since the first sessions with Tony. 
"A funny thing," Tony mentioned as his manager, Marc Gordon, showed up 
to take him somewhere. "We played our new single, 'Runaway' to the people at 
Bell the other day. Everybody liked it except Larry. He said that I was singing 'too 
soulful'. See what 
I mean? Even he thinks we're bubble -gum." 
THOR: A Marvelous Return 
DAWN: A New Day

Capricorn Switches Over 
To Ties With Warner Bros. 
NEW YORK - Capricorn Records 
has entered into an agreement with 
Warner Bros. Recordswhereby War- 
ners will participate in the manufac- 
ture, distribution, merchandising and 
promo of all Capricorn product. With 
the pact effective immediately, Capri- 
corn's first release via Warner Bros. 
will be by Alex Taylor's second album 
"It's Dinnertime," which will be fol- 
lowed in Feb. with the release of the 
Allman Brothers' fourth album, a 
two -record set titled "Eat A Peach." 
Label 
was 
previously 
released 
through Atlantic, which means, of 
course, that distribution remains in 
the W -E -A fold. 
The agreement is the result of ne- 
gotiations between Mo Ostin, pres- 
ident of Warner Bros./Reprise Rec- 
ords, Joe Smith, Warners' execu vice 
president, Phil Walden, president of 
Capricorn Records and Frank Fenter, 
exec vice president of Capricorn.

Atlantic's Top Year Marked 
By 10% Sales Increase In '71 
Label Earns 
24 Gold Awards 
NEW YORK - 1971 was the greatest 
year in Atlantic Records history, re- 
ports Ahmet Ertegun, president. Sales 
were up 10% over 1970, making the 
seventh successive year that the firm 
had enjoyed a substantial sales in- 
crease. This was reflected by 24 
RIAA-certified gold recordings, 13 al- 
bums and 11 singles. 
Atlantic's year was marked by a 
number of noteworthy events. The 
most publicized was Atlantic's acquis- 
ition of distribution rights in the 
United States to recordings by the 
Rolling Stones on their own Rolling 
Stones label. World-wide rights to 
recordings by the rock group were 
signed by Kinney Services last April. 
Other important events included the 
release of two original cast allbums, 
one of the movie sound track to the 
film "Soul to Soul" starring Wilson 
Pickett, Roberta Flack, Les McCann, 
and Eddie Harris; and the other an 
original cast album from the hit TV 
comedy series "All In The Family". 
Both records were best sellers; "All 
In The Family" became an RIAA 
(Record 
Industry 
Association 
of 
America) certified gold album with 
sales of over $1,000,000. 
A new label, Asylum, joined the 
Atlantic -Ateo -Cotillion 
trio 
and 
London: Best Dec., Quarter 
NEW YORK - London Records has 
just accomplished the biggest single 
sales month in its history. The rec- 
ord -shattering Dec. tallies also capped 
the biggest single quarter of sales for 
the firm as it opens its silver an- 
niversary year in business. 
In a year-end appraisal of the 
company's sales posture, Herb Gold- 
farb, vice president for sales and 
marketing, attributed the continuing 
success to a combination of factors, 
not the least of which is the emer- 
gence during the last quarter of 1971 
of singer Al Green. Green, star of the 
London -distributed 
Hi 
Records 
of 
Memphis, has had two million -selling 
singles during that period in the cur- 
rent, "Let's Stay Together," and his 
first major hit, "Tired of Being 
Alone." Green's LP, "Gets Close to 
You," is also riding the album charts. 
But beyond this single factor, Gold- 
farb noted, is the combined impact of 
several multi -LP sets, including the 
new hit Rolling Stones "Hot Rocks," 
two -record set of major past singles 
hits, rush -released in mid -Dec. plus 
the Tom Jones "Live at Caesar's Pal- 
ace" two -disk package. 
The entire Moody Blues family of 
gold record award winning LP's is 
selling at record levels as well, keyed 
by the major success of "Every Good 
Boy Deserves Favour," which has 
been at the top of the album charts 
since its release last fall. 
Contributing in his own measure to 
the sales success story is Engelbert 
Humperdinck, whose current first live 
album, "Live at the Riviera," is also 
doing 
chart 
sales. 
Humperdinck, 
whose entire LP catalog on London's 
Parrot label is in the gold category, 
is to return to the U.S. soon for 
another extended personal appearance 
tour. 
Goldfarb also pointed to the high 
sales plateau occupied by the vet 
maestro Mantovani, the chart success 
of the Savoy Brown group from En- 
gland; 
a 
bonus-pak two -LP John 
Mayall set, and a recently released 
album of earlier, not previously re- 
leased Cat Stevens tracks. Stevens 
composed all the songs in this album, 
which has also just hit the charts. 
Goldfarb also took note of the con- 
tinuing success of the company's clas- 
sical catalog, which features such 
names as Joan Sutherland, Renata Te - 
baldi, Georg Solti, Zubin Mehta, Her- 
bert Von Karajan and the phase 4 
stereo classics which includes major 
successes 
by the veteran Leopold 
Stokowski. 
Branch Success 
In addition to the product itself, he 
stressed, is the added factor of the 
company's six factory owned branch 
operations, which has created a sky- 
rocketing effect to sales activity in 
major market areas. These branches, 
in New York, Boston, Atlanta, Chica- 
go, Los Angeles and San Francisco, 
have also aided in opening up the 
profit well of catalog sales. 
Dr. Goldmark 
Starts New Firm 
For Kinney 
NEW 
YORK - Dr. 
Peter 
C. 
Goldmark is coming out of retirement 
to start a new company in conjunc- 
tion with the Kinney Services, Inc. 
Goldmark was formerly the head of 
CBS 
Laboratories, 
a 
division of 
Columbia Broadcasting System, for 35 
years and was instrumental in the 
invention of the modern LP as well as 
the first color tv broadcast system 
and electronic video recording. 
The new company will be called the 
Goldmark Communications Corp. and 
will serve as a subsid of Kinney. The 
doctor will concentrate his firm on 
the developments and innovations of 
techniques and systems for cable tele- 
vision, satellite communications, elec- 
tronic publishing and educational ma- 
terials for home use. 
Goldmark has begun assembling his 
staff. He claims the major method in 
developing projects would be to blend 
the "software" (information content) 
with the most current technology 
available to meet the demands of con- 
temporary society. He feels that lack 
of this blending has been responsible 
for a number of disappointments in 
recent communications developments. 
Goldmark added .that a bulk of the 
firm's initial thrust would be aimed at 
a Government project to study use of 
communications techniques in rural 
areas.

$Millions To 
Bengla Desh On 
Concert Album 
HOLLYWOOD - Capitol Records, 
has presented a certified check for 
$3,750,000 to Apple Records, Inc. as 
an advance payment on sales of "The 
Concert for Bangla Desh," recording 
of the historic Madison Square Gar- 
den charity concert presented last Au- 
gust by George Harrison and Ravi 
Shankar on behalf of East Pakistan 
(now Bangla Desh) refugees. 
Announcement of the advance pay- 
ment-largest 
in 
Capitol's 
near 
30 -year history-was made by Bhas- 
kar Menon, Capitol's president and 
chief exec officer. 
Apple Records, Inc. will make the 
donation to the Bangla Desh charity 
from remaining funds after deducting 
whatever costs it incurs. 
This album features some of the 
most prominent artists of the day, 
including the aforementioned Dylan, 
George Harrison, Ringo Starr, Leon 
Russell, and Eric Clapton. 
Apple Statistics 
According 
to representatives of 
Apple in Hollyw000d, 900,000 copies 
of the disk and tape (thru Columbia) 
have been sold. Allen Klein of Apple 
estimates a final sale of 3 million 
units, with a total of $15 million to 
the Bengla Desh refugees. Five dol- 
lars for each of the albums sold, at 
$10 dealer cost, will 
be sent to 
UNICEF Bengla Desh Refugee Chil- 
dren's Fund. 
Donald Allan of UNICEF has re- 
ferred to the situation as "the great- 
est, single contribution from a non - 
government source" and specified that 
the money will be used to help about 
20 million people who are badly in 
need of food, clothing, shelter, medi- 
cal services and the transportation of 
supplies to needy areas. 
Klein views the marketing row on 
the album as "unfortunate" and says 
that the marketing terms were de- 
liberately designed "to maximize the 
money for the charity and to preserve 
the artists' integrity." 
He added: "I had a special client - 
10 million starving children. If my 
policies upset people, I'm sorry. I 
think we'll make a heck of a lot of 
people happy. And it's a great album. 
Dealers and buyers should realize this 
is not just another rock record but 
an extraordinary benefit production."

RCA/Musicor's 
Pact On Jones 
NEW YORK-Musicor Records and 
RCA Records have formed an agree- 
ment whereby the recordings made 
by country music artist George Jones 
will be released on the RCA label in 
the U.S. and Canada and through 
RCA's record and tape clubs. The an- 
nouncement was made by Art Tal- 
madge, 
Musicor's 
president, 
and 
Harry Jenkins, RCA Records divi- 
sion vp of country music. 
Talmadge explained that the deal 
covered Jones' entire catalog of 230 
tunes already released on Musicor as 
well as 58 sides that were recorded 
under Jones' Musicor contract but 
not released as yet. Therefore, RCA's 
product will be a number of reissues 
of Jones' Musicor sides in addition to 
some cuts never previously issued. 
Jones recently switched labels from 
Musicor to Epic Records, so the RCA- 
Musicor deal only covers what he 
had recorded before leaving the label. 
Talmadge stated that his label made 
the deal because of its conviction in 
RCA's distribution strength. Jenkins 
verified that RCA intends to give full 
promo treatment to all product, start- 
ing with the initial release of the first 
single under the pact, "A Day In The 
Life Of A Fool." 
Talmadge said Musicor Records will 
continue its own label distribution of 
its other product, concentrating its ef- 
forts to develop new artists through 
its current distrib facilities, as in the 
past.

Tony Bennett: Now TV Special -ist Atlantic's Best Year 
NEW YORK - Tony Bennett has 
pyramided his concert with the Lon- 
don Philharmonic Orchestra into a 
triple threat encompassing the con- 
cert stage, television and an LP. The 
event, now a TV special being syndi- 
cated 
throughout 
the 
U.S., 
also 
helped spur the singer's full-scale en- 
try into television, with additional 
specials and his own musical series 
soon to begin production. 
The concert, held in early 1971 at 
Royal Albert Hall in London, marked 
the first time a vet singer had ever 
performed as guest soloist with the 
103 -member London Philharmonic Or- 
chestra. Bennett packed the Hall with 
an SRO throng of 7,000 patrons, with 
an additional 5,000 disappointed fans 
turned away. The crowd gave him a 
thunderous, standing ovation that 
lated a full ten minutes. 
The concert was filmed by BBC and 
had its first showing in this country 
on Dec. 26 on WNBC-TV in New 
York. The special, "The Tony Ben- 
nett -Super Special," is a one -hour 
colorcast which is being syndicated 
nationally by 20th Century -Fox Tele- 
vision. 
The performance was recorded live 
and the resulting LP is Bennett's cur- 
rent Columbia Records album, "Tony 
Bennett: Get Happy, With the London 
Philharmonica Orchestra." The al- 
bum, packaged with sketches drawn 
by Bennett himself. 
Bennett's television plans include 
two more specials, "Bennett & Basie," 
with Count Basie, and "Bennett & 
Buddy," with Buddy Rich. Both spe- 
cials will be syndicated by 20th Cen- 
tury -Fox Television. 
The singer will begin production on 
Jan. 23 of his new television series, 
"This Is Music," in which he will star 
and will co -produce, through Tony 
Bennett Enterprises, with Thames 
TV. The series, scheduled to air dur- 
ing the 1972-73 TV season, will be

RIAA Re -States 
Role In Gold 
Record Awards 
NEW YORK - The Recording Indus- 
try of America (RIAA) has re -stated 
its role as the certifying agent for the 
industry's gold record award. Respon- 
ding to numerous inquiries on the 
subject, Henry Brief, exec director of 
RIAA, issued the following state- 
ment: 
"To clear up any misunderstandings 
that may exist, we want to emphasize 
that the Gold Record Award is the 
only authorized award 
issued by 
RIAA to recognize sales achievement. 
RIAA does not certify or issue plat- 
inum, silver, diamond or other type 
awards. 
"The establishment of other types 
of awards has been considered in the 
past by RIAA and ultimately rejected 
because they would tend to dilute and 
demean the prestige enjoyed by the 
Gold Record Award. 
"When RIAA initiated its Gold 
Record Award certification program 
in 1958, it did so in response to a 
chaotic indistry situation that pre- 
vailed at that time. There was a pro- 
liferation of awards with no basis in 
fact, no method for verification or 
authentication. As a consequence, the 
veracity of all award claims was held 
in disrepute both in and outside the 
industry. 
"The establishment of the RIAA 
certification program with specific 
sales achievement criteria and an aud- 
it of the company's books by a firm 
of independent certified public ac- 
countants to insure that these criteria 
have been met, has restored prestige 
to the Gold Record Award. 
"In the past 14 years, RIAA has 
relied on the voluntary cooperation 
of companies within the recording in- 
dustry not only to submit their rec- 
ordings for certification but to refrain 
from using gold records to recognize 
other kinds of achievement. 
"We hope this same spirit of coop- 
eration will in the future act to inhi- 
bit the bestowal of non -certified sales 
awards."

E. B. Marks Inks 4 In Expansion 
NEW YORK - Charles Singleton, 
Scott Fagan, Joe Kookoolis and Bob- 
by Donaldson have been signed to 
writer -creative artist contracts by 
Marks Music, according to Hal Fein, 
vice president of the publishing firm. 
Stated Fein: "We're jumping right 
into a heavy schedule of contem- 
porary music and actively welcome 
all writers and all types of material 
to the Edward B. Marks catalog. My 
staff is ready to hear new product at 
anytime." 
Paramuse Opens 
In Mgmt, Prod. 
NEW YORK - Shirley Bernstein, 
Doris Vidor and Bernard Seligman 
announce the formation of Paramuse 
Artists Associates, a new manage- 
ment, consultant and production com- 
pany. The company will represent a 
group of clients to include some al- 
ready firmly established artists, along 
with younger talents who, in the 
opinion of the three principals, show 
the greatest potential for achievement 
and success. 
In addition to creatively and flex- 
ibly advising and negotiating deals 
for projects already brougrt to their 
clients, it will be one of the major 
functions of Paramuse Artists Associ- 
ates to find and help put projects to- 
gether in which the clients' talents 
can best be utilized. Paramuse will also 
take projects in early stages of de- 
velopment and secure monies for the 
artists to make possible the fur- 
therance of these projects. Addition- 
ally, Paramuse will be prepared to 
take options on books, plays, televi- 
sion or film ideas and to provide de- 
velopment monies in order to bring 
these and other properties to a salea- 
ble stage. 
For the past five years Miss Bern- 
stein has been an exec agent for IFA 
(International 
Famous 
Agency). 
Prior to that, she was a Broadway, 
television and motion picture pro- 
ducer. 
Vidor has been a member of the 
story department of Warner Broth- 
ers, worked with the Group Theatre 
in New York, was liaison between 
Darryl Zanuck and his story editor at 
20th Century Fox, worked in the 
story department of United Artists 
and has been actively involved in the 
theatre as a consultant, financier and 
co -producer. Seligman has been an 
agent with the William Morris Agen- 
cy for over 25 years, the last two of 
which were spent as senior executive 
agent in the New York Motion Pic- 
ture Department. 
He has helped 
launch the careers or handled, as an 
agent, the business affairs of more 
than two dozen of the top stars in the 
entertainment industry. 
Paramuse Artists Associates, Inc. is 
located at 745 Fifth Avenue in New 
York. 
SHINING JEWELS-Irene Johnson 
Ware is being congratulated by Jewel 
Records president Stanley J. Lewis. 
Ware had just been appointed vice 
president in charge of gospel promo- 
tions for the label. 
In addition to writing, 
Charlie 
"Hess" Singleton will direct the firm's 
soul music operations. He has just 
completed lyrics for a new song by 
Riz Ortolan, one of the writers of 
"More." Titled "Our Sun ... is Rising 
Now," it is the theme of a soon -to -be - 
released film "One on Top of the Oth- 
er." Singleton has a long list of hits 
including "Strangers in the Night," 
"Spanish Eyes," "Lady," "Mama He 
Treats Your Daughter Mean," etc. 
Fagan and Kookoolis as a team 
have 
been 
connected 
with 
off- 
Broadway activity while Donaldson is 
a writer -performer. Marks Music's 
growth pattern includes major oper- 
ations in Los Angeles and London. 
Concluded Fein: "Our plans are 
ambitious and aggressive. We seek 
the established and non -established 
writers and producers. As to the new 
writers, our staff can polish the rough 
edges around any gifted stones." 
Groove Merchant 
Bows New LP Line 
NEW YORK - Groove Merchant In- 
ternational Records introduced the 
first four albums in their new deluxe 
2200 LP series at the London Records 
distributors conference in Atlanta on 
Jan. 13 & 14. 
Groove Merchant International, an 
independent label headed by Sonny 
Lester, is distributed in many areas of 
the country by London. Sales of the 
first three Groove Merchant LPs 
prompted Herb Goldfarb of London 
to invite Lester and sales manager 
Ery Bagley to Atlanta to introduce 
the new albums to distributors in that 
area. 
The new Groove Merchant LPs are 
"Evergreens" by the Count Basie Or- 
chestra; "Sundance" by Chic Corea; 
"Black & Blues" by Jimmy McGriff 
and "Fusion" by Jeremy Steig, an- 
nounced Sonny Lester, head of GMI. 
The McGriff and Steig sets are two 
records for the price of one. All four 
LPs are also available in tape car- 
tridges and cassettes. 
"We don't want to confine the mu- 
sic we release on Groove Merchant 
International into any limited catego- 
ries. We believe in the talent we re- 
cord and we're confident that they'll 
find an appreciative audience," said 
Lester. 
Bell Drive On 
Lp By Gideon 
NEW YORK - Bell Records will be 
mounting one of its most extensive 
promo and ad campaigns for the San 
Francisco group Gideon 
& Power, 
whose first LP, "I Gotta Be Me," is 
just being released. 
Gordon Bassin, vice president of LP 
sales and merchandising for Bell, out- 
lined details of the program, which 
will support Gideon's personal ap- 
pearances, including the Cellar Door 
in Washington, D.C., the Gaslight in 
N.Y. and the Quiet Knight in Chicago 
and other leading clubs. 
Radio time buys, print ads in local 
underground and soul publications 
and press -on patches which can be 
worn on shirts or dungarees will be 
utilized. More than 1200 press kits 
which include major write-ups on 
Gideon 
from 
Newsweek, 
Rolling 
Stone, the Los Angeles Times, L.A. 
Free Press and the San Francisco Ex- 
aminer are being distributed. Em- 
phasis is being placed on getting the 
press, promo men, distributors and 
key retailers to a live performance in 
their area. Gideon's album was re- 
corded live at the Keystone Korner 
Club in San Francisco. 
Television will play an important 
role in exposing Gideon to the con- 
sumer public. He was on the Sonny & 
Cher Show last summer and when 
they returned to CBS TV this Janu- 
ary, they signed him for a taping on 
March 11 which will air March 20. 
The N.E.T. Network has done an hour 
long special on him and more video is 
scheduled. Gideon toured with the SSu- 
premes last summer. 
GRATEFUL GOLD-Members of the Grateful Dead were joined by Warner 
Bros. Records executive vice president Joe Smith recently at a banquet pres- 
entation held at The Coachman Restaurant in San Francisco. The evening was 
highlighted by the presentation of gold record awards to members of the 
group for their recent Warner Bros. two LP set, "Grateful Dead." Dead mem- 
bers surrounding the Warner Bros. executive include (left to right): Keith 
Godchaux (newest member of the group); Phil Lesh, (Joe Smith), Bob Weir; 
Jerry Garcia and Pigpen. 
Maurer Expands 
Artists Operations 
NEW YORK - Sid Maurer, vet per- 
sonal artist rep, is expanding his Sid 
Maurer Productions to include 
a 
broader spectrum of talent in the 
U.S. and abroad. 
In addition to the New York oper- 
ation at 850 Seventh Ave., reps have 
been appointed in two more key cit- 
ies, Los Angeles and London. Maurer 
has just signed two artists, Ohris 
Montez and Mark Radice, both of 
whom appear on the Paramount la- 
bel. 
Maurer, longtime personal rep of 
Donovan, is exec producer of the 
Warner Bros. -Donovan animated film. 
Originally feature-length, a shorter 
version has 
been 
completed. 
It's 
called "Donovan's Old Fashioned Pic- 
ture Book." Maurer and Tony Bene- 
dict produced. Donovan recently made 
a two visit to Maurer to discuss the 
film and its future. 
ESP Hikes List 
NEW YORK - ESP -Disk has an- 
nounced that effective January 1, 
1972, LP list price is set at $5.98. 
Product previously listed at $4.98. 
Roulette Inks New 
March/Keyes Duo 
NEW YORK - Morris Levy, pres- 
ident of Roulette Records, recently 
broke a long-standing precedent by 
contracting artists following a live 
audition and in the absence of demo 
tapes or a recorded presentation. 
The act, teenage duo Tony & Carol, 
were presented to Levy by producers 
Myrna March and Bert Keyes. Levy 
and other company officials reacted to 
their presentation by immediately ne- 
gotiating a production deal with 
March Keyes' Make Music firm to 
produce Tony & Carol for Roulette. 
Studio 
sessions were completed 
within the next few days. Levy stated 
that an initial release will be issued 
before the end of the month. 
While in business but a year, the 
March/Keyes team has been active, 
currently producing artists for Stax, 
Star -day -King and Paramount in ad- 
dition to their continuing success as 
songwriters. 
The association with Levy and 
Roulette marks a reunion of sorts. 
Keyes, long a successful writer and 
arranger, has written for numerous 
Roulette artists over the past few 
years. 
A HELPING HAND-Bell Records has donated funds to help Reverend O. O. 
Dempsey, pastor of the Upper Park Avenue Baptist Church in New York City, 
in his fight against drugs and crime in the black community. Rev. Dempsey 
was recently honored on his 11th anniversary with the church by members of 
his congregation and friends who hosted a gospel program. Seen above, pre- 
senting a check to Rev. C. Coleman of the Upper Park Avenue Baptist Church 
(center) are Steve Wax, director of national promotion for Bell Records (left) 
and Oscar Fields, Bell's vice president of sales and merchandising (right).

Grammy Finalists 
Mahalia Jackson Dies At 60 
CHICAGO - Mahalia Jackson, the 
most prominent gospel artist ever and 
a prime force in the civil rights move- 
ment, died Jan. 28 in Little Company 
of Mary Hospital in Evergreen Park, 
Ill. At 60 years of age, she had been 
hospitalized a number of times since 
1964 and finally expired from heart 
seizure. 
At the height of her career, she be- 
came a prominent musical figurehead 
who succeeded in bringing black gos- 
pel music to the public -at -large. Her 
annual concerts at Carnegie Hall 
which started in 1950 were major 
events and her records sold in the 
millions. In 1963, she was chosen by 
Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. to sing 
at his March On Washington as a 
preface to his "I have a dream" 
speech. 
Born in New Orleans on Oct. 26, 
1901 in a poor but decent household 
of six children, Miss Jackson was the 
granddaughter of a slave. Her father 
was a longshoreman and barber whö 
doubled as clergyman on Sunday. Her 
mother died when she was six, and she 
was raised by Aunt Duke who brought 
her to Baptist Church every Sunday. 
Because she was poor, Mahalia 
Jackson left school in eighth grade 
and worked as a cook and washer- 
woman. She moved to Chicago in 1928 
and worked as a hotel maid and joined 
the Greater Salem Baptist Church, 
where she became a soloist in the 
chorus. 
She initially gained her popularity 
with black audiences with tunes such 
as "He's Got The Whole World In 
His Hands" and "God Gonna Sepa- 
rate," and a performing style that 
involved high energy rhythm and 
bounce. She moved entire audiences 
to dancing. Her performances for 
white audiences tended to be more 
somber and serious, but she loosened 
up more as she gained more popular- 
ity 
with world-wide audiences 
of 
mixed nationalities. 
Maybelle Smith 
Is Dead At 48 
CLEVELAND-Blue singer Big May - 
belle Smith died in Cleveland Metro- 
politan General Hospital, Jan. 23 after 
prolonged illness. She was 48 years 
old. Her illness was due to withdrawal 
symptoms from a 27 -year long nar- 
cotics habit that she acquired dur- 
ing her singing career, which started 
in the early 1940s. She leaves a daugh- 
ter and five grandchildren behind. 
Featured in a film, "Jazz On A Sum- 
mer's Day" and a headliner at the 
1958 Newport Jazz Festival, Miss 
Smith's 
best 
known 
records 
are 
"Candy," "96 Tear Drops," "Gospel 
Soul" and "So Long." 
Gene Austin, 71 
Dies In Fla. 
PALM SPRINGS-Gene Austin died 
in Desert Hospital of lung cancer, Jan. 
24. The 71 -year -old crooner and com- 
poser was known for his theme song, 
"My Blue Heaven," which sold over 
12 million records during his heyday 
in the 1920s. 
One of the first crooners, Austin's 
RCA recordings of over 100 original 
tunes sold more than 86 million copies. 
Among his hits 
were "Lonesome 
Road" (from the film, "Show Boat"), 
"Melancholy Baby," "Girl 
Of 
My 
Dreams," "Sleepy Time Gal," "Caro- 
lina Moon" and "Ramona." 
Austin also made three Hollywood 
films, "Melody Cruise," "Sadie Mc- 
Kee," and "Gift Of Gab." During the 
50s he made a comeback with tv and 
nightclub appearances. 
Born Eugene Lucas in Gainesville, 
Texas on June 24, 1900, he grew up 
in Louisiana and Maryland. Residing 
in Nevada in 1962, Austin unsuccess- 
fully tried for Democratic nomination 
as Governor of Nevada. He is survived 
by his fifth wife, Maxine, and two 
daughters from a previous marriage. 
Miss Jackson began touring abroad 
in 1952, with special attention in 
France and Israel. She played at the 
Newport Jazz Festivals in this coun- 
try when the fest set aside a special 
segment devoted entirely to gospel. 
Among her top selling Columbia al- 
bums were "Newport 1958," "Bless 
This House," and "I Believe." A two 
volume Columbia collection, "Gospel 
Sounds," contains many of her hits, 
including "When 
I Wake Up In 
Glory," "Just A Little While To Stay 
Here" and "I Will Move On Up A 
Little Higher." 
Mahalia Jackson was married and 
divorced twice and had no children. 
Her first husband was a chemist, Isaac 
Hockenhall. In 
1964 
she married 
Ministers 
Galloway, 
a contracting 
salesman. 
Jean Casadesus 
Killed In Crash 
ONTARIO-Jean Casadesus, 44, con- 
cert pianist, was killed in an auto col- 
lision, Jan. 20. He was enroute to a 
concert appearance in Sarnia. 
The son of pianists Robert and Gaby 
Casadesus, his musical family also in- 
cludes his greatuncles, conductor -com- 
poser Francois Casadesus and violin- 
ist Henri Casadesus. 
Casadesus lived in Paris, but was 
also artist in residence at N.Y. State 
University, Binghamton. He was born 
in Paris and studied at the Paris Con- 
servatory. After his family moved to 
the U.S., he studied under Eugene 
Ormandy. Since 1954, he had been a 
faculty member of the American Con- 
servatory in Fontainbleau. 
He is survived by a wife and daugh- 
ter, his parents, a stepson and step- 
daughter. 
Epilepsy Kills 
Michael Rabin 
NEW YORK - Michael Rabin died 
suddenly of an epileptic seizure in 
his Manhattan home last Jan. 19. The 
concert violinist who made his Car- 
negie Hall debut at age 13 is sur- 
vived by his parents. He was 35. 
Rabin's father was a first chair 
violinist for the N.Y. Philharmonic 
and his mother was a gifted pianist. 
Rabin studied piano under Ivan Gala 
and Galamian and then took further 
musical training at Julliard. In 1949, 
he won the Edgar Stillman Kelley 
Competition of the National Federa- 
tion of Music Clubs. 
Norman Foley Dead 
SCARSDALE, N.Y.-Music publisher 
Norman Foley died in his Scarsdale 
home, Jan. 22, at age 67. Survived by 
his wife, Gwen Williams, and two 
children, he had been retired for the 
last few years. 
Starting with the Feist wing of the 
Big Three in the 1940s, he worked 
up to general professional manager. 
Before that he was a songplugger for 
M. Witmark Publishers. After the Big 
Three, Foley started his own publish- 
ing firm for a few years and then 
joined Sam Fox Music as general pro- 
fessional manager until his retirement. 
Al Klein, Motown 
Alumnus, Dies 
NEW YORK - Al Klein, the former 
Motown album sales director, died 
last week. He had been with Motown 
through its earlier years before he 
went out on his own about four or 
five years ago. 
Harper As London's 
District Manager 
NEW YORK - John Harper has 
been named western regional district 
manager for London Records, ac- 
cording to Herb Goldfarb, sales and 
marketing vp. Harper is replacing 
Bert Annear, who is retiring after 25 
years with the company's San Fran- 
cisco -based post. 
Before coming to London Records, 
Harper worked for Trans -continental 
Distributing Corp. He will now cover 
markets in Seattle, Denver, Phoenix, 
El Paso, Great Falls and Honolulu 
and will coordinate all sales programs 
in the overall California market. Har- 
per will report to Herb Goldfarb in 
London's N.Y. headquarters. 
Famous Picks 
Larry Weiss 
NEW YORK - Marvin Cane, chief 
operating officer of Famous Music 
Publishing Co's., together with Julie 
Chester, have announced the appoint- 
ment of Larry Weiss to the profes- 
sional staff. He'll be responsible for 
acquisition development of Famous' 
contemporary catalog. 
Known predominately as a writer, 
Weiss previously ran an indie oper- 
ation encompassing production, pub- 
lishing, jingles and performing. He 
has also headed Bob Crevee's publish- 
ing, and Calus Ogerman's publishing 
and has worked as a&r man at Kapp 
Records. 
Of Weiss' 300 published songs, 30 
have reached chart positions, includ- 
ing "Bend Me Shape Me" (American 
Breed), "Mr. Dream Merchant" (Jerry 
Butler) and "Help Me Girl" (Eric 
Burdon). Weiss' existing publishing 
firms, Larry Weiss Music Ltd. (AS - 
CAP) and El Double -U Music Inc. 
(BMI), will now fall under the Fa- 
mous Banner for U.S. and Canada. 
Swenson Is 
Tara Veep 
NEW YORK-Dick Broderick, presi- 
dent of Tara Int'l, reports that effec- 
tive Feb. 1, Frank Swenson, former 
marketing director for international 
at MCA Records, will join Tara as 
vice president in charge of interna- 
tional sales. 
Immediate attention will be given 
by Swenson to the growth of South 
American Marketing, Inc., the Vene- 
zuelan company that is the licensee 
for MCA record labels in that coun- 
try. Tara represents SAMI in the 
United States as well as Ember Rec- 
ords and Youngblood Records of Eng- 
land. 
Joe Carlton To 
Hansen As VP 
NEW YORK-Joe Carlton has joined 
Hansen Publications as vice presi- 
dent in charge of Music Retailing 
Operations and Direct Marketing 
(the mail order division.) Hansen is 
the 
world's largest publisher 
of 
printed sheet music and music books. 
Carlton will b operating out of 
New York at Hansen's offices at 
1860 Broadway and will devote his 
efforts to the expansion of the firm's 
retail outlets, improvement of their 
current outlets, and will staff up the 
organization as it expands. 
Hansen owns approximately 40 re- 
tail music outlets and runs some 60 
others through rack jobbers and 
leased operations. 
Carlton is a veteran of the music 
business having served with RCA, 
Mercury, Columbia, ABC, the Rich- 
mond Organization and at one time 
had the hot Carlton label, one of 
the early successful indie manufac- 
turing operations. 
(Cont'd from p. 7) 
mental contributions. In addition, he 
has been picked for an arranging, a 
best musical composition and a best 
motion 
picture 
score 
nomination, 
while his "Theme from Shaft" album 
appears as an engineering finalist. 
Miss King also has been nominated 
as performer and composer, in the 
latter department for "You've Gat a 
Friend," in the former for her "Tap- 
estry" album, picked as one of the 
five best Pop, Rock and Folk Female 
Vocal Performances, where she is 
competing against "Gypsys, Tramps 
and Thieves" by Cher, "Me and Bobby 
McGee," by the late Janis Joplin, 
"The Night They Drove Old Dixie 
Down" by Joan Baez, and "That's The 
Way I've Always Heard It Should 
Be" by Carly Simon. 
Miss Simon has also been nomi- 
nated as Best New Artist of the year, 
along with the jazz-rock instrumental 
group 
Chase, 
two 
vocal 
groups, 
Emerson, Lake and Palmer, and Ham- 
ilton, Joe Frank and Reynolds, and 
singer -composer Bill Withers. 
Withers is also 
up for another 
Grammy for his Best Pop, Rock and 
Folk 
Male 
Vocal 
Performance of 
"Ain't No Sunshine." He competes 
here with Neil Diamond's "I Am, I 
Said," Gordon Lightfoot's "If You 
Could Read My Mind," Perry Como's 
album of "It's Impossible," and James 
Taylor's single of "You've Got a 
Friend." 
Two conductors, each with four 
nominations, head the list of classi- 
cal music nominees. Colin Davis' name 
appears twice on the Classical Album 
of the Year list for his batoning of 
the Berlioz "Requiem" and Tippett's 
"The 
Midsummer 
Marriage," both 
finalists also in the Best Choral and 
the 
Best Opera categories. Pierre 
Boulez has been nominated four times 
also. 
In the rhythm and blues field, last 
year's two vocal winners, Aretha 
Franklin and B. B. King, face strong 
opposition, as 
do Lynn Anderson, 
Ray Price, and Johnny Cash and June 
Carter, all winners in last year's 
country music field competition. 
In jazz, many -time Grammy recipi- 
ent Duke Ellington competes with 
Count 
Basie, 
Maynard 
Ferguson, 
Woody Herman and Buddy Rich in 
the big band division, while Bill 
Evans, last year's Grammy winner, 
heads against two separate groups of 
rivals in Best Jazz Solo and Best 
Small Jazz Group Performances. 
Flip Wilson, who unseated Bill Cos- 
by for a Best Comedy Recording 
Grammy last year, faces the same 
rival, plus several others this time. 
Cosby pops up again in the Best Re- 
cording for Children category, for his 
album of "Bill Cosby Talks to Kids 
About Drugs." 
Ballots, along with complete lists 
of nominations in all of the forty- 
four Grammy categories, go out to 
all Academy voting members the first 
week in February. They will be tabu- 
lated in utmost secrecy by the inde- 
pendent accounting firm of Haskins 
and Sells. Winners will be presented 
their Grammys on the Academy's 
hour -and -a -half 
television 
special, 
"The Grammy Awards Show," to be 
telecast nationally by the American 
Broadcasting Company on the eve- 
ning of Tuesday, March 14. 
The complete list of this year's 
Grammy nominations follows: 
Jones Earns 
Ninth Gold LP 
NEW YORK-Parrot Records art- 
ist, Tom Jones has been certified for 
his ninth gold LP, according to Herb 
Goldfarb, vp for sales and marketing 
at London Records. Parrot is a mem- 
ber of the London family of labels. 
The album, "She's A Lady," was re- 
leased in April. 
Jones recently returned to the U.S. 
for a tour lasting from February to 
September. He is currently on the 
charts with a double -LP set, "Live At 
Caeser's Palace." 
Two years ago, 
Jones received six gold LP's within a 
single calendar year.

Miami Beach To Sponsor 
Summer Fest; Playboy Tie 
NEW YORK - The City of Miami 
Beach, Florida, plans this summer to 
become the first American community 
to sponsor a major music fest. The 
City will base the Festival on Playboy 
Magazine's annual Jazz and Pop Poll 
winners. 
The two-week Miami Beach Play- 
boy Jazz and Pop Festival, in the 
manner of Berlin, San Remo and oth- 
er world cultural centers, has been 
approved and will be funded by the 
city's Tourist Development Authori- 
ty. It will run from Aug. 10 through 
Aug. 23, and will involve hotels and 
businesses throughout Miami Beach. 
The Miami Beach event will offer a 
wide range of top musical attrac- 
tions, many of whom are current or 
past winners of either the Playboy 
Readers' Poll or of the All -Star Musi- 
cians' Poll, made up of the previous 
year's all-star winners. 
TDA has named Charles Cinnamon, 
director of the Youngsummer '70 pro- 
mo and former director of special 
events for TDA, as festival director. 
Arlyne Rathberg, former entertain- 
ment director for Playboy Clubs and 
Hotels, will be the festival's producer. 
Playboy vice president Lee Gottleib 
will coordinate for his organization. 
Six Concert Nights 
The format contemplated for the 
Festival provides for six nights of 
concerts by "superstars" in contem- 
porary music, with two performances 
each night. Both of Miami Beach's 
major arenas, the 10,000 -seat Conven- 
tion Hall and the 3,500 -seat Miami 
Beach Auditorium, will be used. This 
would make a total of more than 120,- 
000 seats available for the 12 Conven- 
tion 
Hall 
complex 
performances 
alone. 
In addition, there will be other con- 
certs and special events to alternate 
with the appearance of the musical 
big guns. Some will feature up-and- 
coming talent. Others will be evenings 
with special theme, style, or ethnic 
appeal, such as Country and Western 
Night,Black is Beautiful Night, Latin 
Night, and others. 
Community musical groups, includ- 
ing the Miami Beach Symphony and 
Greater Miami Philharmonic, will also 
participate actively. The Festival is, 
in fact, planned as a community -wide 
enterprise, and has already been as- 
sured full cooperation of the City's 
hotels and tourist -oriented facilites, 
including 
airlines 
and 
-wholesale 
Certron: 
$9.8 Mil Loss 
In Fiscal '71 
Anaheim, Gal., Jan. 28, 1972. Cer- 
tron Crop. has reported a net loss of 
$9,877,000 and net sales from continu- 
ing operations of $12,466,000 for the 
fiscal year ended Oct. 31, 1971 com- 
pared with a loss of $2,057,000 and 
sales of $14,665,000 for 1970. 
Per share loss was $3.44 for 1971 
compared with .76 cents for the previ- 
ous year. Certron's net loss of $2,057,- 
000 in 1970 was after giving effect to 
a tax recovery of $1,898,000. 
Losses from continuing operations 
in 1971 were $3,743,000. Additionally, 
Edwin R. Gamson, president, said the 
firm incurred a loss of $5,193,000 
from discontinued operations and an 
extraordinary loss of $941,000 in the 
year just ended. 
According to Gamson, the company 
discontinued its proprietary lines of 
"budget music", record rack jobbing 
distribution, and computer tape man- 
ufacturing and distribution during 
1971. Certron manufactures and dis- 
tributes audio recording tape, cas- 
settes, 8 -track cartridges and preci- 
sion plastic products. The company 
believes that by concentrating its 
efforts in these areas, the results of 
its operations will be materially im- 
proved during the current fiscal year, 
Gamson said. 
travel agents. 
Playboy Magazine, with its 6,500,- 
000 circulation, worldwide prestige, 
and almost unlimited facilities for 
publicity and promotion, will cooper- 
ate fully with Miami Beach in ex- 
ploiting the Festival on a worldwide 
scale. According to Mr. Gottleib. the 
magazine has never before permitted 
the use of its Jazz and Pop Poll in 
connection with a commercial enter- 
prise. It is doing so now in the con- 
viction that the association with the 
Festival, backed by the City of Miami 
Beach rather than a private sponsor, 
can only reinforce the Playboy repu- 
tation for knowing and encouraging 
the best in contemporary music. 
Playboy Enterprises' own hotel in 
Miami Beach, the Playboy Plaza, will 
be one of those participating in the 
citywide promo. Playboy also plans 
an Awards Banquet to wind up the 
Festival period, with guests being 
winners of the 1972 Playboy poll. 
To get the Festival underway, TDA 
has allocated an initial $30,000. The 
total proposed budget for talent and 
staff is currently estimated at $360,- 
000. 
Cinnamon said that plans are al- 
ready well advanced for the sale of 
tickets on an international basis, and 
that travel arrangements with partici- 
pating ticket agents and airlines are 
certain to be made. 
The recent approval of TDA, and 
the actual launching of the Miami 
Beach 
Playboy 
Festival, 
climaxes 
more than six months of preliminary 
effort by John Huddy, entertainment 
editor of the Miami Herald, and Cin- 
namon. It was Huddy who originally 
authored the Festival concept for Mi- 
ami Beach. He first proposed the idea 
to the seven -member TDA last Aug., 
1971, but it was only recently that his 
efforts, Cinnamon's, and those of the 
Festival's champions on TDA, led by 
executive director N. Allen Robinson, 
actually bore fruit. The go-ahead on 
the Festival won approval by a five - 
to -two margin. 
Cy Coleman 
Composing 
3 Musicals 
NEW YORK - The forthcoming sea- 
son will be active for composer Cy 
Coleman as he moves in with three 
shows on Broadway. 
The first show will be "Beautiful 
People", (tentative title), which is a 
musical about a 48 -hour marathon 
Encounter session. The show will be 
produced by Herman Levin, who pro- 
duced "My Fair Lady" and "The 
Great White Hope", among many 
other successes. Book and lyrics are 
by James Lipton. 
Also this season Coleman is work- 
ing on a show based upon the play 
"Two For The Seesaw". The show 
will be called "Seesaw". The book is 
by Mike Stewart, who wrote "Hello 
Dolly" and "Bye Bye Birdie". Produc- 
ing "Seesaw" are Joseph Kipness and 
Lawrence Kasha, who are still enjoy- 
ing the fruits of their big hit "Ap- 
plause." Dorothy Fields is writing the 
lyrics. This is the first collaboration 
of Fields and Coleman since their suc- 
cessful Broadway play and motion 
picture, "Sweet Charity." 
Along with `Beautiful People" and 
"Seesaw" there will be a revival of 
"Little Me" with a revised book by 
Neil Simon. 
All of the standard songs from 
"Little Me", which include "I've Got 
Your Number", "Real Live Girl", "On 
the Other Side of the Tracks", and 
others, will be retained, and new 
songs by Coleman and Carolyn Leigh 
will be added. 
Starday-King Plant Up 
For Sale; Seek Cash Flow 
NEW YORK-In a move to generate 
the extraordinary cash flow needed 
to implement Starday-King Records, 
a new "aggressive" policy to "move 
away from the catalogue sales image 
and into heavy recording of new acts 
in all phases of popular music," the 
Nashville based firm is liquidating its 
entire $llia million Cincinnati manu- 
facting complex. 
Starday-King president Hal Neeley, 
who instituted the new thrust sev- 
eral months back, said last week that 
all the pressing, printing, studio and 
lithographic machinery at the Brew- 
ster Street facility is up for sale. The 
real estate itself will also go on the 
market shortly. 
"We're signing many new acts in 
the Rock, R&B, MOR and Country 
areas to augment our present roster," 
Neeley, stated "we are into a heavy 
recording and release schedule now. 
We've reactivated our New York of- 
fices and have Leiber & Stoller doing 
A & R for us there." 
Neeley revealed that cash flow was 
only one of the reasons for putting 
the Cincinnati complex on the block.

Stax Investor 
In 1st Musical; 
Cast LP Outlet 
NEW YORK - The Stax Organiza- 
tion is stepping into the Broadway 
musical area for the first as a major 
investor and original cast LP outlet 
for "The Selling Of the President." 
Show is based on Joe McGinnis' 
best-seller, adapted for the stage by 
Jack O'Brien and Stuart Hample with 
lyrics by O'Brien and music by Bob 
James. Starring is Pat Hingle in the 
role of George Mason, presidential 
candidate for 1976. 
The opening is set for Mar. 29 at 
the Shubert Theatre. While it was 
given a tryout last April at the 
American Conservatory Theatre in 
San Francisco, a Philadelphia run 
will start on Feb. 22. Described as 
"electronic vaudeville," the show will 
be directed by Robert Livingston, who 
directed the hit musical, "The Me No- 
body Knows," John Flaxman is pro- 
ducing in association with Harold 
Hastings and Franklin Roberts. 
Stax is a solid -winner with its first 
soundtrack LP, "Shaft," featuring Is - 
sac Hayes. Al Bell, exec vp of the 
firm, promises "numerous moves" into 
the leisure -time area. 
Bernstein, 
Rodgers Set 
New Musicals 
NEW YORK - Veteran musical the- 
atre talents are planning a return to 
Broadway next season. 
Leonard Bernstein is expected to 
write the music for a treatment of the 
Yiddish stage classic, "The Dybbuk," 
with staging by Jerome Robbins. No 
librettist or lyric writer has been 
named. 
Richard Rodgers is expected to 
team with Sheldon Harnick on a mu- 
sical 
version of "Arsenic 
& 
Old 
Lace." Michael Stewart would do the 
book. 
Of more immediate promise is "Da- 
mon Runyon's Broadway," with music 
by Daniel DiMinno and lyrics by Mor- 
ty Neff. Edward Padula is producing 
for an April opening.

NARM Confab 
Is SRO; Add 
18 New Members 
PHILADELPHIA - NARM's exec di- 
rector Jules Malamud, declares that 
the association's 14th annual conven- 
tion, which will be held 
Mar. 
5 
through Mar. 10 at the Americana 
Hotel in Bal Harbour, Florida, had 
posted its "Standing Room 
Only" 
sign, well before the official closing 
date for convention registration. 
There are no more accommodations 
available at the three convention ho- 
tels (Americana, Balmoral, and Beau 
Rivage). The 66 spots in the Person 
to Person Conferences, which will be 
held in the pool and ocean cabanas, 
have been reserved by manufacturers 
of records, tapes, and allied products. 
18 New Members 
Among the companies registered 
for the convention, are the 18 new 
members, who have joined NARM 
since January 1. New members are 
Berlitz Publications of New York 
City; Camrose Productions of Plain- 
view, New York; Jefferson Depart- 
ment Stores of Miami, Florida; King 
Karol Records of New York; Nation- 
al Record Mart of Pittsburgh; Post 
Records of Philadelphia, Pa.; the 
Post-Pasin 
Organization 
of 
New 
York City; Promo Record Distribu- 
tors of Patterson, New Jersey; Roll- 
ing Stone Magazine of San Francis- 
co; Roper Records of Jenkintown, 
Pa.; Seaway Records of Cleveland; 
Signpost Records of Los Angeles; 
Sounds Distributing Corporation of 
Pittsburgh; TDK Electronics of Long 
Island City, New York; Tracy -Val 
Company of Westville Grove, New 
Jersey; Twinight Records of Chicago; 
Waxie Maxie Quality Music of Wash- 
ington, D.C.; and Wendy Distributors 
of Newark. 
The largest group of regular mem- 
bers ever to attend a NARM Conven- 
tion will hold its annual meeting on 
Monday, Mar. 6, during the conven- 
tion. 
CPM & NEC: 
Meet Seeks 
Stronger Ties 
NEW YORK-Personal manager and 
GWP Records president Jerry Purcell, 
who is president of .the Conference of 
Personal Managers and also is on the 
advisory committee of the National 
Entertainment Conference, has set a 
separate meeting between top officials 
of the CPM and NEC to discuss the 
strengthening of the relationship be- 
tween the two organizations when the 
NEC holds its annual convention in 
Kansas City this Sat. (12). 
The CPM is an organization of 120 
personal managers representing a 
majority of the creative and perform- 
ing artists in show 'business. 
NEC represents the cultural activit- 
ies for more than 500 colleges in the 
United States.

HARVEST-Neil Young-Reprise MS 2032 
No question about it. Neil Young's "Harvest" 
has been the most eagerly awaited LP of the 
new year. It's been well worth the delay. This 
collection of ten songs --all of them Young 
originals-can take its place right up there 
with "After The Gold Rush." More than ever 
before Neil opens himself up, affording us 
more than just a glimpse of the inner work- 
ings of his brain. His hopes, his fears and 
especially his disillusionment are revealed in 
dramatic and bold fashion. Least effective cuts 
are those featuring the London Symphony 
Orchestra; when Neil and his basic accom- 
panists-the Stray Gators-are alone, there is 
magic 
in the air. Singer's current smash, 
"Heart Of Gold," is here too. A bountiful 
harvest indeed. 
I CAPRICORN-Shirley Bassey-United Artists 
UAS-5565 
The cover is gold and shiny-almost blind- 
ing. But what is really blinding is the talent of 
the singer within. Known initially as the "Gold- 
finger" girl, Shirley Bassey has gone on to 
carve out a very special niche for herself 
among distaff vocalists. She has a remarkable 
way with a song and nowhere is this better 
demonstrated than on items like "Where Am 
I 
Going?" (from the show "Sweet Charity" and 
"Where Is Love?" (from Oliver"). Ten other 
tunes round out the package. 
FM 
& AM-George Carlin-Little David 
LD 
7214 
For several years now George Carlin has 
been building a dedicated following composed 
of folks who like their humor imaginative, fast 
and mad. With "FM & AM" he takes a major 
step forward. Even the grumpiest of grumps 
would have to grin as Carlin takes random 
pot shots at everything from birth control to 
Ed Sullivan. As the title might indicate, the 
LP is divided into two parts-one more suit- 
able for AM play, the other a bit freakier. Set 
was recorded at the Cellar Door in Washing- 
ton. Easily one of the best comedy records in 
recent memory. 
"BRIAN'S SONG" THEMES & VARIATIONS- 
Michel Legrand-Bell 6071 
With "Brian's Song" speeding up the singles 
chart and after his great success as composer 
of the "Summer Of '42" theme, Michel Le- 
grand is riding high these days. This album 
represents something of 
a 
greatest movie 
themes type of package-it features the 
maestro on a generous assortment of his film 
compositions, 
including "Summer Of '42," 
"Wuthering Heights," "The Go -Between," and 
his Oscar winner "The Windmills Of Your 
Mind." Set could make a strong bid for chart 
action.

CHAPLIN'S 
BACK-Darius 
Brubeck-Para- 
mount 6026 
In a meticulously premeditated, arranged, 
designed and produced album, Darius Brubeck 
emerges as a musician of great conceptual 
skill and sensitive insight. The son of Dave 
Brubeck who followed in his father's fingertips 
on piano, Darius has assembled themes from 
various Charlie Chaplin films, shedding light 
on the little-known fact that Chaplin composed 
his own film scores on piano. The sound is 
Chaplin and the piano style bears the stamp 
of two Brubeck generations. 
The backup is 
tops, featuring hornman Michael Brecker and 
guitarist Amos Garrett. Chaplin's back and 
Darius has arrived; we will hear more from 
both. 
SILK & SOUL-Lou Rawls-MGM 4809 
Few artists so successfully straddle the MOR 
and soul markets as does Lou Rawls, and his 
second LP for the label should enjoy the suc- 
cess of its predecessor. His new single is here 
("His Sung Shall Be Sung") as well as a beau- 
tiful reading of Lennon-McCartney's "Golden 
Slumbers," the classic "Here Comes That 
Rainy Day" and Michel Legrand's "Watch What 
Happens." On the rousing side, "Hallelujah 
For A Friend" should be in for its share of 
attention. A perfect blend of fireworks and 
felicity.

CABARET-Soundtrack-ABCD 752 
"Cabaret" has come triumphantly to the 
screen as a play with music rather than an 
outright musical comedy. This has necessitated 
plot structure and song changes, but it's all 
for the better in a more realistic screen treat- 
ment. Liza Minnelli may emerge as the first 
superstar in years not out of the rock scene. 
And Joel Grey repeats his masterful portrayal 
as the Kit Kat Club emcee. Wilkomen "Cabaret" 
on screen and this soundtrack LP. 
OH HOW WE DANCED-Jim Capaldi-Island 
9314 
In the past few years, Jim Capaldi has 
undergone transitions, but this is the most 
major one to date. Starting out as the drum- 
mer for Traffic, 
Capaldi was there as the 
group broke and reformed over and over. 
Since the "Live From The Canteen" LP, Capaldi 
switched positions in Traffic from drummer to 
frontstage vocalist. And now he emerges as a 
solo performer, singing his own compositions. 
Although upon inspecting the credits on this 
LP and finding all the old Traffic crew as 
backup, it seems as though this transition is 
merely a change of title, it is not so. The 
Traffic members, in addition to the superb 
Muscle Shoals studio band, have backed Ca- 
paldi in his own distinctive style. The special 
feature of the LP is a rock remake of Al 
Jolson's "Anniversary Waltz." 
LETTERMEN 1-Capitol SW -11010 
Trio has dropped the definite article from 
their monicker but have lost none of the touch 
which has carried them into the Seventies in 
fine fashion. One major difference though: 
there is a good deal more soloing here than 
on previous albums. Lennon's "Oh My Love" 
sets the pace for a bevy of contemporary tunes, 
among them "Day After Day," "Anticipation," 
"Never Been To Spain" and "An Old Fashioned 
Love Song." Chalk up another winning entry 
for this group. 
HEADS & TALES - Harry Chapin - Elektra 
75023 
Even before this album was released, there 
was a considerable amount of buzzing re. the 
talent of Harry Chapin-much of it generated 
by his highly unusual composition entitled 
"Taxi." Now the young singer proves that he 
has the capability to live up to seven the most 
optimistic forecasts. Chapin is literally like a 
breath of fresh air-with his voice he can 
create a mood almost instantly and in many 
of his songs, mood is quite important. For 
example, in "Dogtown," a cold and gray -hard 
recreation of a bustling whaling town. "Could 
You Put Your Light On, Please" and "Some- 
time, Somewhere Wife" are two more sparklers. 
To be sure, "Taxi" is here too. "Heads & Tails" 
signals the arrival of a completely original, 
clear-sighted talent of major proportion. 
THIN 
LINE 
BETWEEN LOVE AND HATE- 
The Persuaders-Win Or Lose SD 33-387 
The line separating this group from other 
r&b acts is a big and bold one. They have a 
strong vocal style and the distinctive use of 
up -front vibes going for them, and that's the 
combination that brought a gold record to the 
title single. You can expect their debut LP to 
continue the ever-increasing trend for soul 
albums to sell heavily in Top 100 markets, 
sparked by their second release "Love Gonna 
Pack Up" and the intricate "Mr. Sunshine" 
which should figure as a key airplay item. 
BEALTITUDE: 
RESPECT 
YOURSELF - The 
Staple Singers-Stax STS -3002 
A 
profoundly religious, yet totally com- 
mercial 
offering, partly 
named after their 
million -selling hit, and partly after verses from 
Matthew. Each tune is about the heavenly 
kingdom, either obliquely or directly, yet each 
can 
be boogied with. The Staples' religious 
message is directed at joy, peace and happi- 
ness and they fear nothing, including success. 
Airplay will no doubt be directed at "I'll Take 
You There," "Name The Missing Word" and 
"Who Do You Think You Are?" They were the 
first 
Jesus -rockers, 
and their 
appeal 
has 
crossed the r&b-pop barrier for good reason.

A&R.

album by Ashton, Gardner, Dyke & 
Co., titled "What A Bloody Long Day 
It's Been." Debut albums by English 
artists Spontaneous Combustion and 
Gallagher & Lyle are also scheduled. 
"Recall The Beginning ... A Journey 
From Eden" is the title of the latest 
album by the Steve Miller Band, also 
inked on March 6.

New Simon LP 
NEW YORK - Polydor Inc. has an- 
nounced the immediate release of Joe 
Simon's new Spring album Drowning 
in the Sea of Love. The album con- 
tains the title song, Simon's recent 
million -selling gold record, and his 
current smash "Pool of Bad Luck". 
The album and the above mentioned 
singles were all produced by soul- 
hitmakers Gamble and Huff. 
Simon, feted by Polydor and Spring 
in honor of his Gold Record at New 
York's Hippopotamus (Feb. 22), has 
just completed an engagement at New 
York's Apollo Theatre, at which he 
broke opening -day attendance records 
for the theatre. Simon is currently 
engaged in an extensive cross-country 
tour, and will continue a heavy sched- 
ule of interviews with both trade pub- 
lications and consumer -oriented music 
magazines which began during his re- 
cent stay in New York. 
Polydor and Spring are sure that 
the album comes at the very crest of 
the wave of Simon's popularity, and 
will atempt to use the album as one 
way of expanding his career to in- 
clude many areas of musical interest 
and taste. 
Advertising plans call for extensive 
use of print advertising in under- 
ground, soul and overground mar- 
kets, as well as radio spots in selected 
markets. 
Promotion will be aimed at MOR, 
top -40 and thythm and blues markets. 
as are "The Best of Buddy Alan" and 
"Praise the Lord" by Wanda Jackson. 
From Island Records, a debut al- 
bum by Claire Hamill comprises the 
Mar. release. Called "One House Left 
Standing," the LP is the first by the 
young British singer -writer. 
Blunstone 
To Promo LP 
NEW YORK - English singer Colin 
Blunstone arrived here last week on a 
promotional visit in connection with 
his debut LP on Epic, "One Year." 
Formerly lead singer for the Zom- 
bies, Blunstone recorded his first solo 
album with production and songwrit- 
ing aid from Chris White and Rod 
Argent, two other Zombies. A tour is 
tentatively being set for mid -May. 
Blunstone will currently remain in 
New York for a week of press inter- 
views and then jet to California for 
several days.

Paperback Deal 
NEW YORK - Kable Books, major 
national newsstand and rack distribu- 
tors, has been granted exclusive dis-

traces the career of Three Dog Night,

Night's personal managers, Reb Fos- 
ter Associates, Inc.

attraction.

of 
its 
ABC/Dunhill albums has been a Gold

190 pages.

8 Albums Spark London's 
Closing Of Fiscal '71-'72 
NEW YORK -A major release, in- 
volving key elements of its catalog, is 
being rushed to market by London 
Records as the firm moves toward the 
close on March 31 of one of its most 
successful fiscal years in history. The 
release, numbering eight new albums, 
is the largest so far to be issued dur- 
ing company's 25th anniversary year. 
The new "Hellhound Train," LP by 
Savoy Brown from England, was the 
subject of a special one -day crash 
meeting of the entire London nation- 
al promo force 10 days ago. The al- 
bum is being rushed to tie in with the 
opening of the group's five -week na- 
tional tour which began Friday (25) 
on the West Coast. 
Chicken Shack, a stablemate group 
of Savoy Brown in its British man- 
agement set-up, will have its first al- 
bum to be released through London. 
The company has major plans for this 
group in terms of special promo and 
merchandising to be set in motion 
when the group undertakes a new 
tour here later this year. 
Next up is a new album by Ann 
Peebles, on the Hi label, distributed 
by 
London. 
She 
is 
now 
being 
groomed to follow in the footsteps of 
her eminently successful label -mate, 
Al Green, who has just scored with 
two consecutive gold singles. The 
Peebles LP is titled "Straight from 
the Heart." 
Also in the works is the latest from 
10 Years After, titled "Alvin Lee and 
Brit. Wave 
Puts London 
On The Alert 
NEW YORK - London Records is 
marshaling its cross-country family 
of promo staffers for long-term Brit- 
ish Sound activity. In fact, two of the 
four acts involved in the latest flurry 
of promotion, Tom Jones and Engel- 
bert Humperdinck, are to be in the 
U.S. for better than six months, once 
they arrive within the next few weeks. 
The armada of attractions leads off 
with the hot group on Parrot, Savoy 
Brown, whose new LP, "Hellhound 
Train," has just been rushed to stores 
to tie-in with the tour promo. The 
tour, which began Friday (25) in San 
Diego, is in every sense a national 
trek, covering states throughout the 
country and concluding April 29 in 
suburban Chicago, after dates in New 
York and New England the week 
prior to the close of the safari. 
Next up is the Moody Blues on 
Threshold Records, distributed 
by 
London, which flies in for one of its 
fortnight, big -dollar grossing efforts, 
including major engagements in large 
arenas in the midwest, east and the 
southwest. Toronto, Ontario, is also 
on the itinerary. The group's current, 
gold -winning LP, "Every Good Boy 
Deserves Favour," has been on the 
national charts since last fall. 
Tom Jones begins his lengthy U.S. 
stay with his first -ever performance 
in the South, in Atlanta on March 14. 
The tour carries on from that time 
until late Sept. Humperdinck arrives 
a month later, playing his first en- 
gagement at Framingham, Mass.

On Son's LP

ther, John S. Stewart, will make his 
record debut on his son's forthcoming 
Warner Bros. LP, "Sun Storn," sched-

His voice is heard on "An Account of 
Haley's Comet" 
on the album in

Comet in 1910 in Lexington, Ken- 
tucky. The younger Stewart worked 
on putting the song together for a 
month, adding a chorus to the narra- 
tive. The background singers include 
John Stewart, 
Buffy Ford, Bryan 
Garofalo and Henry Diltz. The selec- 
tion is produced by John and his 
brother Michael Stewart.

Sporn Opens 
Coast Office 
HOLLYWOOD-Murray Sporn, New 
York music publisher and record com- 
pany exec, has announced the opening 
of Hollywood offices at 6430 Sunset 
Blvd., (213) 466-0498. 
Besides further development of his 
music publishing operations, Sporn is 
president of Angel Music, Inc., and 
Fairland Music Company. Sporn will 
reactivate his record company oper- 
ation under the name of Sparerib 
Records, and will inaugurate a per- 
sonal management division. 
Sporn's background in the music 
business is extensive. He was an asso- 
ciate/consultant to Phillip J. Levin, 
MGM director, and from 1958 to 1966 
Sporn headed up American Metropo- 
litan Enterprises, Ltd., and also was 
president of the ASCAP firm, Broad- 
way Music, Inc., and the BMI firm, 
Tideland Music Publishing Corpora- 
tion and Berkshire Music Corpora- 
tion, and Rush Music Ltd. (England), 
also headed up President Records.

CHICAGO - Mercury Records has

eight -piece group. Senior vp and di- 
rector of marketing Lou Simon dis-

A forecoming nationwide tour is 
being set by Heller-Fichel, Aura's 
new booking agency. Simon said ad- 
vertising would be extensive in the 
contemporary newsprint area as well 
as through paid radio for the Chi- 
cago -based group.

McBride, midwest and international 
director of A&R. 
Lee Morgan 
Fatally Shot 
NEW YORK-Lee Morgan, the jazz 
trumpeter, was shot and killed while 
performing here at Slugs on Sat., 
Feb. 19. Police said a woman, Helen 
More, described as his common-law 
wife, shot him. She was held with- 
out bail until action by a grand jury. 
Morgan, a star on the Blue Note 
label, toured in the 50's with Dizzy 
Gillespie and the Art Blakey Jazz 
Messengers. Morgan, 33, recorded 12 
albums for Blue Note.

Steady Now' Talent Drive 
NEW YORK - Steady Records has 
launched a campaign seeking further 
recognition in the contemporary mu- 
sic field. Activity is spear -headed by 
the patting of what it feels to be 
several important musical artists. All 
are disk acts in keeping with the sales 
phenomena of cafe personal appear- 
ances being used as effective sales 
tools in stimulating the sale of sin- 
gles. 
Among the artists signed are: Phil 
Flowers, Joey Dee, Louis Lee and 
Kaye Stevens. Remaining with the 
company is Eddie Lovette. 
The company also has pacted the 
Original American Touring Company 
and the American Rock Opera Com- 
pany, both of which play numerous 
college concert dates in the U.S. and 
Canada. 
Last year, Steady invested in the 
Broadway production of "Ari", the 
musical adaptation 
of 
Leon Uris' 
"Exodus" and is continuing its partic- 
ipation in Broadway via the Broad- 
way property, 
"Catch 
My Soul," 
which won major awards last year in 
its West End and touring produc- 
tions. Film rights to "Catch My Soul" 
have been sold to Metromedia for an 
undisclosed price. Road show appear- 
ances by the American Original Rock 
Opera Company and the 
Original 
American 
Touring 
Company 
are 
scheduled prior 
to its 
Broadway 
opening. 
A 
deal for distribution in the 
United States was recently signed be- 
tween the Steady Phase II operation 
and Scepter Records. In addition to 
the new artist deals, Steady has com- 
pleted negotiations with Victrix Pro- 
ductions, which recently produced the 
Beverly Bremers chart disk, as well as 
Johnny Maestro who will produce for 
Steady. 
Outside production deals are now 
being set for the artists with Tone 
Production Centers of Miami Beach 
whose current chart productions in- 
clude "Clean -Up Women" and "Funky 
Nassau". 
In the foreign field, Steady is in the 
process of renewing overseas licen- 
sing agreements which expire next 
month. 
Steady President Art Trefferson 
predicted further excitement with the 
evolving trend of Reggae music, the 
Jamaican beat popularized in Aretha 
Franklin's "Rock Steady" and Paul 
Simon's latest single, "Mother and 
Child." Trefferson predicted a trend 
already in evidence in many of Man- 
hattan's discotheques.
