Camden List 
Cut To $2.49 
NEW YORK - RCA Records has re- 
vised the suggested list category of 
Camden Records from $2.98 to $2.49, 
effective Feb. 21. 
Herb Linsky, director of Camden 
product, noted that: "Camden caters 
to an impulse market. It benefits the 
manufacturer, the distributor, and the 
ultimate consumer when this mer- 
chandise is priced to 
obtain the 
greatest possible volume. Many items 
in the Camden catalog have sold very 
well, but the bulk of the Camden line 
is intended for mass merchandising. 
This new price is intended to greatly 
increase our overall exposure of prod- 
uct." 
RCA Records pioneered the econo- 
my priced record market when it in- 
troduced the Camden label more than 
15 years ago. The active catalog con- 
tains the most significant names that 
were ever recorded under the RCA 
banner. 
WB/Reprise 
Switch To

NEW YORK - As part of the compa-

INSTRUMENTAL DIRECTIONS-The Nite Lit- 
ers-RCA LSP-4580 
They're coming on fast on the instrumental 
scene and their name is the Nite-Liters. "Afro - 
Strut," their current single smash, is here and 
it sets the stage for a bunch of superfine 
numbers, among them "Wichita 
Lineman," 
"Cherish Every Precious Moment," "(Them) 
Changes" and a medley of "MacArthur Park" 
and "What's Going On." Oh, and the "Theme 
From Shaft," 
sounding better than 
ever. 
Should win a ready following in no time at all. 
UNCLE JIM'S MUSIC-Kapp KS -3661 
From out of the West (Los Angeles, any- 
way) come Uncle Jim's Music, a very mellow 
five man band. The eleven songs are in 
a 
rock/country vein and among the instruments 
well utilized are harmonica, amplified violin, 
fiddle and pedal steel, the latter played with 
commendable taste and control by one Thomas 
Whitehorse Dunstan. This is a sit back and 
listen kind of LP so all we can say is sit back 
and listen! You'll find it enjoyable. 
TRANQUILITY-Epic E 31084 
What is in a name anyway? A lot in this 
case. Tranquility, a new British group, plays 
music which is well, kind of tranquil. But not 
tranquil in a dull way. More like in a restive 
and laidback way. For their first album the 
quintet has assembled some first class songs, 
most of them composed by vocalist and lead 
guitarist Terry Shaddick. "Look At The Time 
It's 
Late," 
"Walk 
Along The 
Road" 
and 
"Oyster Catcher" deserve your attention. 
Jazz Picks 
CONSTANT THROB-John Klemmer-Impulse 
AS -9214 
Let's put it this way; this isn't exactly what 
you'd call mainstream jazz. On the contrary, 
it's adventurous and innovative jazz-some of 
it high flying, some of it close to the roots. 
Klemmer is a sax player of skill and imagina- 
tion and his accompanists are all of the top 
drawer variety-fellows like Jim Keltner, Shel- 
ley Manne and Howard Roberts. "California 
Jazz Dance" is an eloquent up -tempo thing, 
while "Crystaled Tears" gives Klemmer the op- 
portunity to play softly and movingly. Marni 
Nixon shows up on the title track and acquits 
herself very nicely indeed. Jazz aficionados will 
gobble this LP up but those who normally pre- 
fer other types of music should also find it 
interesting. 
SCIENCE FICTION-Ornette Coleman-Colum- 
bia KC31061 
All through the changing Sixties, there have 
been certain musicians who have proceeded 
ahead, confident that they were in the van- 
guard of things. Ornette has been one of 
these. Though often labeled a jazz musician, 
he truly transcends such classifications. "Sci- 
ence 
Fiction," 
his 
latest release, 
is 
aptly 
named. The eight songs here are voyages into 
the outer limits of arranged as well as impro- 
vised music. "What Reason Could 
I Give," 
featuring a haunting vocal by Indian artist 
Asha Puthli, and "Rock The Clock," a wailer 
on which Dewey Redman contributes some 
highly unusual musette work, are only two of 
the excellent tracks. Ornette, playing his usual 
variety of instruments, is masterful through- 
out. 
THE PHILOSOPHY OF THE SPIRITUAL-Rich- 
ard Davis-Cobblestone 9003 
Richard Davis is the 'bass player; when other 
top bassists talk of virtuosity, style and tech- 
nique, the conversation will inevitably revolve 
around Richard Davis. Aside from his continu- 
ous stream of studio work, Davis plays with 
the Thad Jones -Mel Lewis Orchestra, the N.Y. 
Bass Violin Choir and has sat in with the Bos- 
ton Symphony Orchestra under the baton of 
Igor Stravinsky. This album, on Buddah's Cob- 
blestone subsid, explores new musical realms 
as well as old. The new pieces are from the 
second bassist on the LP. Bill Lee, while Davis' 
revised version of "Dear Old Stockholm" can 
be traced through Miles Davis and Stan Getz 
to Swedish roots. Pianist Chick Corea, guitarist 
Sam Brown, drummer Sonny Brown and per- 
cussionist Frankie Dunlop play for this set.

even as late as '58, they could take a twenties -flavored tune like "Sugartime" 
and turn it into a million seller for Coral records. The McGuire Sisters often put 
their family disagreements out into the open: Phyllis McGuire split from them to 
go solo more times than Ed Sullivan didn't smile. 
TV helped keep Ricky Nelson a powerhouse for Imperial records. While a solo 
performer, much of his appeal beyond the teen audience was attached to his 
family role on ABC's "Ozzie And Harriet" sitcom. TV also worked well for the 
talents of The Everly Brothers. Years before they got a summer replacement 
series of their own in 1970 they became staples of other TV variety shows after 
their first disk, "Wake Up Little Suzie" became a million seller on Cadence. While 
they've certainly known their ups and downs since (and who hasn't), they've 
just released a new LP, "Stories We Could Tell" on RCA. 
As the fifties came to a close, The Isley Brothers established themselves on 
that label with "Shout" and have since known a number of hot periods. Last 
year, they ranked as Cash Box's #2 r&b group. They now record for their own 
Buddah-distributed label, T -Neck. 
The most productive years for family acts were, without question, the 60's and 
early 70's. For those years produced groups that are still giants in the industry 
today. The mid 60's saw the emergence of husband and wife team, Sonny & Cher 
whose "I Got You Babe" in 1965 turned into one of the years biggest. More re- 
cently, the same combo scored million sellers with "All I Ever Need Is You," and 
"Gypsies, Tramps and Thieves," Cher's solo effort. 
In the late 60's, the scene shifted to the entire family as a recording act. The 
Cowsills, via much tv exposure, garnered gold for their "The Rain, The Park And 
Other Things," and "Hair" efforts while three brothers, terribly famous in Austra- 
lia, were preparing to make their American debut. The Bee Gees (brothers Barry, 
Robin, & Maurice) struck it rich with their "New York Mining Dis-ster," "Massa- 
chussets," "Holiday," "Words," and a string of others bringing us to their latest 
goldies, "Lonely Days" and "How Can You Mend A Broken Heart." 
Late in 1969, there emerged a Motown family act who has succeeded in 
recording one million seller after another. The Jackson 5, who debuted on the 
Ed Sullivan Show in Dec. of '69 have a string of million sellers to lengthy to 
mention. And as if that weren't enough, young Michael Jackson, lead vocalist of 
the group stepped out as a solo performer only to prove that their list of hits is 
indeed endless. Michael's "Got To Be There" went on to become an inst-nt num- 
ber 1 single, and his follow-up, "Rockin' Robin" will do the same. Currently the 
subjects of a Saturday morning cartoon show. their exposure on nationwide tv 
has served to further establish the J5 as America's number one family. 
Not too far on the heels of the J5 are The Osmonds who for years were the 
clean cut kids appearing with Andy Williams on his weekly series. Now, with "One 
Bad Apple" and "Yo-Yo" certified as million selling singles, Donny Osmond steps 
out on his own to earn gold awards for his solo efforts, "Sweet & Innocent." 
and "Go Away Little Girl." And it looks as though his re -make of the Paul Anka 
classic, "Puppy Love" will do the same. 
But not all of the family acts were actually families. Many were put together 
for appeal. Case in point: The Partridge Family who have sold millions of records 
based on the popularity of their Friday evening tv show and the youthful appeal 
of David Cassidy who, as a soloist has done exceptionally well with "Cherish" 
and "Could It Be Forever." 
Apart from the aforementioned groups, other Family acts now being repre- 
sented on the charts are The Poppy Family, The Adrissi Brothers and Ike & Tina 
Turner. Interesting, is the fact that a major portion of these success stories were 
written on nationwide television-with The Partridge Family, The Osmonds, The 
Jackson 5, Sonny & Cher, and Ike & Tina Turner all being subject to extensive 
viewing audiences. Even recent newcomers, Karen and Richard Carpenter have 
had tv specials to further their appeal. 
It now seems apparent that the music industry will always serve as an outlet 
for those talented families who have something unique to offer. Because of its 
appeal, and because there are no age barriers to overcome, it looks as though 
the pop music scene will continue to be a family affair. 
Kenny Kerner & Robert Adels 
SOUNDTRACKS-Evolution Records released it's first album, "Paintings" by 
newly signed artist Mike Quatro, and the album received an unusual premiere 
with the Kansas City Symphony. 
Quatro, a keyboard artist, who conceived, arranged, and produced the album, 
filled some 32 basic tracks while playing 8 different keyboard instruments. 
"Paintings", (the album title and one of the 8 original songs) is credited to the 
"Mike Quatro Jam Band", actually composed of only 2 people, Quatro and drum- 
mer Terry Mullens with the only addition to the album being guitar tracks and 
vocals. 
Quatro and the Jam Band on a college concert tour through the midwest and 
just coming off a highly successful concert at the University of Wisconsin, was 
invited to perform as guest artist with the Kansas City Symphony, and as p:rt 
of the arrangement he was asked to do a 40 minute "set" prior to the concert ... 
reproducing "live" his new Evolution album 
. 
. 
. 
a mixture of rock, boogie, and 
classical material. Radio station KBEY-FM taped the set and the concert and 
broadcast both that same night. 
An extra bonus to the evening was the fact that the NEC convention (college 
concert bookers) was taking place in Kansas City the same weekend ... and by 
special invitation of DMA (Diversified Management Associates) of Detroit (Quatro's 
agent), some 200 bookers were present at the concert. 
Leo Fenn, Quatro's manager, reported one interesting sidelight. The audience 
at the Quatro/Kansas City Symphony appeared to be 70% youth oriented (under 
30), an unexpectedly high ratio for a basically classical performance. 
Honk, a four -man group with a sizeable west coast following, has been signed 
to score and write the title theme of a new film, "Five Summer Stories," being 
produced by the award -winning team of Greg MacGillivray and Jim Freeman. 
Two of Honk's original recorded songs, "Don't Let Your Goodbye Stand" and 
"Smoke," on the Prince label, will be used in the production. The Beach Boys 
are also contributing various tunes to the film. 
MacGillivray-Freeman produced the films "Sunshine Sea" and "Waves of 
Chance." The new movie has a March deadline.

out. "Can you think of anything more germane than a guy writing and arranging 
for his sister?" asks Daugherty. 
Richard says "A year or so ago, an interviewer from a magazine asked us each 
a list of questions, separately. The funny thing is, not only did we answer all the 
questions the same, when we were asked things like our favorite groups we'd 
answer in the same order." 
Karen and Richard still live with their parents, in suburban Downey. "We go 
out together a lot. Just yesterday, we all went to the Miller 500." The drive into 
Hollywood is thirty minutes; the two work out song concepts on the way in. "We 
can have the whole album done in half an hour," Karen kids. 
"It's a matter of working together. Richard plays piano, arranges and writes. 
I do most of the singing. And we both know each other's strengths and weak- 
nesses. We consider our groups part of the family, too. We always use the same 
rhythm section on our records, and the band that tours with us has always been 
the same-no one's ever left it. The singers went to school with us, and had the 
same music teacher." 
Anything else about families that enters your career? "We get a lot of families 
at our concerts. Parents and their children get dressed up, go out to dinner, and 
come to see us. They tend to think of us as part of their family. A lot of our fan 
mail has requests from people expecting us to help with their problems." 
Karen and Richard had to return to their recording session. There's an obliga- 
tion, after all. to those families to m'ke good product available to them. We 
promised to meet again, and discuss Karen's statement that their personal musical 
tastes were very decidedly non -MOR. "We like The Beatles, The Chi -Lites, Rare 
Earth, The Stylistics and The Mothers of Invention. But we owe it to our audiences 
to stay within certain musical boundries. A lot of that stuff we couldn't do if we 
wanted to, anyway. You don't have to sound like somebody to like them." 
Karen and Richard Carpenter. Besides being talented, they're 
a couple of 
decidedly nice people. You know ... like part of the family.

NOTES TACKED TO THE HOLLYWOOD RANCH MARKET BULLETIN BOARD 
Lest we forget that the term "artist" refers to people other than musicians, our 
friend John Van Hamersveld has opened a month -long exhibition of his photo- 
graphy under the collective title of "The Interval." The series of photos details 
the collected experience from several recent years of John's life; because he travels 
many of the same paths that we do, a bit of your life might be in there too. 
John is, of course, well known in local record company circles; that and the 
scope of his work as an illustrator can be indicated by his two Grammy nomina- 
tions this year. One is for the cover of Jimmy McGriff's "Black Pearl" album; the 
other, which John co -designed with Ed Thrasher is Warners' "Hot Platters." The 
Long John Baldry cover didn't make the semi-finals. Most of John's work with 
record companies is for album covers, the advertising people haven't figured 
out how to best avail themselves of his talents as yet. 
But as clever and popular as he is as a designer, John's first love is the photo- 
graphy exhibited as "The Interval." It's at 209 San Juan Street (off Main) in 
Venice, afternoons through March 30. All photographs are for sale, including that 
of Kim Fowley standing in front of the Troubadour (two landmarks for the price 
of one). If you're looking for something to remember L.A., or New York, or London, 
or any of a number of shared experiences by, you might do well to stop and 
visit John.

Hughes LP Via 
Double -Shot 
HOLLYWOOD - "Will The Real 
Howard Hughes Please Stand Up ?," 
a comedy album featuring Dave Bar- 
ry & Company, is being rush -released 
by Double -Shot Records here. The la- 
bel's co -presidents, Hal Winn and Ir- 
win Zucker, are also co -producers of 
the album. 
The writers, headed by Martin A. 
Ragaway, 
include Arthur Philips, 
Stanley Ralph Ross and Milt Rosen. 
Ragaway 
is 
an 
"Emmy"-Award- 
winning TV comedy writer. Ross is 
also one of the actors on the album, 
along with Norman Bartold, Eddy 
Carroll, Paul Dubov, Connie Hunter 
and special guest star Selma Dia- 
mond. 
Comedian 
Dave 
Barry 
plays 
Howard Hughes on this comedy LP, 
which 
co -producer Zucker predicts 
"will give the entire industry the shot - 
in -the -arm it needs." Zucker adds: 
"It's an album that will bring in the 
traditional non -record buyer, similar 
to what happened with Vaughn Mead- 
er and the `First Family' LP." 
Barry opens a three-week date 
March 24 at Harrah's in Lake Tahoe 
and then a four -week stand starting 
April 13 in Las Vegas at the Fron- 
tier-a Hughes hotel.

To Project 3 
NEW YORK - The Brass Ring 
featuring Phil Bodner has signed a

label.

baret" b/w a Latin treatment of the

Vic Damone's 
25th Anny 
BEVERLY HILLS - Vic Damone, 
who began his first professional en- 
gagement as a singer on March 8, 
1947, at La Martinique night club in 
New York, this month is marking his 
25th anniversary as an entertainer. 
The singer had been recommended 
to La Martinique's owner by Milton 
Berle, who had heard him sing on an 
amateur program. 
Damone currently co -headlines at 
Las Vegas' Riviera Hotel with Totie 
Fields. 
Island Signs 
First US Act 
MUSCLE SHOALS - London -based 
Island Records have signed their first 
U.S. artists for worldwide distribu- 
tion on the Island label. They are 
Smith, Perkins & Smith from Muscle 
Shoals, Ala. 
All native Alabamans, the grow 
consists of two brothers, Tim (25) 
and Steve (23) Smith, and Wayne 
Perkins (20). 
As a session musician with the 
Muscle Shoals Sound Rythmn section, 
Perkins' guitar playing has appeared 
on numerous albums for a variety of 
musicians, including Joe Cocker, Leon 
Russell, Albert King, Delaney & Bon- 
nie, Lonnie Mack, Percy Sledge, the 
Everly Brothers and Alex Taylor. 
Both the Smith brothers write, pro- 
duce. arrange and play keyboards and 
guitar. All three share vocals. 
Smith, Perkins & Smith's debut al- 
bum, which will be distributed in the 
U.S by Capitol Records, will be re- 
leased in early April, according to 
Liza Williams, President of Basin 
Street West which represents Island 
in the U.S. Immediately following re- 
lease of the album, produced by David 
Hood for Muscle Shoals Sound Pro- 
ductions, the group will begin an ex- 
tensive European tour.

Axioms Prod's. Expands Activities 
HOLLYWOOD - Axioms Produc- 
tions, a locally -based company, 
is 
expanding activities into many areas 
of the entertainment industry. They 
are currently involved with a TV 
show, a comedy radio program in 
syndication, college concerts, record 
production, music publishing and mo- 
tion picture scoring. 
The talent roster includes Paul 
Shapiro, a singer and songwriter, 
whose first album will be released 
this fall. Dick Glass, "The Eloquent 
Elephant," who will star in the com- 
pany's production for television, "The 
Adventures 
of the Eloquent 
Ele- 
phant," has also signed a recording 
contract with the Axioms label. Mario 
Feninger, concert pianist and com- 
poser, 
is 
another 
Axioms 
artist, 
scheduled for a syndicated television 
program, concert tours and recording. 
The Key -Out Players are an im- 
provisational comedy theatre group, 
performing 
in Southern California 
and syndicating their radio comedy 
series, "Rip Rope and His Horse 
String." The company is also current- 
ly producing a college concert pro- 
gram combining the talents of Paul 
Shapiro, Dick Glass and the Key -Out 
Players. The show is called "Beautiful 
Day, Beautiful People." 
Axioms Productions is headed by 
Dale Benson, former independent film 
producer and director. Executive vice- 
president is Ken Gerbino, formerly 
with the Capitol Record Club. 
Ben Smith 
Hospitalized 
NEW YORK, NY - Ben Smith, 
veteran musician and arranger, has 
been admitted to the Sydenham Hos- 
pital 
at 
565 
Manhattan Avenue. 
Smith, suffering a partial paralysis, 
entered the hospital March 8. His 
condition is listed as satisfactory, ac- 
cording to Hospital spokesmen. 
Currently, 
with 
offices at 
1697 
Broadway, Smith has been offering 
professional music services to count- 
less performers and writers since en- 
tering the local scene in 1934. He has 
also been producing independently as 
well as producing for other record 
labels. 
Smith is allowed visitors and visit- 
ing hours are obtainable by checking 
with the Sydenham Hospital.

Broido Joins 
Presser Board 
BRYNMAWR, 
PA. - Theodore 
Presser Co. has announced the elec- 
tion of Arnold P. Broido to its board 
of directors. Broido, who joined the 
music publishing firm as president in 
1969, is also chairman of the board of 
its subsidiary company, Elkan-Vogel, 
Inc. 
Broido previously served in execu- 
tive posts for Boosey and Hawkes, 
Inc., Mercury Music Corp., Edward B. 
Marks Music Corp., Frank Music 
Corp. and the Boston Music Co. He 
was a member of the board of direc- 
tors of the Music Educators National 
Conference from 1966 to 1968, pres- 
ident of the Music Industry Council 
from 1966 to 1968, and served on the 
Rockville Centre, New York, Board of 
Education from 1963 until 1969. He is 
presently first vice-president of the 
Music Publishers Assoc., a member of 
the board of directors of the Ameri- 
can Music Center and a member of 
the board of directors of ASCAP.

Polydor's 5 LP's 
NEW YORK - Polydor Inc. has an- 
nounced a release of five new albums. 
The release includes new albums from 
Mandrill, Jake with the Family Jew- 
els, Roy Ayers Ubiquity, Cat Mother 
and the debut album by Ellen Mcll- 
waine. 
Mandrill's second album, "Mandrill 
Is" continues sojourns into rock, Lat- 
in, soul and jazz. The album, pro- 
duced by Al Brown, is highlighted by 
"Git It All". Tour plans for the group 
are currently being set, with an ap- 
pearance at New York's Academy of 
Music tentatively set for April. 
Ellen Mcllwaine's "Honky 
Tonk 
Angel" is a combination of "live" and 
studio recording, the first side having 
been recorded at New York's Bitter 
End, while the second side was re- 
corded at the Record Plant. Produced 
by Polydor's Peter Siegel, the album 
is Ellen's debut. Ms. McIlwaine has 
recently completed an engagement at 
Philadelphia's Main Point, appearing 
with Polydor's Lily Tomlin. 
There is a new album from Jake 
with the Family Jewels called "The 
Big Moose Calls His Baby Sweet Lor- 
raine". Produced by Ed Freeman, who 
produced Don McLean's "American 
Pie" album and single, the album is 
Jake's (also known as Allan Jacobs) 
second release for Polydor. 
Jake with the Jewels recently com- 
pleted an engagement at New York's 
Folk City and will soon be heard at 
Max's Kansas City. 
A new album from 
Roy Ayers 
Ubiquity titled "He's 
Coming" 
is 
highlighted by Ubiquity's current sin- 
gle "He's a Superstar". The album 
and 
single 
were 
produced 
by 
Myrnaleah Williams, who also man- 
ages the group. Roy Ayers Ubiquity 
recently completed an engagement at 
New York's Pee Wee's. 
A new release from Cat Mother 
titled "Cat Mother" continues that 
band's combination of country and 
city rock and was produced by Cat 
Mother at New York's Electric Lady 
Studios. Currently engaged in a suc- 
cessful tour of England, the group 
(formerly known as Cat Mother and 
the All Night Newsboys) is managed 
by Michael Jefferey, manager of the 
late Jimi Hendrix. 
Niles Inks 
Duberstein 
NEW YORK - Duke Niles has 
signed Chuck Duberstein as an artist 
for his D.N. Productions and as a 
writer for Rayven Music. Niles has 
cut 
four 
sides 
with 
Duberstein, 
formerly a member of the 5th Estate, 
which scored some years ago with 
"Ding Dong! The Witch is Dead." 
PUBLICATION OF THE YEAR'S BIGGEST HITS TO DATE 
Because Cash Box is continually asked to supply a list of the year's leading hits to A&R men, 
record producers and radio stations, etc., Cash Box offers a continuing feature that lists the 
year's Top 50 titles as of the date the feature appears. The feature is published in the last 
issue of each incnth and is compiled from the Cash Box Top 100 Sales Chart. Point system 
operates as follows: For each week a song is m1 on the Top 100 it receives 135 points. Each 
record is awarded 123 points. No. 3 gets 122, No. 4 gets 121, No. 5 gets 116. From No. 6 
thru 10 songs get 115 to 111 points respectively. No. 11 songs get 90 points and so on 
down the line till the No. 50 song which gets 51 points. Only the top fifty titles of any given 
week are included in the survey. Survey begins with the first issue in January.

THEY'RE HAVIN' A PARTY-Columbia Records recently held a party at 
New York's Tavern On The Green in honor of Delaney & Bonnie newly signed 
to the Columbia label, and Kenny Loggins & Jim Messina who have signed 
with Epic. Shown above are Delaney and Bonnie Bramlett with label presi- 
dent, Clive Davis, and Loggins & Messina performing at the affair. 
Others in attendance included Kris Kristofferson, Loudon Wainwright III, 
and Ornette Coleman being embraced by Davis. Affair ended with a jam ses- 
sion by D&B, Rita Coolidge, and John Hammond. 
Jarrett Joins 
Playboy Music 
HOLLYWOOD - Playboy Music's 
After Dark Music, Inc. (BMI) has 
completed negotiations 
with 
Mike 
Campbell, composer Michael Jarrett's 
manager, 
which 
brings 
Jarrett's 
53 -tune catalog into the Playboy Mu- 
sic fold, with current and future song 
publishing to be shared among After 
Dark, Oten Music Pub. (BMI), and 
Little Bit Music Inc. (BMI). Latter 
firm is co -owned by Jarrett and man- 
ager Mike Campbell (Campbell House 
Corp.) . 
Michael Jarrett, who has been writ- 
ing since 1955, took a break from 
touring two years ago in order to 
devote his time to composing. His 
most recent chart -topper was "I'm 
Leaving," recorded by Elvis Presley. 
Jarrett will debut on Playboy with an 
April release featuring ten oringinal 
songs 
published 
under the After 
Dark/Oten Music Pub./Little Bit Music 
Inc. arrangement.

door is

Soul Power 
Label Formed 
SHREVEPORT, LA. - The Jewel 
Record Corp. and Sound/City Rec- 
ording Corp. have formed Soul Power 
Records, with all three labels based in 
Shreveport. Sound/City is responsible 
for all production and Jewel takes the 
ball from there with distribution and 
promotion. 
The first release under the new 
agreement is "It's Not How Long 
You Make It" by Shay Holiday. 
George Perkins has just been signed 
by Soul Power and his first record is 
in the pressing plant and due for 
immediate release. The song "A Man 
In Lone", was written and produced 
by Jerry Strickland. People instru- 
mental in forming the new label are 
Stan Lewis and Gene Kent of Jewel 
and Jerry Strickland, George Clinton 
and Stewart Madison of Sound/City. 
Another Soul Power record due for 
quick release is an instrumental cut 
by the Sound/City staff band, The Af- 
402. Telephone number is (213)-274- 
6741.

`Medicine' As 
CBS Book -Album 
NEW YORK - Columbia Records 
has released "Medicine, Mind and Mu- 
sic, a Consideration of Their Links 
Through the Centuries," thirteenth in 
a series of book -and -record sets in 
the CBS Legacy Collection, prepared 
under the direction of Goddard Lie- 
berson, 
CBS senior vice president. 
"Medicine, Mind and Music" is a two - 
record set with a deluxe 53 -page illus- 
trated book. 
"Medicine, Mind and Music" was 
produced by Lieberson. Fred Karlin 
and Meg Welles Karlin did the musi- 
cal research and Fred Karlin was mu- 
sic director. Mr. Karlin has recently 
been working in Hollywood, where 
his song "For All We Know" from 
"Lovers and Other Strangers" won an 
Academy Award and his score for the 
movie "the Baby Maker" was also 
nominated for an Oscar. 
The performers range from the 
blues team 
of Sonny Terry and 
Brownie McGhee to the distinguished 
classical harpsichordist Igor Kipnis. 
Meg Welles Karlin is heard in several 
English songs. 
Dial: Tex Gold 
And Allmans LP 
CHICAGO - Dial Records is working 
on a number of projects simultane- 
ously, rather than concentrating on 
one specific item, reports Buddy Kil- 
len, vp of the Nashville -based label 
that is distributed by Mercury Rec- 
ords. He claims, "We're in a position 
to pursue a lot of different direc- 
tions." 
What gave them the position to 
move is Joe Tex's "I Gotcha," which 
was recently certified by RIAA as a 
million -selling single. A new Joe Tex 
album, entitled "I Gotcha," is com- 
pleted and set for release soon, ac- 
cording to Killen. 
Also coming soon is a package re- 
corded in the late 1960's by Duane and 
Greg Allman (The Allman Brothers) 
when their group was called Allman 
Joy. Also set for release soon are the 
singles by rock artist Dutch Ross and 
country act Donald Wayne. 
Other artists on the Dial roster in- 
clude Gunilla Hutton of "Hee Haw," 
the Nashville Edition and Johnny 
Lee.

To Atlantic

who

by

soon.

with the success of her soul hit "Make 
Me Yours", in 1967 on the Money 
Records label.

at the Century Plaza Hotel in Los Angeles, on Mar. 14, winning artists dis- 
play their treasured prizes. Shown above are Sam Samudio displaying his 
Grammy and nomination plaque for best album notes, "Sam, Hard & Heavy;" 
Tina Turner winning for the Ike & Tina Turner rendition of "Proud Mary," 
and Charley Pride with two Grammys for best gospel performance (Let Me 
Live), and best sacred performance, (Did You Think To Pray). Pride was 
also a presenter on the program. 
Second row shows Capitol Records president, Bhaskar Menon accepting Gov- 
ernors award honoring Glenn E. Wallichs. Award was presented by a NARAS 
founder, James B. Conkling (left). Best album cover award is received by 
Gene Brownell and Dean Torrance, while Pat Boone and family proudly dis- 
play their nominations for their album, "The Pat Boone Family," which was 
nominated in the category of best sacred performance.

SESAC Vote 
Salute At 
NAB Confab 
NEW YORK -A salute to America's 
1972 Presidential elections and the 
national "Get Out The Vote" cam- 
paign will provide the theme for 
SESAC's popular hospitality suite 
(Room 900) at this year's annual con- 
vention of the National Association 
of Broadcasters, to be held at The 
Conrad Hilton Hotel, Chicago, April 
9-12. 
Designed to highlight the role that 
America's radio and television broad- 
casters will again play in this Pres- 
idential election year, SESAC's Suite 
900 at The Conrad Hilton will feature 
portraits 
of the presidents, from 
George Washington to Richard Nix- 
on, displayed in a colorful patriotic 
motif reminiscent of political rallies 
of years gone by. Live entertainment 
will be provided nightly by Chicago 
pianist Eddie Fritz, a favorite of 
SESAC suite visitors to the N.A.B. 
two years' ago, who will bring back a 
repeat of his "sing -along" stylings. In 
addition, a photographer will be on 
hand to photograph the individual 
convention delegates in the suite and 
then mount their photos on plastic - 
covered 
"campaign 
buttons" 
and 
award them as souvenir mementos. 
One room of the three-room suite 
will be decorated as an old fashioned 
Chocolate Shoppe where, in cooper- 
ation with the Chocolate Manufactur- 
ers Association of the U.S.A., dele - 
vates will be invited to "Explore the 
World of Chocolate" and to enjoy hot 
chocolate and other "goodies" as they 
learn how these delicacies were first 
discovered more than 400 years ago. 
1972 marks the 23rd consecutive 
year that SESAC has opened the 
doors to its hospitality suite at the 
annual 
N.A.B. get-togethers. 
This 
year, the suite will be open daily be- 
ginning Sunday, April 
9, through 
Wednesday, April 12, from 9:00 AM 
to 10:00 PM. SESAC representatives 
scheduled to be in attendance include: 
A. H. Prager, executive vice president 
and managing director; Salvatore B. 
Candilora, vice president and execu- 
tive administrator; Signey H. Guber, 
director of marketing services; Nor- 
man Odlum, director of copyright ad- 
ministration; Charles Scully, director 
of information services; Aleene Jack- 
son, 
public 
relations 
coordinator, 
Nashville 
office; John Eckenrod, of 
the Broadcast License department, and 
field 
representatives Harold 
Fitz- 
gerald, Bob McGarvey, Glenn Ramsey 
and Tom Snowden.

Revives 
Rock Classics

Records.

one of the most successful artists and 
repertoire directors in the history of 
the music industry, has recently been 
conducting 
symphony 
orchestras 
throughout the country. The "Sugar" 
score is by Julie Styne & Bob Mervil-

NEW YORK - Ron Shelley, pres-

The entire series of concerts was pro-

area.

the second.

Werner Ties -Up 
Perf. Rights 
LOS ANGESLES - Fred Werner, 
who composed the Grammy Award - 
winning "Desiderata" narrated by 
Les Crane for Warner Bros. Records, 
has completed negotiations on a con- 
tract with the copyright proprietor of 
the poem, Robert Bell and Crescendo 
Publishing Company of Boston. In so 
doing Werner has legally established 
that "Desiderata" may now be per- 
formed as a musical work only with 
his, Werner's, consent. The composer 
has been "anxious to clear up discre- 
pancies that have existed in the past 
regarding `Desiderata,' " and negoti- 
ated the present contract through his 
Old St. Paul Music Publishing Com- 
pany, a Screen Gems affiliate. 
"Desiderata" has been widely dis- 
tributed in poster form for many 
years, reputedly having its origin in 
Old St. Paul's Church, Baltimore, 
dated 1692 when in fact it was written 
by the late poet Max Ehrmann in 
1927. Werner has been through an 
exhaustive legal search to unravel 
complex details as to how the poem 
come to be printed as a separate 
piece. 
Werner now feels that once the mu- 
sic industry and "responsible parties" 
become aware of the copyright he 
holds, there will be no more infringe- 
ments on his works. 
OLD FRIENDS - Arthur 
(L.) has announced the signing of 
singer -songwriter John Herald (R.) 
to an exclusive long-term manage- 
ment contract with his No Soap Mu- 
sic organization. Herald, formerly a 
member of the Greenbrier Boys, is 
now a solo artist with his own back 
up band. 
In 
addition 
to handling John's 
career as a recording artist and per- 
former, No Soap Music is establish- 
ing a publishing company for John, 
to handle and control his copyrights. 
Among the songs that have brought 
Herald success are "Stewball" and 
"High Muddy Waters" as recorded by 
Joan Baez, Peter, Paul & Mary, and 
Linda Ronstadt.

NEW YORK - Cartridge Television 
Inc. has moved its executive offices to 
larger quarters in New York City, at 
460 Park Avenue. The new offices will 
also 
house the corporation's 
pro- 
gramming department and first New 
York showroom. 
The expanded headquarters facility 
will serve as the primary location for 
Frank Stanton, president of the com- 
pany, 
Samuel 
W. 
Gelfman, vice- 
president of programming and pro- 
duction and Denis B. Trelewicz, vice- 
president, treasurer and secretary of 
the corporation. 
The enlarged programming facili- 
ties at the New York location include 
complete screening and editorial ca- 
pabilities, and demonstration rooms 
for both programming and hardware. 
The eastern institutional sales office, 
the promotional research organiza- 
tion, the movie rental operation and 
other elements of the company's pro- 
gramming department will be housed 
in the New York headquarters. 
Cartridge 
Television 
Inc. 
also 
maintains a marketing and adminis- 
tration facility at Palo Alto, Califor- 
nia, headed by Donald F. Johnston, 
vice-president of marketing, and man- 
ufacturing and engineering facilities 
at San Jose, California, under the di- 
rection of Charles D. Brown, vice- 
president of operations.

LOU DENNIS 
NEW YORK - Lou Dennis has been 
appointed director of tape operations 
for Warner Bros./Reprise Records, re- 
ports Ed Rosenblatt, director of mar- 
keting. Dennis, who will be based in 
Burbank, will report to Roseblatt and 
will oversee Warner Bros. entrance 
into the tape field. Dennis' appoint- 
ment follows the announcement that 
under the recent renegotiated contract 
with Ampex, Warner Bros. will now 
market 
all 
tape 
configurations 
through the WEA national distribu- 
tion system. Ampex will continue to 
manufacture the tapes. 
Dennis has been with Warner Bros. 
since 1967, in the capacity of eastern 
regional sales manager. Prior to his 
assocation with Warner Bros., Dennis 
was the product manager of Smash - 
Fontana Records. In comments on his 
appointment and Warners' commit- 
ment to the tape market, Dennis said, 
"It affords Warner Bros. an opportu- 
nity to utilize its successful WEA dis- 
tribution arm to merchandise and sell 
tapes in a unique and creative man- 
ner. The same innovative techniques 
that have been applied to records will 
now be applied to tapes-and then 
some."

Four Ampex Corp.

SUNNYVALE - GRT Music Tapes is 
placing its promotional muscle behind 
gospel music in a month -long pro- 
gram beginning Monday, April 10, 
titled "Gospel Soul Of GRT." The 
program covers 
69 tapes selected 
from GRT's catalog of naterial from 
the Chess, Checker, Westbound and 
Peacock labels. 
All 69 gospel titles will be released 
in 8 -track, with selected titles in cas- 
sette and open rool, stated Dick 
LaPalm, the company's advertising- 
promQ-tion manager. 
The campaign is the first all-out 
effort by GRT Music Tapes to em- 
phasize gospel music. Two months 
ago, GRT Music Tapes released 20 
gospel tapes, and "the response was 
so good we decided we would devote 
an entire month to promoting the 
music." 
GRT will concentrate on 12 markets 
"where the citizenry appreciates and 
supports such music," LaPalm said. 
These 
cities 
include: 
Philadelphia, 
Washington, Baltimore, Newark, At- 
lanta, Nashville, Dallas, Chicago, De- 
troit, St. Louis, the San Francisco - 
Oakland area and Los Angeles. 
The company will deal directly with 
one -stops and retailers who cater to 
gospel audiences by providing them 
with special order forms, consumer 
pocket catalogs, posters and other 
aids. The company's 16 salesmen will 
call on these accounts to make sure 
they have received this material and 
to explain the program. 
Aretha Franklin heads the list of 
artists in the release. "The Gospel 
Soul Of Aretha Franklin" was one of 
her first recorded efforts. LaPalm 
points out. (Miss Franklin is current- 
ly preparing another LP of gospel 
music.) 
Other gospel performers offered are 
the Mighty Clouds of Joy, Five Blind 
Boys, the Violinaires, the Soul Stir- 
rers and the Rev. C. L. Franklin. 
LaPalm, who selected all the mate- 
rial, says the criterion was on album 
sales and name power in the field. 
NEW YORK - Harry Lefkowitz, 
president of GBC Closed Circuit TV 
Corp. (NASDAQ), reports that his 
company has purchased four oper- 
ating branch offices of the Ampex 
Corp. for an undisclosed sum. 
The offices, which are reportedly 
doing two million dollars in sales an- 
nually, are located in Detroit, Chica- 
go, St. Louis and Indianapolis. Under 
the terms of the purchase, GBC has 
acquired the entire inventory of each 
of the offices, as well as their oper- 
ating personnel. In addition, GBC, 
which claims 
to 
be 
the nation's 
"largest distributor of closed circuit 
television equipment," will also be- 
come the distributor for Ampex prod- 
ucts for the states in which each 
branch is located. 
"GBC intends to continue the dis- 
tribution of Ampex products in these 
particular markets at the same high 
degree of integrity and standards 
which Ampex has always maintained. 
The new offices will serve as GBC 
branches in the same manner as our 
Boston 
office which became 
oper- 
ational 
last 
summer." 
Lefkowitz 
stated.

New Activity For Skye Label 
NEW YORK - The 
Skye Records 
catalog, now being distributed by 
Buddah Records, is experiencing new 
activity. Skye will release product 
from its previously recorded masters, 
the first two to be released on the 
Cobblestone label. They are "The 
Chuck Rainey Coalition" and Bob 
Freedman's "The Journeys Of Odys- 
seus". 
"Coalition" features four drum- 
mers, Bernard Purdie, Ken Rice, Herb 
Lovelle, Jim Johnson; three guitars, 
Cornell Dupree, Eric Gale, Billy But- 
ler; 
two 
percussionists, 
Warren 
Smith, Specs Powell; congas by Mon- 
tego Joe; organ and piano by Richard 
Tee, and additional piano by George 
Stubbs-all led by Rainey himself on 
electric bass. 
"The Journeys Of Odyesseus" is a 
jazz suite for chamber orchestra writ- 
ten by Bob Freedman and featuring 
Hubert Laws, 
Jerome 
Richardson, 
Marvin Stamm, Ron Carter, Richard 
Davis and "Bucky" Pizzarelli-plus 
Freedman's 
"chamber 
orchestra" 
which he conducts. 
A third new Skye album to be re- 
leased has just been recorded in New 
York and is a first for the talented 
young composer/singer, Roger Shriv- 
er. Featured players are Grady Tate 
on drums, Richard Davis on bass, 
Sam Brown and Bob Mann on acou- 
stical guitar, 
Marvin 
Stamm 
on 
trumpet and flugelhorn, and Joe Far- 
rell on woodwinds. The arrangements 
and conducting were done by David 
Krivoshei. 
Other Skye plans for the "future 
include an album of "The Best of 
Gary McFarland, 1968-1971" featur- 
ing the late composer/arranger's top 
recordings on the Skye label.

Mike Nesmith 
CASTAWAYS, NYC - Kenny, who 
runs this upper east side musical 
oasis continues to select from among 
my personal and as yet, unsuperstar- 
ry favorites without prior consulta- 
tion. This gives me a lot of faith in 
the future of the bar/club scene. The 
most recent bravo is connected with 
his booking of RCA's Mike Nesmith, 
a man who has a profound under- 
standing of both people and music 
himself. 
It's now four, going on five LPs 
past the Monkees. The screams have 
been supplanted with quiet admira- 
tion. No one owns just one Nesmith 
LP, and those who have heard him 
collect them like we used to favor 
baseball cards. Fanatics, yes-and for 
good reason. Here is an artist whose 
music is about rather than simply is. 
The object of his focus is western 
music, which reflects more fo1ky roots 
than what Nashville and Bakersfield 
presently call their own. Nesmith is 
one of the few still writing in this 
style, and one of a handful who can 
put across its most memorable stan- 
dards. "Jo -Ann" was his biggest self - 
recorded hit and he's still revered for 
"Different Drum," but before he cut 
one note for RCA, he had assembled 
nine LPs worth of originals, other 
new 
fangled portraits and time- 
honored canvases of the art and is 
just beginning to reveal the complex 
clockwork inside his mind. 
His stage presence is a very posi- 
tive yet laid-back thing which no one 
should miss. His methods cannot fully 
be dealt with here, so watch the "In- 
sights & Sounds" feature for further 
illumination. But we had a real good 
time that we defy anyone to sit 
through a Nesmith set and label him 
just another Monkee who don't stop 
no show. 
r.a, 
David Pomeranz 
Revival 
TOWN HALL, NYC - The crowd 
was small but committed. At this 
point, so is the relative standing of 
Decca's David Pomeranz in the pop 
pantheon. But while so many singer/ 
songwriters are retreating into self- 
made wombs of introspection and in- 
troversion, a few (Polydor's Ellen 
Mcllwainne also comes to mind) are 
not only rebels, but have cause. David 
does not put on an act, but he sure 
knows how to put on a show. 
He opened 
on guitar with "You 
Can't Do That" and encored with 
"Jailhouse Rock." And during each, 
you hardly were conscious of John, 
Paul, George, Ringo or Elvis. They 
came across vibrantly fresh and per- 
sonal, tinged with the jazzy enthusi- 
asm that might be of future extension 
of Cat Stevens when and if he should 
decide to gamble on a new sound 
that'll keep his present fold while im- 
pressing the formerly aloof. David 
mostly plays piano, but is also gifted 
with David Mason in his quartet, giv- 
ing himself the freedom to play either 
keyboard or guitar. His originals are 
all fine, all different. 
So are his 
moods. 
Many artists are pleasant to hear, 
few are interesting. Pomeranz is a 
"few" who in time shall be discovered 
by the many. 
Opening the show, Buddah's Re- 
vival. They are spirited, but have 
seemingly chosen to limit their base 
of operations to the electrified exten- 
sions of pre -progressive folk-rock. 
Things kind of get louder than this 
description might imply, and certainly 
funkier, but the core is unmistakably 
neither nostalgia nor what passes for 
normalcy on the current rock scene. 
Dig their attitude, dig their sound. 
It's that simple. Their music requires 
an open mind. 
r.a. 
Bobby Goldsboro 
WESTSIDE ROOM, L.A. - It was 
Bobby Goldsboro's debut at this Cen- 
tury Plaza Hotel supper club, and the 
United Artists singer handled the oc- 
casion to nearly its-and his-best 
advantage. Sitting on a stool, guitar 
in hand and backed by the string and 
horn -laden Al Pellegrini Orchestra 
and three of his own rhythm players, 
Goldsboro whisked through a dozen 
songs, of which eleven were hits ei- 
ther for or written by the singer him- 
self. His patter was interesting and 
assured, and his guitar playing was 
considerably 
stronger 
than 
just 
"functional." 
During the show, it became clear 
that Goldsboro is perhaps a greater 
talent than the music press generally 
gives him credit for being-"See the 
Funny Little Clown," "I'm a Drifter," 
"Broomstick Cowboy," "With Pen iii 
Hand" and the more recent "Califor- 
nia Wine" are really good songs, and 
Goldsboro wrote them all. 
Other tunes 
performed 
included 
Sonny Curtis' "Straight Life," plus 
"Love 
the 
One 
You're 
With," 
"Watchin' 
Scotty 
Grow", 
"Your 
Song" and, inevitably, "Honey." All 
came through strong and clear in 
Goldsboro's versions. 
t.e. 
Billy Joe Royal 
P.J.'s, L.A. - Billy Joe Royal, the 
man with the biggest sob in his 
throat since Johnnie Ray's heyday, 
made an all -too -infrequent appear- 
ance in this Vegas lounge -styled room 
and proved that he's every bit as 
good as he's always been. 
Backed 
by 
a 
seven -piece 
band 
(three horns) called Thunderchicken, 
Royal combined several of his hits ("I 
Knew You When," "Hush," "Cherry 
Hill Park" and "Down in the Boon- 
docks") with several current successes 
by other artists. The high quality of 
Royal's versions of "Without You," 
especially, and "Honky Tonk Wom- 
an" and "Superstar" (the Murray 
Head number, not the Carpenters') 
indicated that Royal's recent "cool" 
period might be due more to lack of 
the right material than to any lapse 
in his considerable vocalizing ability. 
t.e. 
Honk 
SANTA MONICA CIVIC AUDITORI- 
UM, L.A. - Being the warm-up band 
for a surfer movie isn't exactly ideal 
exposure for a group, even if they did 
the soundtrack for the film. Honk had 
the opportunity and, though they're a 
fine band, muffed it badly. 
The group opened with "When I'm 
Dead and Gone," and the McGuinness - 
Flint jumper was the only uptempo 
tune of the long set. The rest of the 
program consisted of some nice but 
slow-paced originals, a brace of Jack- 
son Browne tunes, and "When Roose- 
velt Came to Trinidad," which they 
took from the most recent Ry Cooder 
album. The set was as dreary as it 
was long; the sound was without 
doubt the least definitive, boomiest, 
bassiest ever heard in these parts 
(and that's saying a lot), and the 
audience was quite justifiably unap- 
preciative. 
All that is unfortunate, though, be- 
cause the group is obviously quite 
good. Your basic country -rock instru- 
mental line-up with especially good 
vocals and part singing, they add 
spice to their sound with harmonica, 
accordion and steel guitar. The drum- 
mer is especially strong, able to gen- 
erate a nice Allman Bros, shuffle 
that, 
under 
other 
circumstances, 
would be nearly irresistible. 
The group would do well to sit 
down, listen carefully to the first 
Buffalo Springfield album and learn 
how to plan a set. Then . 
. 
. watch 
out. 
t.e. 
Pop Best Bets 
BAGS & THINGS-Dennis Lambert-ABC/Dun- 
hill DSX 50119 
The title obviously refers to Lambert's dis- 
taste for musical labels like "pop" and "rock," 
and the music inside attests to the talent be- 
hind that way of thinking. As part of the Lam- 
bert/Potter writing duo, he's been connected 
with charttoppers like "Two Divided By Love" 
and "Don't Pull Your Love" but this LP fea- 
tures none of these. His newies are potentially 
as gigantic however, the best being "I Didn't 
Sing (In The New York Subway)" and "Some- 
body Found Her." This is his first album as 
a singer, but he paid his dues in the early 
sixties on quite a few single efforts and the 
experience thus gained makes 
a potentially 
shakey coming out sound more like a reunion. 
LOU REED-RCA LSP-4701 
The underground 
rock movement started 
with many groups to be sure, but Velvet Under- 
ground certainly was a cornerstone and Lou 
Reed its fountainhead. On his first solo effort, 
Reed continues to take that almost deadpan 
but always brilliant voice of his and use it to 
its fullest and most unique level. Assisting him 
are Yes' Rick Wakeman and Steve Howe as 
well as Hookfoot's Caleb Quaye, among others. 
Musically, 
he has become something quite 
distinct from the Underground, but no doubt 
he will be able to build upon their support. 
As close to 
a rock magician as you'll find 
anywhere, he will establish an occult cult of 
his own in no time. 
CELEBRATION-El Chicano-Kapp KS 3663 
The "Viva Tirado" boys are at it again in an 
aptly named 
LP. Third album for the band 
features a reprise of that hit number, some 
hi-jinks with the likes of "La Cucuracha," and 
some cooking versions of 
Van 
Morrison's 
"Brown Eyed Girl," the Cream classic "I Feel 
Free," Horace Silver's "Senor Blues," and "In 
A Silent Way," which was written by Joe Za- 
winul. Throbbing rhythms and top notch ar- 
rangements make El Chicano a special type 
of group. 
PARIS ENCOUNTER-Gary Burton & Stephane 
Grappelli-Atlantic SD 1597 
Two musicians of unquestionable creden- 
tials have gotten together for an album which 
is a rare listening experience. Vibraharpist Bur- 
ton works neatly with the legendary Grappelli 
over a course of nine songs. There's a touch 
of the old ("Daphne" and "Here's That Rainy 
Day") and flashes of the new as in Steve 
Swallow's "Eiderdown" and "Falling Grace." 
Grappelli's own "Arpege" gets a lovely render- 
ing too. Swallow and drummer Bill Goodwin 
round out the ensemble. A must for every 
serious collector of jazz music. 
LOOSE & FIERY-Roger Whittaker-RCA LSP- 
4652 
Roger Whittaker has been an international 
favorite for some time but has remained on 
the brink of American success. This may well 
be the album which puts him over the top 
here. It's a beautiful assortment of tunes, with 
Roger's solid vocalizing holding them all to- 
gether like a cord. His version of "Mammy 
Blue" 
is unforgettable and other gems in- 
clude "A Taste Of Honey," "By The Time 
Get 
To Phoenix," 
"Scarborough 
Fair" 
and 
"You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling." Hang on, 
Roger, your "new world" is coming. 
SON OF MY FATHER-Giorgio-Dunhill DSX- 
50123 
International singing star Giorgio clicked on 
the American singles front with "Son Of My 
Father" and he could easily duplicate that suc- 
cess in the album field with this identically 
named set. The material here is every bit as 
fascinating as the face of the dog on the 
jacket. Listen to "London Traffic," "Spanish 
Disaster," "That's How I See Her" and "Watch 
Your Step."

Goldstein 
Polydor 
Ad Manager 
NEW YORK - Polydor Inc. has ap- 
pointed Elaine Goldstein ad manager, 
effective immediately. Ms. Goldstein 
was previously account exec with Si- 
cilia Associates and continued in that 
post when Sicilia Associates merged 
with Buddah Records and became 
Buddah's house ad agency. 
Ms. Goldstein, a native New York- 
er, was also assistant ad manager for 
Buddah. She was account exec for 
Ron Delsener, Cable Concerts, and 
Concerts East during her association 
with Sicilia Associates. 
She will report directly to Tom 
Noonan, director of merchandising 
and marketing. 
Tony Taylor 
To Bell Promo 
NEW YORK-Bell Record's director 
of national promo Steve Wax reports 
the appointment of Tony Taylor to 
the Bell promo team. Operating out 
of New York, Taylor will work on all 
product on a national basis, reporting 
directly to Wax. 
Taylor's 12 year background in ra- 
dio and television began in Atlanta, 
where he was program director for 
WQXI for four years, had his own TV 
show and was active in TV production 
nationally syndicated out of Atlanta. 
In 1967 he joined Drake-Chenault, 
consultants at WOR-FM in New York 
as 
producer -announcer. Moving 
to 
WIP in Philadelphia in 1969, Taylor 
win the Bill Gavin "Non -Rock Pro- 
gram Director of The Year" award 
and in 1970, served on the Gavin Ad- 
visory Committee. 
As an air personality, Taylor did a 
stint at KLAC in Los Angeles and, 
most recently, at WNEW in New 
York. He has also hosted TV variety 
shows for Channel 11.

Chairs Bd

&

partment stores in Southern Califor- 
nia and Arizona.

Chester Leaves 
ASCAP Position 
For Free -Lance 
NEW YORK - Mark Chester, AS- 
CAP's assistant pr representative and 
director of photography, has resigned 
from the Society to do free-lance 
photo -publicity. 
The Society's first staff photogra- 
pher, Chester for 3 years has covered 
concerts, press conferences, recording 
sessions, Broadway openings, televi- 
sion tapings, Grammy's and various 
events involving ASCAP members. 
Prior to his joining ASCAP, Ches- 
ter was affiliated with "The Steve Al- 
len Show" on the west coast where he 
served as its publicity photographer. 
In addition to his published works in 
the music trades, Promenade and Mu- 
sic Journal, his travel and reportage 
photographs have appeared in the 
Saturday Review, and other national 
magazines. 
Chester is located at 217 East 17th 
Street; (212) 533-3890.

Mark -Almond Exit 
Blue Thumb 
HOLLYWOOD - British rock group 
Mark -Almond last week terminated 
their recording contract with Blue 
Thumb Records through their attor- 
ney Michael Rosenfeld. 
Cited as among the grounds for 
termination 
were failure 
of Blue 
Thumb to make financial accounting 
of record sales, failure of Blue Thumb 
to release number of Mark -Almond 
recordings required in the contract 
and failure of Blue Thumb to pro- 
mote 
and distribute Mark -Almond 
recordings in accordance with general 
industry standards. 
Mark -Almond's representatives are 
currently in negotiation with "several 
major labels."

Grammy, Promo Revive `Godspell' 
NEW YORK -A Grammy (for best 
show album) Award and an intensive 
promo by Bell Records has revitalized 
the original cast album of the hit mu- 
sical "Godspell." The album has react- 
ed on the charts as 
a result of 
renewed airplay and sales, moving 
from 121 to 91 on this week's chart. 
The album, the label reports, has 
sold over 150,000 copies and the show 
has become an increasingly popular 
international hit with new U.S. and 
foreign productions being scheduled 
each month. But Bell's success with 
the album was the result of much 
advance planning. 
Six 
weeks 
prior 
to the 
actual 
Grammy Awards presentations, Bell 
records began planning its promo 
reaction in the event of a "Godspell" 
win. At 10 am, the morning following 
the awards presentation on national 
television, 1400 LP's carrying a gold 
Grammy Award sticker on the cover 
were rushed, with a personal letter 
Taylor Pres. 
Of Temponic 
NEW YORK-Larry Taylor has re- 
signed as vp of Music Maximus, Ltd. 
to head of all music enterprises of 
Robert G. Friedman, Florida business- 
man, songwriter and entrepreneur. 
Taylor becomes president of Temponic 
Records 
Inc., Temponic Publishing 
Co., Inc. and Temchord Productions 
Inc. 
Immediate projects include five al- 
bums just concluded under Benny 
Carter, who conducted and arranged a 
varied assortment of material written 
by Friedman. Orchestras and choirs 
surround the vocals of Carmen Mac- 
Rae. Joe Williams, Gene Melino, Er- 
nestine Anderson, and Sue Rainey. 
The majority of the sides have been 
recorded 
at 
Capitol's 
Hollywood 
Studios, A & R'd by Dave Cavanaugh 
and Bill Miller. Due to the size of the 
orchestra and chorus, wrap-up sides 
were cut at United's larger studio and 
A 
& R'd by Jack Tracey. A star- 
studded array of many of America's 
greatest musicians are featured on 
the potpourri of songs written by 
Friedman about whom Time magazine 
(April 3) devoted a lengthy article. 
Taylor has been a personal friend 
of Friedman's for many years. 
Taylor joins Temponic with varied 
background in the music publishing 
and recording industry, having held 
top spots at Paramount Pictures Pub- 
lishing Companies and Columbia Rec- 
ords A & R dept. 
Offices will be in the Hollywood 
Versailles 
Tower, 
7135 
Hollywood 
Blvd., Suite 510, Hollywood, Calif. 
Phone: (213) 876-7661.

THE LAST SET AT NEWPORT-Dave Brubeck 
-Atlantic SD -1607 
It was truly the day the music died. July 
3, 1971 was the final night for the Newport 
Jazz Festival. Before the riot put a stop to 
the proceedings though, Dave Brubeck played 
one of the most memorable sets of the en- 
tire event. This album contains that set. The 
sound is excellent and the performances by 
Brubeck and his accompanists, Gerry Mulli- 
gan (baritone sax), Alan Dawson (drums) and 
Jack Six (bass) are top drawer. The perennial 
"Take Five" 
is joined by a stirring "Open 
The Gates (Out Of The Way Of The People)" 
and an ironically well -titled "Blues For New- 
port." One of Brubeck's greatest records to 
date.

THE POPE SMOKES DOPE-David Peel & The 
Lower East Side-Apple SW -3391 
You don't have to be from New York to 
like David Peel but it probably helps. Washing- 
ton Square's first citizen emerges on a new 
label with more of his unusual songs. What 
are David's songs about? Well, a lot of them 
are 
about dope. Some are about politics. 
Others are about the advantages of living 
in New York. The LP was produced by John 
Lennon and Yoko Ono and they have done 
much to make Peel's material more musical. 
If outrageous records appeal to you, then 
"The Pope Smokes Dope" should be on your 
must list. 
HUNGRY CHUCK-Bearsville 2071 
Hungry Chuck is bound to what your ap- 
petite with 
13 tasty treats on the group's 
debut album. The band is new, but the mem- 
bers are all old pros; drummer N.D. Smart 
II (formerly with Barry & the Remains, Kan- 
garoo, Hello People, Mountain), steel player 
Ben Keith 
(Neil Young's "Harvest," Ian & 
Sylvia), guitarist Amos Garrett (Ian & Sylvia, 
Eric 
Anderson), 
pianist 
Jeffrey 
Gutcheon 
(Tom Rush, Mitch Greenhill) bassist Jim Col - 
grove and hornman Peter Ecklund merge for 
a funky set with lots of chuckles, especially 
on "Dorn' The Funky Lunchbox." Also, give an 
ear to "People Do" and "Hats Off, America." 
ESCALATOR OVER THE HILL-JCOA 3LP-EOTH 
This three record set is considered by its 
composers, Carla Bley and Paul Haines, to be 
a "chronotransduction." Others may be more 
inclined to label it an example of avant-garde 
jazz. The list of performers is as varied as the 
musical contents to be found here. Jack Bruce, 
Viva, Linda Ronstadt, Gato Barbieri, John Mc- 
Laughlin, Charlie Haden, Don Cherry and Paul 
Jones are some of the notables. Along with 
the disks comes a helpful and beautifully de- 
signed booklet with photos and lyrics. A fasci- 
nating and bold experiment. 
QUEUES-Vigrass & Osborne-Uni 73129 
Paul Vigrass and Gary Osborne are a couple 
of men who write intelligent lyrics and marry 
them to melodies which seem to be as equally 
influenced by the classics as by the country. 
The result is one of the more pleasant listen- 
ing experiences of the week. A song like "Don't 
You Worry" quickly established a sympathetic 
mood, while "Ballerina" paints a portrait in 
quick graceful lines. Record buyers may soon 
be queueing up to purchase a copy of this in- 
ventive and strangely captivating LP. 
SHIRELLES-RCA 4698 
Shirley Alston, Beverly Lee and Mickie Har- 
ris, collectively known as the Shirelles, have 
been at it for a long, long time, and they get 
better as they go! The girls who first recorded 
"Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow" gained 
prominence with Carole King tunes in the 
early 60's, which aided Carole King when she 
finally made it big over the last couple of 
years. Now, in the early 70's, the situation is 
reversed-the Shirelles open their album with 
"Brother, Brother" (a recent King composi- 
tion), and Carole's new found popularity will 
definitely aid the Shirelles in making it all 
over again. Let's hope so-they sure know 
how to sing songs!

NEW YORK-IMUS-IN-THE-MORNING: TALKIN' DIRTY AND PLAYIN' THE HITS 
Those who have been flipping FM dials waiting for the next innovation 
in 
radio have missed it. And those who feel it could never happen in New York have 
been proved dead wrong. WNBC's newest staff addition, Imus-In-The-Morning is 
not a breeze of fresh air-he's an entire hurricane season. The world is his 
straight man, so everybody duck. 
Careering as dj for less than four years, Imus is now the morning man on 
New York's fastest growing AM station; it seems they are building it all on his 
shoulders. In many cases, their long-established air personalities have had their 
time slots, even their days changed to fit into the "progressive MOR's" new 
image. He has been called an "impudent little bastard" and other more colorful 
phrases. Well, he is a verbal exhibitionist-Archie Bunker turned liberal side out, 
Don Rickles in overalls and Old Glory shirts. And now, thanks to the release of 
his RCA LP "1200 Hamburgers To Go," a recording star. The album features a 
sampling of the characterizations and outrageousity that have brought him from 
Palmdale, California to Cleveland and onto the big one, New York. Folks interested 
in a master success plan for dj's will have to get it from somewhere else, for 
Imus isn't working according to any he'd admit to. 
"My mother-I support her; I'd like to mention that-asked me how 
I kept 
my plans secret from everyone for so long. But I just fell into everything in radio. 
I had a plan, and still do, but to be a rock and roll star." 
First signed to Dooto Records in 1959 as their first and only white act (which 
seemed logical wince he first won his recognition at an all -black talent show at 
LA's Club California), he never waxed an official release for them. He moved 
over to Arvee Records, a logical spot he thought to get The Olympics to record 
his "Gunfight On Sunset Strip" as a follow-up to "Western Movies." Instead the 
label released his master of the tune. 
HOLLYWOOD-DON BUDAY: CHICANO FOR A DAY 
It's all too seldom that we can pick up an album for the first time, put it 
casually on the turntable (in this case, killing time before a movie), and find 
ourselves jumping up and down with excitement. In the case of EI Chicano's new 
Kapp LP, "Celebration," we were so excited that we damn near missed the movie. 
Surprised we were, and pleased too, that the album was produced by old friend 
and fellow rock-and-roll journalist, Don Buday. Naturally, we called him to find 
out what's up. 
"I've been a music critic for about ten years. 
I was writing about jazz for 
Down Beat in 1963, and I've written for the L.A. Free Press, the Staff and various 
men's magazines. 
I knew jazz very well and was asked a couple of years ago to 
produce for Limelight. But it would have entailed moving to New York, and be- 
sides, 
I thought that jazz was dead. 
I still think it's gone so far underground that 
it's not important anymore. 
"I'd first seen EI Chicano at a promotion party. 
I liked their music but felt they 
could be doing it even better. So 
I told them what I thought. They didn't pay any 
attention, so 
I wrote a review, outlining my thoughts." A series of events, articles 
and other meetings transpired, the result being that Kapp's Johnny Musso and the 
group asked Don to produce their third album for the label. 
"They only had two tunes when 
I came in. 
I brought in some things that 
I had 
written, but it turned out that they just didn't fit, and 
I wanted to put the best 
possible tunes on the album. 
"I felt that the group had no identity and no identification, and so 
I wanted 
to establish one with them. 
I tried to get the kind of material any radio station 
could program-and now I'm finding that some very conservative MOR stations 
are playing 'In a Silent Way,' for instance. 
"I tried to pick tunes that had a certain kind of 'Latin credibility,' if you will. The 
IMUS: In The Morning 
DON BUDAY: Celebration 
Up until this current RCA LP, his best review was a B+ in Cash Box for his 
Challenge recording of "I'm A Hot Rodder And All That Jazz." Soon after release 
of that record, he found himself in Arizona pumping gas. There he met his wife 
("who whipped out two kids from a previous marriage .. 
. 
I keep 'em in up in 
the attic now: they don't get as much to eat as the two younger daughters and 
only have a black and white TV"). After jobs as a uranium and copper miner and 
railroad man, back to L.A. and the Don Martin School of Radio. (Lest you be taken 
in by the similarity in names with 
a certain character in Mad magazine, rest 
assured that there is such a place and that it has turned out, in addition to Imus, 
Don Steele, Bob Eubanks and Tom Kennedy.) 
Before completing his course work, he landed a weekend job at a 5 kw rocker, 
KUGY in Palmdale and ever since the morning man "skipped town, on a bum 
check or something" he's been a morning man. A morning man who has pub- 
lished 300 songs with Tree Music, and who still wants that big hit for himself. 
For his next album, he'd like to do a bit of an update on Jimmy Reed B sides. 
"Imagine J. J. Cale singing with The Blossoms backing. That's what it would be 
like. I'm a dynamite r&b singer, and my brother Fred is a strong blues guitarist. 
I'm learning the blues harp now, gettin' ready. There's nothing better than doing 
a session." 
Right now, he's at a point where he's just beginning to believe that while

band itself can play anything it wants to, but a lot of people expect them to play 
certain things. They can boogie, they can play fantastic blues, and they jam like 
few bands do. 
I picked 'Senor Blues,' thinking that it would be a 'Viva Tirado' 
type thing for them. I'd thought of it before even meeting them. It turns out that 
they'd thought of doing it, too, but had never quite dared to. 
I tried to give them 
more of a rock-and-roll identity by getting them to do 'Brown Eyed Girl' and 'I 
Feel Free.' 
I tried to leave room for flexibility-picking material that would be 
new to them and new to me, too. We found a place where our tastes could meet, 
and none of the tunes would become old hat. 
"I made absolutely sure that all composers' names-their full names-were 
on the album jacket, right on the outside where the disk jockey or customer 
could see it. 
I used to manage a retail record store in Baltimore, and that probably 
affects the way 
I look at the packaging of records. Horace Silver's name is there 
to attract the jazz audience. Van Morrison's name is there for his audience. So 
few people bother to consider that when putting together an album, but 
I think 
it's vital."

THE DAY THAT LOVE WALKED IN-David 
Houston-Epic 31385 
"The Day That Love Walked In" is the most 
recent of the string of hits David Houston has 
experienced since he walked into the country 
charts. Houston's growing popularity is due to 
his distinct singing style, which is definitely 
country, but can be distinguished from too 
many other artists who spend their tame imi- 
tating each other. But as distinct as his vocal 
style is, it never becomes pretentious. Listen 
to "I'm Down To My Last 'I Love You' ", "True 
Love's A Lasting Thing," "Livin' In A House 
Full Of Love" and "I Don't Love You Any- 
more." 
DENNIS WEAVER-Impress 1614 
Over the years, we have come to know 
Dennis Weaver as many different people, from 
"Gunsmoke's" Chester to his leading role in 
the "McCloud" tv series. Placing still another 
face forward, Dennis now emerges as a folksy, 
ecology -minded country singer. In an "impres- 
sively" packaged album on Impress Records, 
he runs through a number of well -written origi- 
nals ("Where 
Have The Wild 
Blackberries 
Gone," "I'd Rather Be With You Than Any- 
one"), some popular c&w favorites ("Ode To 
A Critter") and a couple of religious songs 
("I Still 
Sing 
'Jesus 
Loves 
Me,' " "Work 
Through My Hands, Lord"). Gerry Weaver sings 
with Dennis on some cuts. Dennis Weaver isn't 
another actor making a record for kicks- 
he is genuine and serious and makes fine 
music. 
SOMETHING OLD, SOMETHING NEW, SOME- 
THING BLUE-Sammi Smith-Mega 1011 
Sammi Smith has a fine new album that 
displays versatility with something old ("I've 
Got To Have You"), something new ("Ken- 
tucky"), and something blue ("Isn't It Sad"), 
not to mention something borrowed ("Bridge 
Over Troubled Water"). Sammi has earned 
star status in the country field, and the lineup 
of top backup musicians on this set certainly 
proves it. Produced by Jim Malloy and ar- 
ranged by Billy Walker, this LP includes musi- 
cians such as Henry Strzelecki, David Briggs, 
Chip Young, Weldon Myrick, Buzz Cason and 
Jerry Shook. Highlights include "Jody And The 
Kid," "Right Won't Touch A Hand," and "Billy 
Jack." 
CRESCENTVILLE - Larry Groce-Daybreak 
2010 
Larry Groce has a different point of view 
that he expresses in a continuing search for 
reality. Since one of the ways he expresses 
himself is through composing songs, he has 
come up with very different and very real 
lyrics. He is also very honest in his musical 
ballads-a trait that didn't hurt Kris Kristof- 
ferson at all. In "The Bumper Sticker Song," 
Groce's reality is humorous, while songs such 
as the title tune are serious and thought pro- 
voking. "Mr. Hill" concerns the Attica prison 
riot and "Just Another American Dream" has 
a lot to say. Groce is a missing link between 
Kristofferson and Loudon Wainwright III who 
could make it in both folk and country fields.

Rogers/Evans 
TV Specials 
NASHVILLE - Frank Peppiatt and 
John Aylesworth have set a deal with 
Roy Rogers and Dale Evans to pro- 
duce three hour-long holiday specials 
in 1972-73. Specials will be pegged, 
respectively, to Thanksgiving, Christ- 
mas and Easter. 
Specials will be distributed nation- 
ally by Yongestreet Program Serv- 
ices, Inc. in which Peppiatt and Ay- 
lesworth are partnered with Nick 
Vanoff, William O. Harbach and Alan 
D. Courtney. YPS distributes "Hee 
Haw," of which Peppiatt and Ayles- 
worth are executive producers, on 205 
markets. Last major station signed up 
is WBAL-TV in Baltimore, scheduled 
to start the show in May. 
In addition to serving as executive 
producers of the holiday specials, Pep- 
piatt and Aylesworth will be script 
supervisors. Sam Lovullo, producer of 
"Hee Haw," will produce the Rogers - 
Evans shows. "Hee Haw" will begin 
video-taping its next 13 week series in 
June at the WLAC-TV studios in 
Nashville, Tennessee.

Walkway's 
8 New Stars 
NASHVILLE - Eight new stars 
have been added to the "Walkway of 
the Stars", honoring individuals in the 
country music field who have con- 
tributed to the artistic growth of 
country music and to the development 
of the Country Music Hall of Fame 
and Museum. 
Individuals honored at a recent cer- 
emony in Nashville include: Gene Au- 
try, the Statler Brothers, Lynn And- 
erson, Glenn Sutton, Bonnie Owens 
Barbara Mandrell, Dolly Parton, and 
Charley Pride. 
The recent ceremony included re- 
marks by Country Music Foundation 
board of trustees chairman Frank 
Jones, as well as the presentation of a 
"Walkway Certificate" to each new 
member. 
CC's Folk Arts 
Fest At Renwick 
WASHINGTON - Country music 
echoed through the newly -refurbished 
Renwick Gallery recently when the 
Congressional Club kicked off a two- 
day Festival of American Folk Arts. 
Among the performers were head- 
liner Stan Hitchcock, country music 
singer and Caprice recording star 
from Nashville, Tenn., The Ralph 
Case Square Dancers, champions of 
the Asheville, N. 
C. Square Dance 
Festival, Jimmy Driftwood, singer, 
guitarist and dulcimer player from 
Timbo, Ark., and Willie Morrison and 
the Old Americans group from Fox, 
Ark. 
The performers were introduced by 
their respective Congressmen. Among 
those making the introductions were 
Congressmen: Richard H. Fulton of 
Nashville, Tenn., Roy Taylor of Black 
Mountain, N. C., Bill Alexander of 
Osceola, Ark., and John Buchanan of 
Birmingham, Ala. 
The concert was part of a two-day 
festival of folk arts highlighted by an 
exhibit of handicrafts at the Congres- 
sional Club. Attending the festival 
Renfro Valley 
Barndance Agenda 
NASHVILLE - Renfro Valley En- 
terprises have announced the agenda 
at the 
Renfro Valley Barndance, 
which will bring a variety of enter- 
tainment to the valley. 
An Old Time Fiddlers Convention 
has been set for June 9, 10, and 11. 
Authentic fiddlers and other tradi- 
tional front porch rural musicians 
will gather in Renfro Valley to relive 
their early American musical past. 
Participants will bring their fiddles, 
banjos, guitars, harmonicas, singing 
voices and dancing feet to the event, 
expected to draw several hundred 
spectators. 
Other events for the summer season 
at the Valley include a bluegrass fes- 
tival July 14, 15, 16, a giant Ole Time 
County Fair July 28, 29, 30; an All 
Nite Sing, August 5; a championship 
rodeo on August 25-26; and an All 
Day Sing on September 24. In addi- 
tion the regular Saturday night, Ren- 
fro Valley Barndance will be held 
each week-end, along with the famous 
Sunday Morning Gathering on Sun- 
days. 
NCCJ Awards Chet Atkins 
(Cont'd. from p. 37) 
decision to name Atkins as this year's 
honoree was made at a special press 
meeting, April 6, in Nashville. Procla- 
mation came in consideration of the 
continuous efforts Mr. Atkins has ex- 
tended within the music industry to 
further the careers of others, as well 
as his constant gifts of music to the 
public at large. 
In addition, Atkins has fostered 
relationships among the youth of this, 
and other nations, as well as with his 
fellow men through the development 
of the non-profit Chet Atkins Guitar 
Festival and his own golf tourney in 
Knoxville with all proceeds going to 
charity. He has served as a past mem- 
ber of the board of governors for the 
Nashville Chamber of Commerce, has 
been honorary chairman to solicit 
funds for the National Jewish Hospi- 
tal, and currently serves on the Mid- 
dle Tennessee Council executive board 
for the Boy Scouts of America. 
Atkins also serves as honorary fund 
raising chairman for the Kidney 
Foundation, is on the board of direc- 
tors for the Hawaiian Music Assoc., is 
on the board of directors for the Mu- 
sic City Pro -Celebrity Golf Tourna- 
ment, is on the nominating committee 
of the Country Music Hall of Fame, 
and is on the board of directors for 
the Nashville Symphony Assoc. 
He's additionally served a two year 
term as Tennessee's honorary chair- 
man of Cystic Fibrosis in 1969 and 
1970. 
The formulation of FAME, a com- 
pany 
whose 
audio-visual 
guitar 
teaching techniques now available in 
public schools, represents still another 
effort from Atkins to reach the youth 
of our world. "Mr. Guitar" joins the 
list of recipients for the NCCJ Na- 
tional Humanitarian Award, which in- 
cludes Bob Hope, Edwin Gott, and 
Sammy Davis, Jr. 
In charge of Nashville's brother- 
hood dinner to take place May 9th 
will be honorary chairman, and Ten- 
nessee's Governor Winfield 
Dunn; 
chairman, and president of Nashville's 
Commerce Union Bank, Ed Nelson; 
and co-chairman, and president of 
Nashville's section of the National 
Council of Jewish Women, Mrs. Ellen 
Jacobs. 
Invitations are being issued by the 
regional offices of NCCJ in Memphis.

Rev. Davis 
Dies At 76 
NEW YORK-The Rev. Gary Davis, 
an 
influential black ragtime -blues 
singer and guitarist, died of a heart 
attack at Kessler Memorial Hospital 
in Hammonton, N.J., May 5. The 
blind performer, who lived at 109-42 
174th St., Jamaica, Queens, was 76. 
Davis was a unique, self-taught 
stylist who was imitated by many of 
today's younger folk artists. His 
12 -string and six -string fingerpicking 
guitar style is best exemplified by his 
original tunes, such as "Maple Leaf 
Rag," "Baby, Let Me Follow You 
Down" and "A Boy Was Kissin' A 
Girl And Playin' The Guitar At The 
Same Time." 
Davis played throughout the U.S. 
and Canada, as well as appearing in a 
film documentary, "Black Roots." He 
is survived by his widow, the former 
Annie McDowell. 
RC&B Names V -Ps 
BEVERLY HILLS - Jonas Halperin 
and Paul Bloch have been named vice 
presidents of Rogers, Cowan & Bren- 
ner, Inc. 
Halperin, who first joined the agen- 
cy in 1963 in the Beverly Hills office, 
has for the past two years been man- 
aging director of the entertainment 
division in New York. 
Rock Revival's 
L. I. Success 
NEW YORK - The first presentation 
of Richard Nader's Rock & Roll Re- 
vival on Long Island attracted 16,800 
people to the new Nassau Coliseum 
and grossed $80,000. Portions of the 
show, which starred Chuck Berry, 
Bo Diddley, Jay & The Americans, 
Johnny Maestro with the Brooklyn 
Bridge, the Coasters, Five Satins and 
Angels, were filmed for a motion pic- 
ture on the rock revival which will be 
released later this year. 
Volume Nine of the Rock Revival 
at Madison Square Garden is sched- 
uled for June 2 with Little Richard, 
Dion & The Belmonts, (back together 
for the first and only time), Lloyd 
Price, the Clef tones, Danny & The 
Junior, Shirley & Lee, the Exciters 
and Billy Vera and his band. With 25% 
of the tickets already sold, Richard 
Nader is certain to achieve his ninth 
consecutive sellout at the Garden. 
Polydor Archive 
NEW YORK - Polydor Incorporated 
has announced the release of six new 
Archive albums which range from 
early classical flute concertos to a 
collection of 'Monteverdi madrigals. 
The 12's are: "Early Classical Flute 
Concertos," "The Art Of Playing On 
The Violin," "Virtuoso Madrigals Of 
Monteverdi," "Four Concerti Grossi," 
"The Orgelbeuchlein:45 'Organ Chor- 
ales," and "Twelve 'Concerti Grossi." 
ANKA MAN-Buddah Records recording star Paul Anka (second from right), 
on a national tour concurrent with the release of his new single and album, 
"Jubilation," appeared at the Elmwood Casino in Winder, Ontario. With him, 
between sets at the Elmwood are (left to right) program director Alden Diehl, 
music director Rosalie Trombley and air personality Pat Holiday of station 
CKLW in Detroit, Neil Bogart, co -president of the Buddah Group, Ken Benson, 
Buddah promotion director in Michigan, Paul Anka and Jerry Sharell, national 
promotion director at Buddah. Anka will cap his tour with an appearance at 
New York's Persian Room 'at the end of this month. 
Three Dog Night Map 
Summer 'Tour Of Tours' 
HOLLYWOOD - Three Dog Night's 
planned Tour of Tours, a summer as- 
sault on the biggest ballparks and au- 
ditoriums in the nation, will include 
back-to-back return engagements at 
the Dallas Cotton Bowl and Atlanta 
Braves Stadium, August 19-20. 
The Faces with Rod Stewart will 
join the group on the bill, according 
to Burt Jacobs of Reb Foster Associ- 
ates, the Dogs' personal management 
firm. 
He observed that the forthcoming 
Dallas and Atlanta dates may bring 
an audience in excess of 100,000, and 
at least a half -million dollars to the 
box-office. 
The Cotton Bowl and Braves Stadi- 
um were two -third of Three Dog 
Night's concern smash of summer '71, 
a warm-up for this year's record - 
setting journey. Completing their 
"Triple Crown" triumph with Three 
Rivers Stadium, Pittsburgh, the group 
drew total attendance 
of 
83,242, 
grossing more than $374,000.
