Townsend Forms 
Varied Music Co. 
HOLLYWOOD - Ronald Townson, 
one of the members of the 5th Dimen- 
sion, has formed Professional Inter- 
national Productions (PIP), and an- 
nounced the appointment of Ted Baker 
as director of talent. PIP will act as a 
personal management firm, a record 
production company and a packager 
of concerts. The two first two acts 
signed to the personal management 
division are Creative Source, current- 
ly at The Playboy Club in Los Ang- 
eles and Bull, who records for Bell 
Records. 
'Good Foot 
Goes Gold 
NEW YORK - James Brown's Po- 
lydor single "Get on the Good Foot" 
has been certified a million -selling 
gold record by the RIAA. 
Brown, currently in the midst of an 
extensive tour that will take him to 
such cities as Syracuse and Montreal, 
recently completed a successful ap- 
pearance at New York's Apollo The- 
atre. Appearing with 
Brown was 
songstress Lyn Collins, soul singer 
Bobby 'Byrd, the JB's and the other 
members of the James Brown Revue.

RCA strutted its new product in 
two product presentations, 
one in 
Montreal 
the 
other 
in 
Toronto 
(11-12). Getting most of the attention 
was their "live" at the Toronto 
O'Keefe Centre album 
by Harry 
Belafonte. They also released the first 
news of the album, "Oh Say Can You 
See". This album jacket features the 
American flag, upside down and has 
caused a U.S. critic to jump to the 
conclusion that Canada was exercising 
an anti-American attitude within re- 
cording circles. It's now been estab- 
lished that the 
album, featuring 
Charles Linton of Montreal, writer 
and chief performer, used the Ameri- 
can flag only because it happens to 
represent a world power and there 
was no intention of smearing the 
U.S. way of life. The album is in- 
cluded in a multimedia package in- 
volving the set, a television special, a 
book, and a new musical. The musical 
will open soon in Montreal and, hope- 
fully, off Broadway shortly. 
Several Canadian single releases are 
picking 
up 
good 
chart 
numbers 
through the cooperation of radio sta- 
tions. These include Skylark, Vancou- 
ver's latest discovery getting the nod 
from CKLG and other west coast sta- 
tions; Thecycle, picking up good air- 
play from CHED and several Ontario 
and Maritime stations; Abraham's 
Children, now being charted and play - 
listed on principal and breakout sta- 
tions from coast to coast; Roger Ro- 
dier, receiving strong support from 
CFRB and many other MOR stations 
which is now influencing MOT sta- 
tions; April Wine, making a strong 
bid for a national breakout with initi- 
al support from CKGM. 
A&M have appointed Joseph Sum- 
mers to the position of National 
Sales Manager for Canada. Summers 
is a fifteen year veteran in U.S. rec- 
ord sales where he held many impor- 
tant positions, most recent being Na- 
tional Sales Manager of Motown Rec- 
ords. 
Summers climbs aboard the 
A&M ship at a time when the success- 
ful independent is making a bid to 
break a new Canadian find. Lorence 
Hud has been hyped across the na- 
tional for the past several weeks and 
this week is subject of an album re- 
lease. Gerry Lacoursiere, Managing 
Director of A&M Canada threw a. 
bash at his out -of -Toronto hideaway 
(19) to which were invited key deal- 
ers, radio and press VIPs from across 
the country. 
Joh Small takes over as Capitol's 
new national promotion manager, re- 
placing Bill Bannon who assumes his 
newly created position of artist de- 
velopment and marketing coordina- 
tor. Small was former operations 
manager and program director of 
WKNR AM/FM in Detroit and is a 
music veteran of fourteen years hav- 
ing fathered the birth of Detroit "un- 
derground" 
radio as manager of 
WABX.

Osmonds Plan 
Nov. UK Tour 
NEW YORK -The Osmonds' popu- 
larity in England, has prompted plans 
for a concert tour throughout Great 
Britain, probably in Nov. 
It would be the group's first per- 
formance visit, apart from a special 
tip earlier this year to headline a 
Royal Command Performance for the 
Queen. The Osmonds' manager, Ed 
Leffler, of Katz-Gallin-Leffler, is cur- 
rently in 
England concluding ar- 
rangements. 
On British television, meanwhile, 
the Osmonds are now regulars. Their 
animated series has debuted in three 
major independent TV regions, via 
London Weekend, ATV and Scottish 
Television. (It airs 
in the United 
States over ABC-TV every Saturday.) 
The group 
is 
in 
Los Angeles, 
preparing for its first headline en- 
gagement in Las Vegas, beginning 
Thursday, Sept. 28, at Caesar's Pal- 
ace. 
Mendell Back 
From S.A. Trip 
HOLLYWOOD -Lee Mendell, U.A. 
Records vice president for interna- 
tional operations, has returned after 
a month's visit to South America. 
During his tour, Mendell completed 
meetings with USA licenses in all 
major South American markets and 
concluded 
several 
new 
licensing 
agreements. 
Mendell stated that it has become 
most evident, since his visit last year, 
that the growing South American 
market is now becoming much more 
contemporary. Release of product by 
contemporary global performers, he 
said, has increased markedly as has 
the public response to this category 
of music. 
RCA U.K. `Amazing Pace' Confab 
Reveals Happy Sales Statistics 
LONDON - Tagged 
"Amazing 
Pace," RCA U.K. held its annual sales 
confab 
in 
London 
recently 
with 
speeches 
from 
Geoff 
Hannington, 
marketing manager, 
Mike Everitt, 
A&R manager and Graham Heyson, 
RCA Victor label manager. 
Hannington spoke of sales statistics 
for the previous year and revealed 
rises in sales of 40% for singles; 30% 
for full priced albums; 19% for mid 
priced albums; 150% for cassettes and 
140% for cartridges. Outlining future 
policy Hannington said that RCA had 
a sufficient roster of talent to reply 
on sales without the need for gim- 
micks and that in the coming year 
RCA U.K. planned to strengthen its 
artist powers even more. 
Hannington gave delegates news of 
a new "Nostalgia Campaign" that 
RCA is to launch. The series com- 
prises 22 albums culled from RCA 
America's "Vintage" series supple- 
mented with material from the RCA 
catalog. Among the releases is a six 
record set titled "The Dorsey/Sinatra 
Collection," comprising eighty three 
tracks recorded in 1941/42 by Sinatra 
with Tommy Dorsey. The set will re- 
tail at £7150. Other artists being 
featured in the Nostalgia Campaign 
are Maurice Chevalier, Artie Shaw, 
Bing Crosby and Paul Whiteman. The 
campaign will be backed by consumer 
advertising and dealer window dis- 
plays. 
Pop release for the year include a 
massive promotion and marketing 
campaign for Dave Bowie and an al- 
bum 
from 
Brewers 
Droop titled 
"Opening Time" with which a promo- 
tion 
campaign involving 
a 
major 
brewery is currently under negotia- 
tion. 
Other releases from RCA's pop re- 
pertoire 
include 
Natural 
Acoustic 
Band, 
Alan 
Philips 
and 
heavy 
promotion for the forthcoming tours 
by The Everly Brothers and George 
Hamilton IV. In the new year, a dou- 
ble album from Elvis Presley recorded 
live at his Hawaiian Concert will be 
released and a new album from Jack 
Jones. Other artists to receive mar- 
keting campaigns in the new year in- 
clude 
Alan 
Clarke, 
Quintessence, 
Kinks and Jonathan Kelly. Seven 
boxed sets will be issued on RCA's 
classical Red Seal label as a follow on 
from the subscription release of last 
autumn. 
A completely new selling technique 
will be utilized by RCA for the pre - 
Christmas period. Mobile showrooms 
staffed by salesmen will tour the 
country carrying a complete stock of 
the RCA catalog and dealers will be 
invited to browse through to help 
them with their Christmas orders. A 
special discount bulk order incentive 
scheme 
will 
be 
in 
operation for 
Christmas. 
Mike Everitt opened his speech 
with the words, "Catalog artists of 
today were once new artists of yes- 
terday," emphasising the need for a 
continuous flow of new talent without 
relying on past successes. He went on 
to say that RCA would also acquire 
any new labels it felt were worth 
while. In the past year, the company 
acquired Vanguard, Prestige and Fan- 
tasy. From RCA's Victor label, Gra- 
ham Heyson announced albums from 
Henry Mancini, an album from Jim 
Reeves titled "Missing You" and a 
double album from Nancy Sinatra. 
Other releases include albums from 
Chet Atkins, Jerry Reed, Hank Lock - 
lin and Charley Pride. The Barclay 
label is to release Charles Aznavour's 
latest album "Desormais" and Heyson 
added that a number of jazz albums 
from the Victor, Vanguard, Prestige 
and Fantasy labels would follow in- 
cluding Duke Ellington Count Basie, 
Buck Clayton, Miles Davis, Mose Al- 
lison, MJQ, and a live two -record set 
from Buddy Rich. 
Decca 3 Yr 
Ties With 
Brunswick 
LONDON -W. W. Townsley, direc- 
tor of Decca Records has announced 
that his company had clinched a three 
year deal with the Brunswick and 
Dakar labels. Chairman Sir Edward 
Lewis together with senior Decca ex- 
ecutives negotiated 
the agreement 
with Woody Hinderling 
who rep- 
resented Nat Tarnopol, chief of Brun- 
swick and Dakar. Decca have the 
rights for the United Kingdom, South 
Africa, Nigeria and other African 
countries, Turkey, the Middle East, 
India and the Far East. All re- 
cordings will be issued on the Burn- 
swick label and first release will be 
made Nov. 1. 
Four Tops 
To Europe 
HOLLYWOOD - The 
Four Tops, 
newly arrived to ABC/Dunhill from 
their affiliation with Motown, have 
been set for a two -month extensive 
tour of England, Germany, Amster- 
dam and Belgium, beginning Oct. 6 in 
London's reopened Rainbow Theatre. 
The group has just completed re- 
cording their first album for ABC/ 
Dunhill. 
Birtha To Europe 
HOLLYWOOD - Directly 
on the 
heels of their U.S. tour, Birtha is now 
headed for England, Holland, Germa- 
ny and France and is scheduled to 
depart by Oct. 4. Nine of the dates 
for this tour will be with the Kinks. 
Birtha's tour will wrap up back in 
London where they will headline. 
Birtha will go back into the studio 
upon their return. Their premier al- 
bum for ABC/Dunhill is appropriately 
"Births." 
Mendes To Select 
Scholarship 
Student In Brazil 
NEW YORK- Sergio Mendes flies 
to Rio de Janeiro Oct. 10 to assist in 
the final stages of selecting the recipi- 
ent for the $5000, one year full tui- 
tion scholarship he recently estab- 
lished at the prestigious Berklee 
College of Music, Boston, Massachu- 
setts. 
Mendes will meet with a committee 
of musical academicians who will be 
making the final student selection 
based on need and musical ability. 
Any student considered must meet the 
Berklee College of Music's standards 
for admission. 
For the past 10 weeks, all of Brazil 
has been aware of the Mendes schol- 
arship and the opportunity it affords 
a young musician. Flavio Cavalcante, 
Brazil's foremost television personali- 
ty, used his weekly 3 -hour variety 
program to showcase applicants. Up- 
wards of 18,000 letters of inquiry 
flooded Cavalcante's offices. 
The student selected will enter Ber- 
klee in '73 to begin his or her fresh- 
man year. 
GSF Ties In 
Phillipines 
NEW YORK 
-Michael Gusick, di- 
rector of international operations for 
GSF Records, has announced the sign- 
ing of a long-term licensing agree- 
ment between GSF and Empire Inter- 
national of the Phillipines. The deal 
was concluded by Guisick and Hubert 
Co., managing director of Empire In- 
ternational. 
Empire International will distribute 
GSF's singles, albums, 8 -track and 
cassette cartridge tapes throughout 
the Phillipines on the GSF label. The 
first single and LP will be released 
shortly.

Met's 'Carmen' 
To Appear On 
DG Next Year 
NEW YORK - Polydor Internation- 
al will release the Metropolitan Opera 
production of "Carmen" with the Met- 
ropolitan Opera Orchestra conducted 
by Leonard Bernstein. 
Production, debuting at the Met's 
opening night recently, stars Marilyn 
Horne in the title role and James 
McCracken as Don Jose, Tom Krause 
as Escamillo, Adriana Maliponte as 
Micaela 
and 
Donald 
Gramm 
as 
Zuniga. The album, with the original 
opening night cast, is to be released 
on Deutsche Grammophon. 
The agreement was signed at the 
offices 
of 
Amberson 
Productions. 
Those present were: Dr. Hans Hirsch, 
Manager, A&R, Classical Division, 
Polydor International; Schuyler Cha- 
pin, Acting General Manager, Metro- 
politan 
Opera 
Association; 
Jerry 
Schoenbaum, President, Polydor In- 
corporated and Leonard Bernstein. 
Under the baton of Bernstein, the 
recording is currently being taped at 
Manhattan Center in New York City, 
thus marking the first time in seven 
years that a major opera has been re- 
corded in the United States. "Lohen- 
grin" was the last complete opera to 
be recorded in this country. It was 
made in 1965. This production rep- 
resents Bernstein's recording debut 
for Deutsche Grammophon. It is the 
second joint project between D. G. 
and the Metropolitan Opera since the 
classical label's release of the "Metro- 
politan Opera Gala Honoring Sir Ru- 
dolf Bing" earlier this syear. 
This production of "Carmen," con- 
ceived by the late Goeran Gentele, 
Met director killed in an auto accident 
recently, goes back to Bizet's original 
version (with spoken dialog rather 
than recitative), which had its pre- 
miere at the Opera Comique in 1875 
and is rarely performed. 
With this recording, the Met re- 
enters the complete opera field for the 
first time since "Macbeth" was record- 
ed in 1959, while Deutsche Grammo- 
phon makes another step in enlarging 
its position on the American musical 
scene. 
Recording sessions with the Metro- 
politan Opera cast and orchestra con- 
ducted by Leonard Bernstein are ex- 
pected to continue over the next two 
weeks under the supervision of A & R 
producer Thomas W. Mowrey, and the 
album is scheduled for release in the 
United States by Deutsche Grammo- 
phon early in 1973. 
Hirsch, Chapin, 
Schoenbaum & Bernstein

CHICAGO - Mercury Records has 
launched a "Solid Gold Rock 'n Roll" 
program with the re -merchandising of 
seven classic albums currently in the 
label's active catalog, according to 
Lou Simon, senior vice president/ 
director of marketing. Also included 
in the program will be the entire sin- 
gles catalog of Mercury's Celebrity 
Series, Double Hits, and Smash All - 
Time Hits. 
The seven albums are: "Encore of 
Golden Hits" and "More Encore of 
Golden Hits" by the Platters: "Gold 
Vault of Hits -Featuring the sounds of 
Frankie Valli," "Second Vault 
of 
Golden Hits" and "Edizione D'Oro 
(Gold Edition)" by The Four Sea- 
sons; "Golden Hits" by Chuck Berry; 
and "Golden Rock Hits" by Jerry 
Lee Lewis. There are 100 singles in 
the various hit 45's series. 
"These records have been constant 
sellers throughout the years," Simon 
stated, "and because of the renewed 
interest in classic rock and roll, we 
are marketing these albums. There 
will be radio advertising on oldies 
stations as well as on key to 40 out- 
lets. There are also special merchan- 
dising tools for the program includ- 
ing an elaborate browser card and 
poster. 
Extra Discount 
"As a highlight to this whole pro- 
gram we will be offering an extra 
10% discount on the album product to 
distributors and the entire dealer 
trade," Simon continued. "This dis- 
count will be in effect from 10/9 to 
11/9. Since this is just a re -merchan- 
dising and not a re -packaging, the 
Col, Korvettes 
Execs Meet On 
Quad's Future 
Quad Sound was the chief topic of 
discussion at 
a meeting between 
Columbia Records exec and reps from 
all E. J. Korvettes' New York metro- 
politan area stores. 
Representing Korvettes' at the quad 
seminar was a group of 40 audio and 
record merchandising experts led by 
David Rothfeld, vice president of hard 
goods merchandising. Columbia Rec- 
ords' Joe Dash, director of SQ licen- 
sing; Stan Snyder, vice president of 
national accounts; Ron Piccolo, New 
York 
branch manager, 
and Paul 
Smith regional promo manager, New 
York Branch, discussed different con- 
cepts of four -channel merchandising 
with the group. 
In an address before the gathered 
quad 
boosters, 
Columbia's 
Dash 
stressed the importance of SQ mer- 
chandising in both the hardware and 
software category. He indicated that 
the introduction of Columbia's SQ 
system to the public now is as impor- 
tant a step in the field of today's 
musical technology as the inaugura- 
tion of Columbia's first stereo album 
was 17 years ago.

Warners To 
Mkt S'track 
Of 'Marjoe' 
NEW YORK - Warner Bros. Rec- 
ords has completed negotiations for 
the rights to the film, "Marjoe." The 
album will be produced by Howard 
Smith and Sally Kernochan, who pro- 
duced and directed the film. 
Former evangelist Marjoe Gortner 
met Smith, a New York deejay, during 
an interview at which time he di- 
vulged his story of commercial evan- 
gelism. Smith was so impressed with 
Marjoe and the tapes of the interview 
and he decided not to run the show. 
Smith then took the tapes to Don 
Rugoff, who in turn gave Smith the 
go ahead on the movie project. 
The album begins with the widely 
publicized wedding ceremony conduct- 
ed by the young Marjoe (four years 
old) in 1949 and goes through such 
segments as a bombastic sermon de- 
livered by the then eight year old fire 
and 
brimstone hurler; 
some per- 
formances by the adult Marjoe on his 
last tour and songs like "I've Got 
Confidence," performed by the Hol- 
land Sisters, "God I Love You," by 
the Countrymen and "Save All My 
Brothers" the theme from "Marjoe" 
sung by Jerry Keller, the latter tune 
has just been released by Warner 
Bros. as 
a single. As an artist, 
Marjoe is signed to Wes Farrell's 
Chelsea label through RCA. 
After a successful run in New York, 
the film is being released nationwide 
and Warner Bros. plans an extensive 
advertising and promo campaign in 
each city where "Marjoe" plays. 
TA Dividends 
SAN FRANCISCO - The board of 
directors of Transamerica Corp. has 
declared the following dividends on 
stock of the corporation: 
A regular quarterly cash dividend 
of $1.20 on the corporation's $4.80 
convertible preferred stock payable 
Nov. 1, 1972 to holders of record on 
Oct. 10. 
A regular quarterly cash dividend 
of 13% cents a share on Transameri- 
ca common stock payable Oct. 31, to 
holders of record on Oct. 10. 
NEW YORK - Famous Music Corp. 
will release a new rock opera, "Vir- 
gin," written by a Catholic priest, Fa- 
ther John O'Reilly. The album was 
recorded by members of "The Mis- 
sion," 
a singing 
group including 
priests of the Contemporary Mission. 
The double LP set is slated for re- 
lease 
on 
Oct. 
15, 
via 
Famous' 
Paramount Label. 
Special Showing 
Tony Martell, Famous president, 
also announced that the entire rock 
opera will be showcased on Oct. 18, at 
Philharmonic Hall. Performing Virgin 
that night will be the original re- 
cording cast of The Mission, accom- 
panied by a 50 piece symphony or- 
chestra, under the direction of Al Del - 
Monte. Tickets for the occasion are 
by invitation only. The presentation 
"Virgin is far more than a concept 
album," stated Martell. "The individu- 
al performances of lead singers Joe 
DeVito, Dorothy Lerner and Jim Rast 
have to be considered one of the 
strongest combinations of vocal tal- 
ent on any album to date." 
The authors of Virgin represent a 
group of realistic young priests dedi- 
cated to positive change within the 
traditional churches. Their unione life 
style has been the subject of CBS and 
NBC network specials. 
For the past six years, the priests 
have been involved in a musical apos- 
tolate to young people. They have 
toured the nation, live and in concert, 
and have appeared on all of the ma- 
jor network shows. They have dedi- 
cated their lives to helping the disad- 
vantaged and deprived 
of today's 
world. 
Virgin, is based on actual everyday 
living experiences. It reveals the ma- 
jor philosorhical profile of the Con- 
temporary Mission priests. Universal 
yet controversial subjects such as 
birth control, clerical celibacy, pover- 
ty, war, drug addiction receive an un- 
derstanding yet in-depth treatment 
throughout the unfolding of the rock 
opera drama. 
Virgin has been over five years in 
the making. Over five months were 
spent in recording the double album 
set. 
Famous will initiate special mar- 
keting and advertising concepts in a 
full promo campaign. Special packag- 
ing is also being planned for the dou- 
ble LP set. 
O'Reilly, Martell 
ASCAP Revenues 
Up In 8 Months 
HOLLYWOOD - ASCAP showed a 
4.9% increase in revenues for the first 
eight months of 1972 over the same 
period last year, it was revealed at 
the society's west coast meet here last 
week (3). Revenues reached $42,391,- 
000, compared to $40,391,000 in 1971, 
according to Stanley Adams, pres- 
ident. 
Correction 
A story in last week's Cash Box 
indicating a gold record for the Grand 
Funk Railroad album, "Phoenix," was 
in error. The LP has not, as of press - 
time, received gold certification from 
the RIAA.

Garner Is London's 
Nat'l R&B Mgr 
NEW YORK - Emmett J. Garner 
has been named national r & b pro- 
motion manager for London Records, 
according to Sy Warner, director of 
national promotion for the company. 
Garner will cover the entire country 
and will be responsible for the promo- 
tion of all r & b product from London 
as well as the Memphis -based Hi la- 
bel, which includes Al Green, Ann 
Peebles and Otis Clay on its roster. 
Garner, who will operate out of 
London Records midwest branch in 
Niles, Illinois, will report to Dave 
Marshall, national promotion man- 
ager, and Warner, both of whom are 
based in the company's New York 
headquarters.

Great Britain 
Polydor Records has undergone a 
major reshuffle to cope with the ex- 
pansion of the company, which also 
announced that their budget for the 
first eight months showed an increase 
of 50%. Tim Harrold has been appoint- 
ed commercial manager, taking re- 
sponsibilities in marketing, sales and 
operations areas reporting to Polydor 
managing director John Fruin. To 
strengthen the organization of the 
company a new operations depart- 
ment has been set up headed by Don 
Wedge. Marketing manager moves to 
the International London office to be- 
come general manager, his position 
being filled by Mike Hales, previously 
product manager of pop and progres- 
sive music. Malcolm Jones, formerly 
with the Harvest and Cube labels 
takes up the position of pop product 
manager vacated by Hales. Simon Gee 
rejoins the company, after a year at 
Business school, as head of jazz and 
blues product. George McManus and 
Gordan Gray remain in charge of folk 
and country music and easy listening 
and soundtrack music respectively. 
The 
sales 
division 
under 
Eddie 
Webster is to be increased in size. 
Also a new tape sales team is to be 
recruited for sales in non traditional 
outlets. The new team will start oper- 
ating in 1973. Roger Holt becomes 
manager of the promotion division. 
Home sales for the month of June 
stood at £3.9 million, a 32% rise over 
the corresponding month of the pre- 
vious year, according to the Board of 
Trade figures. Exports fell by 1%, but 
figures for the first six months of the 
year compared with that period in 
1971 show an increase of 18% in home 
sales, and a 9% rise in exports. Pro- 
duction for the month of June was up. 
10.5 million records were pressed dur- 
ing the month, 12% than in the previ- 
ous June. Pressings of 45 r.p.m. rec- 
ords was up by 15%, and those of 33's 
by 10%. Total pressings for the first 
six months of the year compared with 
the same period 1971 showed an in- 
crease of 4%. 
In a statement from Derek Everett, 
managing director of MCA Records, 
Peter Robinson and Alan Crowder 
have been given new responsibilities. 
Robinson, formerly the press officer 
now takes up the newly created post 
of marketing co-ordinator. Robinson 
has been with MCA since 1971, .previ- 
ously working on the now defunct 
Music Business Weekly. Production 
co-ordinator Alan Crowder will now 
have 
the added responsibilities of 
handling liaison and licensees. Ev- 
erett stated that the reason for these 
changés were to give more time to 
David Howells who was previously 
handling A&R, marketing and inter- 
national functions, to seek out more 
talent for the label. 
Impresario Robert Paterson and 
George Wein, founder and promoter 
of the Newport Jazz Festival are 
bringing the stars of the 1972 festival 
to London this month. The concerts 
will be at the Odeon Theater. Ham- 
mersmith on the 21st, 22nd. 27th, and 
28th of October. There will be two 
shows each night, and artists appear- 
ing will be The Jimmy Smith Jam 
Session featuring Roy Haynes, Kenny 
Burrell 
Illinois 
Jacquet, 
James 
Moody, Art Famer and Clark Terry, 
plus a first time ever 'drum battle' 
between Elvin Jones, Roy Haynes and 
Art Blakey on the 21st. On the 2nd 
there will be the Charles Mingus Sex- 
tet, with the addition of former Duke 
Ellington Trumpeter Cat Anderson, 
and the Cannonball Adderley Quintet. 
Dave Brubeck will appear on the 27th 
with his present saxist Gerry Mulli- 
gan with the added attraction of his 
old sidekick Paul Desmond. The show 
on the 28th is titled the `Giants of 
Jazz' 
featuring 
Dizzy 
Gillespie, 
Thelonious Monk, Sonny Stitt, Art 
Blakey, Kai Winding and Al McKib- 
bon. The `Giants Of Jazz' will also 
appear at Blightly's Club, Farnworth 
on the 26th and the Cannonball Ad- 
derley Quintet will appear at the Op- 
posite Lock Club, Birmingham on the 
23rd and at Blighty's Club along with 
the Charles Mingus Sextet on the 
24th. 
Richard Dunn has been appointed 
director of Swindon Viewpoint, the 
experimental cable television scheme 
for the Swindon area set up by EMI 
in conjunction with Radio Rentals, a 
British TV hire company, according 
to John Read, chief executive of EMI. 
Dunn, previously executive producer 
of EMI's special films unit, took up 
his new position 
on October 
1st. 
Swindon Viewpoint will be available 
to households' using the 625 lines cable 
relay system at no extra cost. Radio 
Rentals are supplying the relay net- 
work and EMI are responsible for the 
programming.

ter Garden Theater. Evans recorded

and the Broadway show is to be re- 
created on Radio Luxembourg in the 
near future. He was accompanied by 
R. L. general manager Alan Keen's 
assistant June Bryant.

International News Report 
CRMA Is Now 
CRIA; Adopt 
Policy Change 
TORONTO - A recent meeting of 
the Canadian Recording Manufactur- 
ers' Association has resulted in a 
name change to the Canadian Rec- 
ording Industry Association (CRIA) 
as well as policy changes. 
The association's 
new president, 
Phil Anderson, president of Ahed and 
Arc Sound, issued a statement that 
the CRIA will be "the only source -of 
official information" on the Canadian 
recording scene. The membership of 
the CRIA was apparently becoming 
alarmed over the supposed represen- 
tation it had been receiving by those, 
not in authority. Press releases and a 
closer tie with the press is expected in 
the future. 
It was also decided at the same 
meeting that the membership of the 
CRIA should adopt the MAPL system 
of identification for Canadian content 
recordings. Some members had been 
using the star system, initially de- 
signed for CRIA members while oth- 
ers were using the word Cancon. The 
use of the MAPL logo will unify the 
system of Canadian content recogni- 
tion. 
Phonogram 
Gathers 16 
Reps To Baarn 
BAARN - In a meeting held at Pho- 
nograms 
International 
offices 
at 
Baarn recently 
16 delegates from 
Sweden, England, Italy, Norway, Hol- 
land, 
Germany, 
France, Denmark, 
Switzerland and Belgium attended. 
This was the first time Phonogram 
had held such a meeting, and items 
discussed included the possibility of 
frequent and extensive visits of inter- 
national talent to the continent, artist 
exposure on radio and TV, promotion 
film requirements and promotion pub- 
lications. 
The major outcome of the meeting 
was the possibility of better and more 
frequent tours on the continent by 
Phonogram artists. Commenting on 
the event David Hofstede, interna- 
tional artist and record promotion 
manager said, "One of the main ben- 
efits was the fact that our representa- 
tives in the main territories had the 
opportunity of meeting each other for 
a discussion on their policies, plans 
and problems. Many positive results 
have been achieved as a direct result 
of the meeting."

Dureco Celebrates 
20th Anniversary 
BELGIUM - This year Dureco cel- 
ebrates its 20th birthday. The man in 
the middle of this prosperous record 
company is Robert Aardse, commer- 
cial and artistic manager. He became 
representative with Dureco in 1960. 
Till 1968 he remained representative 
and in recent years he was sales pro- 
motor. 
A man who helped to 
establish 
Dureco was Johnny Hoes. In 1964 he 
came over from Phonogram. His first 
album 
was "Een reisje langs de 
Rijn". Robert Aardse still regrets 
that Johnny Hoes started on his own 
at the end of 1967. Dureco lost a sale 
of 2% million records and remained 
with only 1% million records. From 
that time Aardse appeared to be the 
leader of a sinking ship. What was 
left of the repertoire was modernized. 
With the hit "Big bamboo" by The 
Merrymen, 
Dureco 
started 
again. 
With the arrival of Ben Cramer, with 
Shocking Blue and their world hit 
"Venus" and with the introduction of 
writer Pierre Kartner, things were 
getting better and better. 
Producer Pierre Kartner launched 
the Elf Provincien label. This label is 
only meant for Dutch repertoire. Also 
a great deal of Flemish repertoire is 
present. Dureco is really doing well 
now. In 1971 the company had a sale 
of 13% million net. This year the com- 
pany got a new building with its own 
studios. On the occasion of Dureco's 
20th birthday a grand jubilee action 
wa organized. In exchange for an old 
single and a bargain price everybody 
can get a new album entitled "Gouden 
Hitpourri". Names on this LP are 
Corry en de Rekels, Ben Cramer, Ge- 
broeders Brouwer, 
Anja en Johnny, 
Sylvain Poons & 
Oetze Verschoor, 
Wilma en Vader Abraham, Jacques 
Herb en de Riwi's, Anja, De Kermisk- 
lanten, Vader 
Abraham 
met zijn 
goede zonen, De Makkers en Duo X.

To GRT In Can. 
NEW YORK - Metromedia Records 
has switched its distribution in Cana- 
da and will now be represented by 
GRT in that market for both records 
and tapes. Long term deal was an- 
nounced by Jack Wiedenmann, pres- 
ident of Metromedia and Ross Rey- 
nolds, president of GRT of Canada. 
Reynolds has planned rush release 
of recent Metromedia single and al- 
bum product including the 
Bobby 
Sherman LP as well as the new al- 
bums by Peter Allen and Peter Co - 
field. In addition, GRT Canada plans 
a 
massive 
effort behind 
"Buzzy 
Brown," by Tim Davis. 
Deal was negotiated by Tara Inter- 
national's Dick Broderick in conjunc- 
tion with Wiedenmann and Reynolds. 
THE FIRST OF HIS `ART': Violinist 
Joseph Szigeti (right) was presented 
an advance copy of Columbia Rec- 
ords' special six -record set, "The Art 
of Joseph Szigeti," during the Prix 
Mondial du Disque ceremony at Mon- 
treaux, Switzerland. Peter de Rouge- 
mont (left), vice president of Europe- 
an operations for CBS Records Inter- 
national, made the presentation. The 
set was just released here in the U.S 
to honor the artist's 80th birthday.

Knight Sued 
Over Rights 
To Label Name 
HOLLYWOOD-Art Brambila, head 
of Brown Bag Productions here, has 
filed suit in Los Angeles Superior 
Court against Terry Knight and 
Wilkes -Braun from use of the name 
Brown Bag 
Records, 
and 
asking 
$100,000 in general damages and a 
similar amount in punitive and ex- 
emplary damages. 
As early as March, 1970, accord- 
ing to Brambila, he approached the 
then A&R chief of Capitol Records, 
Karl Engemann, with the idea of pro- 
ducing Latin -oriented reck records on 
which Capitol would have first re- 
fusal. Brambila was granted free stu- 
dio time by the company to come up 
with some demos and, he says, by 
December of that year had been for- 
mally granted 100 hours of free time 
under the name Brown Bag Produc- 
tions. 
Brambila further alleges that in 
January, 1971, Ode Records contract- 
ed directly with Brown Bag Produc- 
tions for the services of recording 
artist Mark Guerrero, currently rep- 
resented on the Capitol label with a 
single titled "Rock 'n' Roll Queen" 
and another due for release in the 
next few weeks, "I'm Brown." Capi- 
tol also has an album by Guerrero 
slated for February, 1973, release. 
At press time, Terry Knight said, 
"I have not been served, and accord- 
ing to my attorneys, I have not been 
sued. All I know is that I bought the 
name and concept for Brown Bag 
Records 
from 
the 
Wilkes -Braun 
Graphic Design firm. Since no action 
has been taken to stop the release 
of any Brown Bag Records product, 
I do not intend to delay the release 
of our first LP." 
Welding Assists 
Playboy's Cohn 
HOLLYWOOD - Playboy 
Records' 
exec vice president Larry Cohn has 
named Pete Welding as his assistant. 
The appointment is effective imme- 
diately. 
Welding comes to Playboy from 
two years as west coast A&R direc- 
tor at Epic Records. Before Epic, he 
did graduate work at UCLA in Eth- 
nomusicology and Folklore and was 
Assistant Editor of Downbeat for 
four and a half years before that. 
While at Epic, Welding produced 
Redbone's first two albums for that 
label. He also produced the first 
Quicksilver Messenger Service album 
for Capitol. Most recently, he pro- 
duced the "Where It All Began" al- 
bum by Bo Diddley on Chess. He was 
also responsible for compiling, for 
Chess, retrospective albums on Mud- 
dy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and Sonny 
Boy Williamson. 
White MD Of 
'Earth' Show 
NEW YORK-West Coast arranger - 
composer -conductor Larry White has 
been named music director for the 
upcoming Broadway musical, "Mother 
Earth." The Ray Golden production, 
first staged in California, is being 
presented in New York by Roger 
Ailes. 
The show, now slated for an Oct. 
19 Gotham premiere at the Belasco 
Theater, features singer Kelly Gar- 
rett. 
At one time, White was a member 
of the pop group, the Sandpipers. He 
has also conducted and arranged for 
the 
Osmonds, 
Engelbert 
Humper- 
dinck, Connie Stevens and Nancy Wil- 
son, among others; and was music 
director for two Chevrolet specs un- 
der the title, "The Changing Scene," 
and for a series of eight NBC variety 
shows featuring the Carpenters, Al 
Hirt and Mark Lindsay. 
Price Heads 
Sales At 
Polydor 
NEW YORK-Phil Picone has an- 
nounced that Mel Price has been ap- 
pointed national sales manager for 
Polydor Inc. Price, a vet music busi- 
ness sales exec, was formerly west 
coast sales manager for Polydor. 
Price had previously been associated 
with MGM, serving in various exec 
capacities for seven years, including 
a five year tenure as west coast 
branch manager for MGM. He was 
also national sales manager for MGM. 
Klein, Keller 
Join Staff Of 
April -Blackwood 
NEW YORK - Charles Koppelman, 
vice president and general manager 
of April/Blackwood Music, the music 
publishing wing of Columbia 
Rec- 
ords, has announced two major ap- 
pointments to the firm's East and 
West coast offices. 
Koppelman, 
who 
joined 
April/ 
Blackwood three months ago, has 
named Gary Klein to a newly cre- 
ated post of director of music pub- 
lishing, and Jack Keller to profes- 
sion manager of the Los Angeles of- 
fice. Joel Diamond continues as gen- 
eral professional manager. 
Klein will coordinate April/Black- 
wood's print catalog, exploit copy- 
rights through the special products 
divisions of all record companies, co- 
ordinate the overseas publishing in- 
terests, and audition new writers and 
material. Keller will be responsible 
for the day-to-day operations of the 
West Coast office, his duties to in- 
clude exploiting existing catalog and 
auditioning new writers. 
Both Klein and Keller come to 
April/Blackwood with extensive ex- 
perience in the publishing field. 
Irk 
1967 Klein established the west coast 
office for Koppelman & Rubin's Faith- 
ful Virtue Music and Chardon Music, 
whose catalog represented John Se- 
bastian, Tim Hardin, Bonner and Gor- 
don and others. He later returned to 
New York, first with Commonwealth 
United and in 1969 with Koppelman- 
Rubin Enterprises. 
Keller, for the past 12 years has 
been associated with Screen Gems/ 
Columbia Music. He has produced and 
written many hits, such as "Every- 
body's Somebody's Fool" in 1960, and 
most recently with "Easy Come, Easy 
Go" by Bobby Sherman. He wrote the 
television theme songs for "Bewitch- 
ed" and "Here Come the Brides." He 
had also been instrumental in work- 
ing with and developing several writ- 
ers for Don Kirshner's Aldon Music. 
Kazdin Exec 
Producer At 
Masterworks 
NEW YORK-Columbia Records has 
announced the appointment of An- 
drew Kazdin to exec producer for 
Masterworks and Original Cast re- 
cordings, report Thomas Shepard and 
Thomas Frost, directors of Columbia 
Masterworks. 
Kazdin joined the Masterworks de- 
partment in 1964, and has produced 
albums for Glenn Gould, E. Power 
Biggs, Isaac Stern, Eugene Ormandy, 
George Szell, Pierre Boulez, 
Gary 
Graffman, Philippe Entremont, Leo- 
pold Stokowski and the Philadelphia 
Brass Ensemble. In addition, he has 
produced the soundtracks of "Liza 
With a 'Z' " and the "1776" caster. 
Kazdin, who received his Bachelor 
of Music degree from the New Eng- 
land Conservatory of Music and a 
Master of Science degree from M.I.T., 
has also performed and conducted for 
Masterworks. 
HONORABLE AFFAIR-Some 1,000 persons were at the Waldorf Astoria 
to see Clive Davis, president of Columbia Records, honored as recipient of the 
Ed Wynn Humanitarian Award by the American Parkinson Disease Associa- 
tion. The sixth annual dinner was the most successful held by the association. 
Epic artist Donovan and Columbia artist Maxine Weldon performed. Shown 
in photos above are (top row, left to right), Mr. & Mrs. Clive Davis, and 
Davis flanked by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff of Philaedlphia International 
Records. (second row) Clive Davis with Ornette Coleman and Donovan. Final 
photo captures Donovan in performance at the reception.

marketing

has

Corp. distributes pianos, organs and a

well as motorcycles, skis, snowmo- 
biles, and audio equipment. Yamaha 
Exporting, Inc. is designed to end

Jeromes Sign 
Production Tie 
wgvolution 
NEW YORK-Steve and Bill Jerome, 
riding high with their hit single 
"Popcorn," have entered into a long- 
term production deal with Evolution 
Records. 
The first release under the new 
Evolution deal 
will 
be 
a 
single, 
"Waitin' For the Day to Come," re- 
corded by Steve Feldman and written 
by Feldman with Ellie Greenwich and 
Steve Tudanger. Feldman is a studio 
pianist and percussionist and has 
written material for many major per- 
formers, including Tom Jones. He has 
also been successful writing commer- 
cial jingles. An album is already in 
production with a December/January 
release planned. 
Evolution, currently on the charts 
with "Sunny Days" by Lighthouse, 
plans 
an 
immediate 
release 
for 
"Waitin' For the Day to Come".

Polydor Takes 
Ad Time On 
'Soul Street' 
NEW YORK - Polydor has bought 
ad time on the nationally syndicated 
TV show "Soul Street." 
Initially designed to highlight R&B 
product with the possibility of extend- 
ing the program, says Elaine Gold- 
stein, ad manager, the time buys will 
consist of four weeks of ad spots 
located during the Soul Street Pro- 
gram hosted by soul television per- 
sonality Tommy Russell. The spots 
will be shown in Soul Street's 30 mar- 
kets beginning last weekend (13). 
Markets to be reached include such 
major stations as Chicago (WSNS), 
Washington, D.C. (WDCA), St. Louis 
(KPLR), Cincinnati (WKRC), Den- 
ver (KWGN), Philadelphia (WTAF), 
Baltimore 
(WBFF), 
Houston 
(KVRL), Los Angeles (KBSC), San 
Francisco (KBHK), and Bo s t o n 
(WKBG). 
Polydor has purchased ad spots for 
such soul artists and soul product as 
Lyn Collins' Think About It LP, Mil- 
lie Jackson's Millie Jackson LP, Joe 
Simon's Drowning in the Sea of Love 
LP, James Brown's There It Is, Soul 
Classics and Revolution of the Mind 
albums, Mandrill's Mandrill Is and the 
J. B.'s Food for Thought album. 
Ms. Goldstein has stated that Poly- 
dor will be watching results of the 
television advertising buys 
closely

HOLLYWOOD: VIKKI CARR (from page 18) 
areas that Columbia didn't expect it to sell. It will be released in Mexico in October 
and should be a top seller in that country as well. 
"I'm really thrilled with enthusiasm over this album," said Miss Carr. "This 
album is a little special because it's going to expose the public to some of the 
contemporary Mexican writers, such as Armando Manzareo, who wrote 'It's Im- 
possible' for Perry Como and who wrote 'Somos Novios' in my album. We tried 
to keep everyone happy; we did a song from Spain, a song from Brazil, and we 
decided to keep me happy because 
I wanted to show the people that there are 
other songs that the Latin market has besides 'Granada' and 'Guantanamera.' " 
The album is based on romance, 
and it relates to a lot of people in love. 
"Somos Novios," one of the tender 
love songs contained 
in this album, 
deals with the beginning of a beautifil 
relationship between a young man and 
woman and ends tragically when the 
woman finds out she has been used 
and her man was no good. The songs 
are simple and tender, and Vikki Carr 
makes them sound very caressing. 
Vikki Carr's generosity and concern 
is 
extended 
especially 
to 
Mexican - 
American young people. She has be- 
gun an annual series of $1000 scholar- 
ships to help some of the bright, de- 
serving young 
Chicanos who 
could 
otherwise not afford to go on to col- 
lege, the first grants being awarded 
early in 1971 by the Vikki Carr Scholar- 
ship Foundation. Like her new album, 
this scholarship was a project of love 
for Vikki Carr, the young songstress 
whom everyone knows as a lover of 
milk! 
david gest 
Vikki Carr

NOTES 'N NEWS-According to a press release received from RCA, the sound- 
track album of "The Sound Of Music" on that label is still the largest selling 
album in the history of the record industry. As of the June, '72 audit, domestic 
sales are in excess of 6 million units, and world-wide sales are approaching 13 
million copies. 
Capitol records' Raspberries are currently in the midst of a cross country tour 
with The Hollies 
. 
. 
. "New Blood," first album released from Blood, Sweat & 
Tears in over a year credits six of the 10 group members with the arrangement 
chores. Group played Philharmonic Hall on Oct. 15 & 16 ... Judy Collins will 
be making her first major tour in almost two years beginning on Oct. 26, and 
concluding with two Christmas concerts at Carnegie Hall on Dec. 22 & 23. 
New albums from Santana and Malo being released at the same time by Colum- 
bia and Warner Brothers, respectively. Let's see if blood is thicker than water ..

Andre Kostelanetz conducting The New York 
Philharmonic/The Columbia Symphony Orches- 
tra; Andre Previn, piano-Columbia MG 31415 
A highly commercial, specially priced two - 
disk set of highlights from the spring festivities 
at Lincoln

in

White House Xmas Col Drive On Jazz Catalog 
Favorites On LP 
From Caedmon 
NEW YORK - Caedmon Records is 
rushing 
into 
release 
an 
unusual 
Christmas album, "Christmas at the 
White House," featuring Burl Ives 
singing the favorite carols and hymns 
of America's presidents. The album 
consists of Christmas favorites of 12 
of the nation's chief executives, from 
George Washington to Richard M. 
Nixon. 
The music was arranged and con- 
ducted by Tony Mottola, courtesy of 
Project 3 Records, and played in the 
style of the era in which it was origi- 
nally 
chosen 
by 
each 
president. 
Caedmon is. making two versions of 
the album available: one for the edu- 
cational market, in which Ives intro- 
duces each 
song with information 
about the president and his choice, 
toegether with an anecdote pertaining 
to Christmas at the White House of 
that time; the other version contain- 
ing the twelve carols and hymns only, 
aimed at the consumer market. The 
educational version will also be avail- 
able on cassette, while the consumer 
version will be available on 8 track 
stereo tape. 
Caedmon is mounting a concentrat- 
ed promotion of the Ives package in- 
cluding samples to AM, FM and col- 
lege radio stations, plus a schedule of 
consumer ads across the country. 
MGM To Release 
'Kid Power' Track 
HOLLYWOOD - Mike Curb, pres- 
ident of MGM Records announced last 
week that 
he 
had 
acquired 
the 
soundtrack rights to "Kid Power," 
which has become a hit Saturday 
television series for the ABC Televi- 
sion Network. 
The "Kid Power" track album will 
feature 
8 new songs by arranger - 
composer Perry Botkin, Jr., and lyri- 
cist Jules Bass. 
Cofield Single 
Recall For New 
Edited Version 
NEW YORK - Metromedia Records, 
claiming heavy initial airplay for the 
single from Peter Cofield's album, has 
urged its distributors to return stock 
for the new edited version immediate- 
ly, reports Mort Weiner, marketing 
director of the label. 
Weiner said: "We are so excited by 
the reception Peter Cofield's single 
"Taking Some Time With A Bottle Of 
Wine" has gotten from radio stations 
and trade reviewers that we've asked 
our distributors to return single stock 
on hand for rush shipment of the 
edited, re -mixed single from the al- 
bum, "What Exactly Is A Friend."

'Of Thee I Sing' 
Video Special 
NEW YORK - Columbia Records 
has rush -released the original cast al- 
bum 
of 
this 
week's 
(Tuesday, 
9:30-11:00 p.m. est) CBS -TV special 
"Of Thee I Sing," starring "All In 
The Family" star Carroll O'Connor as 
"presidential candidate" John P. Win- 
tergreen and Academy award winner 
Cloris Leachman. 
To coincide with the presentations of 
the 
1931, 
Pulitzer Prize 
musical 
satire, Columbia is supporting the 
album, produced by Thomas Z. Shep- 
ard, with major market radio spots, 
newspaper ads and an ad in TV Guide 
Magazine's TV listings for Oct. 24. 
The program's sponsor, AMF, has 
launched a promo campaign of its 
own which included mass radio and 
newspaper advertising. Wintergreen 
campaign booths located in Grand 
Central Station and other centers of 
commuter activity, "Wintergreen for 
President" buttons and bumper stick- 
ers and a mock convention held Octo- 
ber 18th in L.A. nominating Winter- 
green for '72. 
"Of 
Thee 
I 
Sing," 
George 
S. 
Kaufman's tongue-in-cheek 
look at 
elections, was the first musical play to 
ever 
win 
a 
Pulitzer 
Prize, 
and 
features the original 1931 score by 
George and Ira Gershwin. Highlight- 
ing the TV special and that cast al- 
bum are such Gershwin standards as

HOLLYWOOD - Groucho Marx has

of

Mouse hats and "The

stations across the country and to all

ords "The Mouse Factory" record al- 
bums.

Chi Starts

Pacific Stereo 
NEW YORK - Pacific Stereo, the 
West 
Coast -based 
hifi 
component 
chain, is expanding its market, and 
Chicago is its first stop. At the open- 
ing of the chain's Oak Lawn store, 
vice-president and general manager 
Tom Anderson indicated that there 
would be four more Pacific Stereo 
stores in the Chicago area. Company 
officials have also talked about expand- 
ing to other areas outside of Illinois 
and Calif. 
Attending the official opening of 
the Oak Lawn store along with Art 
Rivel, vice-president retail distribu- 
tion and audio products at CBS Rec- 
ords, Anderson was joined by Barry 
Taylor, manager store installations; 
Tom Collins, manager of the Oak 
Lawn store; and Bob Schumacher, 
marketing liaison. 
Visitors were led through two sim- 
ulated living rooms, each with diff- 
erent price ranged component systems 
and asked to compare sets. Browsers 
were also 
given a 
four -channeled 
treat in the form of a quad listening 
room.

Chi Fest Boosts Groove Merchant 
NEW YORK - An all-star jazz con- 
cert featuring artists on Groove Mer- 
chant Records, the focal point for a 
massive promo campaign, has "dynam- 
ically" increased the label's sales in 
Chicago. 
Sonny Lester, president of Groove 
Merchant, reports that, "within a 
month of the time we began advertis- 
ing and promoting the concert, our 
Chicago 
distributor, 
Royal 
Disc, 
quadrupled sales in tapes and LP's." 
Groove Merchant had 23 major rec- 
ord store window displays in the Chi- 
cago area, they had radio saturation 
with 220 ad spots prior to the concert 
and they were heavily advertised on 
the Soul Train TV show. "Groove 
Merchant Week" was declared. In ad- 
dition, many thousands of handbills 
and posters were distributed within a 
wide radius of the Auditorium The- 
atre. Advertising and publicity ap- 
peared in virtually every newspaper 
in town. 
The concert featured Groove Mer- 
chant artists Dakota Staton, Groove 
Holmes, 
Jimmy 
McGriff, 
Lucky 
Thompson, 
Reuben 
Wilson 
and 
O'Donel Levy. Shows were at 7 and 
10:30 PM on Saturday, Oct. 14 at the 
Auditorium Theatre in Chicago, with 
each ticket holder receiving a free 
Groove Merchant album at the door. 
In the planning stages since Aug., 
the Chicago concerts are the first in a 
series which will promote the Groove 
Merchant artist roster and establish 
the label's image. Lester is planning 
similar promotions in other U.S. cit- 
Wm. Sheppard New 
Cutlass President 
NASHVILLE-William E. "Bunky" 
Sheppard has been named president 
of Cutlass Records Inc. 
Other exec changes included nam- 
ing William "Billy" Carr senior vice 
president, Stu Tinney as exec vice 
president in charge of sales and Ted- 
dy Boothe as musical director. 
Other recent and new additions also 
include Tom McConnell as national 
director of country and pop promo- 
tion; Mike Roman to handle all of 
Cutless' publishing companies and 
Jan Guenter as executive secretary. 
A 20 -year vet in the music indus- 
try, Sheppard was Ray Charles' pro- 
mo director before joining Cutlass 
three months ago. Carr, too, has been 
affiliated in the production end of the 
business for many years, while Tin- 
ney is a former East Coast business 
executive. Boothe, known profession- 
ally as Teddy B, proclaims a back- 
ground which includes playing saxo- 
phone with several of the big name 
bands, including the late Otis Red- 
ding. 
ies. A 14 -city tour of England and the 
continent is being planned for 1973. 
More to Come 
"We're not in the concert business, 
but we intend to follow this format 
all over the country," said Lester. 
"We're going to employ these tech- 
niques 
in other cities in order to 
achieve the same breakthrough we ex- 
perienced in Chicago. We also expect 
to package this unit for college tours. 
We're not looking to make money on 
the concerts, as long as we can in- 
crease the sales of our albums and 
tapes and build Groove Merchant in 
major record markets. Our first con- 
certs have proved that we can make 
our plan work." 
A highlight of the concerts was the 
first -time -together 
jam 
featuring 
three great organists, Groove Holmes, 
Jimmy 
McGriff 
and 
Reuben 
Wil- 
son, all playing massive Hammond 
organs. 
EMI/Springfield 
(Cont'd from p. 9) 
rather cool reception here this sum- 
mer for reasons that Porter has come 
to understand. He believes that all 
seven on his artist roster, all proven 
as top acts in Australia, have interna- 
tional potential, and if he made some 
miscalculations 
in the way Daddy 
Cool was introduced here, he has by 
no means repeated them in getting 
Rick Springfield off the ground. Dad- 
dy Cool will be back too, and ac- 
cording to Porter, "We expect them 
to break wide open this time." 
Porter drew a parallel between Mel- 
bourne today and the Liverpool of 
the mid -60s, in that he felt there was 
the same bubbling under of creativity 
among both musicians and writers. 
"Up until 1970," he said, "Australia 
was really behind American and Eng- 
land musically. We were turning out 
a lot of mediocre originals and cov- 
ers. But since then, I think, we've 
developed a sound of our own, to the 
point that four or five Australian 
bands are ready to compete in the 
world market." 
The five Sparmac acts standing in 
the wings are Gary Young, Jerry & 
the Joy Band, the B. Bright Band, the 
Hot Dog, and the Mint, all of whom 
are writers. The next one being 
readied for U.S. exposure is Jerry & 
the Joy Band-"a kind of cross be- 
tween Alice Cooper and Tiny Tim, 
visually"-with a record deal pend- 
ing. 
"I like to develop an act at a time," 
Porter said, "so as to get a firmer 
basis for success, and you can only do 
this by concentrating on a single act 
and giving it the time and energy it 
takes to get it rolling."

Ms. & Music 
Doing Fine 
At ASCAP 
NEW YORK - The music and rec- 
ord industry is an area where women 
are, more than ever before, holding 
their own in terms of both business 
and artistic achievement, reports the 
American Society of Composers, Au- 
thors and Publishers. Female member- 
ship in ASCAP is growing, with the 
latest Ms. talents to join being Mimi 
Farina and Candy Staton. 
Some of ASCAP's female members 
who have made important contribu- 
tions to contemporary music are: 
Carole King, Gladys Knight, Judy 
Collins, Jackie DeShannon, the late 
Janis Joplin, Valerie Simpson, Rober- 
ta 
Flack, 
Chi 
Coltrane, 
Dorothy 
Fields, Gladys Shelley and Mary Lou 
Williams, to name a few. The Society 
also points out that there are many 
women, known primarily as ASCAP 
composers and/or artists, who have 
formed their own publishing compa- 
nies, including Janis Ian, Joan Baez, 
Carly Simon, Estelle Levitt and Mel- 
anie. 
To honor the growing activity in 
its female membership ranks, ASCAP 
will run an in-depth article on Carole 
King and a cover story on Dorothy 
Fields in the next issue of its maga- 
zine ASCAP Today.

Seattle Promoter Expands; Changes 
SEATTLE - Northwest Releasing 
Corp., Seattle -based firm that has 
presented name concert attractions in 
the Pacific northwest and western 
Canada for the past 19 years, has 
expanded its sphere of operations, in- 
creased its staff, and shifted top man- 
agement. According to president Bill 
Owens, Jerden Industries, Inc., and 
Potlatch Enterprises, Inc., have be- 
come major stockholders in NRC. 
Under the restructuring, chief ex- 
ecutives of Jerden and Potlatch, Jerry 
Dennon and Jerry Lonn, respectively, 
will become members of NRC's board 
of directors and active in the compa- 
ny. With Owens moving to chairman 
of the board, Dennon becomes pres- 
ident and Lonn vice president and 
general manager. 
Dennon is president of Jerden In- 
dustries, a Seattle -based communica- 
tions and entertainment company spe- 
cializing in records, music publishing, 
radio station ownership, commercial 
productions, and broadcast vocational 
schools. Dennon is a vet of 13 years 
in music and broadcast. Bob Flick, 
former member of the Brothers Four, 
is a Jerden vice president. Jerden has 
interests in Washington, Oregon, Ari- 
zona, and Japan. 
Potlatch Enterprises, Inc., of Seat- 
tle 
and Portland 
is 
an 
advertis- 
ing/promotion firm. It has served as 
the publicity arm of NRC for the past 
three years, and also is NRC's gener- 
al partner for concert presentations 
in Portland. Under the direction of 
Lonn, the firm's founder, Potlatch has 
tripled the NRC concert business in 
Portland during the past two years, 
grossing $900,000 last year for 31 at- 
tractions. 
Erick Justin Kaz 
Signed To Atlantic 
NEW YORK 
- - Eric Justin Kaz has 
been signed to an exclusive recording 
contract with Atlantic Records. A 
singer, songwriter and musician, Kaz 
was brought to the attention of At- 
lantic by producer Michael Cuscuna, 
who also produced the artist's forth- 
coming ablum. 
Kaz has a long history of credits as 
a songwriter, arranger and studio 
sideman. The composer of "Mother 
Earth, (Provides For Me)" for Tracy 
Nelson, he has also written material 
recorded by Tom Rush, Linda Ron- 
stadt, Bonnie Raitt and many others. 
He has also composed the scores of 
two pictures, the well -received "Hi 
Mom," and "Greetings." On his soon - 
to -be -released first album, Kaz sings 
many of his own compositions accom- 
panying himself on keyboards, guitar 
and harmonica. 
The recording contract for Kaz was 
negotiated by Cuscuna and Mark 
Meyerson for Atlantic and Johannan 
Vigoda for the artist. 
CLEAN AND SHINING - Celebrat- 
ing the release of Clean Records art- 
ists Delbert & Glen's first album, At- 
lantic threw a press reception and 
performance at Max's Kansas City 
last Tuesday for New York's music 
journalists 
and 
celebrities. 
Shown 
above (left to right): Glen Clark, 
WXLO-FM DJ Walt Love, Dickie 
Kline of Atlantic, WWDJ's Ronnie 
Grant, and Delbert McClinton. 
Lonn's Duties 
Lonn will take over the day-to-day 
operations as general manager, with 
Owens continuing to oversee all buy- 
ing of attractions. G. H. Burke Gar- 
rett will promote concerts indepen- 
dently in other parts of the country 
not presently served by NRC. 
Last year the company's gross for 
the immediate Pacific Northwest area 
(Oregon, Washington, British Colum- 
bia) surpassed $3,360,000. The compa- 
ny also successfully presented a host 
of performers and concerts in other 
markets across the country. 
Principal cities of operation for 
NRC are Seattle, Spokane, Tacoma 
(Washington), 
Portland, 
Eugene 
(Oregon), 
Honolulu, 
Denver, 
Salt 
Lake City, and the Canadian cities of 
Vancouver, B.C., Calgary, Edmonton, 
Regina, Saskatoon, and Winnipeg. 
Authentic Signs 
Carpenter; Sets 
Singles Re -Issues 
NEW YORK - Authentic Records 
has signed Edward Carpenter, Jr. to a 
long term production agreement. Car- 
penter has produced and assigned 
several masters by The Family Affair 
a group that Carpenter leads, consist- 
ing of his wife and mother, to Au- 
thentic -Records. Their first release 
was "I Had a Friend". Their second 
release, 
"Man from 
the 
Ghetto", 
which was taken from their album 
"The Prophesy" is now being sent to 
radio stations. The album is due out 
in four weeks. 
Julius Dixon, vet composer, pro- 
ducer who heads Authentic says that 
he has now decided to re-release 
several masters from 1958-59. They 
are "Love's Burning Fire" by Beverly 
Ann Gibson, "The Reason" by The 
Chanels, and "The Clouds" by The 
Spacemen. These records were all Top 
100 in a 12 month period.

release plans spotlight three new al- 
bums: "Hatching Out" by Sparrow, 
"Keith Michell Sings Broadway" and, 
on the company's serious music divi- 
sion, Blue Label, "Niccolo Paganini." 
In addition, Spark will be re -servicing 
"My Present," a seasonal single re- 
lease, performed by Jon and Sondra 
Steele. 
"Hatching Out" by Sparrow, is the 
English rock group's first album, fol- 
lowing on the heels of two singles, 
"Rainsun Song" and "I'm Coming 
Back." 
"Keith Michell Sings Broadway," 
the British star's second album, origi- 
nated with a BBC television series 
showcasing Keith Michell's diverse 
talents in over 50 roles. Songs from 
12 of these performances appear on 
the album, among them "Gigi," "01' 
Man River" and "I Only Want to 
Say" from "Jesus Christ -Superstar." 
Michell's first LP, "Keith Michell-My 
Songs/Henry VIII-His Songs," was 
released during the run of his Emmy 
award -winning portrayal of the title 
role in "The Six Wives of Henry 
VIII," broadcast over American net- 
work TV in the fall of 1971. 
"Niccolo Paganini" contains the 
first performance this century of

lin, viola, violincello and guitar, and 
"Quartetto Sonatine" for violin and

ASCAP Tops 
20,000 Mark 
In Membership 
NEW YORK - Membership in the 
American Society of Composers, Au- 
thors and Publishers has passed the 
20,000 mark, ASCAP president Stan- 
ley Adams announced recently. As of 
the end of May, America's oldest per- 
forming rights 
organization num- 
bered some 
5,037 music publisher 
members and 14,829 composers and 
lyricists-a total of 20,166. As of 
Aug. 30, it is 20,343. 
ASCAP has more than doubled dur- 
ing the past decade. At the end of 
1962, membership included 2,072 pub- 
lishers and 6,708 writers. That total 
of 8,780 was itself more than double 
the 1952 figures, 524 publishers and 
2,688 writers-total 3,212. 
The Society, which operates under 
the U.S. copyright law of 1909 to 
license the public performance for 
profit of its members' copyrighted 
works of music, was founded 
in 
N.Y.C. in 1914. At the end of the first 
year, membership was less than 200 
with 170 writers and 22 publishers. 
Today's 20,343 members include ar- 
tists in theatre, film and tv music, 
rock, folk, country, opera, chamber, 
symphonic and religious music. 
previously been eclipsed by Paganini's 
renown as a violinist, are performed 
by the Quartetto Di. Torino.

cashbox/talent on stage 
Quicksilver 
oz Scaggs 
Wishbone Ash 
I. 
The advertising 
read 
"Farewell 
Performance". The original group, 
formed many years ago in California 
under the name of Quicksilver Mes- 
senger Service was indeed excellent. 
After first three Capitol albums, per- 
sonnel started to depart and many 
felt all went downhill. Although the 
current group did perform some old 
favorites, they showed that it was a 
lost cause by putting a good deal of 
the audience to sleep if not driving 
them outside. 
Boz Scaggs was the unfortunate 
loser in the battle with the sound 
system. It got so bad that he even 
took a ten minute break hoping the 
company, Weisberg, could get it to- 
gether. No luck though. Boz opened 
the set with the now traditional "We 
Were Only Sweethearts" and came off 
quite well. 
The only bright spot of the entire 
evening was the opening act, Decca 
recording artists Wishbone Ash. In 
England, their home, they are a head- 
liner; why on the two States tours 
they have been third on a three act 
bill escapes me. "Argus," the latest 
and finest group effort has just been 
voted the #1 album in the 1972 Melo- 
dy Maker Pop Poll. Material from all 
three of their LP's was presented and 
presented well by Andy Powell, Ted 
Turner, Martin Turner, and Steve Up- 
ton. The audience was with them all 
the way and in the end let them know 
it by giving a deserving ovation. This 
group is definitely one to keep your 
eyes and ears on. 
p.a. 
Tim Buckley 
Whole Oats 
BITTER END, NY - Music from 
Philadelphia has come back to nation- 
al attention through the efforts of 
Thom Bell and Gamble & Huff, the 
soul producers who have done so well 
by The Stylistics/The Spinners and 
The O'Jays/Harold Melvin 
& The 
Blue Notes respectively. 
Our last 
strong memories of a white sound 
coming from that city include Bobby 
Rydell, Fabian and Frankie Avalon. 
And then along comes Whole Oats. 
A duo that looks great and sounds 
even better. The keyboard and gui- 
tar/vocal team was ably backed by 
guitar, bass, drums and mellotron at 
their New York debut here. The feel- 
ing was that there will be many more 
return visits in store for them very 
soon. The Atlantic act really shines 
on their reservedly -funky yet ultra- 
cookin' originals like "I'm Sorry" and 
the upcoming single,"Goodnight And 
Goodmornin'." Yet their more pensive 
moments are equally as impressive. 
Their music is distinctive and yet 
familiar-an all too rare combination 
these days. 
Tim Buckley performed much the 
same set that he used to open the 
most recent Zappa visit to our city. 
His non-verbal excesses are 
once 
again limited to "Gypsy Woman." 
With Carter Collins on congas and 
Lee Underwood on guitar, the restor- 
ation of his original artistic level now 
seems at hand after some rather ques- 
tionable self-indulgent albums and oc- 
casional live shows the past two 
years or so. It seems he has re- 
discovered that the soul of jazz-rock 
is to found not in its flamboyant aura 
but in the very mellow and flowing 
energy source itself. 
r.a. 
Elvin ishop 
WINTERLAND, SAN FRANCISCO 
-Elvin Bishop, celebrating his birth- 
day and newly released album on Epic 
Records, "Rock My Soul," turned on 
an enthusiastic crowd to his easy - 
rocking music. 
A great asset of Bishop's is the 
realization of his capabilities as a 
writer, musician, and singer. At the 
first two he is excellent. At the third 
he is good. Yet Bishop has not been 
caught in the trap of thinking that 
every song you write you have to 
sing. For some numbers his voice has 
the right quality, but for other songs 
it could quite possibly be lacking. So 
he wisely has combined his composing 
with Jo Baker, a strong female vocal- 
ist with a lot of heart. 
With his music and her feeling the 
group is guaranteed to bring you up. 
Bishop puts joy into his sound and 
that's really nice. 
The majority of the 
show was 
spent in performing cuts off his new 
LP. And assuming that there are peo- 
ple who enjoy letting music pick them 
up, the album should do well. 
C.C. 
Johnny Rivers 
TROUBADOR, L.A. - All too often 
capable performers become trapped in 
the notion that in order to be ac- 
cepted as a creative artist you must 
produce totally new material. Johnny 
Rivers proved that this concept isn't 
always valid. Mixing his versions of 
old favorites ("Sea Cruise," "Mem- 
phis"), currently popular hits ("Take 
It Easy," "Brown Eyed Girl"), and 
his own creations both new and old 
("Rockin' 
Pneumonia," 
"Summer 
Breeze"), Rivers built a show that 
combined solid material with great 
polish. 
His "take -offs" on other people's 
music are by no means direct copies 
of past hits. Instead, Rivers adds his 
own talent and style to the base that 
other performers have established. 
Rivers clearly is an artist that is 
more concerned with entertaining an 
audience than becoming totally self- 
indulgent in his own creations. He 
gives a crowd the taste of his own 
easy rock, the 50's rock & roll, and 
the folk/country/rock sound all in one 
package. Taking the position of both 
an innovator and creator, Rivers' 
blending of styles is unquestionably 
effective. 
C.C. 
Julie i; uudd 
WESTSIDE ROOM, L.A. - RCA 
Records' wunderkind Julie Budd made 
her first west coast appearances in 
the newly reopened Westside Room 
and most likely won her first-nighter 
audience's admiration if not their 
hearts. At 18 she has not yet really 
learned the art of disclosing vitality 
in 
performance 
while 
concealing 
effort, but she obviously has the vocal 
raw material and probably the talent, 
properly channeled, to emerge as a 
fine entertainer.

The Whispers 
GINZA DISCOTHEQUE, NYC - At 
a swinging cocktail party held Mon- 
day, October 30th, from 6 to 8 PM, 
The Whispers (Chess/Janus) were in- 
troduced locally to the industry and 
trade/press 
personnel. 
Marvin 
Schlachter, president of Chess/Janus 
hosted the well -attended affair that 
served the dual function of unveiling 
the group's 
new LP, 
"Life 
and 
Breath", and as a royal send-off for 
their upcoming tour. 
The Whispers, five soulful singers 
and dancers, opened their preview act 
with a version of the smash O'Jays 
single, "Back 
Stabbers". The 
five 
young men are right in the groove 
with their excellent dance styling and 
vocal deliveries. They are also backed 
by a solid Whispers band. Doing se- 
lections from their LP's, they also 
intro'd 
their 
new 
single 
release, 
"Somebody Loves You" from the 
"Life and Breath" LP. The Whispers 
shape up as a class act! 
d.d. 
:, ette Midler 
CONTINENTAL BATHS, NY - This 
is a hard one to write because this is 
hardly the most ideal hall in the city. 
Besides the steamroom-like condi- 
tions, only a select few of the thou- 
sand -plus audience could view the Di- 
vine Miss M. But everyone could hear 
her, and that's at least part of why 
we were all so cramped together. 
Bette Midler has single-handedly 
put the "show" back into this busi- 
ness. She is Sally Bowles without the 
tragic flaws, the supreme combination 
of a Joplin, a Streisand and the whole 
of Sha Na Na. If you laid all the 
superlatives in the world end to end, 
they couldn't make her a belt. We 
have not seen this kind of showman- 
ship in a new talent for years. May it 
spread throughout the land like the 
news of a Messianic coming. 
She now calls her black -attired fe- 
male back-up trio The Harlettes and 
describes 
them as former cocktail 
waitresses from Encino. Their version 
of "Uptown" even includes the cas- 
tinets part. But Bette is not just 
nostalgia. Her opening number, Buz- 
zy Linhart's "Friends" puts 
that 
across most positively. Whether she's 
doing her "low -rent retro -rock," her 
Laura Nyro impersonation or simply 
singing the hell out of anything she 
touches, Bette Midler is Stolle Stellar 
from the word "go." Our mind is doing 
crazy things in anticipation of her 
Atlantic debut LP. 
r.a. 
Kris Kristofferson 
Rita Coolidge 
TROUBADOR, L.A.-On stage Kris 
Kristofferson is anything but profes- 
sional. Laughing in the middle of 
songs, forgetting lines in others, his 
delivery is uncommonly casual. Yet, 
you can't help but get the feeling that 
although his performance isn't per- 
fect, it is very honest. Kristofferson 
doesn't put on airs when he takes the 
spotlight. He gets on stage and is 
himself. And it's this natural feeling 
that puts an audience at ease and 
open to all the music and meaning of 
Kristofferson. His writing and stage 
presence are effectively consistent in 
that they are both candid and compel- 
ling. 
Rita Coolidge. performing with the 
same band as Kristofferson, did cuts 
off her new A&M LP, "The Lady's 
Not For Sale." She sang with all the 
finesse and feeling that has matured 
her talent from the role of back-up 
vocalist to soloist. She then teamed 
with Kristofferson for a new final 
numbers, 
with 
"Take the 
Ribbon 
From Your Hair" highlighting the 
set. 
C.C. 
Delbert & Glen 
MAX'S KANSAS CITY, NYC - Dig 
it live! Well brother. it's easy when 
it's live in true -grit Texas style con- 
taining 
5 
pieces with that down- 
home, 
country 
funk 
blues 
sound 
which is just great for dancing. The 
kind of dancing one might see at the 
local firehouse or American Legion or 
town hall or any hall for that 
matter. And, that gives you a pretty 
good picture of Delbert & Glen and 
what they're all about. 
Delbert & Glen (Clean Records) 
distributed thru Atlantic got a proper 
New York introduction at an Ahmet 
Ertegun (Atlantic) hosted party held 
in the upstairs room at Max's. It was 
a tremendous party, the place was 
jammed with record celebs and digni- 
taries. There were plenty of refresh- 
ments of all kinds and believe me the 
dance floor was packed. also with 
dancers. And, yes, Delbert & Glen do 
play that get down music. The group, 
led by Delbert McClinton and Glen 
Clark, 
also includes Mike 
O'Neill, 
Matt Betton and David Jackson. They 
played until the wee hours for danc- 
ing, and everyone present enjoyed it. 
A few of the more outstanding selec- 
tions offered by the group included 
"Boxcar Blues". "You Don't Love Me 
No More" and "I Received A Letter". 
The group has their first LP, "Delbert 
& Glen" on the market as well as 
their new single. They sound as if 
they could start a Texas style music 
stampede.

TO 
CASH BOX 
Star,Spanngled 
Women 
For McGovern 
MADISON SQUARE GARDEN, NY 
- We saw a star being born at this 
lavish found -raising event, and not a 
political one either. Her name, Linda 
Hopkins. A virtually unknown singer 
to the audience (despite her Tony 
award for her preformance in last 
season's "Inner City"), she was the 
only artist to get two encores. Even 
The New York Times stood up to 
take notice. 
Linda sang but two numbers. Her 
first was a solo version of a tune she 
once had charted with Jackie Wilson, 
"Shake A Hand." Her finale, "It's My 
Belief" (as encored twice) should be 
the start of a substantial career for 
the RCA artist. The political speeches 
after her appearance seemed anti- 
climactic, even the moving dignity of 
Mrs. Rose Kennedy. 
Shirley McLaine was a most con- 
vivial mc, and considering the scope 
of the show, it all went extremely 
well. Dionne Warwicke opened in her 
street clothes (her bags were some- 
where in Witchita) but they looked 
like the epitome of high fashion from 
the first note. The lovely Ms. Marto 
Thomas read a fable set to music, 
loosely based on "Love Story," fol- 
lowed by a questionably liberated but 
altogether dynamite performance by 
Tina Turner & The Ikettes. 
After intermission, Gwen Verdon 
and Chita Rivera joined Ms. McLaine 
in some music and footwork from 
"Sweet Charity." Bette Davis' reading 
of "Pentagonnorhea" went over well 
as did a musical set from Judy Col- 
lins. We have heard her group in 
better form (there was a definite lack 
of key co-ordination evidenced), but 
when Judy's voice reached up to grab 
the soul of Jacques Brel's "Sons Of 
The Sons," all was forgiven and then 
some. 
The witty highlights of the super - 
bill came fro the trio of Chita Rivera, 
Gwen Verdon and Mama Cass Elliot 
as they top -hatted and caned through 
some 
parodies 
like 
"I 
Wonder 
Where's Kissinger Now?" and "I'm 
Dreaming Of A Free Martha." We 
wish we could have been offered more 
of Mama-she was her usual efferves- 
cent and jolly self; we need a whole 
lot more of that. Melina Mercouri re- 
ceived a standing ovation before she 
launched into some material from her 
"Lysistrada" musical; later she had 
to launch into "Never On Sunday" to 
reprieve herself. Mary Travers looked 
less than 
old-folky 
hi 
her long, 
flowing evening gown but she put 
across our old protestin' favorites 
with more than respectable commit- 
ment and talent. It was Ms. Travers' 
first New York solo concert appear- 
ance in some time and she's been 
missed. 
Bobby 
Rosengarten 
directed 
an 
umpteen -piece orchestra like the pro 
he is; much of the evening's success 
goes to his flexibility as an arranger. 
McGovern with those charts could 
easily sing his way to victory. 
r.a.

Gorov To 
Barnaby 
HOLLYWOOD - Cliff Gorov has 
been appointed director of national 
promotion for Barnaby Records by 
Ken Mansfield, president of the label. 
Gorov thus leaves the same post at 
Pride Records, an MGM subsidiary. 
Earlier as mid -west promotion co- 
ordinator for MGM Records, Gorov 
was helpful in establishing such na- 
tional hits as "Signs" by Five Man 
Electrical Band, "One Bad Apple", by 
the Osmonds and "Candy Man" by 
Sammy Davis, Jr. 
Gorov was previously mid -western 
promotion director for Dot -Paramount 
Records for 3% years. 
16 
Cash Box - November 18, 1972

Oct. Top Month 
For Classics 
Via Phillips 
CHICAGO - Jules Abramson, Mercu- 
ry Records' national sales manager 
reports that "Oct. classical sales had 
exceeded all expectations, setting a 
new record for classical volume in 
one month. Available information has 
made it obvious that volume was con- 
siderably over twice the Oct. sales of 
1971." 
Abramson attributed the increase in 
sales to a combination of Philips' 
Colin Davis Month sales program, the 
acceptance of "Benvenuto Cellini," the 
latest in Philips' Colin Davis -Berlioz 
Cycle, 
plus an "unusually strong 
across-the-board catalog release." 
Steady Growth 
M. Scott Mampe, director of the 
classical Division of Mercury and 
Philips, pointed out that, "this ex- 
traordinary month of record sales is 
merely another indication 
of the 
steady growth of Philips Records 
over the last three years. The long- 
term development of artists has pro- 
duced several young musicians of es- 
teemed international stature-the rise 
and maturity of Colin Davis and Ber- 
nard Haitink for instance, having 
been thoroughly documented on Phil- 
ips Records." Miss Mampe felt that 
the conversion to Imports was the 
spark leading to the growth of Phil- 
ips' Classical Product in America. She 
stated: "Four months ago, in order to 
maintain the quality for which Philips 
is renowned, the list price on Philips' 
Imports was raised to $6.98, against 
dire predictions from the industry of 
plummeting sales. Obviously, the deci- 
sion to raise the price was accurate in 
its assumption that the consumer is 
willing to pay a higher price for a 
top quality product." 
Irwin H. Steinberg, president of 
Mercury, stated: "We are totally com- 
mitted to the classical market and 
fully believe that within the next five 
years we shall be recognized as the 
definitive classical company. I should 
also point out that this extraordinary 
development is being accomplished 
through the company's independent 
distributors, providing yet another 
fine example of the effectiveness of a 
good distribution system of this 
nature." 
Boladian Forms 
Eastbound Label 
Thru Chess/Janus 
NEW YORK - Arman Boladian, the 
Detroit based distributor, producer 
and record company chief (the West- 
bound label) has formed a new label, 
Eastbound Records, which will be dis- 
tributed in the 
U.S. and Canada 
through Chess/Janus. 
Boladian revealed that "Eastbound 
will primarily concentrate on contem- 
porary black artists but will encom- 
pass all types of music." 
Initial releases on the new East- 
bound label, which will be out imme- 
diately, include albums by Bill Mason 
and Gary Chandler and to singles 
from vet Jimmy Delphs and a new 
vocal group, the Unique Blend. 
Chess/Janus president 
M a r v i n 
Schlachter, who has distributed West- 
bound Records since its inception two 
years ago, commented, "Arman Bo- 
ladian's 
success with the Detroit 
Emeralds, Funkadelic, Ohio Players, 
The Counts, Damon Shawn, Teegar- 
den 
& 
Van Winkle 
and 
Denise 
LaSalle, who gave Westbound its first 
gold record with `Trapped 
By A 
Thing Cared Love,' has established 
him as one of the most important new 
record executives in the music busi- 
ness. In addition to presenting the 
industry with an uninterrupted flow 
of hit product, Westbound has become 
firmly established as a growing, vital 
young label. We look forward to sim- 
ilar success with Eastbound Records."
