Cap In Million $ 
Deal With RCOA 
HOLLYWOOD - Capitol Industries, 
Inc., and Record Club of America, 
Inc., have announced the conclusion 
of long term contractual arrange- 
ments under which Record Club of 
America has been licensed to manu- 
facture albums, cartridges and cas - 
sets from the Capitol catalog for 
release by RCOA through its mail 
order operations in the U.S.A. and 
Canada. The club will pay Capitol 
minimum royalties over a period of 
years in excess of $1,000,000. 
Bhaskar Menon, president of Capi- 
tol 
Industries, 
said, 
"Capitol 
is 
pleased with the new arrangement, 
which will bring additional exposure 
and promotion of Capitol's recordings 
and artists to the members of RCOA. 
Because of other Capitol licensing 
agreements we do not anticipate that 
the RCOA arrangement will have any 
appreciable near term effect upon the 
company's earnings. However, we be- 
lieve its long term effect will be 
beneficial." 
Complementing Menon's remarks, 
Sigmund W. Friedman, president of 
Record Club of America, stated, "This 
is the most substantial license RCOA 
has entered into, and it is a reflection 
of our enthusiasm for Capitol and 
confidence in its products. We believe 
that our over 4 million members will 
enthusiastically welcome the inclusion 
of Capitol and Angel product in our 
club and that should be of substantial 
benefit to our operation." 
The lawsuit against Capitol Indus- 
tries, Inc., and Capitol Records, Inc., 
instituted by RCOA for alleged anti- 
competitive practices, has been termi- 
nated 
by 
RCOA. 
The 
settlement 
agreement states that these defen- 
dants expressly deny engaging in any 
illegal or wrongful activity.

In Kirshner's

NEW YORK - "In Concert," the 
first in a series of rock specials to be 
produced by Don Kirshner for ABC- 
TV will air on Nov. 24, at 11:30 p.m. 
(EST) and will feature performances 
by Alice Cooper, Curtis Mayfield, Bo 
Diddley, and Seals & Crofts. A second 
show slated for Dec. 8, will feature 
the Allman Brothers, Poco, Blood, 
Sweat & Tears, and Chuck Berry. 
According to Don Kirshner and 
Dave Yarnell, "the tapings of the 
shows turned out to be a mini Wood- 
stock, with performers and audiences 
remaining in the studio around the 
clock, and everyone giving 100% to 
make the shows come off properly." 
Yarnell commented that more than 
two-thirds of the hour and a half 
special will be entirely devoted to mu- 
sic with less than one-third for com- 
mercials. "There will be no emcee to 
introduce the groups," continued Yar- 
nell, "just music." 
Reach Major Markets 
The broadcast will be stereo simul- 
cast in many major markets includ- 
ing New York, Los Angeles, Pitts- 
burgh, Detroit, Chicago and Houston, 
as well as being FM simulcast in other 
areas.

Rudolf Friml Dies 
NEW YORK - Rudolf Friml, who 
along 
with 
Victor 
Herbert 
and 
Sigmund Romberg wrote America's 
most memorable operettas, died in 
Hollywood on Sat., Nov. 12, at the 
age of 92. 
The Prague -born composer's output 
included 33 operettas, the three most 
important being "Rose Marie," "The 
Vagabond King" and "The Three 
Musketters," 
His 
first hit, 
"The 
Firefly," was written in 1912. A movie 
version of the latter work in the 30's, 
starring Allan Jones, included an ad- 
ditional song, "Donkey Serenade." 
Friml, who continued composing 
until his death, was honored by AS - 
CAP on his 90th birthday, an event at 
which he showed his youthful flair at 
the piano. He was an ASCAP charter 
member. 
His standards, besides "Donkey Ser- 
enade," include "Indian Love Call," 
"Only a Rose," "Song of the Vaga- 
bonds," "Totem Tom Tom," among 
others. 
Friml started his music career as a 
composer and pianist of serious mu- 
sic. He first came to America, in 1901, 
as an accompanist to the noted violin- 
ist Jan Kubelik. 
Friml is survived by his fourth 
wife, two sons, a daughter and six 
grandchildren.

announced the re-signing of It's A 
Beautiful Day to the label. Negotiat-

WB Music Reps 
Bowen, Howe 
NEW YORK - Warner Bros. Music 
Publishing, in accord with its acquisi- 
tion policy, has recently concluded cat- 
alog presentation deals with 
two 
key American record producers, Jim- 
my Bowen and Bones Howe. 
Bowen has 
been 
a 
well-known 
figure on the music scene over the 
last decade. Once a pop star himself, 
as an artist he recorded a rock & roll 
classic, "Party Doll". He has produced 
numerous million -selling records for 
many artists, including Frank Sina- 
tra, Dean Martin. and Kenny Rogers 
and The First Edition. His current 
activities 
include 
recording 
Lee 
Hazlewood and Bert Kaempfert. 
Howe has produced all of the Fifth 
Dimension hits, including the million 
selling "One Less Bell" and "Didn't 
Get To Sleep." His various other re- 
cording activities have included pro- 
duction for Shirley Jones, the Associ- 
ation, and Punch. 
Ed Silvers, president of Warner 
Bros. Music, states that Warner's has 
already 
secured many 
cover re- 
cordings of compositions from both 
catalogs. 
Letter To Editol 
Right On! 
This week's Cash Box editorial 
("The Liner -Note Vacuum") 
com- 
menting on the absence of liner notes 
evident in today's product is a valid 
commentary. With so many manufac- 
turers wondering how to launch a 
new group or present a new artist, it 
seems a paradox that the potential 
consumer is given so little informa- 
tion. 
There is a root cause, though. As 
one who spent a number of years 
with various manufacturers, invested 
endless 
hours 
of 
discussion with 
countless new artists and written 
scores of liners, I experienced a de- 
veloping disdain for liner notes-not 
from the manufacturer, but from the 
artist and/or producer. As the indus- 
try passed into the era of the self- 
contained artist and the independent 
producer in the post Beatle period, 
more and more "independence" was 
asserted by these people. So called ar- 
tistic considerations took precedence 
over marketing considerations and 
the new breed of music makers said 
"the music speaks for itself 
. 
. 
. 
what's in the grooves is our state- 
ment". Great, except few people got 
to hear their "message" because they 
weren't sufficiently motivated by the 
written word to pick it up! 
The information provided by jazz 
authorities such as Feather, Gleason, 
Gitler, etc. et al is, as you stated, an 
anthology of the period and the music. 
Unless one saves random in-depth re- 
views of current pop and rock rec- 
ords, there is no archive for this peri- 
od. 
With everyone in the industry com- 
plaining, though, will they ever really 
go forward into the past in search of 
good old days? 
Marty Hoffman 
Goody 9 Mos.: 
Higher Sales, 
Profit Loss 
NEW YORK - Sam Goody, Inc. has 
reported results for the nine months 
ended Sept. 30. 
Sam Goody, president, said that 
sales for thé nine months ended Sept. 
30, increased to $19,362,571 compared 
with $17,864,129 for the year earlier 
period. There was, however, a loss of 
$93,455 or 14e per share for the cur- 
rent period, compared with a profit of 
$253,509 or 37e per share for the 
same period a year ago. 
Goody noted that the loss for the 
nine months is attributed to the open- 
ing of five new stores located in Liv- 
ingston, N.J., Pennsauken, N.J., North 
Philadelphia, Pa., Raleigh, N.C. and 
the Radio City area of New York. 
In commenting on projections for 
the year, he said that given the va- 
garies of buying patterns in the 
Christmas season, we may still reach 
our projection of net earnings of 
$475,000 or 70e per share.

Vanguard Bows 
Six Albums; 
1st Hopi Set 
NEW YORK-Vanguard Records has 
released six new albums. The four 
pop, blues and folk recordings in- 
clude: "Carmilla: A Vampire Tale" 
by the ETC Company of La Mama, 
the original cast recording; "Voice of

Vanguard album by this sensitive folk 
instrumentalist; "Hold That Plane" 
by Buddy Guy, the great blues -gui-

by Mississippi John Hart, the actual 
last sessions recorded by the folk 
and blues singer. 
The two classical recordings in- 
clude: "Las Cantigas de Santa Maria" 
performed by the Waverly Consort, 
recreating a series of tales relating 
the miracles performed by the Virgin 
Mary; and Cherubini's "Missa Solem- 
nis in D Minor" performed by the 
Clarion Concerts Orchestra and Cho- 
rus conducted by Newell Jenkins and 
featuring Patricia Wells, Maureen 
Forrester, George Shirley and Justino 
Diaz.

Grammy Awards 
Entries Screened 
NEW YORK-Dozens of the record- 
ing field's producers, musicians, ar- 
rangers, composers, record company 
execs, reviewers, authors and trade 
paper representatives gathered 
in 
New York's Essex House on Nov. 9 
for a full day screening of thousands 
of entries submitted for this year's 
Grammy Awards competition. The 
purpose of the record Academy's 
(NARAS) annual event was to in- 
sure proper category placement for 
recommendations submitted by mem- 
bers and companies and also to screen 
out. all ineligible material. 
Throughout the morning, separate 
committees met to review all entries 
in their specific fields, occasionally 
huddling with other committees to 
discuss duplicate entries. In the after- 
noon, the various committees com- 
bined forces to solve all remaining 
category problems and also to review 
all entries for the Best New Artist 
category. 
The pop, rock and folk committee 
meeting was supervised by Atlanta's 
Bill Lowery, assisted by Mary Tall- 
ent. Chicago sent Bill Traut; Los An- 
geles winged in Jack Daugherty and 
Don Ralke; Nashville supplied Don 
Gant 
and John 
Sturdivant. 
The 
trades were represented by Bob Adels 
of Cash Box, Mike Sigman of Record 
World and Sam Sutherland of Bill- 
board. Nancy Ehrlich sat in for Rec- 
ord Source International, while Co- 
lumbia and RCA sent over Mickey 
Eichner and Bruce Summerfield, re- 
spectively. 
Chicago producer Sam Brown su- 
pervised the rythm and blues screen- 
ing with able assistance from Jim 
Delehant of Atlantic, Cecil Holmes of 
the Buddah Group, Phil Jones of Mo- 
town, Buzzy Willis of RCA and Tim 
Whitsett of Stax, along with Tony 
Heilbut, 
author 
of 
"The 
Gospel 
Sound: Good News and Bad Times," 
and producers Joe Kennedy and. Hor- 
ace Ott. 
Dan Morgenstern, editor of Down 
Beat and a New York chapter Gover- 
nor, piloted the Jazz committee that 
included Atlantic's Michael Cuscuna, 
CTI's Gregg Hall, trumpeter Joe 
Newman 
and 
reviewers 
Stanley 
Dance, Ira Gitler and Father Norman 
O'Connor. 
Musicologist 
David 
Hall 
again 
chaired 
the 
Classical 
committee 
screening, aided expertly by producer 
Jim Frey, Scott Mampe of Philips 
and Tom Shepard of Columbia. And 
once more this year, author and 
teacher Henrietta 
Yurchenko and 
historian Ray Kennedy reviewed all 
the entries on the Ethnic/Traditional 
category.

Paul Williams 
In Mini -Pilot 
HOLLYWOOD -A "mini -pilot," 
something new for television, is being 
peddled to networks and syndicators, 
the show starring singer -composer 
Paul Williams. Pilot is being handled 
by Pierre Cossette and Jerry Frank 
of Hollywood, who put on the Johnny 
Mann "Stand Up and Cheer" show. 
A nine -minute segment of Wil- 
liams' appearance on that program 
was lifted and edited "to show a taste 
of Paul's personality," according to 
his manager, Denny Bond. The vi- 
gnette shows Williams singing, and 
talking. 
Pilot show is being offered as a 
late -night, 
primetime 
TV 
vehicle, 
since the A&M recording artist is 
well known in that time slot, having 
guested many times on the "Tonight" 
show. 
The segment was shot at KTLA 
studios in Hollywood, with John Mof- 
fitt directing from a script by Rod 
Warren and Ken Shapiro.

Boot Promo

Agape label in mid 1972.

Melvin's Gold 
NEW YORK - Harold Melvin and 
the Bluenotes, one of Philadelphia In- 
ternational's most popular recording 
acts, have struck gold with their 
smash single, "If You Don't Know 
Me By Now." The record has been 
certified gold by the RIAA, signifying 
sales of over one million units. 
"If You Don't Know Me By Now" 
was produced by Ken Gamble and 
Leon Huff, and was culled from Har- 
old Melvin and the Bluenotes' current 
chartclimbing LP on the Philadelphia 
International label, "I Miss You."

Yes 
NASSAU 
COLISEUM, LONG IS- 
LAND - Ordinarily, I would wait 
until a group came to closer grounds 
before seeing them. Carnegie Hall. 
The Felt Forum. Or, as a last resort, 
Madison Square Garden. But Yes are 
a very special group. They are one of 
a kind. For apart from creating their 
very 
own 
sound, they 
have 
also 
created a new kind of music. Yes mu- 
sic. Music that displays their techni- 
cal virtuosity as well as their creativ- 
ity as composers and arrangers. 
Yes opened their Nassau Coliseum 
date with "Siberian Khatru," a song 
that combines, in a little more than 
eight minutes, all that Yes is about. 
Superb vocal harmony. Tight musical 
interplay. And a dramatic flair for 
astounding dynamics. Yes leave no 
room for mistakes of any kind. They 
are too well rehearsed. Too profes- 
sional. Too dedicated. They can and 
do produce, note for note, every 
sound that appears on their albums. 
A spectacular accomplishment when 
you consider the complexity of their 
arrangements! 
The songs themselves are not com- 
plex, but rather bits and pieces of 
themes contributed by the individual 
group members and woven carefully 
into near epic proportions to demon- 
strate what can be achieved when ev- 
eryone gets into the act. Apart from 
performing their entire "Close To The 
Edge" album, (Close To The Edge, 
And You And I, Siberian Khatru), 
Yes also treated the capacity crowd 
to "Roundabout," "Your Move," "I've 
Seen All Good People," "Heart Of 
The Sunrise," two solo ventures-one 
by guitarist Steve Howe, and one by 
keyboard man, Rick Wakeman-and 
an encore of "Yours Is No Disgrace." 
Yet, as the huge crowd filed slowly 
out of the arena, I couldn't help but 
wonder why they came. Was it be- 
cause Yes has attained supergroup 
status and one is expected to attend 
such functions-or was it that the 
people realized that there, before 
their very eyes, is a group the likes 
of which may never come again? 
Those who came to get high, play 
with 
balloons, 
or throw frisbee's 
around can't be expected to achieve 
any degree of musical sophistica- 
tion-but those who came to listen 
and learn were rewarded by THE 
group that has reached for and has 
conquered new levels of musical depth 
and intensity.

Paull Williams 
to patter with him and do an effective 
job on a number of her own. More of

gab and hip humor. He also needed a 
better sound system.

Hot Tuna 
New Riders 
Wishbone Ash 
PALLADIUM, L,A. - An evening of 
inconsistent music battled head on 
with the sound difficulties and poor 
acoustics that so often plague the 
vastness of the Palladium. 
Hot Tuna headlined this triple bill 
and turned in a less than satisfying 
performance. Of course, the Palladi- 
um didn't help much. The music of 
Hot Tuna is better suited to smaller 
clubs, and their sometimes too -loose 
style failed fully to come across to 
the huge crowd. Hot Tuna is certainly 
capable of putting on a good show 
with the proper location, atmosphere, 
and attitude. It really 
should be 
chalked up to just one 
of those 
nights. 
The New Riders of the Purple Sage 
were back in town for another fine 
set. Pleasant vocals and crisp guitar 
work are the New Riders trademark, 
and this performance was no excep- 
tion, proving again that they are 
there own strong band and not just 
an extension of another. 
Britain's Wishbone 
Ash encoun- 
tered some early sound problems, but 
it didn't prove to be a terrible hin- 
drance. As a total unit, Wishbone Ash 
keeps their set tight, but allows ample 
freedom for instrumental creativity.

CARNEGIE HALL, NY - Rock the- 
atre that isn't serious drag or ultra - 
violence ? Yes, Elton John brought it 
to Carnegie. But we also thank the 
good Muse that there was 
some 
meaty music on those bones of stage 
business. 
Let's dispense with the obvious 
visual elements of the evening first. 
Elton set the tone with his outfit: a 
red, silver and blue Uncle Sam -type 
suit. Ex -Bonzo "Legs" Larry Smith 
made two guest appearances. The first 
was as "Wedding Man," kind 
of 
a limp-wristed Kaiser headed for the 
church on time. His/her train was 
supported by two militarily -donned 
dwarfs. His second shot was in a 
trench coat, as he dueted "Singing' In 
The Rain" with Elton, supported by 
eight chorus girls, a black -tie pianist 
and the dwarfs again. The "rain" was 
first flung about by a thirties -garbed 
dancer, but by song's end, it was com- 
ing down in tinsely torrents from up 
above the lights. And of course on his 
own time, Elton kicked the stool back 
and played piano standing, crouching 
and jumping depending on the occa- 
sion. 
Musically, Elton garners hushed 
silence or frenzied audience participa- 
tion as most befits the song. He un- 
veiled a number of new tunes from 
his upcoming LP, "Don't Shoot Me, 
I'm Only The Piano Player." The first 
was "Daniel," a piano/vocal solo of 
a 
dreamy nature with somewhat 
amorphous, 
though 
poetic 
lyrics. 
"Crocodile Rock," his just -released 
single about the days when music was 
pre -camp shtick went down well. The 
closest thing to a blues he and the 
band has ever done-"Have Mercy On 
The Criminal"-was a successful ex- 
tended number. 
The time champ of the evening, 
however, was one of longest jams on 
"Madman Across The Water" we've 
heard. The set which ran well over 
two hours, was 
spiced by "Your 
Song," "Take Me To The Pilot" and 
the enormously well -received "Rocket 
Man." Dee Murray, Nigel Olsson and 
the 
newest 
band 
member 
Davey 
Johnston (on guitar and mandolin) 
was very much on a winning streak. 
The evening went by with melody, 
style and fervor. 
English quintet Family opened the 
show. They came out with a negative 
attitude about the audience and were 
a self-fulfilling prophecy. 
r.a. 
Johnny Nash 
illy Paul 
I. 
BITTER END, NY - When this club 
goes for the black audience, they do 
it in style. Nash has always been a 
vocalist of merit, but his newfound 
group, Sons Of The Jungle, will truly 
cement his relationship with an audi- 
ence. 
Something like a War with mel- 
lotron (or a Moody Blues with conga 
and bells?), this nine -man 
band 
shocked the audience with a sound 
that completely takes you by sur- 
prise. They play and sing/chant on so 
many levels of music, it is inaccurate 
to view them merely in the light of 
the afro -rock scene. While the sets 
bands usually play before introducing 
the vocalist typically make you fidg- 
ety, 
theirs 
hardly 
seemed 
long 
enough. 
Nash continued in the groove of 
their excitement with songs from his 
"I Can See Clearly Now" LP, inter- 
spersed with oldies like "You've Got 
Soul" and "Hold Me Tight." "Stir It 
Up," his single release prior to his 
#1 "Clearly Now" went over ex- 
tremely well. He's been around the 
business for a long, long time. It 
shows in all the right places. 
We were unfortunate in that we 
obviously caught Billy Paul on an off 
night. His voice was not in top form; 
because of his normal use of his 
range, the loss of the high notes were 
particularly missed. The back-up for 
the inventive Philadelphia Interna- 
tional artist seemed a bit too freeflow 
to 
our liking. 
The tightness 
he 
achieves so easily in the studio was 
just not there. "Me & Mrs. Jones" has 
made him the star he deserved to be. 
Now he has to learn to make every 
performance count. 
r.a. 
Ted Turner and Andy Powell are 
powerful and intricate lead guitarists 
who weave through melodic musical 
journies like "Phoenix" and "War- 
rior." The very enthusiastic response 
was well deserved. 
111.11. 
Tom Rush 
Lindisfarne 
PHILHARMONIC 
HALL, 
NY - 
Columbia folkie Tom Rush, with that 
tender fist of a voice, played to an 
eager audience here. Appearing with 
bass (Wayne Leslie) drums (Brian 
Post) and long-time guitarist/friend 
Trevor Veitch (the audience loves him 
almost as much as Rush), he proved 
himself still very much the master of 
his musical fate. Whatever the state 
of the relative popularity of acoustic 
folk or amped folk -boogie, Rush will 
command an enviable following. 
He has only one "gimmick" per se- 
that's his frog -in -heat voice which 
first came to light on "Who Do You 
Love?" and which he also uses on his 
interpretation of Randy Newman's "A 
Lover's Prayer." Aside from this en- 
joyable trickery, Tom gives it to you 
plain, straightforward and strong. 
The group harmonizes well vocally 
(as on "Merrimac County") and apart 
from not playing upon this facet of 
their talents quite enough, his set was 
well-paced-full of slight variations 
on the theme that brought him fame 
that won't quit. 
Elektra's English quintet, Lindis- 
farne is not yet half the draw here 
they are in Merry Olde. They have 
three albums out (the latest, "Dingly 
Dell"), but of the eight tunes they 
did, four were taken from their first, 
"Slightly Out Of Tune." For good 
reason. The LP still ranks with the 
finest ever recorded by any group; it's 
a harder act to follow when it's your 
own. The finale, "We Can Swing To- 
gether" and quite a few standing ova- 
tionary fans proved their worth to 
this side of the Atlantic.

POP PICKS 
A 
LOOK 
INSIDE-Joe South-Capitol 
ST - 
11074 
For perhaps the first time since his debut 
LP, Joe's material and vocals are met on their 
genius level by acute, ballsy production and 
arrangements. This one thus proves that Joe 
South is country, soul, progressive and Top 
40-alternatively and simultaneously. "Misun- 
derstanding" is by far the best track he's ever 
laid down-the rhyme scheme is devastating 
and it has all the guts of an Aretha winner. 
"Imitation Of Living" 
is 
a 
stone country 
smash. while "All Nite Lover, All Day Friend" 
and "Save Your Best" are hits in any idiom 
you care to name. South is every direction! 
SPIN 
AWAY-Lettermen-Capitol 
SW -11124 
This album could represent a turning point 
in the trio's career. In addition to their now 
familiar MOR softsell, there's a very substan- 
tial guitar -dominated 
version 
of America's 
"Sandman." Should this see release as a sin- 
gle, this album will have an even greater ap- 
peal to the younger buyer. LP also includes a 
live medley of two Nilsson songs "Don't Leave 
Me/Without Her" and a beautiful interpreta- 
tion of the Elton John-famoused "Love Song," 
written by Lesley Duncan. 
elti,.., 
SOUL 
OF 
THE 
BIBLE-Cannonball Adderly 
presents the Nat Adderley Sextet; narrated by 
Rick Holmes-Capitol SABB-11120 
From the folks who brought you the suc- 
cessful) two -record set "Soul Zodiac," comes 
another lookin' and soundin' just as strong. 
Probably more so, since there's material here 
for a few singles if properly edited. The gospel 
tradition is expanded into the jazz/r&b constel- 
lation, and the music moves. The album's pro- 
gression from "In The Beginning" to the 
"Space Spiritual" is as natural a winner as 
you're gonna read about in the Good Book. Or 
anywhere else for that matter. 
THE SEA HAWK: THE CLASSIC FILM SCORES 
OF ERICH WOLFGANG KORNGOLD'S-Charles 
Gernhardt, National Philharmonic Orchestra- 
RCA LSC-3330 
This seems to be the kind of "classical" LP 
only the public wants. For too long, film scores 
have been the sole providence of soundtrack 
LPs, even when a full symphonic treatment 
seemed only fitting to the work. Korngold's 
career as a Hollywood scorer of merit is here 
traced from his first, "Captain Blood" (1935) 
to his last, "Deception" (1946). Initial public 
response indicates this LP could be a har- 
binger 
of 
a 
new 
marketing approach for 
orchestras. 
FOCUS 
MOVING WOVES 
JAZZ PICKS 
N-- 
MOVING WAVES-Focus-Sire SAS -7401 
First album released through the label's new 
affiliation with Famous Music is the second for 
this Dutch group. It far surpasses their early 
'71 effort both in ambition and scope. Here are 
four musicians who know the happy medium 
between mood -creation 
and technical skill. 
They chiefly use voice for coloration only, but 
there is one vocal track here, "Moving Waves" 
with English lyrics. "Hocus Pocus" is a hard 
rocker equipped with yodels, while many of the 
other short pieces play upon the nuances of 
mellotron, harmonium and flute. Side Two is 
an extended emotive piece, "Eruption." A to- 
tally remarkable package on all fronts. 
CLEAR SPOT-Captain 
Beefheart And 
The 
Magic Band-Reprise MS 2115 
Wherein Don Van Vliet and 
his band of 
reknown meet up with hit producer Ted Tern- 
pleman (most recently of Doobie Brothers 
fame) and thereby take to creatin' some heavy 
and rather commercially viable rock. That's 
right, Beefheart's gone "meaty music." There's 
still that cryptic Bayou voice of his in the freak 
column, but here it is used to create a mood 
that fits in with the more garden variety sound 
of today. More than just a new experiment in 
packaging. It asks the question, "Can a Cap- 
tain from a far-out neighborhood find boogie 
happiness at the house of Burbank?" 
CLASSICAL PICKS 
LAST 
SESSIONS-Mississippi 
John Hurt- 
Vanguard VSD-79327 
O. frabjous joy! And so unexpected too! 
Vanguard has come up with previously unre- 
leased performances by the country blues mas- 
ter produced by Patrick Sky in early and mid - 
1966. In addition to his own tunes and tradi- 
tional songs, there's material here from Bukka 
White and Leadbelly. John was in a class all by 
himself as a blues musician-but more impor- 
tantly as a blues person. The totally unpreten- 
tious and ever -human figure left more than a 
mere legacy. He left his entire being in his 
music. 
YOU ARE THE MUSIC . 
. 
. WE'RE JUST THE 
BAND-,-Trapeze-Threshold THS-8 
This trio will not be called "Threshold's oth- 
er acri for too much longer. The Moody Blues 
have teir thing going, and Trapeze now most 
assuredly have theirs as well. Very much a 
drum and vocal band (which is not to dismiss 
the contributions of Glenn Huges on bass and 
Mel Galley on guitar), they get everyone's 
rocks off with "Keepin' Time," "Feelin' So 
Much Better Now" and the title cut. Rod Ar- 
gent guests on two tracks. 
POP BEST BETS 
WITH 
LOVE-Joe Williams-Temponic 
TB - 
29561 
There's a song on this LP called "Once 
Upon A Happy Time (The Big Band Days)," 
which does more than bring back memories. It 
gives modern day validity to the approach 
which spares no expense to create fullness. So 
do most of the cuts on this album. Williams 
sings more effortlessly than ever, and he's 
backed by eight trumpets, nine trombones, 
nine saxophones, two pianos, three drums, 
bass, four french horns, two vibes, three gui- 
tars, four violas, four cellos, twelve violins and 
a chorus of twenty-one. What you call really 
big band-and really big music.

BERLIOZ: BENVENUTO CELLINI-Colin Davis, 
conducting the Chorus Of The Royal Opera 
House, Covent Garden and the B. B. C. Sym- 
phony Orchestra; Nicolai Gedda, tenor-Philips 
6500-494 
Colin Davis' Berlioz cycle has come in for 
tremendous critical acclaim. His "Les Troyens" 
package paved the way for substantial sales 
in the classical market for this 4 -LP set. This 
recording of the 1838 opera is the first com- 
plete available, and it features several un- 
published scenes from the original version. 
THE EXCELLO STORY - Various Artists - 
Excello DBL 28025 
A specially -priced two -record oldies collec- 
tion with much to recommend it. Firstly, it 
carefully illustrates the evolution of rock 'n 
roll, as many of the cuts by artists like 
Lightnin' Slim and Slim Harpo show just how 
the down home 
blues came to figure into 
r&b's, then rock's scheme of things. Collectors 
will also note that this is the first oldies pack- 
age to include the original "Oh Julie" by The 
Crescendos and "Little Darlin' " by The Gladi- 
olas. Other gems from Lillian Offitt, Arthur 
Gunter and a host of blues performers. 
UNDER MY WINGS-Smith Connection-Music 
Merchant MM105 
This vocal trio deals in silky soul with full, 
inventive arrangements courtesy of McKinley 
Jackson & Paul Riser. The sum total of their 
abilities could make for an act in the success- 
ful Stylistics bag. Title tune which provides the 
theme for the cover photo brings in sound 
effects to create 
a very immediate mood. 
"Wish 
I Had You" allows the group to show off 
their vocal range. "You Ain't Livin' Unless 
You're Lovin' " is a tuneful treatment of a 
catchy phrase. Album also includes soulful 
remakes of " 'Til There Was You," "Rainy Days 
& Mondays" and "My World Is Empty Without 
You."

Jasper Cook 
MAX'S KANSAS CITY, NYC-When 
T -Bone picks up that guitar of his 
and gets into that nasty low down 
blues groove, one can easily under- 
stand why T -Bone is considered a 
father of the blues. I must go on 
record and say that T -Bone has one 
of the finest blues bands that I have 
heard in sometime. His one night, 
December 5th stand at Max's drew a 
packed audience and the show was 
electrifying. The 6 piece band opened 
with, "The Ghetto" and T -Bone at 
the keyboard; he is as adept on the 
keyboard as he is on the guitar. But, 
when he goes into the blues using the 
guitar. the guitar actually becomes 
the vocal extension of his emotional 
blues feelings. 
"Crazy About 
My 
Baby" and "Come On Woman" are 
given T -Bone treatments that makes 
one feel as if he were witnessing a 
performance that one might expect, 
may have come straight from the 
heart of early New Orleans blues. 
"Goin' Back To Jackson" and "I Woke 
Up This Morning" brought the audi- 
ence to its feet and, needless to say, 
when it comes to the blues T -Bone 
carry's the whole hag! 
Jasper Cook, a young 4 piece R&B 
type rock band, opened the show and 
they proved above average in their 
performance.

wisdom 
(as

"Friends").

VILLAGE VANGUARD, NYC - No 
stranger to Jazz aficionados or Jazz 
orientated fans, Chick Corea & Re- 
turn To Forever, recently made an 
appearance at this underground vil- 
lage "in" spot that can always be de- 
pended upon to offer the unique in 
musical fare; and Chick's stint was 
no exception. 
Nightly, overflow crowds gathered 
to enjoy the solid offerings of Chick, 
keyboard; and his members, Stanley 
Clarke, Bass; Airto Moreria, Drums; 
and Flora Purim doing special vocal- 
izations. 
The musical content of the set that 
I 
caught 
included, 
"Time 
Lag", 
"You're Everything" and "Matrix." 
This a very cool closely knit unit that 
kept the audience in rapt attention. 
When the sounds and melodies are 
right, as they were on this set, it 
only takes three selections to make a 
night. Chick has that special ability 
to communicate. Definitely an artist 
worth seeing. 
Incidentally, Chick will soon have a 
new 
LP 
entitled, "Light 
As 
A 
Feather" on Polydor who has signed 
Chick Corea and the group to an In- 
ternational World -Wide contract.

Bonnie Raitt 
Maria Muldaur 
SPRAGUE HALL, NEW 
HAVEN, 
CT.-Throughout the past three or 
four generations, there have been 
countless definitions of the blues, in 
both musical lyrics and written word. 
But as many times as people have 
tried to pin it down, the blues re- 
mains undefined-it is a feeling, not 
a bunch of words. There are many 
performers who assume the style of 
the blues and mimic the originators, 
but somehow they miss the point and 
wind up with a bunch of words and 
notes instead of the real thing. And 
there are a few that have a line on 
the feeling-they have the intangible 
essence that is the blues. I suppose 
that at this dramatic point in the re- 
view, I'm supposed to say that Bonnie 
Raitt is one of these few people, but 
she isn't. She's two of them. 
Yes, folks, just like Cert's Mints, 
Bonnie has that two -in -one quality. 
When she plays bottleneck slide on a 
Spanish National guitar, she leaves 
no doubt in mind that she knows 
where it's at as far as traditional 
blues goes. But on top of this, Bonnie 
can take the blues idiom and success- 
fully apply it to contemporary lyrics 
and feeling. Perfect examples of this 
are Joel Zoss' "Too Long At The 
Fair" and Stephen Stills' "Bluebird." 
She takes these two distinctive lyrics 
and melodies and adds herself to them 
. 
. 
. something old, something new, 
something borrowed and something 
blue. 
When she's done with these 
tunes, a transfixed listener can easily 
imagine Zoss and Stills commenting, 
"Why didn't I write it like that to 
start with?" 
In short, Bonnie Raitt has the 
magic of making the listener feel 
the way she does. It is the fine l'ne 
of class that separates the true artist 
from the technician. 
Backed up by her faithful sidekick 
Freebo on Fender fretless bass, Bon- 
nie was joined for the evening by 
pianist Lou Terriciano, whose gifted 
fingers touched the soul of Sprague 
Hall every time they touched the 
ivory keys. In addition to songs from 
her two Warner Brothers albums, 
such as "Love Has No Pride," "Since I 
Fell For You" and "Under The Fall- 
ing Sky," Bonnie was loose enough to 
unleash her recently written "Blend- 
er Blues," which quickly whipped, 
chopped and pureed the receptive 
audience. Bonnie provoked two solid 
and genuine standing ovations from 
this Yale University crowd, and she 
received similar response from U. of 
Hartford students the night before. 
Both these audiences are hard to 
please, and judging from their re- 
sponse, she's the new college cult 
heroine. 
With Maria Muldaur also on the 
bill, the concert achieved a strong 
thematic unity. An alumnus of the 
Even Dozen Jug Band and the Jim 
Kweskin Jug Band (both as Maria 
DiAmato, before she married Geoff 
Muldaur), Maria knows what sweet- 
ness is, be it blues, rags or ballads. 
She has been away from live per- 
forming for awhile but is now back 
full steam, perhaps due to Bonnie's 
incentive. Freebo and Lou Terriciano 
also backed Maria, and were joined 
by guitarist David Nicturne (who also 
backs up David Bromberg). When 
Maria -received superlative audience 
response for tunes such as "Chauffer 
Blues" and Mississippi John Hurt's 
immortal "Richland Lady Blues," she 
showed us that the era of female folk 
performers is upon us once again. 
Once she set up the audience with 
her singing and strumming, Maria 
simply bowled them all over with a 
spry and funky fiddle hoedown. 
As would be fitting for a show of 
this calibre and cohesiveness, a high 
energy jam served as grand finale. 
Bonnie and Maria merged their tal- 
ents for the Barbara George r&b 
classic, "I Know." Backed by Freebo, 
Terriciano and Nicturne, these two 
"fragile" chicks soon had the crowds 
doin' the boogie in the aisles, a feat 
which is hard enough for an electric 
rock band to achieve. By the end of 
the tune, two members of the audi- 
ence jumped onstage to add totally 
spontaneous 
flute 
and 
harmonica 
solos. One of those special and rare 
concerts that will be filled 
in the 
memory banks forever! 
m.p. 
Woody Herman 
Wayne & Puma 
HALFNOTE, MANHATTAN, NYC - 
Woody 
Herman and 
his 
(young) 
Thundering 
Herd 
came 
into 
the 
Halfnote, Nov 
27, and they were 
greeted 
by 
a 
packed 
pre -opening 
press and trade party. Woody, still 
feeling fit and full of fire, as he has 
so often done in the past, has again 
assembled a 15 piece band including a 
top notch funky rhythm section. And, 
Woody and His Herd really had the 
popular 
Jazz 
spot 
jumping 
all 
through his week long stand. I at- 
tended the second night first show 
and Woody opened with a Broadbent 
tune, "Adams Apple" and then the 
band went into one of his all time 
greats, "Woodchopper's Ball". "Ear- 
ly 
Autumn", 
that 
had 
originally 
served as a proper musical setting for 
Stan Getz so many moons ago, got a 
beautiful treatment from the band. 
As is to be expected with the Her- 
man bands, he has a talented array of 
musicians and they displayed their 
stuff with a funky version of "Water- 
mellon Man", and a great Stapleton 
arrangement of "It's Too Late". Sta- 
pleton is a member in the Horn sec- 
tion. Woody also pulled out a '47 
Jimmy Guifre arrangement of "The 
Four Mothers" and the audience loved 
it. Gregory Herbert on tenor sax 
seems to be a coming figure on the 
Jazz scene. He did an outstanding 
solo bit on the beautiful "Summer of 
'42". Also, Gregory was brilliant with 
his piccolo solos. 
At a Seminar last summer that was 
conducted by Woody, he was asked 
whether this Herman band was his 
best and Woody replied, "Yes, this 
band, a year from now". The year is 
almost up and 
from the youthful 
looks and the sounds these cats are 
putting together, my guess is this 
Thundering 
Herd band 
will keep 
Woody in the forefront for another 
decade. Woody has a new LP release 
on Fantasy, "The Raven Speaks." 
Chuck Wayne & Joe Puma, a guitar 
duo, a la the Bucky Pizarelli duo, 
supplied the pre Woody listening mu- 
sic and it was pleasant.

Harry Chapin 
Whole Oates 
TROUBADOUR, L.A.-Harry Chapin 
is a monster performer. He opened 
here 
to a less than capacity but 
warm 
responsive 
audience. 
The 
erudite Mr. Chapin is a master at the 
art of vocal storytelling with his ivy - 
league air, vague'y reminiscent of the 
1950's campus favorite, Tom Lehrer. 
His tremendous insights and empathy 
for the "human condition" reach out 
and touch all who hear him. With 
compositions like "Sniper" and "Bet- 
ter Place To Be" (his new single-it's 
a killer), he makes cerebral demands 
on his listener as well as being one of 
the only performers who can success- 
fully produce vocal audience partici- 
pation. He is a 20th century pied 
piper with the inate power to corn- 
p'etely mesmerize those who see him 
in person. He is tightly backed up by 
three consumate musicians: Tim Scott 
on cello; Ron Palmer on lead guitar 
and vocals, and John Wallace on elec- 
tric bass. If you've any of his live 
engagements, beg borrow or steal his 
new LP on Electra Records. 
Polished, 
professional, 
well -re- 
hearsed and exciting-watch out for 
Atlantic's Whole Oates. Not only does 
this group have all of the basic ingre- 
dients to be a smash, they've put them 
all together and then some. Variety 
and versati'ity are the focal points in 
their performance, and they utilize 
them skillfully. With total accom- 
plishment, they combine sensitive lyr- 
ics, imaginative changes, and orignal 
material, i.e. "Had I Known You Bet- 
ter" arranged for acoustic guitar, and 
"Lily" featuring Chris Bond on Me- 
lotron. Vocals are pure, strong and 
controlled with interesting and struc- 
tured harmonies. Whole Oates is a 
group to watch. 
I.e.

Playboy Sets Jan. Packages 
HOLLYWOOD - Larry Cohn, exec 
vice president of Playboy Records, 
has announced a mid -Jan. release of 
three albums, featuring rock artist 
Brenda Patterson's debut for the la- 
bel, singer -songwriter Laurie Kaye 
Cohen, and rock band Brownstone, 
spotlighting lead vocalist Barbara 
Lopez. It marks Playboy's first major 
Buchanan 
Mcllwaine 
Polydor LP's 
NEW YORK - Polydor rock guitar- 
ist Roy Buchanan is currently putting 
the finishing touches on his second 
album for the label. Produced by Poly- 
dor's a&r director Peter Siegel, the 
album is being recorded at New 
York's Record Plant, with sidemen 
being flown in from Montreal and 
Nashville for the sessions. 
Also, Ellen Mcllwaine has com- 
pleted her new Polydor album, "We 
the People." The album, produced by 
Polydor's a&r director Peter Siegel, 
was recorded at New York's Record 
Plant. The title cut, "We the People", 
however, was recorded live at Ms. 
Mcllwaine's recent concert at New 
York's Carnegie Hall. 
Included in the album is Ms. Mcll- 
waine's current single, "I Don't Want 
to Play" and her rendition of the 
hymn "Farther Along", on which Ms. 
Mcllwaine is backed up by acapella 
group, the Persuasions. Percussionist 
Candido also appears on the album. 
album release since spring and the 
label's first under Cohn. 
Six additional releases have been 
scheduled through March, including 
first offerings from Alladin & Aum, 
IS, Sharon Cash, Sam Russell and 
Ivory. 
"Playboy is looking for longevity," 
said Cohn. "We're not interested in 
the quick hit and the inevitable fade 
into oblivion. The artists must be 
unique in whatever their presentation 
and truly have a personality all their 
own." 
Playboy will support all releases 
with a substantial advertising and 
merchandising campaign coordinated 
and directed by Rocco Catena, direc- 
tor of merchandising. 
Vanguard Promos 
Kaplan's Hopi LP 
NEW YORK - Vanguard Records is 
launching their first album release on 
Hopi Records "Confessions of a Male 
Chauvinist Pig" by Artie Kaplan. 
Harold Lewis, sales manager and 
Eddie O'Keefe, director of radio pro- 
motion for Vanguard went out into 
the field three weeks ago to bring 
advance play of the album to dealers, 
radio stations, one -stops and racks in 
several major markets. Initial adver- 
tising includes full page print ads in 
consumer papers and trade magazines 
and is being backed by radio spots. 
Additional promo includes a special 
women's mailing; a press kit mailing, 
containing lyric sheets and singles as 
well as bios, pictures, and reviews.

IT'S PLATIN L M- following his Carnegie Hall sell-out appearance in New 
York, Elton John and members of his band were presented with platinum LP's 
by Rick Frio, vice-president and director of Marketing for MCA Records. Elton 
received platinum LP's for four LP's: "Elton John", "Tumbleweed Connec- 
tion", "Madman Across The Water", and "Hanky Chateau". 
Pictured at the Essex House presentation are, standing, left to right: Nigel 
Olsson, Elton John, Bernie Taupin, Davey Johnstone, and Dee Murray. Bottom 
left is John Reid, president of Rocket Records (a new record company formed 
by Elton and other musical business associates), and Rick Frio. 
UA Publishing 
Issues Super 
`Sawyer' Demo 
HOLLYWOOD - The United Artists 
Publishing Group has put together a 
deluxe promo package for the score 
of the upcoming musical film "Tom 
Sawyer," produced by Arthur Jacobs' 
APJAC Productions in 
association 
with the Reader's Digest for UA re- 
lease. The unit is made up of an al- 
bum box containing an illustrated 
folio with the complete score, both 
music and lyrics, and a demonstration 
disc with the nine tunes written for 
the picture by Richard M. and Robert 
B. Sherman. It is being shipped to 
recording artists, record companies 
and record producers throughout the 
world. 
The film "Tom Sawyer" is slated 
for theatrical release in the summer 
of 1973. The original motion picture 
soundtrack album will be issued in 
May by United Artists Records con- 
taining two tracks by Charlie Pride, 
who is heard under the main titles 
and end titles of the film. RCA will be 
releasing a Charlie Pride single in 
conjunction with the motion picture 
release. 
Melvin Lastie Dies 
NEW ORLEANS - Melvin Lastie, 
noted r&b trumpeter, died in New Or- 
leans on Mon. Dec. 4. He was 41. 
Lastie performed with King Curtis 
and Willie Bobo, and played solo 
trumpet on the Barbara George sin- 
gle, "I Know." Funeral services were 
held in New Orleans on Sat. Dec. 8. 
WEA's Neal 
Dies In Fire 
CHICAGO - Marshall Neal, Jr., a 
sales representative for WEA Dist. in 
suburban Des Plaines, Ill., died of 
burns suffered in the tragic fire which 
destroyed Sanders One Stop on Nov. 
22 and claimed the lives of four cus- 
tomers. At the time of the tragedy 
Neal was making his regular sales 
call at the store. 
Newspaper accounts of the incident 
stated that the fire was touched off by 
two men who allegedly had robbed 
the store and poured gasoline over 
the premises. Ironically, the store was 
normally a Thursday stop for Neal 
but, because of the Thanksgiving Day 
holiday, he was making his call on 
Wednesday. 
Neal is survived by his widow, 
Goldie, and five children, ranging in 
age from two years to twenty-one. 
PAN-TASTIC-Columbia Records has just signed Pan, a four piece group via 
a master purchase agreement with Pan Productions. Group consists of ex 
Beau Brummel Ron Elliot, Keith Barbour (Echo Park), Arthur Richards, and 
Val Garay. Pictured at group signing are (1-r) Richards, Barbour, Abe Hoch, 
manager, Val Garay. Shown seated are Allan Rinde, Columbia's western a&r 
director, and Ron Elliot.

formed RSO Records in the U.S., and 
has named Johnny Bienstock as man-

ly head of singles sales for Atlantic 
Records, which will distribute the new 
label.

of

picture music during the past decade. 
- 
"Man Of La Mancha" follows hard on 
the heels of UA's "Fiddler on the 
Roof," one of the best-selling film LPs 
of all time. 
Inspired by the Spanish classic by 
Cervantes, "Man of La Mancha" is an 
original work by Dale Wasserman, 
who 
has brilliantly 
combined the 
character and spirit of Cervantes with 
the splendid lunatic fantasies of the 
author's fictional creation Don Quix- 
ote. 
"Man of La Mancha," adapted for 
the screen by Wasserman, has been 
described as a musical within a play, 
but it actually defies convention. Au- 
diences around the world, however, 
have agreed that it is a unique dra- 
matic experience. 
Peter O'Toole as Cervantes/Don 
Quixote, 
Sophia 
Loren 
as 
Dul- 
cinea/Aldonza, and James Coco as 
Sancho 
Panza, 
inherit 
roles 
per- 
formed 
in 
theatrical 
productions 
presented in 22 languages in 45 coun- 
tries. 
The 
original 
stake 
version 
opened in New York on Nov. 22, 
1965, and later swept the Tony and 
Drama Critics Awards as Best Musi- 
cal. It has been brought to the screen 
with its prize-winning songs and mu- 
sic, inciding such favorites as "The 
Imposslble Dream" and "Dulcinea." 
For pr ducer-director Arthur Hiller, 
"Man Of La Mancha" caps a career 
that indludes, "Love Story" and "The 
Hospital."

At Chicago Meet: 
Indie Distributors Vote To 
Seek Gains In NARM Framework 
NEW YORK - Dispelling rumors of 
a separate indie distributor organiza- 
tion, a group of indie distributors 
meeting in Chicago on Fri., Dec. 8, 
voted unanimously to work within the 
framework of NARM, the merchan- 
diser -manufacturer association. 
The meeting of 22 distributors was 
called in the wake of problems faced 
by this 
segment of the business, 
which in recent years has been con- 
fronted with the growth of branch 
operations and charges by labels util- 
izing such a network that indie dis- 
tributors 
are 
failing 
to 
provide 
sufficient promo support on product 
and are slow in payment of bills. 
The 
Chicago 
meeting also 
saw 
plans developed for an expanded role 
of the indie distributor in NARM, 
originally organized 
to 
serve the 
rack -jobber 
area, 
but 
which 
has 
evolved as an association of wider 
industry purpose. 
The first order of business at the 
Chicago meeting was a unanimous 
vote of the 22 distributors present to 
remain in NARM, and to continue to 
work as members of NARM, for the 
best interests of their segment of the 
industry. 
Plans 
were 
developed 
whereby the indie distributors could 
achieve their objectives within the 
framework of the established industry 
association. 
Working 
with 
Jules 
Malamud, NARM exec director, Dave 
Press, NARM president, and Earl 
Kintner, general counsel, who attend- 
ed 
the 
meeting, the 
distributors 
present worked out a set of initial 
plans for their expanded role 
in 
NARM. Foremost and of the most 
immediate importance was the role 
MCA Shows Video Disk; Sees 
Pricing Along Lines Of LP 
UNIVERSAL CITY - MCA Disco - 
Vision, Inc., unveiled its eagerly antic- 
ipated video disk last week for the 
MCA board members, industry execs 
and press, highlighted by a seven - 
minute demonstration 
drawn from 
the Universal Pictures archives. 
The record itself proved to be a 
paper -thin, 12 -inch silver mylar disk 
with a playing -time capability of at 
least 40 minutes, at 1800 r p.m., for 
either color or black -and -white pro- 
gram material, thus far outdistancing 
the capabilities of existing audio- 
visual disk systems. It can be pro- 
duced for about 40 cents and pressed 
in virtually the same way an ordi- 
nary LP record is pressed. It is also 
just about indestructible. Price to the 
consumer will be along the lines of 
LP pricing. 
Opening the first public demonstra- 
tion was Lew R. Wasserman, pres- 
ident and chief exec officer of MCA, 
Inc., who aster a few brief remarks 
introduced the newly appointed pres- 
ident 
of 
MCA 
Disco -Vision, 
Inc., 
John W. Findlater, a veteran MCA 
senior officer and vice president. 
Said Findlater, "We believe we've 
achieved 
the 
ultimate 
concept 
in 
home entertainment and information 
storage and retrieval systems, and 
that both the hardware and the soft- 
MCA's Video Disk Player 
ware will be sold to the consumer at 
popular prices."

around $500. Prototypes of both were

10 Jan. LP's 
Due From GSF 
NEW YORK - GSF Records will 
release 10 new albums in Jan. The re- 
lease marks the largest quantity of 
releases since the inception of the 
company and the initial releases of 
the newly formed jazz label, En- 
counter Records, which will be dis- 
tributed by GSF. 
The five albums that will appear on 
the GSF label are: "Joe Quarter - 
man", "Coldwater 
Stone", "Classic 
Example", "Skull Snaps" and "Sound 
Experience". Quartermen's new al- 
bum, which follows his current sin- 
gle, is produced by Bill Tate and 
Cotter Wells and the Classic Example 
album is being produced by Mickey 
Stevenson. 
The Encounter albums are "Seldon 
Powell", "East Coast", "Harold Vic" 
"Frank 
Owens", 
and 
"Sands 
of 
Time". These five albums are being 
produced by Lloyd Price and Bernard 
Purdie, the principals of the label. 
BASF Debuts 
Classic Line 
BEDFORD, MASS. - In January, 
1973, BASF Records will debut their 
classical line. Highlighting the initial 
release will be the beginning of a 
series of historic recordings of Ger- 
man opera repertory from the early 
1940's, previously unavailable in re- 
corded form. 
The first three recordings in this 
series will feature highlights from 
three operas - "Carmen" featuring 
Elisabeth Hongen, Josef Hermann and 
conducted by Karl Bohm; "Othello" 
featuring Helge Rosvaenge, Maria 
Reining, 
Hans Reinmar-conducted 
by Karl Elmendorff; "Capriccio", the 
third album of this series, will be of 
special interest as it is the world 
premier cast of Strauss' last opera 
featuring Viorica Ursuleac, Franz 
Klarwein, Hans Hotter, Georg Hann, 
Georg Wieter and conducted by its 
co -librettist, Clemens Kraus. 
From BASF/Harmonia Mundi, the 
following 
releases 
are 
scheduled: 
"Ave 
Maria 
Kaiserin", 
Aachener 
Domchor led by Rudolf Pohl; "El 
Siglo De Oro" featuring characteris- 
tic works of the most important mas- 
ters of the school 
of Montserrat, 
based on Gregorian melodies; "Bach- 
Three 
London 
Symphonies", 
per- 
formed on original instruments by 
the 
Collegium 
aureum; 
"Francois 
Couperin's

`Kennedy Wit' Spurred By Book 
NEW YORK - Immediate best seller 
status for a new book about the late 
John F. Kennedy has resulted in 
massive new interest in an RCA al- 
bum, "The Kennedy Wit", and RCA 
Records has announced a new adver- 
tising, promotion and publicity cam- 
paign on the album. 
Dave Rothfeld, vice president and 
divisional merchandising manager of 
Korvettes stores, first alerted RCA 
that the book, "Johnny, We Hardly 
Knew Ye," by Kenneth P. O'Donnell 
and David Powers with Joe McCar- 
thy, had brought a new rash in the 
never -far -from -the -surface interest in 
the late President and that the inter- 
est had spilled over into the record 
field, specifically on RCA's album. 
The 
book, 
published 
by Little, 
Brown, already is in its third print- 
ing and is a selection of such book 
clubs as Literary Guild, Book Find, 
Fortune Book Club, Playboy Book 
Club and Saturday 
Review 
Book 
Club. 
RCA's 
album 
was 
first 
issued 
shortly after Kennedy's assassina- 
tion. It contains a collection of the 
very best 
of the wit for which 
Kennedy was famous, taken from his 
speeches, remarks during his cam- 
paign, his televised press conferences 
and his years in the White House. 
The album was edited by Bill Adler 
who had written the book on which it 
was based, has an introduction by the 
late Adlai E. Stevenson and is nar- 
rated by David Brinkley of NBC-TV 
News. 
An RCA spokesman said: "The al- 
bum has sold consistently since it 
was released in 1964, but the new 
Kennedy book has created a strong 
fresh interest in the album. We plan 
a campaign to bring the album to the 
attention of the millions who may 
have missed it but who now want this 
memento of the voice of the late 
President issuing some of his famed 
witicisms." 
Good Noise's 
Artist Roster 
MONTREAL - Andre Perry, pres- 
ident of Good Noise Ltd., has an- 
nouned the artists he and his staff 
have produced for which he is now 
negotiating American record deals. 
Good Noise,. a creative musical com- 
plex, has finished product on Man - 
Made (a progressive group), Ronney 
Abramson 
(a 
solo artist/writer); 
Jackson and Hawk (a group their 
producer Frazier Mohawk has de- 
scribed as "Children of the media"); 
and Brian Blaine (a singer/songwrit- 
er). 
Ronney Abramson, a young lady 
whose first album is already available 
on Canadian Capitol Records, is cur- 
rently working on her second album. 
Jackson and Hawk are a duo that are 
at one moment blues artists, another 
moment pop and another folk, their 
first album is now in the final mixing 
stages; Brian Blaine was formerly a 
record producer, his single includes 
session -work by drummer Jim Gor- 
don and Tom Malone of the Mothers 
of Invention. Man -Made, produced by 
Andre Perry, have completed 
one 
high -voltage progressive album, one 
side of which is conceptual.

PolydorIDG"s 
Limited Editions 
NEW 
YORK - Three specially 
priced multi -volume limited editions, 
representing three genres of classical 
music, have been released 
on the 
Deutsche Grammophon and Archive 
label recordings. Polydor Incorporat- 
ed is the U.S. distributor for the two 
imported classical labels. 
The three Limited Editions include 
Beethoven's Nine Symphonies with 
maestro Karl Boehm conducting the 
Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra and 
Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau's third vol- 
ume of Schubert Lieder, including 
"Die schone Mullerin," "Winterreise" 
and 
"Schwanengesang", 
both 
of 
which are on the Deutsche Grammo- 
phon label. The Archive label is rep- 
resented by J. S. Bach's Cantatas for 
the Advent and Christmas with Karl 
Richter directing his Munich Bach 
Choir 
and Orchestra and 
soloists 
that include Edith Mathis, Sheila 
Armstrong, Anna Reynolds, Ernst 
Haefliger, Peter Schreier, Dietrich 
Fischer-Dieskau and Theo Adam. The 
LPs sell for $4.50 per disc (suggested 
retail price) as opposed to the usual 
$6.98 (suggested list price) import 
price. Deutsche Grammophon Limited 
Editions have been marketed this 
pre -holiday season by a blanket in- 
sertion of 1,000,000 4 -color posters in 
college newspapers in cities ranging 
from Cambridge, Massachusetts to 
Portland, Oregon. Additionally, just 
two weeks ago, the same poster, with 
order blank imprinted on the back, 
was inserted in 100,000 copies of the 
Chicago Tribune. 
The Limited Editions were con- 
ceived some ten years ago with the 
packaging of the Herbert von Kara- 
jan -Berlin 
Philharmonic 
Orchestra 
interpretation of the Beethoven Nine 
Symphonies, 
and 
carried 
through 
with special editions of the Bruckner 
Symphonies (14 discs), complete Mo- 
zart works (the Sonatas, the early 
Symphonies, later Symphonies and 
Concertos), and with the recording of 
"Music of the New Viennese School" 
as interpreted by the LaSalle Quartet 
this year (a recording that has gar- 
nered numerous international awards 
in its short life). 
Polydor International 
is 
already 
preparing several additional limited 
editions to be released on Deutsche 
Grammophon next season as part of 
their SKL series. 
Farrell Sets 
Coast Meeting 
NEW YORK - Key executives of 
the Wes Farrell Organization flew to 
Los Angeles recently from their New 
York offices for a week long meet- 
ing. 
Two of the executives are Steve 
Bedell, vice president of the Farrell 
production and commercial divisions, 
and Bob Harrington, regional pro- 
motional director. The duo, along 
with other WFO staffers, will confer 
regarding planning various activities 
in 1973 of Farrell's Chelsea Records, 
Coral Rock Productions and the vari- 
ous publishing companies owned by 
WFO. 
Farrell's chart activity 
includes 
nine records in the national charts. 
This covers 
five 
discs under the 
Chelsea Records banner-three sin- 
gles and two LPs by Austin Roberts, 
Wayne 
Newton 
and 
Willie 
Roundtree; under Coral Rock Pro- 
ductions, chart records include the 
Partridge Family single and LP; the 
Richard Harris LP and the David 
Cassidy LP. In the WFO publishing 
division, more than 20 tunes are cur- 
rently on the national charts.
